papers.abstract: Generating novel views from limited observations requires preserving both the appearance and spatial structure of a scene. Although recent approaches exploit fine-grained geometric cues, they do not explicitly model high-level semantic and spatial properties such as object identity, attributes, and inter-object relationships. In this work, we investigate whether 3D language understanding can provide complementary supervision for novel-view generation. We introduce Ask4NV, built on a pretrained unified multimodal model with a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture. Our model incorporates camera geometry into both VAE and ViT representations and leverages understanding features during generation through joint self-attention with a modality-aware attention masking strategy. Experiments demonstrate strong image quality and geometric consistency in novel-view generation, alongside competitive 3D language understanding. Further analysis shows that joint training improves cross-view correspondence in VAE representations and similarity in a 3D-aware feature space.
authors: Jahyeok Koo, Hyeonseo Yu, Seungho Jang, Jaewoo Jung, Jiwon Kang, Seokju Cho, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Targets the challenge of preserving both scene appearance and spatial structure from limited observations.
Introduces Ask4NV, built on a pretrained unified multimodal Mixture-of-Transformers model.
Encodes camera geometry in VAE and ViT representations and integrates understanding features via masked joint self-attention.
Achieves strong image quality and geometric consistency while maintaining competitive 3D language understanding.
Joint training improves cross-view correspondence and 3D-aware feature similarity.

papers.title: Can Learning to Answer Spatial Questions Improve Novel-View Generation?

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
authors: Shaoyuan Xie, Zihan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Jiashu Qu, Xiaoqing Liang, Lingdong Kong, Junchi Lu, Henrik I. Christensen, Qi Alfred Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark jointly evaluating navigation following, conflict awareness, and adversarial robustness.
Predicts three navigation-compliance modes to separate conflict reasoning from action generation.
Uses navigation-conditioned world-model rollouts that simulate strictly following instructions to assess their safety.
Achieves 88.16 Driving Score and 68.64% Success Rate on Bench2Drive.
Improves closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 versus the best SimLingo variant.

papers.abstract: Representation-alignment methods effectively accelerate the diffusion transformer training. REPA, for example, uses a pretrained vision encoder to supervise an intermediate layer through an MLP projection head which is discarded after training. It aims to import semantics from the vision encoder to the diffusion backbone. While this objective is achieved at early layers by back-propagating the alignment loss, there is no guarantee that later layers, supervised by the velocity prediction loss alone, can well access such semantics. We propose a simple solution, representation conditioning (RECON), to improve semantics in later layers. During training, we feed the pretrained vision encoder tokens into later layers; during inference, because we no longer have the clean image, we reuse the MLP head (as a proxy to the vision encoder) and project its output tokens to the later layers. Our method adds no parameters and leads to much faster convergence: RECON is $63\times$ faster than SiT and $25\times$ faster than REPA. Code is available at https://github.com/saeidrazavi/RECON
authors: Saeed Razavi, Xingjian Leng, Liang Zheng
bullets: REPA aligns early diffusion layers with a pretrained vision encoder, but later layers may not access those semantics effectively.
RECON feeds vision-encoder tokens into later layers during training.
At inference, it reuses the discarded MLP projection head as a proxy for the vision encoder to generate conditioning tokens.
The method adds no parameters and reports convergence 63× faster than SiT and 25× faster than REPA.
Code is publicly available on GitHub.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Representation Conditioning (RECON) to improve semantics in later layers of diffusion transformers by reusing vision encoder tokens. This offers a training efficiency improvement for video/image diffusion models.
papers.title: Representation Conditioning for Generation
papers.tldr: RECON conditions later diffusion-transformer layers on pretrained vision representations, improving semantic access and substantially accelerating convergence without adding parameters.

papers.abstract: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
authors: Zhefei Gong, Hefeifei Jiang, Zehao Wang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of fine-tuning high-dimensional, tightly coupled mobile-manipulation systems on real robots.
Fine-tunes a frozen base policy with additive residuals, separated into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning.
Uses sparse human interventions covering under 20% of training to reshape value estimates and guide exploration.
Real-world experiments on TIAGo++ report improved task performance with about 30 minutes of online interaction across base-policy architectures.
Scope: demonstrated for dynamic, human-centric real-world mobile manipulation; specific task details and quantitative gains are not provided in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HiRe-MoMa Framework enables policy-agnostic real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulators through an asynchronous residual reinforcement learning paradigm. (Right) Shared-Control Rollout: an onboard rollout worker augments a frozen base policy with learnable residuals; sparse human interventions during critical or hazardous phases are stored in an expert buffer. (Left) Asynchronous Central Learner: the residual policy is optimized along two pillars: a) a Hierarchical Residual Architecture (Sec. 4.1) that decouples the residual into mobile and manipulator heads with unidirectional conditioning, embedding the platform’s physical hierarchy directly into the policy; and b) an Expert-Guided Value Alignment loss (Sec. 4.2) that fuses sparse environment rewards with sparse human corrections to reshape the critic toward expert-preferred behaviors.

Figure 4: Training Dynamics. Comparison across methods over training time, where we construct the figure along the actual training time. (a) Success rate: HiRe-MoMa(full) attains a consistently higher success rate throughout training, validating the effectiveness of our design combining hierarchical residual architecture and alignment. (b) Human intervention steps: HiRe-MoMa requires fewer human interventions and converges faster than the baselines, and the comparison with and without alignment (+Hierarchical Decoupling) demonstrates the effectiveness of the extra alignment loss.

Figure 1: HiRe-MoMa System Overview. (a) Training Paradigm: A real-world dual-unit configuration consisting of an onboard controller for real-time interaction and a computing unit for policy optimization and action prediction. (b) Coordinated Execution: The red dashed lines illustrate the stringent spatiotemporal precision required for base-arm synchronization. In mobile manipulation, marginal tracking deviations are often magnified by kinematic coupling, causing even routine grasping maneuvers to fail.

Figure 7: Training-Step Progression vs. Wall-Clock Time. HG-DAgger advances through training steps faster than the SAC-based residual methods, but its higher step throughput does not translate into higher success rates (Fig. 4(a)). HiRe-MoMa adds only a modest per-step overhead over +Flat Residual (1–2×) while delivering clear gains in success rate and episode length.

Figure 3: Real-World Experimental Tasks. Our evaluation encompasses three tasks, Place Only, Sweep Litter, and Pick Place, that demand varying levels of inter-module coordination. These tasks are particularly challenging for mobile manipulators as they require the simultaneous optimization of base positioning and arm reaching, where minor misalignments in the platform’s pose propagate as significant errors at the end-effector.

Figure 6: Residual Correction Visualization. Base longitudinal velocity and manipulator vertical position throughout the Place Only task. HiRe-MoMa applies coherent corrections at critical trajectory phases, most notably during base acceleration and the manipulator’s lay-down motion.

Figure 5: Disentangling Decomposition and Conditioning. Training-time success-rate curves for +Flat Residual, +DecompositionOnly, and +Hierarchical Decoupling on Place Only and Sweep Litter; see App. A.1.

Table 3: Policy-Agnostic Generalization. Our HiRe-MoMa yields consistent gains when applied to ACT [47], demonstrating architecture-independent efficacy. While the performance ceiling is inherently tied to the base policy’s quality, the results confirm HiRe-MoMa’s capacity to fine-tune diverse base policies.

Table 4: Decomposition vs. Conditioning within Hierarchical Decoupling. Decomposition alone provides the dominant gain by mitigating gradient interference (+30 pt average success rate). Conditioning adds a targeted improvement (+5 pt on average) that manifests on the coupled dual-arm task (Sweep Litter).

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/
authors: Huixuan Cheng, Bike Zhang, Shankar Sastry, Koushil Sreenath
bullets: Targets direct generation and analysis of learned humanoid-control network weights, rather than conventional policy training alone.
Uses a linear autoencoder to compress actor parameters and a Diffusion Transformer to model their latent distribution.
Trained on reinforcement-learning policies for the Unitree G1, it generates real-world networks performing walking, dancing, and spin-kick motions.
Finds a consistent kinematic-prior structure in first-layer weights under both reinforcement and imitation learning.
Scope: results focus on Unitree G1 policies and initial understanding of the learned weight space.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
bullets: Addresses trajectory errors caused by action representations that are disconnected from visual dynamics.
Uses a visually derived motion scaffold plus a compact residual encoding for centimeter-scale corrections.
A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.

papers.abstract: Achieving general spatial intelligence requires a unified understanding of both static 3D and dynamic 4D. However, we find that existing models struggle to excel at both: 3D post-training can weaken dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models often lack strong static 3D reasoning. Our analysis reveals that this spatial--dynamic interference is highly non-uniform across parameter groups, with the balance between static and dynamic capabilities particularly sensitive to changes in late-layer MLPs. To address this interference, we propose DynThinker, a unified framework for jointly strengthening static and dynamic spatial reasoning. Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) applies configurable group-wise averaging to constrain drift in interference-sensitive pretrained parameters while preserving flexibility for capability enhancement. Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) complements D-EMA by selectively integrating spatial and temporal priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate VLM representations under semantic guidance. Across ten metrics spanning nine static 3D and dynamic 4D benchmarks, DynThinker achieves the highest average score among all evaluated models. Notably, DynThinker achieves 56.0 on ReVSI, 67.2 on DSR-Bench, and 51.2 and 40.1 under the sample-wise and group-wise evaluation protocols of DSI-Bench, respectively, setting new state-of-the-art results among the compared open-source models across all four evaluations within a unified model.
authors: Qihang Cao, Haoyuan Li, Zihan Guo, Sensen Gao, Zihui Gao, Huixin Zhang, Fan He, Jianhua Han, Hang Xu, Xiaodan Liang, Jia-Wang Bian
bullets: Existing models face a trade-off: improving static 3D reasoning can harm dynamic understanding, while 4D-specialized models may underperform on static tasks.
The interference is non-uniform across parameters and is especially sensitive to late-layer MLP changes.
Decoupled Exponential Moving Average (D-EMA) stabilizes interference-sensitive parameter groups while allowing capability improvements elsewhere.
Spatial-Dynamic Fusion (SDF) selectively injects temporal and spatial priors from a dynamic geometry encoder into intermediate vision-language representations.
Across ten metrics on nine benchmarks, DynThinker obtains the highest average score among evaluated models and sets open-source results on four reported evaluations.

papers.abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Kun Xiang, Yunshuang Nie, Tao Tang, Xinlong Zheng, Jia-Wang Bian, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational overhead caused by external 3D geometry encoders in geometry-aware MLLMs.
Transforms intermediate MLLM hidden states into predictive representations of current geometry and future semantics.
Uses two-stage training: lightweight latent frame prediction heads first learn from geometry and next-frame semantic targets, then the external expert is removed during joint optimization.
Introduces Spatial-Grounded Temporal Fusion to selectively integrate self-predicted spatial-temporal priors.
Reports latency reduction from 1.45 s to 0.40 s while retaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the GeoThinker-F pipeline. The framework adopts two decoupled training stages to internalize geometric and temporal representations within the MLLM. Stage 2 (Right): The external geometry encoder is removed from the pipeline. The resulting geometry and future-semantic representations are selectively integrated by SGT-Fusion modules inserted at intermediate MLLM layers for spatial reasoning.

Figure 3: Efficiency and throughput comparison. (a) Compute vs. throughput trade-off, showing GeoThinker-F positioned in the ultra-efficient zone with minimal FLOPs and superior throughput. (b) Relative speedup over the highest-accuracy baseline among the compared methods within each backbone family, reaching an 8.8× acceleration on Qwen2.5-VL-7B compared to Cambrian-P and a 3.6× acceleration on Qwen3-VL-8B compared to GeoThinker.

From top to bottom, we show the input RGB frames, geometry representations predicted by LFP head, and the corresponding feature targets from offline VGGT expert. The predicted features demonstrate remarkable structural alignment with the offline-expert feature targets.

Figure 7: Qualitative limitations of endogenous geometry prediction. For each sequence, we show the input RGB frames (top), LFP-predicted geometry representations (middle), and the corresponding VGGT feature targets (bottom). Top: In the presence of rapidly changing non-rigid structures, the predicted representations exhibit weaker correspondence with the VGGT targets. Bottom: The predicted maps display coarser spatial variation than the corresponding VGGT feature targets. These examples illustrate conditions in which endogenous geometry prediction does not fully recover the geometry-related structure captured by the external expert.

Figure 6: Qualitative semantic selectivity under visually ambiguous conditions. For each sequence, we show input RGB frames (top), LFP-predicted geometry representations (middle), and the corresponding VGGT feature targets (bottom). In these selected snow and driving examples, the VGGT targets exhibit comparatively diffuse or background-dominated activations, whereas the endogenous predictions remain concentrated around the primary human or vehicle. This case-level contrast suggests that prediction from MLLM hidden states can preserve semantically relevant spatial focus when low-level visual cues are ambiguous.

Figure 5: Qualitative structural correspondence in standard scenes. For each sequence, we show input RGB frames (top), LFP-predicted geometry representations (middle), and the corresponding VGGT feature targets (bottom). In these selected scenes with clear foreground subjects and structured motion, the endogenous predictions preserve coherent object-centered activation patterns and broad spatial correspondence with the VGGT targets across consecutive frames. This qualitative agreement illustrates that GeoThinker-F can recover useful geometry-related structure from intermediate MLLM hidden states.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods enable efficient reconstruction of 3D scenes from sparse multi-view images in a single forward pass, without scene-specific optimization. However, existing feed-forward scene-coding pipelines first generate a complete Gaussian representation and then encode its geometry and appearance attributes separately, often involving non-differentiable operations. The resulting 'generate-then-compress' pipeline requires complex attribute-specific codec designs and limits rate-distortion performance by restricting the exploitation of cross-attribute redundancy. We propose multi-view feature coding for Gaussian splatting (MFGS), an end-to-end feed-forward framework for scene coding. Instead of compressing an explicit Gaussian representation, MFGS extracts multi-view features from the input images and encodes them into a compact bitstream. Through end-to-end rate-distortion training, MFGS learns compact multi-view features that jointly represent geometry and appearance, enabling the receiver to predict Gaussian attributes from the decoded features. We further introduce importance-guided Gaussian selection to accommodate different rendering budgets, allowing the receiver to adjust the number of Gaussians used for rendering from the same bitstream. Across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, MFGS achieves 99.76-99.86% bitrate savings over the generate-then-compress pipeline, as measured by BD-rate, while reducing total GMACs by 52-55% and providing an approximately 12 times end-to-end speedup.
authors: Seungmi Choi, Ji-Hyoun Choi, Suhyun Jo, Tae-Gwon Park, Hui Yong Kim
bullets: Avoids the conventional generate-then-compress pipeline and its separate, non-differentiable attribute codecs.
Uses end-to-end rate-distortion training to encode multi-view image features into a compact bitstream.
Predicts Gaussian attributes from decoded features while exploiting redundancy between geometry and appearance.
Importance-guided Gaussian selection supports adjustable rendering budgets from a single bitstream.
Across RE10K, ACID, and DL3DV, reports 99.76–99.86% BD-rate savings, 52–55% lower GMACs, and about 12× faster end-to-end processing.

(b) The MFGS framework compresses multi-view features with an established learned image codec and predicts Gaussian attributes from the decoded features at the receiver. This unified path simplifies coding, exploits cross-attribute redundancy, and enables end-to-end rate–distortion training, while compact latent grids reduce computation.

papers.abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.
authors: Walter Simoncini, Dheeraj Varghese, Gertjan J. Burghouts, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of offering transformers in only a few fixed sizes under changing hardware and workload constraints.
Jointly ranks individual MLP neurons and attention heads on a shared importance scale using differentiable soft pruning across multiple sparsity targets.
Evaluated on 27 vision and text transformer encoders spanning 22M–8B parameters, with smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity.
Pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters with only a 0.8% ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy drop.
At 60% sparsity, AugReg ViT-B/16 reaches up to 1.80× higher throughput and 1.26× lower single-query latency on an A100; models are built in minutes without retraining.

Figure 1 Differentiable soft pruning. Initial importance scores for MLP neurons and attention heads are transformed into learnable log-scores and median-centered by type, aligning their reference points without changing within-type rankings. At each optimization step, the joint ranking determines a threshold κb and soft mask Mb for each sparsity target b ∈ B. We run the same calibration batch through the frozen model under each mask, average losses across targets, and update only the log-scores. Mask gradients concentrate near each threshold, so multiple targets expose different regions of the ranking to useful gradients. The optimized ranking can then be hard-pruned to any inference budget without further optimization.

Figure 5 Ranking optimization changes both cross-block sparsity allocation and within-block selection. papers.selection_reason: Retraining-free elastic pruning of transformer neurons/heads enables adaptive compute; fits Efficient AI.
papers.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
papers.tldr: A retraining-free method turns fixed-size transformers into smoothly adjustable models that trade accuracy for compute across a continuum of sparsity levels.

papers.abstract: We introduce Continuum Attention (CA), a causal Transformer attention operator that replaces discrete key and value lookup with integration over a continuous, piecewise linear memory curve. Each query induces an exponential relevance density along the curve. Integrating the density and interpolated values yields exact normalized attention from closed form exponential moments, including half token boundary contributions. The gradients follow analytically from moments of order at most two, enabling parallel GPU implementations while retaining quadratic sequence complexity and the standard Transformer decoder. Compared with ordinary softmax and focal attention, CA reduces mean validation negative log likelihood by 0.0200 and 0.0480 nats per byte, respectively, winning all paired comparisons. An additional disjoint validation slice yields a 0.0457 nats per byte advantage over the strongest selected softmax baseline, with a paired 95% confidence interval. These findings motivate continuous integration as a promising attention alternative while leaving larger scale generalization open.
authors: Afshin Khadangi
bullets: Uses a continuous piecewise-linear memory curve instead of discrete keys and values.
Computes query-dependent exponential relevance densities and exact normalized attention via closed-form moments, including boundary contributions.
Provides analytic gradients using moments up to order two, supporting parallel GPU implementation.
Outperforms ordinary softmax and focal attention on reported validation comparisons.
Larger-scale generalization remains untested.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.

papers.abstract: Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control. The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements. In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance. In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student model on its own rollouts with token-level supervision from a teacher, assuming that the teacher can reach a correct answer from any prefix the student writes. We call this property the recoverability of the teacher and show it fails on incorrect rollouts: the teacher follows student errors, although it recognizes them. We propose CriticOPD, using error recognition to restore recoverability. The teacher critiques an incorrect rollout, allowing the student to rewrite its solution following the error. The resulting output, including the critique as privileged information, is scored by the teacher while the student uses the revision without the critique for training. On two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves OPD, with the largest gains on competition problems.
authors: Kaixiang Zhao, Tianrun Yu, Shangzhe Li, Yuxiao Yang, Amanda Hughes, Weitong Zhang, Taylor W. Killian
bullets: OPD assumes the teacher can recover from any student-generated prefix, but this fails when the teacher follows recognizable student errors.
CriticOPD uses the teacher’s error critique to guide the student in rewriting its solution.
The teacher scores the critique-assisted revision, while the student trains on the revision without access to the critique.
Across two Qwen3 students and six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CriticOPD improves over standard OPD, especially on competition problems.

papers.abstract: Long-form agentic video generation must turn a screenplay into shots that remain spatially and temporally consistent across nonconsecutive requests. Passing prompts or recent frames between shots does not provide a shared spatial frame for revisiting a scene or a time-indexed record for replaying an earlier event. We present Any Time, Any Space (ATAS), which compiles a screenplay into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references. Before generation, it retrieves relevant evidence from a scene memory of registered static geometry and an event memory of dynamic observations indexed by scene, event, and time. After generation, ATAS reconstructs and registers the clip. It updates memory only when review and state checks accept the observation, while film delivery remains independent of memory admission. Across four video generators, ATAS improves all reported cross-shot consistency measures and achieves the highest aggregate benchmark score for each backbone. It also outperforms the compared agents and 3D-guided methods on target-image spatial revisit, leads three event-recapture criteria, and receives the highest human ratings on all six criteria. The video results and code are available on our project page: https://lhmd.top/atas/.
authors: Weijie Wang, Haomin Zhang, Ye Li, Akide Liu, Zeyu Zhang, Haoyu Zhao, Yefei He, Donny Y. Chen, Feng Chen, Bohan Zhuang
bullets: Addresses the lack of shared spatial and time-indexed state when generating nonconsecutive shots.
Compiles screenplays into shot requests with explicit location, camera, and event-time references.
Retrieves evidence from static scene memory and dynamic event memory before generation, then reconstructs and registers generated clips.
Admits new memory only after review and state checks, while keeping film delivery independent of memory updates.
Improves reported cross-shot consistency across four video generators and receives the highest human ratings on all six criteria.

Fig. 2 Workflow of ATAS. A high-level prompt is parsed into multi-shot requests and bounded shot requests. Each request contains a description, scene, spatial anchor, camera, time interval, and optional event. The shot prompt and the context-dependent prompt condition the video generator. Scene memory supplies static point-cloud references for the requested scene, while event memory supplies dynamic references for the requested event. Shot validation either requests another candidate or sends the accepted observation to the state update. The generated shot remains available as film independently of whether the observation is added to persistent state.

papers.abstract: Automated research with LLM agents has shown promising results in various domains. Through iterative refinement and scored verifiers, LLM agents are capable of discovering new ideas. There are different ways to scale automated research: let one agent iterate for longer, run several agents in parallel, or further let the parallel agents communicate and build on one another's candidates. However, we find that all three strategies eventually plateau as the agents accumulate history. Each agent becomes anchored to its own past attempts, making fewer and smaller edits. Beyond this point, additional budget brings little further improvement. In this paper, we show that the key to scaling discovery further is to forget. Periodically discarding the search state, including every agent's session and the candidate history, and restarting from the best candidate found so far, unblocks the search and pushes the same budget further. We implement forgetting in a team of agents with communication and evaluate it on four tasks spanning heuristic programming, kernel optimization and model training. The results show up to 15% improvement compared to parallel agents, and up to 39% compared to a single agent. Our results suggest that, for open-ended discovery, what an agent is allowed to remember matters as much as how much compute it is given.
authors: Shangyin Tan, Ben Zhou, Lakshya A Agrawal, Jialin Zhang, Yilin Chen, Qiuyang Mang, Donghyun Lee, Dennis Jacob, Koushik Sen, Alex Dimakis, Matei Zaharia
bullets: Parallelism, longer iteration, and agent communication eventually plateau as accumulated history anchors agents to small edits.
The proposed strategy periodically discards agent sessions and candidate history, then restarts from the best candidate found.
Implemented in a communicating multi-agent system and evaluated across four tasks in programming, kernel optimization, and model training.
Forgetting improved results by up to 15% over parallel agents and up to 39% over a single agent.
The findings suggest memory management is as important as compute for open-ended automated discovery.

The agent then edits a candidate and the judge scores it. The harness records the new candidate with its score in the search state and the turn in the agent sessions. A team runs four such loops at once, each with its own state, and the candidates of an agent’s peers come from the other three loops.

papers.abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.

bullets: Targets difficult compositions such as hanging, gravity-driven settling, and hidden containment that static coordinate or image-generation approaches often mishandle.

papers.abstract: Interactive video generation commonly relies on small bidirectional chunks to reduce response latency. Yet our preliminary experiments show that larger chunks improve video quality and better utilize GPU parallelism, allowing more latents to be sampled with only a modest increase in sampling time. Motivated by these observations, we propose Speculative Sampling, a strategy that combines the modeling power of large bidirectional windows with the low-latency interaction of small ones. It expands the modeling window by appending noise latents as padding and caches the resulting predictions for reuse when the condition remains unchanged. Predictions are delivered incrementally, while the uncommitted future remains replaceable. Our latency analysis shows that this removes the waiting-time lower bound imposed by chunk boundaries, shifting the optimization focus from reducing chunk size to accelerating per-chunk sampling. Bidirectional window size thus becomes a decision variable for jointly optimizing visual quality and sampling time, rather than a necessary constraint on low-latency interaction. This opens a path to serving large bidirectional models in interactive streaming systems without complex streaming post-training.
authors: Yubo Huang, Yuxuan Zhang, Jiaming Liu, Sirui Zhao, Enhong Chen
bullets: Interactive video systems use small bidirectional chunks for responsiveness, but larger chunks can improve quality and GPU utilization.
The method expands the modeling window with noise padding and reuses cached predictions when conditions remain unchanged.

The approach removes the waiting-time lower bound caused by chunk boundaries, shifting focus to faster per-chunk sampling.

papers.abstract: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Multimodal code intelligence connects the symbolic world of programs with the visual world their execution creates. Interest in this capability is burgeoning, as models are increasingly asked to produce charts, webpages, animations, and semi-structured documents. Recently, proprietary models have pushed far ahead, producing interactive artifacts even from a text description or a screenshot alone. Yet their data and training remain closed, and open progress is held back by the quantity and quality of available data and by the pipelines and methods for producing it. Quality is the harder of the two, since a sample must be correct as a program, well built, and above all visually right once rendered. No existing signal covers all three. Execution often returns just a pass or fail, code similarity does not map to the visual output, and task-specific verifiers do not generalize. To push open progress further, we start from the data side with PrismaForge, a hierarchical data pipeline centered on a synthesized rubric that decomposes these factors into checkable criteria. The same rubric serves as both filter and reward: it curates the supervised corpus, then drives reinforcement learning on visual-coding tasks. Leveraging PrismaForge for data synthesis and filtering, we build PrismaCoder-2M, the most diverse open dataset for multimodal code intelligence and the largest to date. On the model side, we train PrismaCoder-9B and PrismaCoder-35B on this data and release both. They lead the open state of the art by a wide margin and rival leading proprietary systems. Our analyses further show that the proposed rubric-based pipeline improves multimodal coding performance across model backbones. We release our code and data at https://qiushisun.github.io/PrismaCoder-Home/.

papers.abstract: We introduce an approach for self-supervised representation learning designed to be used as a tokenizer for generative modeling. Our objective supervises a representation loss by factorizing the pointwise mutual information of the data, which we estimate by taking information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model. We justify our algorithm theoretically and empirically, demonstrating that our generative approach to representation learning avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression in cases where commonly used methods like DINO and LeJEPA fail. Moreover, we show our representation learning technique is scalable; expending more compute leads to predictably better latent tokenization. For the first time, we perform a careful analysis of the combined flop efficiency of tokenizer and generative model and demonstrate that our approach is a compute-optimal improvement over direct diffusion for pixel-space generation, obtaining an FID-50K of 2.18 with JiT-L. Applied to ImageNet and the text-to-image dataset GPIC, we show tokenizer encoder scaling laws for diffusability, where extrapolating our approach achieves representations in 7x fewer FLOPs than DINOv2 on ImageNet and 8x fewer FLOPs than WebSSL on GPIC.
authors: Alan Baade, Kyle Sargent, Vincent Sitzmann, Eric Ryan Chan, Justin Johnson, Li Fei-Fei, Gordon Wetzstein
bullets: Factorizes pointwise mutual information using information differences between conditional predictions from a learned generative model.
Theoretically and empirically avoids dimensional collapse and feature suppression observed with DINO and LeJEPA in tested settings.
Scaling compute yields predictably better latent tokenization and favorable tokenizer–generator compute trade-offs.
Achieves FID-50K 2.18 with JiT-L and reports projected 7× and 8× lower FLOPs than DINOv2 and WebSSL for studied datasets.
Scope includes ImageNet, GPIC, and pixel-space diffusion comparisons; some efficiency claims rely on extrapolation.

papers.abstract: Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act. We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken. After every recognized word, a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold tau set by the user, so 1 - tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object. Otherwise, it waits or asks. The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate, and evaluate. On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92 percent of the time when it commits at tau = 0.9, and needs 31 to 35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.
authors: Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Addresses robots’ tendency to wait for complete instructions before acting.
Uses a fine-tuned text encoder to score scene objects word by word and commits when the best calibrated probability reaches a user-set threshold.
Supports waiting or asking when confidence is insufficient, with 1 − τ representing accepted error risk.
On instructions with unseen words, it commits correctly 1.6–2× as often as keyword matching and is at least 92% correct at τ = 0.9.
Runs in 31–35 ms per word on consumer GPUs and includes streaming, data-generation, training, calibration, and evaluation tools.

Right: the loop that runs after every recognised word. The judge scores each scene object, the probabilities are calibrated, and the robot commits, waits for the next word or asks which object is meant. The evaluation feeds generated words to the judge directly, without speech recognition.

papers.abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.
authors: Yushen Liang, Yue Peng, Baosheng Jin, Tianluo Zhang, Xinyu Zhang, Shuyi Zhou, Zhuoran Chen, Xinqi Liu, Shenji Wan
bullets: Problem: Standard robot memories treat each update as equal time, so identical observations over different durations can produce inappropriate actions.

Method: TFP learns memory dynamics where observations and prior memory determine transitions, while measured elapsed intervals control state evolution; it conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Results: Controlled comparisons with Diffusion Policy and π₀.₅ show higher average success than matched recurrent, state-space, and interval-gated memories.
Evidence: Memory readouts recover event timing and motion after occlusion, while changing supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions.
Scope: Real-robot timing and memory tasks plus LIBERO evaluations indicate benefits for physical and general manipulation.

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation provides dense supervision for reasoning models via a privileged self-teacher. However, this supervision reflects local token preferences rather than the expected return of an unguided student continuation. Recent methods combine this signal with GRPO. They use GRPO for update directions and the teacher for signal scaling. However, we demonstrate a more effective integration within PPO. Specifically, we identify complementary positional dynamics: privileged information enhances a critic's value-prediction accuracy toward the response's end, whereas self-teacher guidance is strong initially, drops mid-generation, and rebounds finally. These insights motivate Value-Augmented Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (VASPO), wherein a self-teacher and critic evaluate identical privileged information at student-generated prefixes. The critic computes token-level PPO advantages from predicted continuation returns, while the self-teacher modulates selected positive advantages via bounded probability ratios. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 and 1.81 percentage points on Qwen3-4B and OLMo3-7B variants, respectively, and achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves. Our code is available at https://github.com/cii030/VASPO.
authors: Fei Wu, Zhenrong Zhang, Jianshu Zhang, Jun Du
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between local self-teacher preferences and the expected return of student continuations.
Uses a critic and self-teacher on the same privileged information at student-generated prefixes.
The critic computes token-level PPO advantages, while bounded teacher probability ratios modulate selected positive advantages.
Across six math reasoning benchmarks, VASPO improves mean accuracy over PPO by 2.59 points on Qwen3-4B and 1.81 points on OLMo3-7B.
Achieves the highest mean accuracy among evaluated methods on Knights and Knaves.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at: https://gr-bc.github.io
authors: Xiaoman Li, Zhiqiang Yang, Jiayu Hu, Jipeng Kong, Yang Zhang, Jingwei Zhang, Fangzheng Yan, Chunhua Shen, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality long-horizon demonstrations containing detours, failures, hesitations, and imperfect recoveries.
Builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over successful and failed intervention-assisted rollouts.
Uses reverse graph search to estimate minimal remaining steps and reweight chunks by their reduction in this potential.
Reuses recoverable segments and intervention paths without reward models, critics, progress predictors, trajectory comparisons, or progress labels.
Evaluated on four manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, reaching 91% success after a few offline iterations.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting multiple tokens per step, yet feature-based drafters rely on target hidden features whose contextual emphasis may not align with the needs of subsequent draft positions. Hybrid linear attention (HLA) models maintain compact recurrent states that accumulate historical associations, offering an efficient source of complementary context for speculative drafting. We introduce ReaDy, the first speculative decoding method, to the best of our knowledge, to leverage HLA recurrent states for position-specific context retrieval during drafting. ReaDy equips each draft position with a learned query to retrieve supplementary context directly from the target's committed recurrent states. A lightweight state reader integrates this context into draft representations through residual updates, while low-rank state reads and fused operators keep additional computation and I/O overhead low. Building on DSpark's parallel backbone and sequential prediction head, ReaDy employs a lightweight two-stage adaptation strategy, with reader capacity, state sources, and residual placement examined through ablation studies. Across seven benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and dialogue, ReaDy achieves an average $3.16\times$ decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding with Qwen3.8-27B on a single NVIDIA B200 GPU. It outperforms DSpark on every benchmark, improving throughput by 7.97% and acceptance length by 8.50% on average. Our code is available at https://github.com/StartLuxLabs/ReaDy.

papers.abstract: Low-light video processing remains an underexplored problem in computer vision, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality ground-truth data. Existing public datasets exhibit several limitations, including restricted motion diversity, limited scene coverage, weak degradations, reliance on auxiliary modalities such as event data, and misalignment between low-light inputs and ground truth. Furthermore, current datasets typically address either low-light enhancement or scene understanding, whereas these tasks should be considered jointly. We introduce \textbf{OLiVES}, a benchmark dataset for outdoor low-light videos with dynamic scenes, designed to support both low-light video enhancement (LLVE) and video object segmentation (VOS). The dataset addresses key content gaps by incorporating a diverse range of natural textures, animals, occlusions, dynamic activities, and close-up scenes. To the best of our knowledge, OLiVES is the first outdoor low-light video dataset captured using professional cinema-grade cameras. It provides over 25,000 aligned normal- and low-light frame pairs, along with over 46,000 VOS annotations. We benchmark state-of-the-art LLVE and VOS methods on OLiVES and show that training on it improves performance on both tasks. The OLiVES project page is available at: https://anonymous-OLiVES.github.io/.
authors: Yini Li, Joanne Lin, David Blackham, David Bull, Nantheera Anantrasirichai

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains language models from checked task outcomes, but assigning a terminal reward to individual reasoning tokens or actions remains difficult. Group-relative methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) sample several attempts per prompt, but lose their reward-based learning signal when all attempts receive the same outcome. We propose Hindsight-Privileged RLVR (HP-RLVR), a single-rollout method that turns a completed trajectory's own future into token-level update weights. The generating policy snapshot scores each eligible token under its causal history and under a hindsight context containing the realized future and verifier feedback. A normalized Jensen--Shannon divergence between the two views weights the reward relative to a historical baseline, yielding bounded token credit for both successful and failed attempts, with no reference solution or learned critic. In paired Qwen3-8B runs over a shared $100$-step schedule, HP-RLVR trains $1.21\times$, $1.46\times$, and $2.30\times$ faster than GRPO on mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld, using one eighth the rollouts per prompt. Accuracy is comparable overall, with HP-RLVR ahead on mathematics at all three sizes and GRPO ahead on code and ALFWorld. In ALFWorld, $43.2\%$ (4B) and $49.0\%$ (8B) of GRPO's gradient-norm records are zero, versus none for HP-RLVR.
authors: Wei Chen, Yubing Wu, Zhou Xu, Haoyue Zhang, Delu Zeng, Jiahao Wang, Junmei Yang, Pan tiewen, Jingfeng Liu, Zhiheng Zhou, Bo Li, Min Chen

Uses one eighth the rollouts per prompt and trains 1.21×–2.30× faster than GRPO across mathematics, code generation, and ALFWorld in the reported schedule.
Achieves comparable overall accuracy: stronger on mathematics, while GRPO leads on code generation and ALFWorld.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, an agent must explore an unknown environment to learn how to make good decisions. Unlike methods that can freely sample any state--action pair, an agent learning from a single trajectory must spend additional time navigating between states. It is therefore natural to expect that learning from a single trajectory requires more experience. In this paper, we show that this additional cost is not always necessary. For average-reward reinforcement learning, we develop an algorithm that learns where to collect information while ensuring that the required samples can be obtained efficiently. We establish an upper bound on the number of interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove a matching information theoretic lower bound, showing that, for a broad class of environments and at sufficiently high accuracy, learning from a single trajectory is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted access to state action samples. Our results reveal that the additional complexity cost of navigation can be avoided by adapting information gathering requirements to how the environment provides information.
authors: Tongxi Wang
bullets: Studies policy identification when learning must follow one continuing trajectory rather than freely sampling state–action pairs.
Introduces an algorithm that adaptively chooses where to gather information while navigating efficiently.
Provides an upper bound on interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy.
Proves a matching information-theoretic lower bound for broad environment classes at sufficiently high accuracy.
Shows that, in the worst case, single-trajectory learning can be no harder than unrestricted state–action sampling.

papers.tldr: Single-trajectory average-reward reinforcement learning can identify near-optimal policies without the expected extra navigation cost in broad settings.

papers.abstract: We study how to improve LLM reasoning at inference time without updating model weights or using external reward models. Recent reward-free power-sampling methods define the sequence-level power target $\pi_\alpha(y\mid x)\propto p_0(y\mid x)^\alpha$, where $\alpha>1$, which increases the relative probability of completions that are already likely under the base model. Existing methods use Metropolis--Hastings or Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) to approximately sample from this target. However, two challenges arise at different levels. At the target level, full-sequence sharpening can concentrate probability on a few exact reasoning--answer trajectories, suppressing alternative paths that support the same answer. At the sampler level, finite-particle SMC can suffer from path collapse when resampling repeatedly duplicates a few high-weight prefixes. To address these challenges, we propose Decoupled Marginal Sharpening (DMS), which separately controls how strongly the model favors particular reasoning paths and how strongly it favors final answers after aggregating support across those paths. At the target level, DMS first samples from a sharpened reasoning distribution, then marginalizes the model's answer probabilities over the resulting weighted reasoning population and sharpens the induced answer marginal. Separate exponents allow mild reasoning sharpening to encourage exploration of diverse paths, followed by stronger answer-marginal sharpening to concentrate probability on answers with greater aggregate support across those paths. At the sampler level, we develop Fully Adapted Annealed SMC, which combines an annealed sequence of power targets with locally fully adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling. Experiments on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models show that DMS achieves the highest mean pass@1 among the compared methods in all tasks.
authors: Weixin Wang, Wei Deng, Anderson Schneider, Yuriy Nevmyvaka, Pan Xu, Andrew Bennett
bullets: Addresses two issues in reward-free power sampling: loss of alternative reasoning paths and SMC path collapse.
Separates reasoning-path sharpening from final-answer sharpening through independent exponents.
Introduces Fully Adapted Annealed SMC with adapted proposals and predictive ancestor resampling.
Evaluated on MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, HumanEval, and AIME24/25 across three base models.
Achieves the highest mean pass@1 among compared methods on all reported tasks.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.

bullets: Targets failures in pretrained vision-language-action models on unseen long-horizon tasks.

On 50 RoboCasa365 target tasks, success on unseen composite tasks increases from 4.6% to 13.8% without human demonstrations.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, uses 28% of GPU time and 22% of self-collected demonstrations while achieving slightly higher success.

papers.abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.
authors: Parham Nooranbakht, Seyed Mahdi Basiri Azad, Joschka B\"odecker
bullets: Uses an adaptive action grid: high-value regions gain bins, while low-value bins are pruned.
Across eight DMControl tasks, SGQN is best on four and near-best on three; it trails Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run.
Analysis finds growth effectively activates all candidate bins, resembling uniform growth, while pruning has little impact.
Coarse initialization is important; starting with all bins causes collapsed seeds, and annealed softmax selection sharply reduces return.
Results may also reflect an uncontrolled difference in update frequency versus baselines.

papers.title: Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN): An Analysis of Adaptive Action Grids in Decoupled Q-Learning
papers.tldr: SGQN is a competitive continuous-control Q-learning method, but its gains appear driven by coarse initialization and epsilon-greedy action selection rather than adaptive grid growth or pruning.

papers.abstract: The scaling relationship of compute and performance for language models (LMs) has been extensively studied; more recently, models are being designed to scale memory use, as well. In particular, adding embeddings for n-grams scales memory separately from compute use, because each pass only processes individual embedding rows, which are much smaller than the storage used for the whole embedding table. However, existing methods train embeddings from scratch, which needs expensive GPU memory for fast reading and writing. Meanwhile, the ordinary memory of the host system is cheap and underutilized by these training methods. To scale on host memory, we introduce COUNT (Counting Offline Unlocks N-gram Transformers), which builds n-gram embeddings without adding learned parameters by storing precomputed n-gram counts on host. We use the corpus frequencies to weight together the LM's own unembeddings of the next tokens most often following the current n-gram history. At a fixed compute budget, COUNT can be added as an additional input embedding for pretraining 1B-parameter LMs to improve validation loss as much as an LM with 57% more compute. If GPU memory is limited, using COUNT to let backbone parameters fill GPU memory gives better performance than splitting memory with additional learned n-gram embeddings. Beyond efficiency, COUNT allows switching in a different table of n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time to adapt to a new task without any training.
authors: Ian Magnusson, Noah A. Smith, Pang Wei Koh
bullets: Addresses the GPU-memory and training cost of learned n-gram embeddings.
Builds n-gram embeddings from corpus frequencies and the LM’s next-token unembeddings, without adding learned parameters.
Stores count tables in inexpensive host memory while accessing only relevant embedding rows during inference or training.
For 1B-parameter LMs at fixed compute, COUNT improves validation loss by as much as 57% more compute.
Supports training-free adaptation by swapping in n-gram counts from a domain-specific corpus at inference time.

papers.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
papers.tldr: COUNT uses offline n-gram counts stored in host memory to provide training-free, domain-adaptable embeddings that improve language-model efficiency and validation loss.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.
authors: Chonghan Qin, Dongming Wu, Kaituo Feng, Jiaxu Wang, Xinlei Yu, Peiwen Sun, Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Bingao Chen, Weitong Lian, Ryan Ji, Wenqi Ren, Xiaobin Hu, Dahua Lin, Yu-Gang Jiang, Xiangyu Yue
bullets: Motivation: Existing studies are rapidly expanding but lack a consistent framework for integrating agentic functions into complete robot systems.
The paper traces the evolution from robot policies to vision-language-action, world, and world-action models.
It organizes research into 17 categories across four domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness.
The survey covers agent-driven learning, data collection, world and task construction, evaluation, and capability orchestration.
It identifies open challenges and future directions toward more capable, reliable, and adaptive robots.
