papers.tldr: This paper unifies emerging research on agentic robots—systems that reason, learn, plan, act, and autonomously adapt in real-world environments.

papers.abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. Link for the webpage \href{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}
authors: Zeji Yi, Soham Dasgupta, Xinyang Zhang, Koushil Sreenath, Guannan Qu, Xi Chen, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi
bullets: Compares continuous and discrete single-step regression and multi-step flow policies in single-task and multi-task training, across simulation and real hardware.
Even naive uniform-bin quantization achieves comparable or better task success than continuous-action policies.
The key weakness of discrete policies is factorization error from product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions, rather than insufficient precision.
Iterative computation in discrete flows and classifier-free guidance improve responsiveness within predicted action chunks.
Geometric corruption processes inspired by continuous flow matching do not consistently improve discrete policies.

papers.title: When Do Discrete Actions Make Good Continuous Controllers?
papers.tldr: Discrete action policies can match or outperform continuous controllers in robotic VLA tasks, with factorization—not action precision—as their main challenge.

papers.abstract: This paper considers reliable in-sequence molecular communication, where bio-nanomachines exchange molecule-encoded information in a specified order, and investigates a new simulation-based method to incrementally evaluate communication protocols by gradually increasing the complexity of experimental settings. The proposed method, called Affine Memory Replay (AMR), builds a continual learning (CL) model to estimate communication performance between bio-nanomachines. AMR stores past simulation samples and synthesizes additional replay samples through interpolation and extrapolation between past samples. Through incremental performance estimation tasks, it replays both past and synthetic samples to regularize model updates, helping the model adapt to new experimental settings while retaining knowledge from earlier ones. Experimental results show that AMR significantly outperforms existing CL methods in maintaining overall estimation accuracy across sequentially learned estimation tasks. It effectively balances memory stability and learning plasticity under moderate training cost.
authors: Siddhant Setia, Junichi Suzuki, Tadashi Nakano
bullets: Addresses incremental performance estimation for bio-nanomachine communication protocols.
Uses a continual-learning model that replays stored simulation samples alongside interpolated and extrapolated synthetic samples.
Regularizes updates to balance adaptation to new settings with retention of earlier knowledge.
Outperforms existing continual-learning methods in overall estimation accuracy across sequential tasks.
Maintains memory stability and learning plasticity at moderate training cost.

papers.abstract: For the fundamental problem of prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether one could compete with a comparator that switches $k$ times among only $m$ experts. For a discrete set of experts, this problem was resolved by Bousquet and Warmuth (2020), who gave an efficient algorithm with optimal regret matching the information-theoretic limit. We study the analogous problem in online convex optimization, where the action space is continuous. An inefficient algorithm can be derived by discretizing the action space and applying the Bousquet--Warmuth algorithm, giving regret of $\widetilde{O}(md+k)$, while the best known efficient algorithm for this problem has regret $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. We show that this computational inefficiency is inherent, establishing a separation between the information-theoretic and polynomial-time regret achievable for this problem. Specifically, under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, we show that for every polynomial-time algorithm there exist instances for which it incurs at least $(k\sqrt d)^{1-o(1)}$ regret.
authors: Angelos Assos, Anand Brahmbhatt, Elad Hazan
bullets: Studies prediction with expert advice when the action space is continuous and the comparator switches k times among m experts.
An inefficient discretization-based method achieves regret approximately Õ(md+k), matching the information-theoretic scale.
The best known efficient method has regret approximately Õ(dk), revealing a computational gap.
Under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, every polynomial-time algorithm suffers at least (k√d)^(1−o(1)) regret on some instances.
Establishes a separation between achievable regret with unlimited computation and with polynomial-time algorithms.

papers.title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization
papers.tldr: The paper proves that efficiently tracking a comparator switching among a small set of experts in online convex optimization inherently requires substantially more regret than the information-theoretic optimum, assuming the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture.

papers.abstract: Momentum is a classical tool for accelerating convex optimization and a standard component of modern large language model training. Yet recent empirical work has questioned the usefulness of first-moment momentum in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We study this question through a bandit formulation of RLVR with bias-corrected exponential moving average (EMA) momentum, where the EMA coefficient $\beta$ controls how quickly the weights on past gradients decay. When policy gradients are evaluated exactly, we prove that increasing $\beta$ within a range that prevents overshoot strictly accelerates optimization. When gradients are estimated from sampled responses, a positive expected gain can be obscured by sampling fluctuations. We show that as the learning rate $\eta$ decreases, the expected gain with fixed $\beta$ vanishes faster than these fluctuations, whereas increasing $\beta$ to keep $\eta/(1-\beta)$ within the safe regime preserves a nonvanishing gain that eventually dominates them. Bandit simulations quantitatively validate these predictions. RLVR experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base using SGD with EMA and AdamW support our principle of choosing larger coefficients in practical LLM post-training. On Qwen2.5-32B with AdamW, simply increasing $\beta_1$ improves mean validation accuracy by nearly $2$ percentage points over the conventional choice, demonstrating the principle's effectiveness at a larger model scale.
authors: Kaifei Wang, Zikang Shan, Liwei Wang, Yinyu Ye, Han Zhong
bullets: Models RLVR as a bandit problem using bias-corrected EMA momentum, with β controlling gradient-memory decay.
With exact policy gradients, increasing β within a safe, non-overshooting range strictly speeds optimization.
With sampled gradients, fixed-β gains can be hidden by sampling noise; scaling β to keep η/(1−β) safe preserves gains that eventually dominate fluctuations.
Bandit simulations and Qwen experiments support using larger momentum coefficients; increasing AdamW’s β₁ improved mean validation accuracy by nearly 2 percentage points on Qwen2.5-32B.
The analysis is scoped to the proposed bandit formulation and tested RLVR settings; larger momentum must remain within a safe regime to avoid overshoot.

papers.abstract: We develop a self-supervised reinforcement learning algorithm that learns to build towers of up to eight cubes from scratch, without prior data, rewards, demonstrations, or pretrained models. Our method, Contrastive Planning via Spherical Linear Interpolation (C-Slerp), uses contrastive representations as reusable building blocks and repeatedly composes them to infer a sequence of intermediate waypoints. Under our hyperspherical parameterization, the learned representations allow intermediate waypoints to be inferred in closed form through spherical linear interpolation, without training a separate high-level policy or performing graph search. Importantly, the representation geometry also tells us how to adjust the number of waypoints based on the difficulty of each goal-reaching problem. Experiments show that our method succeeds on long-horizon navigation and robotic manipulation tasks, including settings where strong baselines fail to achieve a single success. Ablations further show that using a fixed number of waypoints substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of adapting the plan to task difficulty.

bullets: Learns from scratch in a self-supervised reinforcement learning setting, including tower-building tasks with up to eight cubes.

Adapts the number of waypoints to goal difficulty based on representation geometry.
Succeeds on challenging navigation and manipulation tasks where strong baselines may fail entirely; fixed waypoint counts perform substantially worse.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning makes language models better at solving tasks, but the same mechanism also rewards guessing. When success is the only way to earn reward, opting for a safe fallback is always worse than a long-shot attempt. When a wrong action can corrupt a database or ship broken code, that incentive can be costly. Therefore, we propose training models to fail gracefully: to preserve successful behavior whenever possible while learning to execute a safe fallback policy when acting would be unreliable. However, naively using policy gradients with intermediate reward for fallback behavior is brittle due to unfavorable optimization dynamics. We address this challenge with GracefulRL, which reshapes the optimization landscape to promote graceful failure. Importantly, this behavior emerges directly from outcome-level reward signals, without annotations specifying when to fall back or additional inference-time machinery such as a verifier. Across a range of tasks and scales, we train models that largely preserve their task-solving capability while selectively falling back when acting would be unreliable. More broadly, our results show that reinforcement learning can not only incentivize models to succeed, but also to reason about the limits of their capabilities and change course when they determine that success is out of reach.
authors: Daman Arora, Xuecheng Liu, Himanshu Gaurav Singh, Fahim Tajwar, Abitha Thankaraj, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Haiwen Feng, Yuda Song, Andrea Zanette
bullets: RL can encourage risky guessing because success is rewarded more than safe abstention.

Across tasks and scales, models largely retain task-solving ability while selectively avoiding unreliable actions.

papers.abstract: Context can improve large language model performance, but these gains may be lost after context removal. Inspired by biological systems consolidation, we formulate Memory Consolidation (MC) as internalizing these gains while preserving non-target capabilities, connecting context-specified editing, skill learning, and behavioral steering under a common objective. We introduce a five-task-family testbed measuring consolidation and retention under single, batch, and sequential updates. We propose Cortex, which generates prospective queries to anticipate uses of context and distills context-conditioned outputs into mergeable low-rank or structural feed-forward network updates. Across 4B--120B dense and mixture-of-experts backbones, including both text-only and multimodal models, Cortex lies on the empirical consolidation--retention Pareto frontier in most evaluated settings. After 50 sequential factual edits on a 14B model, Cortex-Structural recovers 88.9% of the context-induced gain while retaining 99.8% of original non-target performance.
authors: Jintian Zhang, Feng He, Xinnian Liang, Ziwen Xu, Haoming Xu, Haojing Huang, Shuangzhi Wu, Ningyu Zhang

Tested on 4B–120B dense and mixture-of-experts text-only and multimodal models.

papers.abstract: Anatomical labels help 3D Gaussian splatting preserve vessels in cinematic renderings of CT, but the representation is still found by optimising each patient's scene, where densification decides where Gaussians go, while real-time displays cap their number. We address one part of this process: deciding where a fixed budget of B Gaussians should be placed. We propose a reusable, labelaware allocation front end that maps a patient's CT, labels and transfer function to a density over 2mm cells and draws exactly B positions from it without per-patient optimisation; the other Gaussian attributes are still fitted per patient. The front end is learned once from per-patient optimised scenes and implemented as a population-trained neural prior and an interpretable seven-parameter visibility-aware closed form (VACF). With identical attribute fitting on 20 held-out patients at 10K-100K Gaussians, both raise vessel-masked PSNR over uniform allocation by 4.5-7.1dB and over pruning a dense voxel-aligned model by 1.6-3.3dB. The neural prior does not differ significantly from per-patient optimised allocation at any budget, and VACF is within 0.6dB of it on vessels; on 19 external patients the neural prior again matches it on vessels and VACF is within 0.7dB. As an initialisation for position optimisation, VACF allocation beats per-patient densification on vessels at 10K Gaussians and, at 25K, reaches a higher vessel PSNR after 118s of optimisation than densification after 248s. Under altered rendering presets, VACF transfers to new colours and lighting but not to a label-free transfer function, whereas the neural prior shows the opposite pattern.
authors: Bowen Xiang, Dingjie Su, Jon S. Heiselman, Michael I. Miga
bullets: Addresses budget-constrained Gaussian placement for cinematic CT rendering, while per-patient fitting still determines other Gaussian attributes.
Maps CT, anatomical labels, and a transfer function to a cell-level density and samples exactly B Gaussian positions.
Introduces a learned neural prior and an interpretable seven-parameter visibility-aware closed form (VACF), trained from optimised scenes.
Across held-out and external patients, both methods outperform uniform and dense-model-pruning allocations; the neural prior matches per-patient optimisation, while VACF remains close.
VACF improves vessel quality and optimisation speed as an initialisation, but transfer depends on the rendering setup and availability of labels.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method. (a) For each training patient, CT and labels are classified by a TF and path-traced from 256 training views on a sphere; a per-patient 3DGS model (teacher) optimised on these views defines the oracle allocation, the count of its Gaussians per 2 mm cell. A simple distortion model (Proposition 1) suggests that one density per patient can serve a range of budgets. (b) The allocation front end predicts this density from per-cell features without per-patient optimisation, implemented as a visibility-aware closed form (VACF) with six tissue weights and a visibility exponent, or as a neural prior (3D U-Net). Both are fitted to the oracle densities of the training patients by minimising the KL divergence (dashed) and then frozen. (c) For a new patient and any budget B, exactly B positions are drawn from the density; colour, opacity, scale and rotation, and optionally the positions, are then fitted to path-traced views of that patient, and the result is rendered by splatting in real time. All images are data of MSD test patient 372: CT slice with labels (vessels red, tumour yellow, liver outline green), teacher Gaussians (coronal projection, darker = more opaque), cell features (one axial 2 mm slice), densities (22 mm axial slab, square-root scale), sampled positions (18 mm coronal slab) and a rendering after VACF allocation with optimised positions at 10K Gaussians.

Figure 3: Image quality as a function of the budget B (log scale) after fitting all attributes at the allocated positions with the same protocol for every method. Top (a–c): 20 held-out MSD patients; bottom (d–f): 19 external 3D-IRCADb patients. (a, d) Vessel-masked PSNR, (b, e) thin-vessel PSNR (r < 1.5 mm), (c, f) foreground PSNR. The neural prior tracks the per-patient oracle density (dashed); VACF is close below it; both stay well above uniform voxel allocation and pruning of a dense voxel-aligned model by LightGaussian significance, and their advantage over the anatomy heuristic is largest on thin vessels and at small budgets. Dotted (a–c): per-case 3DGS at budget B, which also optimises positions (Section 5.3). Means over patients; paired statistics in Tables 2 and 4.

Figure 4: Thin-vessel regions of two MSD test patients rendered with 10K Gaussians (preset A). First column: ground-truth crop (top) and the full view with the crop location (bottom). Other columns: renderings after allocation and attribute fitting (top; crop PSNR in dB) and the absolute error averaged over colour channels (bottom; white 0 to black 0.08). Uniform allocation blurs branches and leaves errors along every vessel edge; differences among the anatomy-aware allocators are subtle in single crops (patient-level statistics in Tables 1–2). The last column shows VACF followed by joint optimisation of positions. Crops are chosen automatically as the 112 × 112-pixel window with the most thin-vessel pixels in the view.

Figure 1: The problem. (a) Cinematic rendering path-traces a CT volume classified by a transfer function (TF); it conveys depth and shape but takes minutes per frame. (b) 3D Gaussian splatting renders such scenes in real time, but head-mounted displays, tablets and browsers cap the number of Gaussians B, so their positions must be chosen. Shown are B = 10,000 positions (in an 18 mm coronal slab) drawn uniformly over the organ and by our visibility-aware closed form (VACF), which concentrates them on vessels and the visible surface. (c) With identical fitting of all other attributes, the two allocations give different images: crops of a held-out view, absolute error and crop PSNR (MSD test patient 372); and vessel-masked PSNR against the budget on 20 held-out patients, where the neural prior matches the per-patient oracle, VACF comes close, and uniform allocation stays 4.5–7.1 dB lower.

Figure 7: How the per-patient oracle spends its budget (20 MSD test patients). (a) Share of the budget per region for the anatomy heuristic, VACF, the neural prior and the oracle (hatched). Regions are assigned per 2 mm cell: a 2 mm shell below the liver surface, interior parenchyma, parenchyma within 2 mm of a vessel, vessels by radius, tumour rim and core, and cells outside the liver. Relative to the heuristic, the oracle spends more on the surface shell, thin vessels and tumour and much less around vessels. (b) Log-ratio between the oracle’s and each method’s budget share as a function of depth below the liver surface. The heuristic over-spends deep inside the organ and under-spends near the surface; VACF halves this bias (from about +0.7 to +0.5 near the surface and from −0.85 to −0.35 deep inside) and the neural prior removes it.

Figure 5: Allocation as initialisation for position optimisation. (a–c) Test-view PSNR against optimisation time at 25K Gaussians (means over 10 MSD test patients; evaluation time excluded): VACF allocation with positions frozen (the evaluation protocol) or optimised jointly with the other attributes (15K iterations), and per-case 3DGS grown by budget-capped densification (30K iterations). (d, e) Vessel-masked and thin-vessel PSNR at 10K for four initial allocations with positions frozen (open circles) and optimised (filled circles); dotted line: per-case 3DGS. Position optimisation helps every allocation, but uniform initialisation remains far behind, and VACF with optimised positions exceeds per-case 3DGS on vessels.

Figure 9: Supporting analysis (training patients). (a) Under uniform allocation the MSE falls as a power of the budget, reaching a floor above about 50K Gaussians; fitting D = AB−β+C gives β = 0.96 on the foreground, with steeper slopes on vessels and thin vessels than on parenchyma. Geometric means over five patients. (b) Budget invariance: Jensen–Shannon divergence between the normalised allocation densities of budget-capped per-patient models at different budgets (bars), compared with the divergence between two optimisation seeds at the same budget (dashed: 25K; dotted: 200K), at 8 mm and 4 mm resolution. Densities at different budgets differ about as much as two seeds do.

Figure 6: Rendering presets (10 MSD test patients; all allocators fitted or trained on preset A). (a–c) One test patient under preset A, preset B (unseen colours, extinctions and lighting) and preset C (unseen label-free TF). (d) PSNR relative to the oracle of each preset at 10K Gaussians on vessels, thin vessels and the foreground. VACF stays at the oracle level under preset B but not under preset C, where appearance no longer follows the labels; the neural prior with TF inputs shows the opposite pattern; without TF inputs it behaves like VACF. (e) Preset-C renderings of one view at 10K Gaussians (foreground PSNR) and absolute errors: label-driven allocation (anatomy heuristic, VACF) leaves large errors along the liver surface, where the preset-C oracle spends almost a third of its budget.

Figure 8: Allocation densities of one patient (MSD test patient 372). Left: a path-traced view of the patient (display copy rendered at 1024×1024). Right: allocation densities shown as coronal projections of the number of Gaussians per 2 mm column, on a common colour scale. Uniform voxel allocation spreads the budget over the organ; the anatomy heuristic concentrates it on large vessels and blurs it into their surroundings. The per-patient oracle follows the vessel tree down to small branches while keeping a broad coverage of the parenchyma. VACF and the neural prior reproduce this pattern without per-patient optimisation.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses budget constraints in 3D Gaussian Splatting for medical imaging by proposing a reusable, label-aware allocation front end and neural prior.
papers.title: Where Should the Gaussians Go? Reusable Label-Aware Allocation for Budget-Constrained Gaussian Splatting of Cinematic CT
papers.tldr: A reusable label-aware Gaussian allocation strategy places a fixed rendering budget where CT vessels matter, improving vessel quality and speeding position optimisation without per-patient allocation search.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates LLM generation through lightweight drafting and parallel verification. It is particularly promising for long inputs, where KV-cache access costs can be amortized over multiple accepted tokens. Yet most drafters are trained on short sequences and degrade on long inputs, while long-context training is costly. Existing training-free approaches restrict the context window, rescale positions, or augment recent context with retrieved distant entries. Drafters, however, read target hidden states that already encode contextual and positional information, and their lightweight architecture makes full-history attention affordable. We propose FOLD, a training-free method that preserves exact local positions and treats all distant entries as far memory at a shared position. To counter attention dilution as the memory grows, we sharpen attention within it to emphasize relevant entries while separately controlling its total weight relative to the local window. Across six target-drafter pairs and diverse benchmarks of up to 256K tokens, FOLD predominantly delivers the highest speedup, with the best case more than doubling the speedup over autoregressive decoding, from 2.08$\times$ to 4.22$\times$.
authors: Shuxuan Li, Jialiang Kang, Yanghao Zhou, Ziye Zhu, Xiao Yang
bullets: Addresses drafter degradation on long inputs without costly long-context training.
Preserves exact positions for recent tokens while assigning distant entries a shared far-memory position.
Sharpens attention over distant memory and controls its total influence to reduce attention dilution.
Evaluated across six target–drafter pairs and benchmarks up to 256K tokens.
Predominantly achieved the highest speedups; the best case improved from 2.08× to 4.22× over autoregressive decoding.

The outputs are merged by their masses.

papers.abstract: With the rapid development of vision-language models (VLMs), Web-GUI agents have achieved promising performance in interacting with real-world interfaces through screenshot-based grounding. However, high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn histories introduce excessive visual tokens, causing substantial inference overhead. Existing token pruning methods, mainly designed for natural images, often select tokens independently based on importance scores, which can fragment the local visual structures required for recognizing small GUI elements such as buttons, icons, and hyperlinks. In this work, we propose STP-GUI (Spatially-aware Token Pruning for GUI agents), a query-guided token pruning framework that preserves fine-grained instruction-conditioned token scoring while performing spatially coherent window-level selection under aggressive token reduction. A lightweight selector is optimized through policy learning while the VLM backbone remains frozen. Experiments on Online-Mind2Web show that \papername achieves a favorable efficiency-performance tradeoff under low token budgets. At 21% token retention, it preserves 77.7% of full-token performance while reducing inference latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%. Results on Android in the Wild further suggest that the method transfers to mobile GUI environments.
authors: Shuo Wang, Sifan Zhou, Xiaobo Wang, Tianyu Fu, Chenxu Zhao, Anyang Su, Hanning Wang, Ping Jiang, Minghui Wu
bullets: Addresses inference overhead from high-resolution screenshots and multi-turn visual histories.
Uses query-guided token scoring with spatial window-level selection to avoid fragmenting small GUI elements.
Trains a lightweight selector with policy learning while keeping the VLM backbone frozen.
On Online-Mind2Web, retaining 21% of tokens preserves 77.7% of full-token performance, reducing latency by 31% and FLOPs by 57%.
Results on Android in the Wild suggest transfer to mobile GUI environments.

papers.abstract: Agents for mixed-degradation image restoration typically learn what a tool does to an image only after running it: failed calls waste computation and harmful outputs go unnoticed until too late. We propose PreActIR, an agentic restoration framework that predicts tool consequences before execution. For each candidate tool, a tool-conditioned world model forecasts changes in residual degradation, image quality, and fidelity, together with the risk of harm and the uncertainty of the prediction. The agent executes the top-ranked candidate, and an independent verifier commits or rolls back its output before the agent replans from the observed state. PreActIR also audits whether performance is limited by the selector or by the candidate space, and studies targeted tool adaptation as a controlled way to expand that space. In a controlled evaluation that fixes the candidate pool, verifier, and budget and employs reference-annotated degradation states, PreActIR uses 42.5% fewer real tool calls and 63.4% fewer rejected calls than reactive, execute-then-evaluate trial and error, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB.
authors: Xu Zhang, Jun Wan, Lefei Zhang, Liangpei Zhang
bullets: Addresses inefficient mixed-degradation restoration agents that discover tool behavior only after acting.
Uses a tool-conditioned world model to predict degradation changes, quality, fidelity, harm risk, and uncertainty.
Ranks candidate tools, then uses an independent verifier to commit or roll back results before replanning.
Audits whether limits come from tool selection or the candidate space and studies targeted tool adaptation.
In controlled evaluation, reduces real tool calls by 42.5% and rejected calls by 63.4%, while improving Y-PSNR by 0.92 dB versus reactive trial and error.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of PreActIR. The world model predicts action consequences before execution, while the predict–act–verify controller executes and verifies the selected action with commit or rollback. papers.abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models activate only a few experts per token, yet all expert weights must be stored. Mixed-precision quantization reduces this storage cost by assigning higher bit-widths to sensitive experts and lower bit-widths to resilient ones, but expert rankings alone do not determine how strongly to weight their errors. To address this gap, we propose NatScale, a contrast-calibrated allocation framework for mixed-precision MoE quantization. It uses a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based expert weights to an information-theoretic contrast target while preserving rankings. We jointly evaluate each expert's gate, up and down configurations to estimate its output error. We then combine these errors and calibrated weights with an existing prior based on weight spectra, variance and precision decay to select configurations under a storage budget. Across three models, NatScale achieves the lowest native-to-quantized KL divergence and the highest top-token agreement in all nine settings against five allocation baselines. It also yields the lowest perplexity in seven settings. These findings highlight the importance of objective-aware precision allocation.
authors: Renjie Xie, Juncheng Yang, Aoting Hu, Yan Liang, Mingxi Zhang, Zheheng Hong, Wei Xu, Yanzhi Chen
bullets: MoE models require storing all expert weights, making quantization important despite sparse activation.
Expert sensitivity rankings do not indicate how strongly each expert’s errors should affect precision allocation.
NatScale applies a model-specific power transformation to calibrate gradient-based weights while preserving rankings.
It jointly evaluates experts’ gate, up, and down configurations, combining output errors with calibrated weights and prior statistics.
Across three models and nine settings, it achieved the lowest KL divergence and highest top-token agreement in every setting, plus the lowest perplexity in seven.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of NatScale. (a) Contrast Calibration: Maps gradient scores gi via a power transformation wi = gβτ i , where the exponent βτ is calibrated using a symmetric KL divergence target τ to control expert storage competition. (b) Joint Error Estimation: Evaluates quantization distortion by jointly quantizing gate, up, and down projections over replay inputs while incorporating structural priors. (c) Budgeted Allocation: Synthesizes calibrated weights, structural priors, and joint errors into expert costs, solving the global storage allocation by linear-programming (LP) relaxation and feasible rounding under a storage budget B.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models have made significant progress in referring expression comprehension (REC), yet most REC benchmarks still focus on final-target localization. Complex queries often involve intermediate visual references with different dependencies on prior grounding, but final-only evaluation leaves this process unexamined. To address this gap, we formulate trajectory-level REC, in which models receive an ordered sequence of grounding steps constructed from a single complex query and localize the target regions associated with each step. We instantiate this setting in ReferFlow-Bench, which characterizes structured region transitions through four trajectory types, namely Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture. Experiments show that current models struggle to consistently ground intermediate visual references across successive steps. We further propose ReferFlow, which decouples interleaved text-latent trajectory generation from coordinate decoding. Specifically, Stateful Region Latent Reasoning represents each target region as an object-indexed state composed of continuous latents, with explicit visual and spatial supervision to preserve region information for subsequent grounding. Trajectory-Aware Parallel Decoding then recovers all coordinate blocks in parallel through four geometry-constrained refinement rounds, with each block conditioned on its corresponding trajectory prefix, thereby reducing within-box sequential dependencies and eliminating cross-box autoregression. We further apply Grounding-Aware GRPO to promote consistent grounding across steps and learn adaptive trajectory generation from complex REC queries. ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.
authors: Tianyi Gao, Han Fang, Xin Wei, Yaoyao Zhong, Zhaoyan Pan, Weijie Zhu, Hongbo Sun, Zhiyu Lin, Kaicheng Yang, Jinglin Xu, Ye Yuan, Hao Li, Hao Sun, Jingmin Xin
bullets: Introduces trajectory-level REC, evaluating ordered grounding steps rather than only the final target.
Presents ReferFlow-Bench with four region-transition types: Refinement, Shift, Reset, and Mixture.
Uses stateful region latent reasoning to preserve visual and spatial information across grounding steps.
Employs trajectory-aware parallel coordinate decoding with geometry-constrained refinement to reduce sequential dependencies.
Grounding-Aware GRPO encourages consistent multi-step grounding; ReferFlow achieves leading performance on general REC benchmarks and ReferFlow-Bench.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are today used largely for pretraining vision-language-action models, with little ability to use the same data for target-embodiment or task-oriented training, which scalable deployment of robots in industrial and general environments depends on. A human demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device such as a mobile phone can serve as post-training data for a robot whose body differs in structure and capability from the human who recorded it. This is made possible not by retargeting the hand's motion but the object's. A capture yields a body-free record: the object's pose over time, its contact intervals, and a reconstructed 3D object with provenance. Any robot, given as a URDF and a short descriptor, is solved against that record and scored in simulation against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth: the human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer, measured per robot. Each (robot, episode) pair gets one outcome: pass, failure with a named mode, or refusal, with its reason, before any motion. The method runs as a working system over a growing collection; the set analysed here is a sample of it: 42 captures solved on 8 robots, 157 pairs, of which 31.2% pass, 52.2% fail, 14.0% are refused and 2.5% are unauditable (kinematic feasibility, +/-50 mm / +/-15 deg, in simulation). Refusals held up: every pair the checks refuse on stored evidence yet ran anyway failed (13 of 13; 5 on a body whose public model welds its hand). A description file could not be shown to screen a robot: its outcomes were barely more predictable than guessing. No policy has yet been trained on the record. The record decides what a robot may post-train on; whether the policy then works on the real robot is the simulation-to-robot question, answered downstream.
authors: Nagasrikanth Kallakuri
bullets: Phone-recorded demonstrations capture object poses, contact intervals, and reconstructed 3D objects without tying data to a human body.
Each robot, specified by a URDF and brief descriptor, is evaluated in simulation against the demonstrated object motion before any policy execution.
For 157 robot–episode pairs across 42 captures and 8 robots, 31.2% passed, 52.2% failed, 14.0% were refused, and 2.5% were unauditable.
Refusal checks were reliable: all 13 pairs that ran despite being refused failed.
The study assesses data eligibility for robot post-training; it does not yet train policies or establish real-robot performance.

papers.abstract: We study the finite-sample convergence of Q-learning algorithms for the average-reward formulation of Reinforcement Learning (RL) with options. While options allow temporarily extended and hierarchical actions, the average-reward formulation incorporates continual tasks beyond discounted and episodic RL. We establish the first $\tilde{O}(1/\text{iterations})$ convergence guarantees, in the mean-square sense, for average-reward option Q-learning algorithms in both the inter- and intra-option settings. First, we prove that both inter- and intra-option Bellman operators satisfy multi-step span contractions under unichain assumptions. Then, we propose synchronous estimators of these multi-step option Bellman operators leading to two variants of option Q-learning. Finally, we extend the stochastic approximation framework to prove convergence rates of these two algorithms under the minimal assumptions used in the literature.
authors: Kintan Saha, Ahana Deb, Anders Jonsson, Debabrota Basu
bullets: Addresses continual-task RL with average rewards and temporally extended, hierarchical actions.
Shows that both inter- and intra-option Bellman operators satisfy multi-step span contractions under unichain assumptions.
Introduces synchronous estimators of these operators, yielding two option Q-learning variants.
Proves the first \tilde{O}(1/iterations) mean-square convergence rates for these algorithms.
The guarantees rely on minimal assumptions commonly used in prior work.

papers.tldr: This work provides finite-sample, mean-square convergence guarantees for average-reward Q-learning with options in both inter- and intra-option settings.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction builds 3D scenes directly from input images for novel view rendering, but learning Gaussian attributes from predicted geometry for high-quality rendering under large viewpoint changes remains challenging. We analyze limitations in Gaussian attribute learning and introduce InfiniSplat v2, which improves rendering quality through architectural and training changes. Our method decouples geometry and attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch, aligns predicted Gaussians using ground-truth camera poses during training, and adopts large-angle target view supervision. Across six datasets, the feed-forward outputs of the same trained model achieve state-of-the-art mean LPIPS and DISTS among the evaluated methods in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings. In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS decrease by 25.8% and 32.9%, respectively, compared with the strongest evaluated baselines. We further find that opacity learned with only image reconstruction supervision suppresses geometrically inconsistent points. Project page: https://zju3dv.github.io/InfiniSplat2/
authors: Yongzhen Hu, Hao Yu, Jiawei Wang, Xianming Zeng, Jianyun Xu, Xingliang Liu, Ruizhen Hu, Xiaowei Zhou, Hujun Bao, Sida Peng
bullets: Targets high-quality novel-view rendering from input images, especially under large viewpoint changes.
Decouples geometry and Gaussian-attribute prediction with a frozen geometry branch.
Uses ground-truth camera poses for Gaussian alignment during training and large-angle target-view supervision.
Achieves the best mean LPIPS and DISTS among evaluated methods across six datasets in both pose-conditioned and pose-free settings.
In the pose-conditioned setting, mean LPIPS and DISTS improve by 25.8% and 32.9% versus the strongest evaluated baselines; scope is feed-forward reconstruction under the tested settings.

papers.abstract: The success of transformers is attributed to several factors, including their capacity to express formal languages over variable-length inputs, and ability of the attention mechanism to focus on relevant input features. However, there is limited understanding of the training dynamics of shallow transformers, specifically how to decouple the learning of the attention and the output (feedforward) layer. A natural extension of the theory of one-step gradient feature learning in feedforward networks suggests that one could first learn the attention weights with a single gradient step, and then train the output layer. We show that this fails for a shallow transformer trained to recognize a star-free language from unbounded-length input. We prove that the transformer can be trained to recognize the language with a three-phase gradient descent: the output layer is updated first, followed by an attention update, and the output layer is fine-tuned in the third phase. In contrast, the language cannot be learned by training only the attention or output layer, or by a single attention-layer update followed by finetuning the output layer. We empirically show that ``attention learning lagging output layer learning" is beneficial in other language recognition, regression, and in-context learning tasks as well.
authors: Yaomengxi Han, Debarghya Ghoshdastidar
bullets: Studies how attention and output-layer learning interact in shallow transformers.
Shows that a one-step attention update followed by output training fails on a star-free language.
Proves a three-phase schedule—output update, attention update, output fine-tuning—can learn the language.
Establishes that training only attention or only the output layer is insufficient for this task.
Empirical results suggest delayed attention learning also helps language recognition, regression, and in-context learning.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied robot learning requires large and diverse manipulation datasets, but collecting real-world demonstrations remains expensive in human effort and robot time. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, yet converting a real workspace into a robot-learning-ready environment still requires substantial manual effort for object extraction, asset processing, coordinate calibration, and trajectory specification. We present AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to real framework that converts scanned real-world workspaces into reusable embodied simulation assets and scalable manipulation data. Given multi-view observations, robot states, and open-vocabulary semantic queries, AutoRSR reconstructs the workspace, extracts individual object assets, and automatically registers the reconstructed scene to the robot base frame at metric scale. Starting from a small number of reference motions, AutoRSR then generates executable manipulation trajectories and scales them through trajectory interpolation and domain randomization. After workspace scanning and semantic queries, the remaining pipeline requires no manual object annotation, scene-to-robot calibration, or robot teleoperation. Across three real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained on 1K automatically generated episodes per task achieve 73.3--86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to pi 0.5 trained from 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while reducing the human time required for data generation by an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that real-world observations can be converted into metrically aligned, executable, and scalable simulation data with substantially reduced human effort.

The reported scope covers three real-world manipulation tasks and depends on workspace scans, semantic queries, and reference motions.

papers.abstract: Document understanding systems are typically evaluated as separate components via layout analysis, optical text recognition, reading-order prediction, and image captioning. This separation leaves scientific figures, captions, and visual semantics weakly connected, and fails to measure whether a model can produce a single page-level parse that is both structurally faithful and semantically accessible. We introduce Read-Parse-Describe, a unified dataset for document parsing with visual element description generation. Given a page image, models are required to output an ordered list of layout elements containing bounding boxes, semantic labels, reading-order indices, recognized textual content, and alternative text descriptions for visual elements. The benchmark is built from 2,402 documents, comprising 18,163 continuous pages, 125,218 layout elements, and 11,338 visual instances. Besides, we further propose a plug-and-play space-awareness enhancer that reuses multi-layer visual features and injects grid-aware spatial guidance into vision-language tokens for layout-aware generation. Experiments across end-to-end VLMs and pipeline parsers show that existing systems still struggle to jointly recover reading order and visual semantics, while our enhanced model achieves strong joint performance. These results highlight the need to move beyond isolated document parsing modules toward unified models that jointly read, parse, and describe complex documents. The new dataset and code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yufanchen96/RPD
authors: Yuheng Chen, Yufan Chen, Zhuojun Cai, Ruiping Liu, Junwei Zheng, Jiale Wei, Di Wen, Weijia Fan, Kunyu Peng, Jiaming Zhang, Rainer Stiefelhagen

papers.abstract: A ReAct-style agent accumulates observations, intermediate results, and failed attempts in a single context. As this context grows, stale and off-path information consumes its limited capacity and obscures relevant evidence, making focused reasoning increasingly difficult. We introduce TreeFlex, a framework in which the agent's own policy decides where to search. The agent records each intermediate state, with a short summary, as a node in a search tree maintained by the harness. The policy is a single language model that acts in two roles. In the Reflection role, it has a global view of the tree through these summaries and picks a node to resume, together with an instruction. In the Execution role, the harness restores the path that led to that node, and the model carries out the instruction with the usual task tools until it saves a new node or proposes a solution, which Reflection then approves or sends back to another node. Through these choices, the policy decides whether to deepen the current line, branch from or revisit an earlier state, verify a proposal, or stop, without a fixed traversal order or a score for each node. We train navigation, task actions, checkpointing, and proposal review jointly with a tree-aware adaptation of GRPO, using task-level outcome rewards augmented by process rewards. After small-scale RL of a 4B model, with the same active-context limit for all methods, TreeFlex reaches 48.8% accuracy on a challenging deep-research benchmark, versus 41.5% for flat ReAct and 42.8% for FoldAgent, and its Pass@8 is about ten points higher than either. On SWE-bench Verified, with all three systems trained with RL from the same 9B model, TreeFlex resolves 54.9% of tasks, versus 43.3% for FoldAgent and 45.2% for its step-wise variant.

With matched active-context limits, achieves 48.8% on a deep-research benchmark and 54.9% on SWE-bench Verified, outperforming the compared baselines reported in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Controlling an agent in an environment solely perceived through onboard vision is challenging: perception yields noisy, variable-length, and partially occluded context, while onboard compute is shared between perception and control, limiting the planning horizon executable in real time. We propose VIGOR-MPC, a modular student-teacher framework, agnostic to the perception pipeline, which addresses reference tracking across navigation tasks by distilling a privileged, field-of-view-aware long-horizon MPC into a computationally lightweight short-horizon MPC whose cost parameters are determined online from vision. The teacher operates in simulation with full state knowledge and a multi-trajectory formulation that guarantees the agent can stay within its field of view. The student observes only the noisy, occluded context produced by a perception module and learns, via a multi-level recurrent mapping, to infer cost parameters that aim to recover the teacher's behavior despite missing information. We evaluate VIGOR-MPC on vision-based autonomous racing in simulation and on hardware. Using only onboard perception of the track, VIGOR-MPC generalizes to tracks unseen during training and approaches the lap times of the privileged long-horizon teacher while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow matching are now dominant frameworks for generative modeling in continuous domains, but they typically require multiple network evaluations at inference. This has motivated extensive research on one-step generative modeling primarily built on diffusion and flow, though existing approaches often rely on complex training machinery. In this work, we introduce Priming Models, a simple two-stage framework for training one-step generators. Motivated by the difficulty of distributional training from scratch, Priming Models are first trained on a reconstruction objective, e.g., pixel-space denoising at a fixed noise level, before undergoing feature-space distributional post-training. Our central scientific finding is that this simple reconstruction stage is already enough to entirely alleviate the difficulty of distributional training. Empirically, across class-conditional image generation, text-to-image generation, and world modeling, Priming Models significantly advance the Pareto frontier of training compute vs. generation quality. On ImageNet at $256 \times 256$ resolution, we achieve a state-of-the-art FID of $1.19$ among one-step generators using approximately one-tenth the training compute of prior methods with comparable FID. We open-source our codebase at https://github.com/JaeyeonKim01/priming.

bullets: One-step generators avoid costly multi-step inference but are difficult to train directly with distributional objectives.

papers.abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

Uses TacClaw, a tactile-enabled handheld interface that synchronously records vision, fingertip touch, and end-effector trajectories without a target robot.
Aggregates over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames across more than 1,000 task types and diverse real-world environments.
Provides trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and annotations for contact segmentation, subtasks, and spatial grounding.
Demonstrates cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints. We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate. Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions. Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.
authors: Motasem Alfarra, Pietro Mazzaglia, Markus Peschl, Daniel Dijkman, Christos Louizos

A score-based memory prioritizes hard, low-value observations and uses importance sampling under limited compute.
Improves performance across simulated robots and shifts, with gains up to 80%, and transfers to a physical Go2 with added payload.

papers.abstract: Orthogonal transforms have emerged as an effective tool for low-bit quantization of large language models (LLMs), as they reshape activation distributions without changing the underlying model function. Existing approaches typically rely either on fixed data-agnostic transforms, such as Hadamard rotations, or on calibration-time optimization of learned rotations. We study rotation selection from first principles and show that maximizing covariance leads to spectral alignment and provides a principled criterion for constructing quantization-friendly orthogonal transforms. Based on this insight, we propose SpectrumQuant, a closed-form rotation method that estimates activation covariance from calibration data and uses it to construct a covariance-aware orthogonal transform for post-training quantization. Our formulation characterizes quantization-friendly rotations as compositions of alignment and mixing components, while recovering Hadamard matrices as a special case. Interestingly, a class of butterfly matrices belongs to this category. In the realm of LLM quantization, SpectrumQuant bridges the gap between data-agnostic structured rotations and learned rotations, providing an effective and efficient data-aware alternative for post-training quantization. Experiments on Llama and Mistral models show that SpectrumQuant is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation strategies while requiring less than one-third of the GPU memory and significantly less time than learned rotations approaches like SpinQuant and DartQuant.
authors: Dwaipayan Haldar, Indranil Patra, Azhar Yousuf, Chandra Sekhar Seelamantula
bullets: Identifies covariance maximization and spectral alignment as principles for selecting effective orthogonal transforms.

On Llama and Mistral, is competitive with state-of-the-art rotation methods while using less than one-third the GPU memory and substantially less time than SpinQuant and DartQuant.
Targets efficient, data-aware post-training quantization rather than fully data-agnostic or learned rotation strategies.

papers.abstract: An agent can improve its behavior within an unresolved problem by changing how it acts and which experience it retains. We propose MMLA-RSI, a recursive self-improvement scheme with two implementations in Memory-Mediated Learning Architecture: Reasoning-Time Training (RTT) changes the policy state $\Phi$, while Reasoning-Time Memory Adaptation (RTMA) changes authoritative memory $M$. Each route also makes its adaptation method an object of improvement. A current numerical updater trains the policy proposing its successor; a current memory manager chooses the records available to the process proposing its successor. An independently admitted successor takes over the same role in the next generation. We give bounded executable rule languages, shared task/proposal interfaces, and one algorithm for either route or their composition. The RTT instance changes scalar schedules in a clipped-momentum update. The RTMA instance chooses NULL or a complete-row write with possible eviction. A fixed interpreter, trusted committer, and independent evaluator bound what can change. State versions, read closures, and conditional properties describe causal execution, accepted transitions, and finite work. Existing numerical-component studies motivate the construction. In four-candidate program selection, retaining LARC feedback updates reduces expected error by 24.65 and 36.65 percentage points for two trained initializations. In chronological continuous-integration replay, feedback binding is positive while retention increases loss. Completed SQL studies improve substantially over an unadapted substrate but do not establish the required additional online benefit. These results characterize their declared components. The two recursive routes and their joint realization are specified here; their beneficial recursive chains and discovery efficiency remain to be evaluated.
authors: Junyi Zou, Avrova Donz
bullets: RTT adapts the policy state, while RTMA adapts authoritative memory and its retention decisions.
Each route recursively improves the mechanism that proposes the next policy or memory-manager successor.
A shared framework uses bounded rule languages, fixed interpreters, trusted commits, independent evaluation, versioned state, and causal execution controls.
Component studies show mixed outcomes: feedback retention helps in program selection, while retention increases loss in continuous-integration replay; SQL studies improve over an unadapted substrate.
The paper does not yet establish the benefit or discovery efficiency of complete recursive chains or their combined realization.

papers.abstract: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) holds that increasingly capable models converge toward a common representation. However, recent studies have shown different views on aligning representations via their neighborhoods, spanning trees, and distances. We show that these views can differ because the alignment criteria behind them sit at different points of one lattice, and we formalize this explanation as the Lattice Representation Hypothesis (LRH). Under the LRH, the convergence claimed by the PRH is agreement at the top of the lattice, whereas its evidence comes from neighbor overlap, a criterion near the bottom. The Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis (ARH) restricts convergence to local neighborhoods because calibration keeps the growth of neighbor overlap with model size but largely removes that of centered kernel alignment. We show that this removal can come from calibrating a maximum over layers, so global convergence remains open. Back into Plato's Cave (BPC) infers coarse shared structure from the collapse of neighbor overlap on larger evaluation sets, whereas we trace it at least partly to a fixed number of neighbors covering shorter distances. We show that the spanning-tree overlap used by Structure over Geometry (SOG) mostly repeats one-nearest-neighbor overlap. The LRH also extends to independently trained models, whose training procedure and objective decide the criteria met reliably across runs. We prove this claim for the training procedure in a linear autoencoder and for the objective in a finite contrastive Gibbs model. Experiments on dozens of pretrained vision and language models and thousands of runs of both theoretical models support these conclusions. We hope this work paves the way toward a general theory of representation hypotheses, with a framework to analyze them and compare their evidence. Project page: https://eethanshi.github.io/LRH
authors: Dai Shi, Andi Han, Xiaoyu Li, Luke Thompson, Jos\'e Miguel Hern\'andez-Lobato
bullets: Different alignment criteria—neighbor overlap, distances, centered kernel alignment, and spanning-tree overlap—occupy different levels of a representation-criteria lattice.
The Lattice Representation Hypothesis (LRH) reframes the Platonic Representation Hypothesis as convergence at the lattice’s strongest criterion, while existing evidence often tests weaker criteria.
The Aristotelian Representation Hypothesis (ARH) limits reliable convergence to local neighborhoods; calibration can preserve neighbor overlap while removing centered-kernel alignment.

Some reported effects are reinterpreted: large-set neighbor-overlap collapse can reflect fixed-neighbor, shorter-distance coverage, and spanning-tree overlap largely duplicates one-nearest-neighbor overlap.
Experiments across pretrained vision/language models and theoretical linear-autoencoder and contrastive-Gibbs settings support the framework; global convergence remains unresolved.

papers.abstract: Nanosatellites (e.g., CubeSats) have the potential to carry out useful science and exploration activities for outer solar system exploration, but their small size leads to tradeoffs between attitude control and science capabilities. Magnetorquers offer a unique compromise as compact actuators that enable three-axis attitude control, but suffer from a loss of control authority and require full knowledge of the planetary magnetic field. In this work, we present a learning-based adaptive model predictive control (MPC) algorithm that plans rotational trajectories for the satellite while accounting for this loss of control authority. Key to our approach is the inclusion of a learned magnetic field model that is trained in simulation using low-fidelity magnetic field data. Using measurements collected online, our proposed algorithm adapts this learned magnetic field model using a simple last-layer update scheme, allowing the MPC controller to quickly adapt to the true planetary magnetic field model and more effectively plan attitude trajectories. We demonstrate the results of our proposed approach for two use cases, (1) Earth-orbit and (2) Uranus-orbit, and show that our learning-based adaptive MPC algorithm improves controller success for these system simulations by 5% and 61%, respectively.
authors: Patrick Schwartz, Abhishek Cauligi
bullets: Magnetorquers enable compact three-axis control but have limited authority and depend on accurate planetary magnetic-field knowledge.

Evaluation is limited to Earth- and Uranus-orbit system simulations.

papers.abstract: Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift. We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures. The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty. Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy-filter mismatch during training. In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.
authors: Siwei Ju, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Targets safety failures that develop over multiple steps rather than occurring instantaneously.
Learns an ensemble safety critic using horizon labels, temporal-consistency constraints, and smoothness regularization.
Uses conservative uncertainty aggregation and a closed-form differentiable CBF-style filter to minimally adjust actions.
Integrates the shield with PPO through an anticipation loss to reduce policy–filter mismatch.
In simulated quadruped locomotion, improves robustness and reduces catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the training pipeline. Rollouts are collected in simulation under domain randomization and disturbances, and states are labeled by horizon-H safety to populate separate safe/unsafe buffers (with discounted weighting for delayed violations). A predictive safety critic is trained with a composite objective (labeling, temporal consistency, and smoothness), and an ensemble is aggregated via CVaR to obtain a conservative safety estimate and uncertainty σt. At each step, a differentiable closed-form safety layer projects the raw policy action to a minimally modified safe action, which is used both during PPO training (with an anticipation loss to reduce interventions) and at deployment for safety-shielded control.

Fig. 2: Top row: success rate; bottom row: average return. Columns correspond to four evaluation suites (action-noise and external-perturbation, each on flat terrain and heightfield terrain). The x-axis denotes the perturbation/noise sampling probability.

The plot compares success rate (top row) and average return (bottom row) across different levels of action noise and external perturbations. Both methods show similar robustness under action noise, but our method outperforms SafeFall when faced with perturbations, demonstrating its superior generalizability.

Fig. 5: Comparison of state-only and state-action safety critics. The state-action safety critic demonstrates better generalizability and robustness, particularly under perturbations and domain shifts. The results are shown for success rate (top) and average return (bottom) across different perturbation settings. The result is aggregated over 5 seeds, and the shaded area shows the standard error. The state-action model outperforms the state-only model under external perturbation and domain shift.

Under heightfield terrain with enlarged perturbations, the nominal estimate can diverge substantially from the next-state reference (e.g., around t ≈ 175–190), leading to spurious risk alarms and unnecessary interventions.

papers.abstract: Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present GLoD-LVSM, a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, GLoD-LVSM learns a continuous field that initializes a flexible number of anchors to match the desired budget. A condenser then aggregates scene information into these anchors, with both the field and condenser trained end-to-end. Second, the condenser infers reference-token and anchor geometry to guide compression through geometry-grounded attention, improving rendering quality and enabling frustum culling during decoding. Compared with existing LVSM scene-compression baselines, GLoD-LVSM achieves the best trade-off between rendering quality and scene token count. Compared with the uncompressed base model, GLoD-LVSM reduces the scene-token count by 33.4% and accelerates rendering by $1.23\times$ with no quality loss. Under a relaxed quality-loss budget, the reduction increases to 85.5%, with $3.00\times$ rendering speedup. Further analysis reveals that view-synthesis supervision yields emergent scene depth and self-organized anchors that align with surfaces and adapt their density to local texture complexity. Beyond rendering, we further show that our scene representation also supports scene-semantic understanding, highlighting its potential for broader downstream tasks.
authors: Weikai Lin, Nicholas Milef, Carl S Marshall, Grant Kaijuin Yang, Todd Keeler, Yuhao Zhu
bullets: Addresses token redundancy that increases LVSM storage and rendering costs.
Learns a continuous field to initialize flexible numbers of scene anchors for different token budgets.
Uses an end-to-end condenser with geometry-grounded attention to guide compression and enable frustum culling during decoding.
Reduces scene tokens by 33.4% with no quality loss and provides a 1.23× rendering speedup; under relaxed quality loss, reductions reach 85.5% with 3.00× speedup.
Learned anchors self-organize along surfaces and adapt density to local texture complexity; the representation also supports scene-semantic understanding.

papers.abstract: Multilingual models share capacity across languages, so adding languages can hurt performance on existing ones. Mixture-of-experts models expand this capacity with little additional per-token computation. Given this extra capacity, does adding experts reduce what each additional language costs? To answer this question, we propose a repetition-aware joint scaling law relating number of active parameters, training tokens per language, number of experts, and language coverage. Fitted on 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations, our law reduces prediction error on held-out configurations by 28% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. At matched number of active parameters and training tokens per language, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of expanding from 12 to 200 languages by 83% compared with a dense model. Our law further shows that broader language coverage favors more experts across a wider range of compute budgets, guiding capacity allocation as multilingual models scale.
authors: Joel Dag, Nikit Srivastava, Hamada M. Zahera, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo
bullets: Adding languages can degrade existing-language performance because model capacity is shared.
The study proposes a joint scaling law linking active parameters, per-language training tokens, expert count, and language coverage.

With matched active parameters and per-language tokens, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of scaling from 12 to 200 languages by 83% versus a dense model.
Broader language coverage favors using more experts across a wider range of compute budgets.

papers.abstract: Offline navigation demonstrations are multimodal, because one observation often allows several valid actions, such as passing an obstacle on either side. Behavior cloning averages these actions, potentially leading to unsafe routes. Multimodal policies must discover the alternatives from the data, but similar states can lead to different routes whose current actions overlap. In navigation, the alternatives have a geometric cause and can be computed from one observation. We propose a hierarchical neural-network policy that computes candidate modes from local geometry and learns from demonstrations which mode to follow and how. A high-level policy selects a mode using the goal and its previous choice among a set of candidate modes, and a low-level policy turns it into an action. In simulation, the policy succeeds in over 95\% of seen and unseen test cases, compared with at most 43\% and 20\% for four offline learning baselines and 79\% and 67\% for a heuristic that uses the same modes without learning. The simulation-trained policy also transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.
authors: Chengyang Peng, Zhihao Zhang, Upama Pant, Yiming Wang, Keith A. Redmill, Ayonga Hereid
bullets: Addresses behavior cloning’s tendency to average distinct valid routes into unsafe actions.
Computes alternative navigation modes from local geometry rather than discovering them solely from data.

The simulation-trained policy transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.

papers.abstract: A multiplayer world model must predict how the independent actions of several players change a shared environment, including changes outside a player's current field of view. A point-of-view (POV) video captures such changes only after they enter its field of view, whereas panoramic video records the surroundings in every viewing direction and has served as an intermediate representation of the world state in recent world models. Learning this task therefore requires synchronized POV and panoramic videos of interacting players together with their actions, yet no existing dataset provides this combination in Minecraft, an established testbed in which players act independently in a shared, modifiable 3D world. We present PAWA, a dataset and framework for action-conditioned panoramic multiplayer world modeling. The dataset pairs each player's POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions. Its distributed pipeline decouples CPU gameplay capture from GPU rendering, scales beyond 64 simultaneous players, and re-renders each recorded session under new observation configurations without replaying the gameplay. On this dataset, we develop a dual-tower model that jointly predicts POV and panoramic video and couples the two streams through cross-attention that aligns tokens observing the same direction in a shared world frame. We further introduce a quadratic-phase player encoding that provides many more player codes than existing rotary codes at the same embedding dimension. Experiments show that PAWA outperforms state-of-the-art multiplayer world models in POV prediction quality while also producing high-fidelity panoramic predictions. The dataset and collection pipeline are open source to support further research on multiplayer world models.
authors: Siqi Yang, Yimu Wang, Ziqi Cai, Chengxuan Zhu, Shuchen Weng, Erwin Wu, Zhaofei Yu, Kaipeng Zhang, Boxin Shi
bullets: Addresses the lack of synchronized multi-player POV, panoramic video, and action data for shared-world modeling.
Pairs each player’s POV video with world-stabilized panoramic video and aligned actions; supports scalable capture and re-rendering under new observation configurations.
Uses a dual-tower predictor with cross-attention to align POV and panoramic tokens viewing the same world direction.
Introduces quadratic-phase player encodings to support more player identities at the same embedding dimension.
Outperforms prior multiplayer world models on POV prediction while generating high-fidelity panoramic predictions; the dataset and pipeline are open source.

papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) excel on graph-structured data but suffer catastrophic forgetting when classes arrive sequentially. In class-incremental graph learning, predictions are often dominated by recently learned classes, causing severe recency bias. Dynamic expansion can isolate knowledge across sessions, but many methods assume task-incremental settings and require task identities at test time to select branches or heads---information unavailable in class-incremental learning. Learnable routers offer an alternative, yet continual fine-tuning the router on new data can bias routing toward recent components. We propose MAEM, a replay-free, capacity-controlled dynamic mixture-of-experts framework for class-incremental graph learning. MAEM builds representations with Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and trains a dedicated expert for each new session, then freezes it to protect prior knowledge. For routing without task IDs or a shared trainable router, each expert uses a masked autoencoder (MAE); test nodes are assigned to the expert with the lowest reconstruction error, reducing routing-level recency bias. When the expert pool reaches a fixed capacity, MAEM merges the least-used experts via Git Re-Basin alignment and further distills them into a fused expert using topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions (DeepInversion-style), without storing or revisiting historical graph data. On four class-incremental graph benchmarks, MAEM mitigates recency bias, outperforms strong continual graph learning baselines, and keeps model capacity bounded under strict replay-free learning.
authors: Junlin Chen, Wenhao Wang, Junchao Xu, Qingsong Yao, Fei Xue, Li Sun, Xiao Wang, Ruijie Wang
bullets: Addresses class-incremental GNNs that forget earlier classes and overpredict recently learned ones.
Trains a separate SGC-based expert per session, then freezes it to preserve prior knowledge.
Routes test nodes without task IDs using each expert’s masked-autoencoder reconstruction error.
Bounds capacity by aligning and merging the least-used experts, then distilling them with topology-aware pseudo data synthesized from MAE distributions.
Experiments on four benchmarks show reduced recency bias, stronger performance than continual graph-learning baselines, and bounded capacity without replaying historical graphs.
