papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.
authors: Huailiang Ma, Yuxuan Li, Ziyi Zhao, Xinkai Wang, Mingyu Li, Xinyu Guo, Lifeng Zhu, Aiguo Song, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
bullets: Targets weak fine-grained object understanding in existing image-level VLA models, especially under layout, clutter, and background shifts.
Encodes observations into temporal object slots with separate representations for persistent identity and changing object state.
Routes VLM attention toward relevant object tokens using identity-guided modulation.
Trains an action-conditioned dynamics module to predict future object states, while avoiding future prediction at inference.
Improves generalization across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation with novel arrangements and backgrounds.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive generation underlies real-time, causal video synthesis and is the backbone of video world models. Today's dominant approach distills a bidirectional diffusion model into a causal few-step student, but existing pipelines make this conversion prohibitively expensive, requiring offline Probability Flow ODE} (PF-ODE) trajectories that cost tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of storage. We show it can be made dramatically more efficient. Pushing this efficiency to its extreme, we reduce trajectory supervision to a single sample, the strictest setting possible, and find that it causes severe quality collapse. We trace this to the teacher's trajectory geometry: the high-noise regime, governing semantic layout and motion, and the low-noise regime, governing fine texture exhibit fundamentally different curvature and optimization behavior, so a single monolithic student cannot jointly fit both, causing severe representation interference. Motivated by this, we propose Glance Forcing, a lightweight distillation framework that decouples the denoising trajectory into two complementary slow and fast experts, each guided by a tailored, stage-specific objective, while keeping the pretrained teacher entirely frozen. This decoupling further reveals a general mechanism underlying few-step distillation: PF-ODE distillation mainly straightens the few-step trajectory geometry, while the subsequent distribution-matching stage independently governs distributional quality. Using only one PF-ODE trajectory, Glance Forcing already surpasses the fully-trained state-of-the-art baseline, raising the VBench Total score from 84.04 to 84.22 while cutting trajectory-collection cost from thousands of GPU-hours to about one A100-GPU-hour, with markedly larger gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, and instruction-following, and consistent preference from human raters over strong baselines.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Junchao Yi, Hu Jian Guo, Linjie Li, Rui Zhao, Alex Jinpeng Wang
bullets: Existing causal distillation pipelines require tens of thousands of GPU-hours and terabytes of PF-ODE trajectory data.
The authors attribute single-sample quality collapse to different optimization geometry in high-noise semantic/motion and low-noise texture regimes.
Glance Forcing uses two frozen-teacher-guided slow and fast experts with stage-specific objectives to decouple these regimes.
With one PF-ODE trajectory, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.22 and reduces trajectory collection to about one A100-GPU-hour.
It also reports gains in dynamic degree, VisionReward, instruction following, and human preference over strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Building foundation models for MRI has emerged as a promising direction for advancing medical image analysis and improving accessibility of task specific models. Existing approaches primarily focus on effective pretraining strategies and evaluating their performance across diverse downstream tasks. While these methods show performance gains, limited attention has been given to understanding task alignment between pretraining and downstream objectives. Unlike language models, where the two stages are naturally aligned, such alignment is less evident in vision based applications. Motivated by this gap, we explore continual pretraining. Specifically, continually pretraining a pretrained ViT encoder using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) on a prostate segmentation task to enhance task alignment and downstream performance. We further perform layer-wise representational analysis using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) to assess representational shifts and their correlation with task outcomes. Our experiments show improved performance in 3 of 6 downstream tasks and comparable results in the others. Our Feature analysis reveals that, for segmentation tasks, continually pretrained encoder features exhibit greater similarity to those of the finetuned encoder than the original pretrained encoder, correlating with observed performance gains.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird's-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments. BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors. Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance. Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC. This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.

papers.abstract: Parallel drafters such as DFlash and DSpark reduce proposal latency, but early mismatches limit how much of each block can be accepted. Retaining alternatives introduces parent states and candidate choices that reference-conditioned training does not directly supervise. We introduce TreeSpark, a unified training and inference framework extending the semi-autoregressive DSpark architecture. It constructs parent-conditioned candidate trees from one backbone pass and replays their expansion, pruning, and budgeted packing during training. Survival negative log-likelihood weights retained edges by reference-derived path mass, while a capped coverage hinge promotes target-important alternatives near local selection boundaries. Both objectives reuse reference-chain target distributions without additional target forward passes. We evaluate greedy decoding with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B on nine general benchmarks and six writing domains. Across targets and suites, TreeSpark improves mean acceptance length over DSpark by 23.4% to 31.6% and mean single-request throughput by 15.1% to 25.0%. Batched Qwen3-4B throughput improves by 12.6% to 17.2%. At fixed attention capacity and inference policy, the proposed supervision further improves mean acceptance length by approximately 6.4% and mean system throughput by 4.2% to 5.0% on Qwen3-4B.

papers.abstract: Learning world models across diverse domains calls for a unified control space, yet ac- tion interfaces vary across domains and action annotations are often scarce. Latent ac- tions learned directly from videos offer a promising way to establish such a space without explicit action supervision. However, learning shared latent actions across domains re- mains challenging, as variations in appearance, embodiment, and dynamics can entangle domain-specific visual cues with transferable transition structure. To this end, we intro- duce OneLA, a simple framework that learns continuous latent actions through a shared orthogonal dictionary and a common predictive objective, without task-specific designs or cross-domain alignment losses during latent action pretraining. These latent actions pro- vide a shared conditioning interface for world models, with lightweight adapters mapping native control commands into the same space. Conditioned on latent actions and the cur- rent visual state, the world model predicts context-dependent transitions for controllable rollout. OneLA improves action readout across domains and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline. A joint-training comparison further shows a 20.5% improvement in Human Preference Score v3 (HPSv3) for real- scene generation. These results suggest a path toward general-purpose world models that learn from diverse videos and support flexible control through latent action space.

Improves action readout and reduces action cycle-transfer rotation error by 24.8% over the strongest evaluated baseline.
Joint training improves HPSv3 by 20.5% for real-scene generation.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
authors: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang, Kai Hu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses underspecified task instructions that do not clearly specify the next physical interaction.
Uses a vision-language reasoner to infer the next local motion from instructions and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict video and action chunks.
Builds temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
Introduces Execution-Grounded GRPO to train motion descriptions for appropriateness and execution success while keeping the WAM fixed.
Achieves 39.6% task success with default instructions and 31.6% with vague instructions in RoboLab real-to-sim evaluation.

After each sampling round, one of the highest-reward endpoints is randomly selected as the starting state for the next round.

papers.abstract: In various industries, smoke and fire are two of the most important threats in the workplace. One of the common methods for detecting smoke and fire is the use of infrared thermal and smoke sensors, which cannot be used in outdoor applications. Therefore, the use of vision-based methods seems necessary. The problem of smoke and fire detection is spatiotemporal and requires spatiotemporal solutions. This paper presents a method that uses spatial features along with temporal-based features to detect smoke and fire in the scene. It consists of three main parts; the task of each part is to reduce the error of the previous part so that the final model has a robust performance. This method also uses transformer modules to increase the accuracy of the model. The results of our model show the proper performance of the proposed approach in solving the problem of smoke and fire detection and can be used to increase workplace safety.

bullets: Addresses the limitations of infrared thermal and smoke sensors in outdoor environments.
Models smoke and fire detection as a spatiotemporal vision problem.

Incorporates transformer modules to improve detection accuracy.

papers.abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.
authors: Zhuobai Dong, Xiaobing Tu, Xiantao Zhang, Jinkui Ren, Yinggui Wang, Yue Ma, Linfeng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the high latency and non-causal processing of existing video object removal methods.
Transfers erasing capability from a text-to-video foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser.
Uses sliding-window causal attention, attention sinks, self-rollout, and KV-cache rolling to maintain fixed-context, constant-speed generation.
Reports sub-second latency and up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU.
Introduces the LongErase benchmark and supports interactive, infinite-length video erasing with strong real-world generalization.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are moving onto edge devices, but little is known about how much energy they draw on single-board computers with NPU or GPU accelerators, or where that energy goes. We measure total-system energy, latency, and thermal behavior of Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct and its text-only sibling on a Raspberry Pi 5 with a Hailo-10H NPU and on a Jetson Orin Nano Super, on both CPU and accelerator, and separate the fixed energy of each request from the energy that grows with output length. Because the accelerators use different quantization and serving software, we compare deployment stacks rather than silicon. Three findings stand out. First, NPU offloading makes the Pi a much more efficient VLM platform: it cuts energy per generated token by about two-thirds, leaves the host CPU largely free, and avoids the thermal throttling that the CPU backend reaches in sustained use. Second, an image adds both fixed and per-token energy, but at typical response lengths generating the answer costs far more than processing the image. Third, the Jetson GPU favors short responses through its lower fixed cost per request, whereas the Pi NPU favors longer ones through its lower cost per output token; their energy curves cross near 40 output tokens.
authors: Junlin Liao, Harshit Kondle, Di Liu, Zonghua Gu
bullets: Measures system energy, latency, and thermal behavior across Raspberry Pi 5 CPU/NPU and Jetson Orin Nano Super CPU/GPU deployments.
Separates fixed per-request energy from energy that scales with generated output length, while comparing deployment stacks rather than hardware alone.
Pi NPU offloading reduces energy per generated token by about two-thirds and prevents the thermal throttling seen with sustained CPU inference.
Image inputs increase both fixed and per-token energy, but answer generation typically dominates total energy at common response lengths.
Jetson GPU has lower fixed request cost; Pi NPU has lower per-token cost, with energy curves crossing near 40 output tokens.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.
authors: Kiyanoush Nazari, Luchen Li, Haoshu Fang, Nima Fazeli, Zhibin Li, Fumiya Iida, Thomas George Thuruthel
bullets: Reviews tactile representation learning, policy learning, foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and cross-domain generalization.
Organizes prior work by touch’s functional role throughout the learning and control pipeline.
Highlights challenges in learning transferable physical representations and linking semantic reasoning with contact-level control.
Examines scaling across objects, tasks, sensors, robot embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer.
Proposes future directions toward tactile foundation and world models for predicting, reasoning about, and adapting physical interactions.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Representative architectures for integrating tactile information into foundation models for robotic manipulation. The paradigms include (a) direct multimodal conditioning, where tactile tokens are fused with vision, language, and proprioception within a VLM/VLA backbone; (b) semantic alignment of tactile representations with vision and language prior to policy conditioning; (c) physical grounding of tactile features through force-aligned representations; (d) predictive architectures that use tactile world models to generate future visuo-tactile interaction states for action generation; and (e) tactile-augmented reasoning, where tactile observations and retrieved interaction memories condition a VLM/VLA for semantic understanding and decision making.

papers.abstract: Human mesh recovery (HMR) provides a geometric foundation for understanding human motion, but accurately reconstructing both body motion and fine hand articulation from videos remains challenging, especially in real-world scenes where occlusion and partial visibility are common. Video generation pretraining offers rich spatial and temporal priors for this task, but its focus on visual synthesis leaves a gap between these representations and explicit human geometry. We present DreamHMR, a general framework that adapts video generation priors for complete body-and-hand reconstruction. It follows a global-to-local strategy, first grounding video representations in human geometry and then refining body and hand detail with reliable local evidence. Global Body Representation Transfer trains the video backbone to predict complete human renderings, turning its native prediction task into a means of learning surface correspondence and posed geometry. Local Joint Feature Enhancement combines contextual estimates with reliable local evidence to recover fine body and hand detail, while limiting interference from occluders and background. Experiments on five datasets with four video backbones demonstrate strong reconstruction performance across backbone families. Under a unified evaluation protocol, our best model outperforms the best existing methods on all reported metrics of 3DPW, EMDB-1, and RICH, reducing body MPJPE by 4.2%, 4.7%, and 6.1%, respectively. In more challenging occlusion settings on held-out BEDLAM and EgoBody sequences, DreamHMR reduces overall body and hand MPJPE by 7.0% and 10.0%, respectively. Our code will be made publicly available.
authors: Zhengjie Xu, Ruihao Gong, Xianglong Liu
bullets: Addresses the gap between video-generation representations and explicit human geometry in human mesh recovery.
Uses a global-to-local design: first learns complete human geometry, then refines body and hand details from reliable local evidence.
Global Body Representation Transfer trains the video backbone to predict complete human renderings and learn surface correspondence.
Local Joint Feature Enhancement combines contextual predictions with local evidence while reducing interference from occluders and background.
Across five datasets and four video backbones, it reports improved body and hand reconstruction performance, especially under occlusion.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. HM3D-M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation-assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL. We further contribute two baselines. HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis. Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16--27% SR, while our baselines reach 38--41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes. Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team. Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/
authors: Hongyu Ding, Kanyu Xu, Mingjia Chen, Zixuan Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yifan Zhang, Yang Gao
bullets: Targets the previously uncombined setting of multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation in photorealistic indoor scenes.
Episodes involve K agents searching for an unordered set of M goals expressed as open-vocabulary categories, instance images, or descriptions.
Provides 1,000 validation episodes, 3,926 goals across 379 categories, 100K training samples, and team-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL metrics.
Introduces HiGA, a trained hierarchical goal assigner, and LaViRA-M3, a training-free VLM-agent team with shared mapping and progress analysis.
Adapted and zero-shot methods achieve 16–27% SR, while the proposed baselines reach 38–41%; LaViRA-M3 is also deployed on three heterogeneous robots.

papers.abstract: We present several advances on neural operators by viewing the action of operator layers as the minimizers of Bregman regularized optimization problems over Banach function spaces. The proposed framework allows interpreting the activation operators as Bregman proximity operators from dual to primal space. This novel viewpoint is general enough to recover classical neural operators as well as a new variant, coined Bregman neural operators, which includes the inverse activation operator and features the same expressivity of standard neural operators. Numerical experiments support the added benefits of the Bregman variant of Fourier neural operators for training deeper and more accurate models.
authors: Abdel-Rahim Mezidi, Jordan Patracone, Saverio Salzo, Amaury Habrard, Massimiliano Pontil, Remi Emonet, Marc Sebban
bullets: Recasts neural-operator layers as minimizers of Bregman-regularized problems on Banach function spaces.
Interprets activation operators as Bregman proximity operators mapping dual spaces to primal spaces.
Recovers classical neural operators and defines a new Bregman neural operator with an inverse activation operator.
The Bregman variant retains the expressivity of standard neural operators.
Experiments indicate improved training of deeper and more accurate Fourier neural operator models.

papers.abstract: Distilling pretrained video diffusion models into few-step autoregressive (AR) generators typically combines student initialization with distribution matching distillation (DMD). An intermediate AR teacher can provide causally compatible targets for ODE initialization. However, causally compatible targets alone do not ensure high-quality generation under a short sampling schedule. We analyze the posterior-mean predictions favored by direct latent regression and empirically find that causal ODE initialization alleviates blur but still leaves fine detail unresolved. To address this limitation, we propose Representation Forcing, which learns few-step causal initialization through representation-space supervision rather than intermediate-teacher trajectory regression. The student is trained with teacher forcing by comparing clean predictions and training targets through normalized features of a frozen video diffusion transformer. This phase reuses the synthetic videos generated by a bidirectional model for AR teacher training and replaces both teacher training and causal ODE distillation, without generating additional causal ODE trajectories. The subsequent asymmetric DMD procedure remains unchanged. Empirical results show that, at four sampling steps, RepForcing better preserves generation quality than intermediate-teacher-based initialization before DMD. After DMD, our four-step chunk-wise model improves VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 (+0.62 points) and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 (+59.25%) over the reported causal-ODE-based baseline.
authors: Siming Fu, Zheming Fu, Lianrui Mu, Haoyang Huang, Chaojie Gu, Ruizhe He
bullets: Causal ODE initialization reduces blur but can leave fine details unresolved under short sampling schedules.
RepForcing uses teacher forcing to match clean predictions and targets through normalized features from a frozen video diffusion transformer.
It reuses synthetic videos from bidirectional-model training and avoids additional causal ODE trajectory generation.
At four sampling steps, it better preserves quality before DMD than intermediate-teacher initialization.
After DMD, it raises VBench Total from 84.04 to 84.66 and VisionReward from 6.326 to 10.074 over the reported causal-ODE baseline.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Representation Forcing Initialization Pipeline. Training videos are encoded into clean latent blocks by a VAE encoder. The trainable causal DiT reconstructs clean blocks from noisy inputs, conditioned on preceding clean blocks under teacher forcing. The predicted and target video latents are passed separately through the same truncated, frozen Wan2.1-14B to obtain features f̂ and f . A token-wise cosine loss compares these features, with stop-gradient (sg) on the target branch. Gradients propagate through the frozen extractor to update the causal DiT. This initialization replaces intermediate AR teacher training and causal ODE distillation.

Table 1: Comparison with existing methods. Dynamic., Vision., and Instruct. denote Dynamic Degree, VisionReward, and Instruction Following. papers.selection_reason: Representation-space initialization for distilling video diffusion into few-step autoregressive generators.

papers.tldr: RepForcing improves few-step autoregressive video diffusion distillation by learning causal initialization in a pretrained representation space instead of regressing intermediate teacher trajectories.

papers.abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.
authors: Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Hanjun Wei, Qinghao Zhang, Zhixi Cai, Shiwen Ni
bullets: The method reads action choices from hidden states of a frozen vision-language generator processing the goal and screenshot.
Heads predict the action type, select numbered visual targets, or choose text options and WRITE slots.
A confidence cascade uses head decisions when confident and otherwise falls back to generator decoding from the same forward pass.
Across seven offline test sets, heads controlled 12–64% of steps with performance within 1.4 points above or 0.3 points below the generator under a strict threshold.
A looser threshold improved WebArena success and used less than half the generated tokens, but results varied across benchmarks.

Decision heads read a learned mix of five of its layers and return a distribution over action types, boxes and options (with a WRITE slot). When the confidence ct reaches τ the agent acts at once or, for WRITE, lets the generator write only the text; otherwise the generator decodes the whole action from the same KV cache.

papers.abstract: We investigate two aspects of multilingual pre-training with limited data, namely how language exposure is distributed across English, Dutch, and Chinese, and how that exposure is ordered during training. In particular, we compare balanced multilingual exposure to language-dominant exposure, where one language is exposed with more training data than the others. We also compare mixed training, where multilingual training data is used throughout training, with curriculum training, where monolingual exposure of the dominant language is followed by balanced multilingual exposure. Our results show that multilingual BabyLM performance varies with both the amount and order of language exposure. Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning across all 15 matched configurations, indicating that simultaneous multilingual exposure is more effective than staged exposure in our setting. Several language-dominant mixed training configurations achieve higher scores than the balanced configuration, suggesting that a balanced distribution is not necessarily the highest-performing configuration in our setting. Interestingly, the Dutch-primary configurations achieve the best overall performance.
authors: JiWoo Hwang, Lukas Edman, Alexander Fraser
bullets: The study examines English, Dutch, and Chinese under balanced versus language-dominant exposure.
It compares mixed multilingual training with a curriculum that starts monolingual and later becomes balanced multilingual.
Mixed training outperforms curriculum learning in all 15 matched configurations.
Some language-dominant mixtures outperform balanced exposure, with Dutch-primary configurations performing best overall.

Figure 1: Mixed and curriculum training for the Dutchprimary 60/20/20 configuration. Mixed training shuffles all 100M tokens in a single stage, whereas curriculum training first uses 40M Dutch tokens and then a balanced multilingual stage containing 20M tokens from each language. papers.title: Language Exposure Matters: Distribution and Order in Multilingual BabyLM Pre-training
papers.tldr: Multilingual BabyLM performance depends on both how much exposure each language receives and when that exposure occurs.

papers.abstract: Video scene graph generation (VidSGG) aims to capture objects and their evolving relationships in videos. This requires accounting for both the persistence of object identities and abrupt changes in relationships. Existing methods aggregate information across frames to exploit temporal context, but an emphasis on consistency can obscure these changes. As a result, a model may retain its previous prediction even after the underlying relation has changed. We refer to this failure mode as relational semantic inertia. To address this issue, we propose Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer (RTAformer), a one-stage framework that separately models entity persistence and relation changes. It injects calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries to guide predicate updates, while cross-frame instance alignment during training helps reduce cross-frame representational drift. Experiments on Action Genome show improvements in recall and mean recall over existing methods, with ablation studies supporting the contributions of the proposed components and comparisons using matched backbones showing larger gains on relation-transition frames than on non-transition frames.
authors: Jaeyeon Heo, Geuntaek Lim, Yukyung Choi
bullets: Addresses the failure of temporal consistency methods to update predictions when video relationships change.
Uses a one-stage Transformer that separately models entity persistence and relation transitions.
Guides predicate updates with calibrated differences between adjacent-frame relation queries.
Applies cross-frame instance alignment during training to reduce representational drift.
On Action Genome, improves recall and mean recall, with larger gains on relation-transition frames.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overall framework of RTAformer. (a) Frame-wise spatial triplet parsing produces instance-pair and relation queries for target and reference frames. (b) Disentangled Temporal Aggregation (DTA) refines the target queries with separate instance and relation streams, where TADI injects relation-transition cues. FFN heads produce the instance and relation predictions that form the output triplets. (c) Spatio-Semantic Instance Alignment (SSIA) aligns adjacent-frame instance-pair queries during training.

Fig. 5: Qualitative comparison around relation transition boundaries. The participating entities remain visible across adjacent frames, while predicates for ‘person–broom’ and ‘person–door’ change. RTAformer updates the changed predicates, e.g., ‘person– holding–broom’ and ‘person–not contacting–door’, whereas OED preserves previousframe relations such as ‘person–not contacting–broom’ and ‘person–touching–door’.

Fig. 3: Transition-Aware Delta Injection (TADI). TADI uses the adjacent-frame relation-query displacement ∆q = Qrel tar,q−Qrel prev,q as a transition cue. The displacement is decomposed into its numerically stabilized root-mean-square (RMS) magnitude rq and RMS-normalized direction ∆dir q , while the scale gate gq and foreground confidence cq modulate the injection strength.

Fig. 1: (a) Relational semantic inertia: the ‘person–cup/glass/bottle’ pair persists across frames, but its relation changes from looking at to not looking at, while the baseline [29] retains the previous predicate in the target frame. (b) Our reimplementation of the baseline exhibits an 11.6-point gap in SGDET R@10 between the non-transition and relation-transition frame subsets.

Table 1: Experimental results on Action Genome under the SGDET protocol. We report Recall@K (R@K) and mean Recall@K (mR@K) under With Constraint and No Constraint settings. ‘–’ indicates that the metric is not reported.

Table 3: Ablation on relation-stream transition injection design. Starting from the spatial+SSIA baseline, we compare temporal aggregation without transition injection and three relation-displacement injection variants. All variants use the same spatial branch and ViT-B/14 backbone.

Table 2: Module ablation. Starting from the frame-wise spatial baseline, we evaluate SSIA and DTA individually and jointly. The spatial baseline performs frame-wise triplet parsing without temporal refinement. DTA denotes the full temporal module with TADI. All variants use the ViT-B/14 backbone.

papers.selection_reason: Relation-transition-aware transformer for video scene graph generation, directly relevant to video understanding.
papers.title: RTAformer: Relation-Transition-Aware Transformer for Video Scene Graph Generation
papers.tldr: RTAformer improves video scene graph generation by modeling persistent entities separately from changing relationships to reduce relational semantic inertia.

papers.abstract: Pairwise preference feedback has become a widely adopted supervision signal for reinforcement learning in video generation models, as pairwise comparisons provide a more reliable alternative than pointwise scalar ratings for evaluating the quality of generated videos. Specifically, we define a preference graph for each GRPO group under a pairwise evaluator, where nodes represent sampled rollouts and edges encode pairwise preferences. Auditing 6,976 on-policy comparison graphs, we find that cyclic preferences are prevalent and persist throughout training. Naive pairwise reward aggregation based on average win rates discards the underlying comparison structures and treats each rollout independently, which may introduce unreliable advantage estimates for certain rollouts and consequently affect reinforcement learning optimization. Therefore, we propose the \emph{Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk} (\ours{}), a graph-aware advantage aggregation method that strengthens the global preference signal from win rates with reliable relational evidence from cyclic preference graphs through a reliability-guided preference walk. Under matched evaluator, comparison protocol, group size, prompt schedule, and query budget, \ours{} requires no additional evaluator queries beyond the observed comparisons within each rollout group and improves over Pairwise-GRPO across controlled comparisons, transfer settings, and blind human evaluations.
authors: Xinrui Lin, Fan Li, Shumin Wang, Dehong Kong, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Pairwise preferences for video rollouts often form cycles, which persist during training.
Win-rate aggregation ignores relational structure and can yield unreliable rollout advantages.
Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk combines global win rates with reliability-guided evidence from preference graphs.
It uses only comparisons already observed within each rollout group.
The method improves over Pairwise-GRPO in controlled, transfer, and blind human evaluations, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RAP-Walk. Top: methods share the Pairwise-GRPO pipeline and differ only in advantage construction. Bottom: (a) same-prompt videos exhibit quality trade-offs; (b) pointwise rewards are normalized independently; (c) v1, v2, and v3 form a directed cycle yet have identical row-wise win rates, so win-rate aggregation assigns them identical advantages; (d) RAP-Walk uses reliable edges and multi-hop paths to correct the win-rate anchor.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison across eight prompts. Each prompt shows four frames from videos generated by Pretrained, Pairwise GRPO, and RAP-Walk. Pretrained denotes the original Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B model without LoRA post-training. All methods use matched prompts and initial noise.

Figure 2: Five-node illustration of cyclic preference propagation. (a) A cyclic preference graph with reliability-aware propagation. (b) Normalized preference credits from rowwise win-rate aggregation and RAP-Walk. Win-rate aggregation only considers direct comparison outcomes, while RAP-Walk exploits reliable multi-hop support and reduces the influence of conflicting local structures.

Table 2: Quantitative comparison on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with Qwen3-VL-30B/235B evaluators. Within each evaluator, runs share group size, prompt schedule, and budget; pairwise methods also share the bidirectional comparison protocol and query count. Best/second-best are bolded/underlined.
Table 4: Ablation study on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B with Qwen3VL-235B. Win-rate Pairwise-GRPO is the reference; best/second-best values are bolded/underlined.
Table 3: Results across generator backbones with a fixed Qwen3-VL-235B evaluator. Best/second-best values are bolded/underlined per generator.

papers.selection_reason: Graph-aware preference aggregation for RL fine-tuning of video generation models, relevant to video diffusion training.
papers.title: When Pairwise Preferences Cycle: A Reliability-Anchored Preference Walk for Video GRPO
papers.tldr: A graph-aware preference-walk method uses cyclic pairwise-comparison structure to produce more reliable advantages for video GRPO without extra evaluator queries.

papers.abstract: Synthetic data is increasingly used in language-model pretraining. Existing knowledge-corpus synthesis pipelines, including WRAP and Nemotron-CC, usually take a source passage or document segment as input and generate rewritten or QA-style samples from that text. This can improve surface form and prompt diversity, but it does not explicitly require fine-grained source facts -- especially secondary entities, list/table entries, and precise temporal attributes -- to appear in the synthesized corpus. We propose AFCS (Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis), a pipeline that first extracts source-supported atomic facts and then uses each retained fact to drive generation. AFCS uses structure-aware extraction over the document tree, source-grounded verification, local context expansion, and multi-format generation. In continued-pretraining experiments with OLMo-3-7B and a 32B base on the same FineWiki source corpus, AFCS outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA. Granularity ablations show that fact-level synthesis improves over chunk-level, paragraph-level, and entity-level synthesis; and a 100B-token mid-training integration improves factual benchmarks and raises the 12-task general benchmark average by +1.09.
authors: Yunhao Wang, Feng Zhang, Tinghao Yu, Xing Wu, Jiang Zhou
bullets: Targets missing fine-grained facts, including secondary entities, list/table entries, and temporal details.
Extracts source-supported atomic facts with document-structure awareness and verifies them against the source.
Expands local context and generates diverse samples in multiple formats from each retained fact.
Outperforms WRAP and Nemotron-CC on SimpleQA, SimpleQA Verified, PopQA, and HotpotQA in experiments with 7B and 32B models.
A 100B-token integration improves factual benchmarks and increases the 12-task general benchmark average by 1.09 points.

figures.caption: Figure 1: AFCS pipeline and source-fact coverage. Source-conditioned synthesis (top) segments the web corpus and asks an LLM to synthesize from each segment, so the generated corpus tends to preserve salient facts while under-covering fine-grained facts in lists, tables, and secondary mentions. Atomic-fact-conditioned synthesis (bottom) first extracts structure-aware atomic facts from the same source corpus and then conditions generation on source-anchored assertion cards. Each card marks the local anchor (e.g., a document scope, list item, table row, or date cell), the natural-language assertion, and the highlighted value structure (e.g., a role binding, multi-element set, compound clause, or bibliographic record). These cards are generation targets rather than canonical entity–relation KG triples.

Figure 2: Training dynamics across factual QA benchmarks. The x-axis is aligned by consumed training tokens: 1k steps correspond to 2B tokens for 7B models and 4B tokens for 32B models. Solid lines denote 7B models and dashed lines denote 32B models. AFCS maintains consistent gains over source-conditioned baselines across the average score and individual factual QA benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Atomic-fact-conditioned synthesis improves factual knowledge pretraining; relevant to LLM pretraining methods.
papers.title: AFCS: Atomic-Fact-Conditioned Synthesis for Factual Knowledge Pretraining
papers.tldr: AFCS improves factual knowledge pretraining by generating synthetic data directly from verified atomic facts rather than only source passages or document segments.

papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) has shown strong effectiveness for text-based LLMs and LLM systems, but its application to audio-visual understanding systems requires suitable textual interfaces through which multimodal reasoning can be exposed to text-based optimizers. We investigate how the design of textual interfaces affects prompt optimization for multimodal reasoning, on the audio-visual question answering task. We compare three interface designs, including a direct inference system consisting of a single omni-modal large language model (OmniLLM), a captioner-reasoner system, and an agentic architecture in which a primary agent orchestrates subagent OmniLLMs. Experiments with Qwen3-Omni and Gemini show that direct prompt optimization provides model-dependent gains; the captioner-reasoner system and the agentic system expose more interpretable optimization interfaces but are harder to optimize, where error analysis of cases affected by optimization is conducted. Our study highlights textual interface design as an important factor in making prompt optimization effective for omni-modal reasoning systems. Our implementation details are specified in GitHub repo.
authors: Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Tong Lei, Dahan Wang, Peter Bell
bullets: Studies prompt optimization for audio-visual question answering through text-based interfaces.

Finds direct optimization produces model-dependent gains, while more interpretable interfaces are harder to optimize.
Uses Qwen3-Omni and Gemini, with error analysis of optimization-affected cases.
Highlights interface design as a key factor in optimizing omni-modal reasoning systems.

papers.abstract: Visual world knowledge is a core capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), underpinning knowledge-intensive visual question answering and fine-grained visual reasoning. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in two key respects. First, their category coverage is narrow: most benchmarks span only a small number of categories across a few domains, falling far short of the open-ended scale of real-world visual entities. Second, their task construction is often insufficiently rigorous: models can answer correctly using coarse-grained cues, vague associations, or elimination strategies without truly mastering precise concepts, making it difficult to accurately assess their knowledge of fine-grained entities. We introduce VisualWorldBench, a taxonomy-grounded multi-task benchmark built on a hierarchical taxonomy of 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances whose ground-truth labels cover 15,479 categories across four complementary tasks: closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming, covering different directions of knowledge retrieval and varying degrees of answer openness to comprehensively evaluate visual world knowledge. Most questions are constructed from taxonomically proximate categories, forcing precise discrimination among fine-grained entities. Experiments reveal that the strongest closed-source model achieves only 80.4% average accuracy, exposing capability gaps hidden under conventional benchmarks. We further construct VisualWorldBench-50K, a training resource covering 50K+ categories. Fine-tuning on VisualWorldBench-50K yields over 21 percentage points improvement on VisualWorldBench, with consistent transfer to public fine-grained recognition and visual knowledge benchmarks.
authors: Chen Chen, Zheming Liang, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Covers 21,291 leaf-node classes across 8 visual domains, with 32,541 evaluation instances spanning 15,479 categories.
Uses four tasks—closed-set recognition, contrastive selection, precise localization, and open-world naming—to test varied knowledge retrieval abilities.
Emphasizes taxonomically similar categories, requiring precise discrimination rather than coarse cues or elimination strategies.
The strongest evaluated closed-source model reaches 80.4% average accuracy, indicating limitations on fine-grained visual knowledge.
VisualWorldBench-50K covers 50K+ categories; fine-tuning improves benchmark performance by over 21 percentage points and transfers to other benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of VisualWorldBench. The benchmark spans 8 visual domains—Animal, Plant, Fungus, Food, Scene, Transport, Artifact, and Other—with a taxonomy of 21,291 leaf-node classes and 32,541 evaluation instances covering 15,479 ground-truth categories. The benchmark evaluates four complementary tasks: closed-set recognition (MCQ), contrastive selection (Grid-Sel), spatial localization (Grid-Loc), and open-world naming (Open-QA).

Figure 2: Taxonomy-grounded construction and four-format evaluation design of VisualWorldBench. (a) Benchmark construction: a hierarchical taxonomy (illustrated with an example subtree), multiformat task generation, and two-stage quality control (model-assisted triage by three frontier models followed by human verification and release balancing). (b) The four evaluation formats—MCQ for closed-set recognition, Grid-Sel for contrastive selection, Grid-Loc for precise localization, and Open-QA for open-world naming—with their task setup, sample counts, and design choices.

Figure 3: Examples of the four VisualWorldBench tasks, all grounded in a shared 21,291-class taxonomy. MCQ (closed-set recognition): the model selects the correct category from 20 taxonomyaware options (sibling, near, and random distractors). Grid-Sel / Grid-Loc (contrastive selection and precise localization): the model identifies or localizes the target category among visually similar alternatives in a composite grid. Grid-Sel requires selecting the correct cell, while Grid-Loc requires outputting a precise bounding box on the same grid layout. Open-QA (open-world naming): the model generates the fine-grained category name without any candidate set.

Figure 4: Capability profiles vary substantially across visual domains, taxonomy depth, and category exposure. (a) MCQ accuracy by visual domain (red ⋄: proprietary; blue ◦: open-source). Crossdomain gaps exceed 33 pp within individual models. (b) Grid-Sel accuracy by taxonomy depth for four open-source models (Qwen3.5-27B/9B/4B, Qwen3-VL-8B) at 2×2 and 3×3 resolutions. Performance degrades substantially at the deepest levels (7+). (c) Memorization vs. generalization (Qwen3-VL-2B): Base = instruct baseline (no SFT); Holdout = fine-tuned excluding records with held-out ground-truth labels; Full = fine-tuned on the complete SFT data. Selection and localization improve on categories held out from SFT target labels, with smaller gains on MCQ.

Figure 5: MCQ and Open-QA task examples. (a)–(d) MCQ: closed-set recognition with 20 taxonomyaware options including sibling, near, and random distractors drawn from the taxonomy hierarchy. (e)–(f) Open-QA: the model must generate the precise fine-grained category name without any candidate set.

Figure 6: Grid task examples (2×2). (a)–(b) Grid-Sel: the model selects which cell contains the target category from a composite grid of taxonomically similar images. (c)–(d) Grid-Loc: the model outputs a bounding box to precisely localize the target object within the grid. Red boxes indicate the ground-truth bounding box. All distractors are sibling or near categories from the taxonomy.

papers.abstract: Accurate nuclei segmentation underpins quantitative computational pathology, yet remains challenging due to morphological variability, weak boundaries, nuclear crowding, and pronounced domain shifts arising from differences in tissue preparation, staining, and acquisition. While deep learning and recent foundation models have improved segmentation performance under matched distributions with the original training data, their generalization across heterogeneous histopathology domains remains limited. We introduce GDBA-Net, a parameter-efficient nuclei segmentation framework built around the proposed Gated Dual-Branch Adapter (GDBA). GDBA-Net adapts a frozen SAM2 encoder by integrating pretrained semantic representations with explicit frequency-derived structural priors. The complementary representations are independently transformed through Grid MLP branches and dynamically integrated using sample-adaptive channel-wise gating, selectively emphasizing structural cues relevant to nuclear delineation. Despite using only 4.3 million trainable parameters, GDBA-Net achieves state-of-the-art in-dataset performance and consistently superior cross-dataset generalization across six diverse nuclei segmentation benchmarks under fully supervised, cross-dataset, and five-shot adaptation protocols, outperforming competing CNN-, transformer-, and foundation model based methods. Comprehensive ablations confirm that these gains arise from the coordinated design of semantic-frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity. By uniting transferable semantic representations with explicit structural priors, GDBA-Net provides a robust, annotation-efficient solution to domain variability in nuclei segmentation. https://github.com/biplabpoudel25/GDBA_Net
authors: Biplab Poudel, Betserai Albert Magarire, Anish Kumar Shah, Jiacheng Xie, Dong Xu
bullets: Addresses domain shifts caused by tissue preparation, staining, acquisition, and challenging nuclear morphology.

Ablations attribute the gains to semantic–frequency complementarity and adaptive gating rather than increased model capacity.

papers.abstract: MeanFlow predicts interval-average velocities, but conventional few-step sampling ties the interval queried from the model to the duration of the state update. We separate these two quantities at inference, fixing the model, update grid, and number of queries while varying the prediction horizon. Our central finding is that the horizon response depends on both query position and the states entering that query. Across seven independently trained CIFAR-10 checkpoints at classifier-free guidance (CFG) scale 2, a longer horizon worsens FID at early steps but improves it at the midpoint. To probe whether query time alone determines this response, we fix the midpoint query and current/subsequent guidance while changing only earlier CFG. In held-out factorial outcomes on five previously studied checkpoints, the mean midpoint horizon benefit increases from 0.109 to 1.308 FID, indicating sensitivity to the incoming-state distribution. A frozen four-query rule reduces mean CIFAR-10 FID by 2.023 without retraining or extra queries, including gains on five checkpoints trained after rule selection. A milder rule also improves mean FID by 1.041 on a stronger frozen grid, with fixed-rule FID gains on the evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints. However, matched-budget calibration favors query-start shifting in historical CIFAR tests, and the tested Horizon allocation adds no FID benefit beyond Grid+Start on two public ImageNet models. Thus, prediction horizon is a distinct, position- and state-sensitive inference control, but not a universally preferred one.
authors: Tinglan Wang, Haixu Liu, Shaobo Chen, Nuo Qian, Qi Gao, Kai Wen, Yu Yao

Fixed-rule gains also appear on evaluated public ImageNet-256 and AFHQ checkpoints.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates inference dynamics in MeanFlow (video generation), specifically decoupling model queries from state updates, which is relevant to video generation and understanding.
papers.title: Rethinking Prediction Horizons: Decoupling Model Queries from State Updates in Few-Step MeanFlow
papers.tldr: Decoupling MeanFlow’s model-query horizon from the state-update duration reveals a position- and state-sensitive inference control that can improve FID without retraining or extra queries, but is not universally best.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently encounter conflicts between internal parametric knowledge and external contextual knowledge, yet the mechanisms governing this selection remain unclear. We show that the choice between context and parametric knowledge is linearly represented and can be controlled along a single direction in the model's residual stream. We first demonstrate that this direction generalizes across factual-conflict settings, including context formats, knowledge categories, and datasets, while consistently shifting behavior between parametric and contextual answers. We then transfer a direction learned from simple factual conflicts to three more complex task families: RAG, memory, and rule following, where models must acquire information from retrieved documents, interaction histories, or explicit rules. Across four model families and multiple transfer settings, steering consistently improves the use of prompt-provided information over the unsteered model. These results suggest that the direction captures a transferable preference for external knowledge rather than a mechanism specific to factual conflicts.
authors: Yibin Lou, Yi Hu, Jianhui Chen, Chenpeng Wang, Muhan Zhang, Liangming Pan
bullets: Knowledge selection between parametric and contextual information is linearly represented along a single model direction.
The direction generalizes across conflict formats, knowledge categories, and datasets.
A direction learned from simple factual conflicts transfers to RAG, memory, and rule-following tasks.
Steering consistently improves reliance on prompt-provided information across four model families and multiple settings.
The findings indicate a transferable preference for external knowledge, not merely a factual-conflict-specific mechanism.

papers.abstract: We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector's surroundings. External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost. FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on $\pi_{0.5}$ in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8% success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1%, versus 52.1% for the wrist-equipped $\pi_{0.5}$. Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
authors: Bingao Chen, Lihan Zha, C. Karen Liu, Guy Tevet
bullets: Addresses the limited scene coverage of wrist cameras and the low-resolution detail of external views.
Predicts the next interaction region alongside each action chunk, then receives original-resolution crops plus full images.
Built on π₀.₅ in Single and Dual configurations using one or two external stereo cameras with RGB-D inputs.
On four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single and Dual achieve 70.8% and 77.1% success, compared with 52.1% for wrist-equipped π₀.₅.
Matches the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improves performance with distractors, cloth, and far-away objects.

papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of large vision language models (LVLMs) has made geolocation inference from images highly accurate and accessible. This poses serious privacy risks: a passive adversary with black-box LVLM access can infer a user's location from a single photo with no metadata. Existing protection methods rely almost exclusively on adversarial perturbation, which introduces perceptible visual artifacts and utility degradation. We identify the visual-geolocation asymmetry: geolocation-decisive clues, such as street signs, tend to be visually peripheral but dominate location inference. Exploiting this asymmetry, we propose GeoCloak, an agentic framework for semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection. It acts as a clue-aware planner that analyzes each image to identify geolocation-relevant clues, dispatches targeted semantic edits to directly suppress peripheral clues, and autonomously configures adversarial perturbation to further suppress residual geolocation features, all under iterative utility-aware feedback. We evaluate GeoCloak on four diverse datasets spanning 108 countries and 576 cities against five LVLMs and three inference methods. GeoCloak reduces overall city-level accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9%, approximately half of the best-performing baseline, while achieving substantially superior utility preservation both qualitatively and quantitatively. We hope this work takes a meaningful step toward practical, semantics-preserving geolocation privacy protection, giving users greater control over the location information inadvertently embedded in their shared images.
authors: Yixin Wu, Mingjie Li, Yun Shen, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
bullets: Targets the risk that black-box vision-language models can infer locations from ordinary photos without metadata.
Exploits the asymmetry that geolocation-critical clues, such as street signs, are often visually peripheral.
Uses an agentic planner for clue detection, targeted semantic edits, adaptive perturbation, and utility-aware iteration.
Evaluated across four datasets covering 108 countries and 576 cities, with five LVLMs and three inference methods.
Reduced city-level geolocation accuracy from 41.2% to 9.9% while preserving utility better than the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: In recent years, with advances in multimodal interaction technologies and the growing demand for intelligent emotional support, Multimodal Emotional Support Conversation (MESC) has emerged as an important task. However, existing systems still suffer from shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies due to weak semantic feedback, cross-dimension reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision. To address these challenges, we propose FACES, a fine-grained gated semantic alignment framework for MESC. Specifically, FACES integrates multi-source rewards to construct multidimensional semantic and functional alignment signals, employs a non-compensatory gated fusion mechanism to reduce cross-dimension reward offset, and leverages structured Chain-of-Thought (CoT) anchors to perform token-level credit assignment. Under a controlled response-length protocol, FACES improves the average MLLM-based evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04 and achieves an 80.22% pairwise win rate over SOTA. Human evaluation under the same protocol yields a 75.3% preference rate. Results on three external datasets further support transferability. The code and dataset are available at https://github.com/OCT-ARR/arr.
authors: Hang Ren, Peidong Wang, Yichen Gao, Wen Zhang, Jiayang Yu, Xiaocui Yang, Shi Feng
bullets: Targets shallow responses and inappropriate support strategies caused by weak semantic feedback, reward compensation, and coarse reasoning supervision.

Under controlled response length, improves the average MLLM evaluation score from 3.61 to 4.04, with an 80.22% pairwise win rate and 75.3% human preference rate.
Results on three external datasets support transferability; code and dataset are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision-language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct, a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision-language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy's computational dependency: vision-language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over $\pi_{0.5}$. Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
authors: Ziyan Liu, Jiting Liu, Weihong Zhong, Wenda Yu, Yeqiu Chen, Jason Li, Xiaojiang Peng, Shuyuan Hu, Kai Wang, Bo Zhao
bullets: Fixed shared parameters can struggle when different robot operations require competing updates.
MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank updates for both vision-language and action modules.
Coupled generators follow the policy’s dependency structure, letting vision-language updates influence action-side parameter generation.
The framework is trained with the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
It reports gains of up to 16.30% on LIBERO and Meta-World and up to 14% over π₀.₅ in real-world evaluation.

papers.abstract: Chemistry evaluation has moved past multiple-choice probes toward open-ended expert problems, yet the benchmarks that define the current frontier still score answer endpoints alone. Such scoring conflates memorized facts with stepwise derivation, treats visual and textual inputs as interchangeable, and confounds long-horizon planning with stepwise execution. These blind spots prevent any diagnosis of where the reasoning chain breaks in a model. We present ChemArgus, a competition-level chemistry benchmark drawn from chemistry competition material, textbooks, and research papers, whose scoring replaces the answer endpoint with three measurement properties. Fine-grained scoring grades every subquestion point by point with partial credit, so a score lands at the level of the step rather than the outcome. Multimodal capability is priced on every problem containing a real image, paired with a controlled text description, so visual understanding is measured against text on identical tasks. Diagnostic attribution reads paired metrics that share one scoring unit and differ only in context construction, so a gap between two scores isolates a single cause, namely integration, propagation, or local reasoning. GPT-5.6-Sol scores 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving against 28.8% and 30.4% under the two sequential metrics, a gap measuring the integration burden. Through rubric partial credit and these cause-isolating score gaps, ChemArgus shows not only whether a model answers chemistry correctly but where its reasoning chain fails, so that every score it reports doubles as a diagnosis, a readout of the chain rather than a verdict, aiming to guide language models step by step on their path toward chemistry expertise, one corrected step at a time, each step priced by the rubric, point by point.
authors: Hanyao Guo, Mo Cui, Zihan Tan, Leixin Sun, Yichun Wang, Yinan Shen, Guojun Zhu, Jia Jiang, Erhao Chen, Zui Chen, Wenzhe Gao, Zhihao Yu, Qijun Wang, Yetian Zhu, Jiande Chen, Chuhang Pei, Yao Jiang, Yichen Fan, Pinhan Wang, Xiaorui Pan, Qianyi Zhu, Yang Liu, Mang Ye, Guancheng Wan
bullets: Targets blind spots in endpoint-only evaluation, including memorization versus derivation, visual versus textual understanding, and planning versus execution.
Uses point-by-point rubric scoring with partial credit to evaluate intermediate subquestion steps.

Compares sequentially constructed metrics to attribute score gaps to integration, propagation, or local reasoning.
For GPT-5.6-Sol, reports 23.2% on unassisted whole-problem solving versus 28.8% and 30.4% on the two sequential metrics, illustrating an integration gap.

papers.abstract: Scaling self-supervised contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL) to 1000-layer Euclidean neural networks has enabled state-of-the-art goal-reaching performance, yet wall-clock time scales linearly with depth. We find that changing the geometry achieves stronger performance with far shallower networks. This matters in complex navigation environments, where walls can make route distance deviate substantially from Euclidean distance. In a U-shaped maze, we show that the longer the route, the more it deviates from Euclidean distance. Hyperbolic CRL addresses this mismatch by replacing Euclidean distances in CRL's contrastive objective with geodesic distances in hyperbolic space. On hard navigation tasks, inductive bias beats scale: depth 64 hyperbolic agents outperform 1024-layer-deep Euclidean networks while training more than $12 \times$ faster and using about $13 \times$ fewer parameters. We observe that hyperbolic agents behave qualitatively better in hard humanoid mazes, where they follow corridors to reach goals, whereas Euclidean agents try straight-line shortcuts over walls. Our results show that matching the representation geometry to the task can substitute for substantial network depth. Code is at https://github.com/Probabilistic-and-Interactive-ML/HypGCRL .
authors: Timo Klein, Thomas Lang, Andrii Shkabrii, Lukas Miklautz, Yllka Velaj, Sebastian Tschiatschek
bullets: Euclidean distance poorly reflects route distance in environments with obstacles and walls.
Hyperbolic CRL replaces Euclidean distances in the contrastive objective with hyperbolic geodesic distances.
Depth-64 hyperbolic agents outperform depth-1024 Euclidean agents on hard navigation tasks.
Hyperbolic agents train over 12× faster and use about 13× fewer parameters.
In hard humanoid mazes, hyperbolic agents follow corridors instead of attempting straight-line paths through walls.

papers.abstract: Transformers can perform in-context reinforcement learning without parameter updates. However, existing theoretical constructions often require context sizes that grow with the number of sampled transitions, leading to increasing memory costs in large-scale problems. This raises a fundamental scalability question: how much context is intrinsically necessary to carry out such learning? We answer this question for fixed-policy TD evaluation. We show that, with a shared linear decoder, the minimum context dimension required to exactly reproduce the first $L$ TD iterates is the Krylov dimension induced by the sampled transitions. When the available context dimension $m$ falls below this threshold, exact reproduction is no longer possible. In this regime, we characterize the optimal approximation error and show that it decays as $\Theta(\gamma^m\max\{1,1/(m(1-\gamma))\})$ where $\gamma$ is the discounting factor. Moving from representation complexity to actual memory cost, we characterize the optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations as $\Theta(nk_L)$ and show experimentally that on a sampled task whose exact rank is full but whose numerical rank is small, a context accurate to $10^{-2}$ is $88.7\%$ smaller than the sparse sufficient statistics of TD. Finally, we establish the learnability of the shared executor through pretraining by proving global convergence of an auxiliary objective over effective attention parameters under suitable task diversity. Experiments across diverse TD evaluation problems validate parameter recovery and the predicted context--accuracy tradeoff.
authors: Yajie Zhao, Yingjun Mo, Zhiyong Wang, Bo Tang, Chao Xu, Fang Kong
bullets: For fixed-policy TD evaluation with a shared linear decoder, exact reproduction of the first L TD iterates requires context dimension equal to the transitions’ induced Krylov dimension.
Below this threshold, exact reproduction is impossible; the optimal approximation error decays as Θ(γ^m max{1, 1/[m(1−γ)]}).
The optimal retained memory for exact continuous representations scales as Θ(nk_L).
On a sampled task with full exact rank but low numerical rank, context accurate to 10⁻² used 88.7% less memory than TD’s sparse sufficient statistics.
The paper also proves global convergence for pretraining the shared executor under suitable task diversity, with experiments validating parameter recovery and the context–accuracy tradeoff.

papers.abstract: Reconstruction of 3D structures using under-ice AUV video footage has been inaccurate, although it is not certain whether this is due to shortcomings in the methods or an inherent deficiency of the capture system. We test four different models for reconstruction on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream): classical feature matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model. All four fail, each in a distinct way: near-total registration yielding almost no structure, geometrically broken output despite healthy photometric metrics, a persistent coverage artifact, and unstable cross-chunk scale. We show that all four are consistent with the same capture regime, a small camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio. Following our analysis, we propose a detection system that flags this type of failure in minutes, rather than hours of wasted compute.
authors: Ana-\c{S}tefania Kog\u{a}lniceanu, Kl\'ara Orb\'an, Ashwin Nedungadi, Stefan L\"udtke, Kuderna-Iulian Ben\c{t}a
bullets: Evaluates four reconstruction approaches on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video.
All methods fail differently: insufficient registration, geometric distortion, coverage artifacts, or unstable scale.
The failures share a common cause: a low camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio.
Proposes a detector that flags likely reconstruction failure within minutes instead of after extensive computation.
