papers.abstract: Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents. Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy-goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues. We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths. Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal's location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0% to 95.3%. Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6% to 84.3% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works. Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
authors: Julia Barth, Armin Sommer, Kunvar Thaman, Jannik Schilling
bullets: Identifies functional target substitution, policy shortcuts, and cue competition across Procgen and robot tasks.
Traces whether goal information is retained internally, influences the policy, and reaches the final decision.
Shows that steering can recover behavior when the goal reaches the decision, while new downstream wiring is needed when it does not.
Recovery fails when the goal is inert, linking intervention effectiveness to the depth of misalignment.
Frames goal misgeneralization as multiple policy-alignment failures rather than a single representation failure.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes goal misgeneralization in learned policies across robot tasks, relevant to embodied robot learning and alignment.
papers.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
papers.tldr: Goal misgeneralization arises from three distinct alignment failures, and recovery depends on how deeply the intended goal is disconnected from action selection.

papers.abstract: Video large language models (Video LLMs) often generate responses unsupported by the input video. Contrastive decoding (CD) can mitigate these hallucinations, but its effectiveness depends on how the negative branch weakens visual evidence. Existing methods rely on predefined perturbations or masking guided by question reconstruction, offering limited control over the model's visual reliance during answer generation. We introduce Attention-guided Representation Perturbation for Contrastive Decoding (ARP-CD), a training-free framework for constructing contrastive negatives directly in representation space. ARP-CD uses the attention mass assigned to visual tokens at the answer-prediction position to guide bounded gradient updates of the language model's input visual hidden states. These updates reduce visual attention and produce a negative input, whose predictions are contrasted with those of the original branch throughout generation. Experiments across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks show that ARP-CD outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model--benchmark settings, reducing hallucinations while improving general video understanding. Further analyses show that attention-guided perturbation directions improve negative quality and that the resulting negatives provide effective contrastive references for correcting the original predictions.
authors: Zhixin Cai, Ruoqi Yuan, Xinchen Yang, Zhuofan Chen, Jun Bai, Chuantao Yin, Wenge Rong
bullets: Targets unsupported video-grounded responses in Video LLMs.
Uses visual-token attention at the answer position to guide bounded gradient updates to visual hidden states.
Contrasts predictions from the perturbed negative branch with the original branch during generation.
A training-free method evaluated across four Video LLMs and four benchmarks.
Outperforms representative training-free baselines in most model–benchmark settings while improving general video understanding.

papers.abstract: We present a Generative World Simulation framework that couples persistent shared world state with continuous first-person audiovisual generation. The framework integrates DAO, a computable world engine, and JING, an Egocentric Interactive Experience Model, to support sustained interaction for humans and agents. DAO maintains the states of characters, objects, and spaces and their relationships, advancing the world according to interaction rules and world time while preserving the consequences of past actions. From this evolving state, DAO derives observer-specific conditions for JING, which combines these conditions with character, object, and scene references, observation history, and current actions to generate each observer's audiovisual experience. Users can explore environments, manipulate objects, and communicate with characters through viewpoint control and text instructions, with their actions shaping both the shared state and subsequent experiences. By connecting world-state evolution with experience generation in a continuous interaction loop, the framework offers an approach to building interactive worlds that retain their history, evolve through action, and persist beyond any individual observer.
authors: XGEN Team, Guohao Cai, Haoxuan Che, Frank Fan, Chenran Huang, Junjia Huang, Jiayi Jiang, Yanheng Li, Leon Liu, Shaoteng Liu, Xi Liu, Feng Nie, Zhefan Rao, An Wang, Hanwen Wang, Pengxiang Yan, Jieming Yu, Qian Zha, Wentao Zheng
bullets: Targets interactive worlds that retain history and persist beyond any individual observer.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Data pipeline overview. (c) Local readout combines the world state with an observer’s pose to provide observations for an experience interface. (d) World snapshots and event history preserve state across interactions.

papers.abstract: Interpreting an ambiguous utterance in real-world interactions often requires context beyond a single utterance. When the utterance refers to objects in a visual scene, it is necessary to maintain and update the set of plausible referents as context accumulates, without assuming that the available information identifies a unique object. However, prior work on interactive visual grounding, which localizes objects referred to by linguistic expressions, has focused on identifying a unique object once sufficient dialogue context becomes available. To address this gap, we propose Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG), a task for estimating the set of objects consistent with the given dialogue context. We further introduce CandVG, a benchmark that evaluates how the candidate set changes across dialogue turns. Our evaluation of vision-language models shows that stronger visual grounding capability does not necessarily yield better CSVG performance. In particular, models have difficulty predicting the complete candidate set, owing to challenges in candidate generation and premature commitment to a small set of candidates in early turns. Nevertheless, we find that this limitation can be partially mitigated in the evaluated large-scale models using instructions designed for CSVG.
authors: Shun Inadumi, Lee Sangmyeong, Koichiro Yoshino
bullets: Ambiguous referring expressions may remain compatible with multiple scene objects as dialogue unfolds.
Candidate Set Visual Grounding (CSVG) estimates the full set of plausible referents rather than selecting one object.
CandVG benchmarks how candidate sets change across dialogue turns.
Stronger conventional visual grounding does not necessarily improve CSVG performance.
CSVG-specific instructions partially mitigate incomplete candidate generation in evaluated large-scale models.

papers.abstract: Learning robust driving policies that generalize beyond their training domain remains a central challenge in motion planning. We propose an uncertainty-driven self-play scheme, in which half of the agents are rewarded for increasing their neighbors' epistemic uncertainty, while the other half learn to drive safely as the exploring agents continuously seek out their weaknesses. Epistemic uncertainty indicates where the policy is least confident and serves as an automatic proxy for scenario difficulty. Exploring agents use this signal to seek out hard cases, generating a challenging curriculum without manual scenario design. The resulting policy outperforms standard self-play, achieving best-in-class zero-shot transfer to nuplan Val14 (99.12% vs. 97.97%) and Argoverse 2 (82.39% vs. 78.03%) without fine-tuning, while also improving performance over standard self-play on Waymo. Our diversity-driven approach achieves 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage than the baseline, indicating a much richer set of behaviors. Further analysis shows that epistemic uncertainty serves as a calibrated difficulty detector, with highest-uncertain agents exhibiting 14.8 times the combined failure rate across collision, off-road, and DNF, of lowest-uncertain agents, enabling automatic prioritization of challenging scenarios without ground-truth labels.
authors: Sajad Marvi, Julian Schmidt, Alessandro Canevaro, Julian Jordan, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Exploring agents seek states that increase neighboring policies’ epistemic uncertainty, while other agents learn to drive safely through these challenges.
Epistemic uncertainty acts as an automatic difficulty signal, enabling curriculum generation without manual scenario design or ground-truth labels.
The approach improves zero-shot transfer on nuPlan Val14 and Argoverse 2 and also outperforms standard self-play on Waymo.
It produces 85% higher LSTM hidden-state coverage, suggesting a broader range of learned behaviors.
Highest-uncertainty agents have a 14.8× higher combined collision, off-road, and DNF failure rate than lowest-uncertainty agents.

papers.abstract: Multi-session agents can switch between LLMs to balance performance and inference cost. Such switches require transferring a history for continuity, yet their effects on the recipient remain underexplored. Through controlled experiments with multi-session tasks, we uncover behavior transfer: recipients tend to adopt reasoning and action patterns from the models that generated their histories. This effect is most evident with raw-history transfer but is substantially reduced by summarization. Based on these findings, we propose Direction- and Authorship-aware Summarization of History (DASH) that preserves stronger-model behavior while minimizing weak-to-strong transfer via summarization. Experiments with repeated swaps show that DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines. These results suggest that effective multi-model orchestration requires considering not only which model to use, but also which behavioral patterns to carry forward.
authors: Youngbin Choi, Sehyun Hwang, Suhyeon Jun, Seoyeon Lee, Sunghyun Choi, MoonJeong Park, Dongwoo Kim
bullets: Model swaps can cause recipient LLMs to adopt the reasoning and action patterns embedded in prior histories.
Behavior transfer is strongest with raw-history sharing and is substantially reduced by summarization.
DASH uses direction- and authorship-aware summarization to preserve desirable behavior and limit weak-to-strong transfer.
Across repeated swaps, DASH outperforms raw-history transfer and naive summarization baselines.
The findings highlight behavioral history—not just model selection—as a key factor in multi-model orchestration.

papers.abstract: Mamba models underperform Transformers on in-context retrieval. This gap is usually attributed to Mamba's fixed-size recurrent state, which loses information as the context grows. We challenge this assumption by focusing on query-first retrieval, a setup in which the query precedes the context and state capacity should not be the binding constraint. We show that even in this setting Mamba lags substantially behind Transformers, despite its selection mechanism, which was designed to distinguish relevant content from distractors. We then demonstrate that the Mamba selection gates have sufficient control over the state updates to influence the model output: intervening on specific gates alone can swing accuracy between extremes. However, as gates are input-dependent, they require the incoming token's representation to encode its relevance to the query. We therefore probe token representations across layers, and find that the relevance signal emerges only gradually with model depth, and that the gates begin to reflect it only several layers deeper. Crucially, we find that gates in retrieval-critical layers are not yet aligned with relevance. The selection mechanism is thus expressive enough to solve the task, but it commonly operates on a relevance signal that has not yet arrived. Mamba's retrieval bottleneck therefore extends beyond state capacity: even when capacity is sufficient, the delayed emergence of relevance information across depth often prevents successful retrieval.
authors: Nir Yarden, Amit Ben-Artzy, Roy Schwartz
bullets: Query-first retrieval removes state-capacity pressure, yet Mamba still substantially trails Transformers.
Mamba’s selection gates can strongly control outputs, showing that the mechanism is expressive enough for retrieval.
Gate decisions depend on token representations encoding relevance to the query.
Relevance signals emerge gradually across layers, while retrieval-critical gates often act before those signals are available.
The bottleneck is therefore delayed cross-layer relevance alignment, not capacity alone.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mechanistic overview of query-first retrieval in Mamba Guided by the design principles behind Mamba’s architecture, we trace the flow of information across the layer and tokensequence axes, examining under a magnifying glass the mechanisms involved at query-first retrieval in Mamba, in search of the source of its degraded performance. Specifically, we zoom in on the following processes: (a) As token representations are mixed across layers, a relevance signal is encoded. (b) The selection gate responds to this signal by ‘opening and closing’, selectively writing relevant content to state while suppressing distractors. (c) The recurrent state stores the target information while being repeatedly updated, which requires protecting it from decay. (d) Finally, the target information is extracted from the state to generate the output token.

Figure 2: A local relevance flag in the target entry enables Mamba to identify and encode relevant information earlier, substantially improving long-context retrieval. (a) Evaluating the model on the query-first phonebook dataset, with and without a local relevance flag. The flag drastically improves Mamba’s accuracy on longer phonebooks. (b) Probing recurrent states for the target information reveals that the local relevance flag enables target decodability to emerge in earlier layers and with greater strength. (c) Calculating the difference between Mamba’s selection gates for target and distractor tokens demonstrates that the selection gate distinguishes token relevance earlier and more effectively when the local relevance flag is included. Showing results for Nvidia-Mamba; See fig. 6 for Codestral-Mamba results.

Figure 6: Codestral-Mamba exhibits trends similar to Nvidia-Mamba when a local relevance flag is added to the target entry: (a) overall model accuracy improves, (b) the decodability of the target information in the recurrent state becomes stronger, and (c) selection gates better distinguish between target and distractor entries.

Figure 4: Relevance information emerges gradually through the network, with delays both in contextualizing token representations and in aligning the gates with the resulting relevance signal. (a) Layer-wise linear probing shows that relevance becomes readily decodable from token representations much later when a local relevance flag is not present. (b) Layer-wise probes reveal a further delay: relevance becomes decodable from the gates only several layers after it emerges in the corresponding representations. (c) Cumulative layer-wise patching of either target information gates or representations shows that accuracy gains are concentrated in the early-to-middle layers, including layers where relevance is already decodable from representations but not yet adequately reflected in the gates.

Figure 3: Manipulating the gates corresponding to the target information tokens governs performance. (a) Patching the unflagged prompt with flagged gating values recovers full flagged accuracy, whereas the reverse substitution reduces flagged accuracy to unflagged levels. (b) Oracle-scaling the target information tokens gates of the unflagged prompt can bring Mamba to near-perfect or near-zero accuracy.
Figure 5: A sample of unflagged vs. flagged datasets. A single word addition, encoded to merely zero to two tokens, improves Mamba’s accuracy substantially.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes Mamba's retrieval bottleneck and selection gates, relevant to LLM architecture.
papers.title: Beyond State Capacity: Why Retrieval Breaks in Mamba
papers.tldr: Mamba’s retrieval failures are not just caused by limited state capacity: relevance information often reaches its selection gates too late for effective retrieval.

papers.abstract: Recent video world models have increasingly adopted 3D memory mechanisms to integrate historical observations into a lightweight and persistent scene representation. This naturally raises a complementary question: if 3D representations can serve as an effective mechanism for memorizing observed scenes, can they also be directly used as the latent space for reconstructing and generating scenes? Motivated by this idea, we represent a scene as a compact and unstructured 3D-anchored latent space (\textbf{SceneAE}). Each latent combines an explicit 3D position with an implicit content feature and is spatially grounded to describe its local scene region, forming a sparse latent point cloud. Unlike conventional video-VAE latents that describe how a scene appears from particular viewpoints, our representation directly describes the scene itself, making it naturally applicable to both reconstruction and generation. For reconstruction, once the scene has been generated, our persistent 3D representation can be projected and decoded into RGB-D observations by different target cameras, without the need to regenerate a video for each new camera trajectory. For generation, we leverage the geometry-content separation to first generate camera-controlled 3D geometry and then synthesize content conditioned on it, reducing camera-appearance entanglement and improving camera controllability. Experiments show that this 3D latent achieves superior generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Wenzhao Zheng, Yunpeng Zhang, Yi Wu, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Addresses whether 3D memory representations can serve directly as latent spaces for scene reconstruction and generation.
Represents each scene with spatially grounded 3D positions plus implicit content features, forming a sparse latent point cloud.
Projects the persistent representation into RGB-D views from new cameras without regenerating videos for each trajectory.
Separates geometry generation from content synthesis to reduce camera–appearance entanglement and improve camera control.
Experiments report improved generation quality, computational cost, and camera controllability.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Motivated by this, we propose Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA), a two-stage method for making more effective use of a fixed rank budget. After the first stage, ReGRA estimates task gradients on a calibration set and removes their projections onto the two-sided subspace induced by the first-stage update. It then aggregates the residual-gradient directions to initialize a second-stage adapter without changing the first-stage update. An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to capture complementary directions. Both updates can be merged into the pretrained weights, incurring no additional inference overhead. Across diverse benchmark sets, ReGRA achieves stronger performance than alternatives with the same total rank and even matches LoRA adapters with twice the rank. Ablation studies and further analysis support the contribution of its core design choices. Code is available at https://github.com/Fanyao-Li/ReGRA.
authors: Fanyao Li, Yuxi Liu, Xiaohao Liu, He Chang, Zhaoxin Wang, Zhulin Tao
bullets: Higher LoRA rank can introduce harmful directions: in a rank-16 diagnostic, keeping only top singular components performed best.
ReGRA uses a two-stage process: it projects calibration-set task gradients away from the first adapter’s induced subspace, then initializes a second adapter from residual directions.
An orthogonality regularizer encourages the two updates to learn complementary information.
Across diverse benchmarks, ReGRA outperforms same-total-rank alternatives and matches LoRA with twice the rank.
The two adapters can be merged into pretrained weights, adding no inference overhead.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall framework of Residual-Gradient Adaptation (ReGRA). ReGRA first trains Adapter 1 to learn an initial task-specific update. It then projects the task gradient away from the subspace already captured by Adapter 1 and extracts the dominant residual directions via SVD. These residual directions are used to initialize and guide Adapter 2 toward complementary taskrelevant information. The two adapters are finally combined with the frozen backbone to form the final model.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves reasoning in language models, but scalar outcomes provide coarse supervision over response trajectories. Self-distillation offers denser token-level guidance by comparing an unassisted policy with a feedback-informed self-teacher, yet the teacher evolves with the student, creating unstable targets and motivating additional regularization. We introduce Function-Space Policy Optimization (FSPO), a single-policy framework that combines current privileged adaptation with function-space temporal consolidation. FSPO stores sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, providing temporal separation without maintaining a persistent teacher model. It further introduces privileged disagreement correction to explicitly suppress locally overvalued actions, reliability-adaptive grounding that strengthens reference supervision when self-generated evidence repeatedly fails, and quality and coverage-aware temporal memory that retains verified behaviors and improves privileged demonstrations. Across reasoning and tool-use benchmarks, FSPO achieves the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour training budget, improving over the strongest baseline by approximately 4% points on average while reducing peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.
authors: Aryan Das, Arnab Bhattacharya, Vinay Kumar Verma
bullets: Addresses coarse scalar supervision and unstable moving targets in RL with Verifiable Rewards.
Uses a single policy with sparse historical next-token distributions as fixed temporal targets, avoiding a persistent teacher model.
Adds privileged disagreement correction, reliability-adaptive grounding, and quality- and coverage-aware memory.
Reports the highest average accuracy under a 5-hour budget, with roughly 4 percentage points over the strongest baseline.
Reduces peak memory from about 70 GB to 56 GB on Olmo3-7B-Instruct.

papers.abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) changes logit margins among non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes. Matching a local reference distribution keeps those probabilities and also penalizes margin expansions. We ask whether a soft auxiliary can preserve selected local non-target margin relations without freezing that distribution. We introduce \textbf{Selective Rank-Preserving SFT (SRP-SFT)}, a soft margin target: a hinge on reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs from the reference's top-$K$ non-target tokens, applied at fixed teacher-forced prefixes. The hinge stops once the requested bound is met. We derive the KL cost of violating a margin, characterize the feasible region and its conditional utility, and give a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations. In one-epoch experiments on Qwen3-4B-Base and UltraFeedback, this target raises MATH-500 and code-generation scores over CE and LP-SFT at all three training seeds. At seed 1234, MATH-500 pass@1 rises from 49.56\% to 54.56\% and the four-metric code mean rises from 65.91\% to 69.50\% relative to LP-SFT. Ranking controls, held-out cache diagnostics, sensitivity sweeps, and six additional backbones show where these score changes appear.
authors: Yuxuan Wang, Guangxiang Zhao, Xinyu Tan, Yahui Han, Xinxiang Yin, Zhonghai Wu, Xiangzheng Zhang, Lin Sun, Tong Yang
bullets: SFT can alter non-target logit margins even when matching a local reference distribution.
SRP-SFT applies a hinge loss to reference-scaled lower bounds for pairs among the reference model’s top-K non-target tokens at teacher-forced prefixes.
The hinge stops penalizing a pair once its requested margin bound is satisfied, allowing distributional flexibility.
The paper derives the KL cost of margin violations, characterizes feasibility and utility, and provides a finite-step condition for reducing aggregate violations.
On Qwen3-4B-Base with UltraFeedback, SRP-SFT outperformed CE and LP-SFT across three seeds in the reported MATH-500 and code-generation evaluations.

papers.title: Beyond Distribution Matching: Selective Margin Preservation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: SRP-SFT preserves selected non-target logit margins without forcing the full reference distribution, improving math and code-generation scores in reported one-epoch experiments.

papers.abstract: World models trained via latent dynamics offer a scalable path for embodied planning, yet existing methods suffer from representational collapse, computational overhead, and limited long-horizon capability. We introduce a memory-enhanced latent world model that augments JEPA-style prediction with a content-addressable memory bank. Our approach learns high-level representations directly from observations, operating at multiple temporal scales within a shared latent space, and conditions predictions via adaptive layer normalization. To prevent collapse and ensure effective memory usage, we design two complementary losses that encourage slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization. Experiments on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture, outperforming conventional latent world models on long-horizon planning tasks.
authors: Yuwei Sun, Siyu Zhu
bullets: Targets representational collapse, computational overhead, and weak long-horizon performance in latent world models.
Uses a content-addressable memory bank with multi-timescale representations in a shared latent space.
Conditions predictions through adaptive layer normalization.
Introduces losses promoting memory-slot diversity and balanced temporal utilization.
Evaluated on PushT, Tworoom, Reacher, and OGBCube, achieving state-of-the-art performance with a lightweight architecture.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The scheme of the memory-enhanced latent world models.

Figure 3. Visualization of memory slot usage. We observe distinct activation patterns across planning stages. In the PushT environment, the first slot exhibits peak activation when the agent starts to approach the T-shaped block, whereas the fifth slot dominates when the agent initiates pushing the block toward the target area. papers.abstract: Accurate 3D reconstruction in real-world environments remains a significant challenge due to the coexistence of reflective and non-reflective surfaces, which pose distinct modeling demands. Existing methods often treat these surface types separately, limiting their generalizability and physical plausibility. To bridge this gap, we propose MicroSDF, a novel neural implicit framework that facilitates geometry and reflectance modeling through microfacet theory. Our approach incorporates three core innovations: (i) a microfacet-guided geometry model that extracts multi-scale surface normals (macroscopic and microfacet) from a signed distance field (SDF), regularized by a proposed microfacet normal consistency loss to enforce physically plausible surface orientations; (ii) an enhanced dual-branch color model, where the specular branch leverages the microfacet normals to model high-frequency reflectance, and the vanilla branch, unlike prior works, uses reflection direction (instead of viewing direction) to better model diffuse and low-frequency specular components; and (iii) a detection-guided color blending strategy that adaptively fuses the color outputs based on reflection priors, providing more physically intuitive blending than implicitly learned blending weights. Combined with a tailored multi-stage optimization scheme, the proposed MicroSDF achieves robust and high-fidelity reconstruction across reflective and non-reflective surfaces. Extensive experiments on DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, establishing a new direction for physically grounded neural reconstruction.
authors: Lejia Ye, Yuhua Xu, Yulan Guo, Lian Xu, Xiaohu Zhang
bullets: Targets the difficulty of modeling mixed-reflectance scenes with a unified neural implicit framework.
Extracts macroscopic and microfacet normals from the SDF and enforces their consistency for physically plausible geometry.
Uses dual color branches: microfacet normals for high-frequency specular effects and reflection direction for diffuse and low-frequency components.
Adaptively blends color predictions using reflection priors rather than implicitly learned weights.
Reports robust, high-fidelity reconstruction and state-of-the-art performance across DTU, Shiny Blender, Ref-NeRF, and DeepVoxels.

papers.abstract: Executing a vision-language-action (VLA) policy involves deciding when to continue an attempt and when to intervene to improve its chances of success. We introduce ACRO, an Actor--Critic rollout orchestration layer that makes these decisions for a fixed VLA. ACRO seeks interventions that offer a more promising continuation, are physically feasible, and leave sufficient time to complete the task. A Critic learned from policy rollouts estimates success prospects to decide when to intervene and select a re-entry target along the executed trajectory. Trajectory Retraction shortcuts the visited path to return the robot to that target, where the same VLA resumes execution from a fresh observation. We evaluate ACRO with GR00T N1.7 and $\pi_{0.5}$ across SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and real-robot manipulation. Under the same physical execution budget, including all return motion, ACRO improves success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points, respectively. It also completes additional tasks as the execution budget grows. These results show that controlling when and where a policy resumes can turn its existing capabilities into more successful task executions. Project page: https://junhoo.me/acro
authors: Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Baekseung Kim, Minkyu Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak

Evaluated with GR00T N1.7 and π₀.₅ in simulation and real-robot manipulation, improving success by 10.4, 7.3, and 21.7 percentage points across the reported settings.
Also completes additional tasks when the available execution budget increases.

papers.abstract: Geometry foundation models estimate camera poses and 3D scene structure from video sequences, but maintaining consistent reconstructions over long horizons remains challenging. Feed-forward models process long sequences as independent, fixed-length frame windows and align their predictions, causing pose and reconstruction errors to accumulate across windows. Streaming models retain information from past frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when later observations reveal errors. To address this, we introduce Scaffold MemOry for Revision (SMORE), a framework equipping frozen geometry foundation models with a revisable external memory for long-horizon inference. Inspired by hippocampal associative memory in biological brains, which links spatial context with sensory experience, SMORE associates where an observer is with what it observes, enabling past observations to be stored, retrieved, verified against new evidence, and revised when inconsistencies are detected. We evaluate SMORE with eight competitive geometry models on five datasets spanning camera pose estimation, multi-view depth estimation, 3D point-cloud reconstruction, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), and novel view synthesis. Across all evaluated models, SMORE consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, reduces multi-view depth error by up to 58%, reduces Chamfer distance for 3D point-cloud reconstruction by up to 43%, and achieves average trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM. By retaining corrected poses and observations, SMORE further improves the fidelity and spatial consistency of large-scale 3D scene reconstruction. These results establish revisable external memory as a flexible interface for extending pretrained geometry models beyond fixed-context prediction toward iterative, error-correcting inference over long visual sequences.
authors: Soumick Sarker, Mengmi Zhang
bullets: Addresses error accumulation from fixed-window and non-revisable streaming inference on long video sequences.
Associates spatial context with observations so past geometry can be stored, retrieved, checked against new evidence, and revised.
Evaluated with eight geometry models across five tasks, including pose, depth, point-cloud reconstruction, SLAM, and novel view synthesis.
Consistently improves long-sequence pose estimation, with reported reductions of up to 58% in depth error and 43% in Chamfer distance.
Achieves trajectory error as low as 2.9 cm in long-horizon SLAM and improves large-scale scene consistency.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Limitations of existing 3D geometry models for long horizon and overview of our SMORE. A Limitations. Feed-forward models process long sequences in separate windows and subsequently stitch their predictions, causing errors to accumulate at window boundaries and yielding inconsistent camera poses and 3D geometry. B Limitations. Video streaming models retain information across video frames to inform future predictions, but cannot revise earlier estimates when subsequent observations reveal errors, leading to persistent pose drift and distorted geometry over long sequences. C SMORE Overview. SMORE introduces four memory operations: Store retains frames, camera poses, and 3D point maps in the content bank, while the scaffold associates spatial and visual information. Retrieve uses the current frame’s visual descriptor to find candidate past frames. Verify jointly processes the current window and retrieved pairs to see whether their past poses support consistent window placement. Revise uses the accepted evidence to update the global placements of affected windows, moving their stored cameras and geometry together.

papers.abstract: Action-chunking vision-language-action (VLA) models predict sequences of future robot actions. Under fixed-horizon execution, the robot executes a fixedlength prefix of each predicted chunk before invoking the policy again, leaving the remaining predictions unused. For a given number of executed actions, short execution horizons require more policy calls. Extending the execution horizon amortizes policy inference cost over more actions. However, uniformly applying long horizons across episodes can limit opportunities for precise corrections. To address this limitation, we propose PICES (Perturbation-Informed Chunk and Execution Horizon Selection), a training-free method that jointly selects an action chunk and the number of actions executed before the next policy call. Within a single policy call, the action expert generates a batch of action chunks from multiple initial noise samples and their locally perturbed counterparts, using the same conditioning features across all samples. PICES exploits differences between corresponding actions in each nominal chunk and its counterpart to determine candidate-specific execution horizons and select a nominal chunk for execution. Experiments on simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that PICES achieves speedup by up to 2.3x in wall-clock policy inference time on Jetson Orin and Thor relative to fixed horizon baselines while improving the success rate.
authors: Jehun Lee, Hajun Lee, Jimin Ryu, Youhan Lee, Beomseok Kang, Jonghyun Choi, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Fixed-horizon execution can waste predicted actions and incur excessive policy calls at short horizons.
PICES is training-free and jointly selects an action chunk and how many actions to execute before replanning.
It compares nominal action chunks with versions generated from locally perturbed noise samples under shared conditioning features.
Experiments in simulation and real-world manipulation show up to 2.3× faster wall-clock inference on Jetson Orin and Thor, with improved success rate.
The method targets adaptive execution: longer horizons for stable predictions and shorter horizons for precise corrections.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of PICES. Step 1: Draw N initial noise samples and construct a perturbed variant of each sample. Step 2: The action expert processes the resulting N(1 + 1) inputs in a single batch under the shared condition C, producing N nominal action chunks and their corresponding perturbed chunks. Step 3: Stepwise action sensitivity G (n) k is computed by comparing each nominal chunk with its perturbed counterparts. Step 4: Compute a sensitivity score Si for each nominal chunk by averaging its sensitivity over the first W steps and use this score to determine its execution horizon hi. PICES retains candidates whose scores are at or below the median and selects the nominal chunk with the longest execution horizon from the pool.

Figure 1: High-level idea of the PICES. papers.abstract: Hyperspectral imaging distinguishes RGB-similar objects, but a pretrained vision-language-action model needs a state its frozen decoder can use. SPECTRA-VLA provides a native-width spectral upgrade without retraining the visual encoder or action decoder. A learned continuous residual enriches each target token through its own normalized false-color reference; projection, norm control and validation-calibrated injection regulate the change. Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category balanced accuracy rises from 0.812 to 0.883. With identical residuals and scale, own-token addition improves reuse of an external category-derived probe on frozen decoder logits: 0.701 versus 0.590 with pooled replacement, at similar image-disjoint recognition. Five grouped tests covering the same 86 acquisitions recover within-category spectral shape with $R^2=0.802/0.337$ from continuous and posterior-code states. Category-matched spectral swaps further show that own-token composition approximately doubles the target-specific recovery increment after frozen decoding. Spectral enrichment and receiving-token preservation thus work together at the pretrained interface.

Uses native-width residual enrichment based on each token’s normalized false-color reference, with projection, norm control, and validation-calibrated injection.
Across 86 held-out acquisitions, category-balanced accuracy increases from 0.812 to 0.883.

papers.abstract: Typed decision models need an interface that can use additional reasoning while retaining candidate outputs. We train a shared candidate-answer reader on a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone to unify direct decisions with on-demand, interruptible reasoning. The reader returns distributions from empty and partial reasoning prefixes. A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests explicit reads, and an entropy rule accepts acquired answers and cancels generation. Measurements distinguish answer-query work, generated output, and pipeline time. Across 768 questions from ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge, accuracy rises from 70.96% for direct reading to 84.38%. Relative to 512-token terminal reading, accuracy improves by 7.29 percentage points with 2.25% more mean output work. Relative to 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time falls by 46.30% with an accuracy difference of -1.17 points. Exact-prefix controls isolate the saving from interruption, while read-scheduling controls distinguish reduced observation work from shorter response time.
authors: Bin Zheng, Zheng Chen
bullets: Addresses how typed decision models can invoke additional reasoning without discarding candidate outputs.
Uses a shared candidate-answer reader over a frozen Qwen3.5-4B backbone, supporting direct decisions and partial reasoning prefixes.
A benefit gate starts reasoning, a natural-state trigger requests reads, and an entropy rule accepts answers or interrupts generation.
Across 768 ProofWriter, LogiQA 2.0, and ARC-Challenge questions, accuracy increases from 70.96% to 84.38%.
Compared with 1,024-token terminal reading, pipeline time drops 46.30% with a 1.17-point accuracy decrease.

papers.title: Selective Reasoning for Typed Decision Models: When to Start, Read, and Stop
papers.tldr: A selective reading-and-stopping interface improves typed decision accuracy while reducing unnecessary reasoning and pipeline time.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning provides a direct mechanism for optimizing task objectives in large language model-driven agents, but task rewards are typically sparse trajectory-level signals that only evaluate task success, without directly supervising action-conditioned environment transitions, leaving the model with limited explicit understanding of action consequences and environment dynamics. Recent work introduces auxiliary supervision through policy and world modeling co-training, yet typically treats complete environmental observations uniformly as world modeling targets, overlooking the varying decision relevance of observation content. We propose DGS-WM (Decision-Guided Selective World Modeling), a decision-guided policy-world modeling co-training approach for language agents. DGS-WM employs a Decision-Guided Observation Selection component that filters observation units with decision value as world modeling targets based on their support for subsequent policy responses, and a Confidence-Adaptive Weighting component that adaptively adjusts supervision strength according to the model's prediction confidence on selected targets. Together, these components form a decision-aware auxiliary world modeling loss, jointly optimized with the RL loss on the same policy model. Across multiple benchmarks covering single-hop/multi-hop question answering and interactive web tasks, DGS-WM achieves consistent improvements under different model scales and RL algorithms, demonstrating more stable and effective performance compared to full-observation world modeling methods.
authors: Maolin Ran, Minda Chen, Di Huang, Wei Xiong, Fei Huang, Weiwen Liu
bullets: RL agents receive sparse task-level rewards, which provide limited supervision about action consequences and environment dynamics.
DGS-WM selects observation units for world-model training based on their value for subsequent policy decisions.
It adaptively weights selected targets according to the model’s prediction confidence.
The decision-aware world-modeling loss is jointly optimized with the RL objective on the same policy model.
Experiments across question-answering and interactive web tasks show consistent, more stable improvements across model scales and RL algorithms versus full-observation modeling.

Green highlights indicate selected content; gray text indicates filtered noise.

papers.abstract: Gaze coordinates attention in human interaction through coupled eye, head, and eyelid motion. A humanoid robot must choose where to look while generating a suitable movement toward that target; fixed tracking rules alone do not model the temporal structure of human gaze. We separate these tasks with an asynchronous vision-language model that selects a scene referent, a reactive perception module that maintains fixation, and a Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) that generates target-conditioned motion. RGT is a Transformer-VAE trained on markerless human recordings retargeted to the robot's 11-DoF joint space: self-supervised pretraining encodes recent full-head history, and autoregressive fine-tuning exposes the model to its own predictions during rollout. At inference, a four-dimensional binocular-eye trajectory conditions coordinated neck and eye motion; an auxiliary blink predictor triggers eyelid templates during playback. On a two-second benchmark in which all controllers receive the same ground-truth target, RGT-Base obtains the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE, and physical demonstrations show the integrated targeting and control pipeline. The evidence establishes robot-space kinematic fidelity and real-time RGT inference; perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary target-selection accuracy remain questions for controlled evaluation.
authors: Yuhang Hu, Junlin Lyu, Yuan Fang, Xiaoying Shen, Lechen Zhang, Jiong Lin, Judah Goldfeder, Steven Tian, Hod Lipson
bullets: Separates gaze target selection, fixation, and target-conditioned motion generation.
RGT uses a Transformer-VAE trained on retargeted markerless human gaze recordings in an 11-DoF robot joint space.
Self-supervised history encoding and autoregressive fine-tuning support realistic rollout behavior.
On a two-second shared-target benchmark, RGT-Base achieves the lowest reported overall seven-joint MSE.
Physical demonstrations show integrated targeting and control, while perceived naturalness and open-vocabulary selection remain unevaluated.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT) pipeline. The left panel illustrates our hierarchical perception system operating on a real humanoid robot. Egocentric video from the camera-embedded eyes, together with high-level natural language instructions, is processed by a slow-system VLM that reasons over the environmental context and designates salient targets. A fastsystem Visual Perception Module then tracks the selected faces in real time to produce a continuous target gaze direction. The right panel depicts the RGT architecture: a History Full-head Motion Tokenizer encodes recent facial dynamics while an Eyeball Trajectory Generator encodes the target gaze, and a Transformer-VAE fuses both streams into a latent representation from which it predicts future motion. The Action De-Tokenizer maps the near-future tokens to 11-DoF joint commands on the physical robot. The quantitative benchmark evaluates motion generation with ground-truth eye targets; target selection is illustrated by the physical demonstration.

Figure 2: Full pipeline of the Realistic Gaze Transformer (RGT). Top: Data preprocessing stage. Raw human motion sequences (head pose, eye gaze, and blinks) are segmented into clips. Blink events are detected and extracted as separate blink templates (small eyelid motion sequences), and those blink segments are removed from the sequences to produce blink-free training data. Bottom: Model architecture and inference. Given a past full-head motion sequence and a planned eyeball motion sequence, the Transformer-VAE model (encoder and decoder) predicts a future blink-free trajectory along with blink probabilities for each future frame. At inference time, when a blink is predicted (high probability), a corresponding blink template is injected into the generated trajectory, yielding the final full-head motion with realistic blinks (red frames show the injected blink).

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of gaze behaviors across controllers. Each row shows a time sequence of robot face images during a representative leftward gaze shift. Top: Ground-truth human motion (GT) exhibits coordinated eye–head motion, with eyes leading the head. Second: RGT reproduces the illustrated sequence’s eye–head timing. Third: Eyes-Only rotates the eyes to mechanical extremes while keeping the head fixed, resulting in strained, unnatural motion. Bottom: Head-Only turns the head abruptly toward the target while leaving the eyes static, exaggerating head movement and yielding sluggish gaze redirection. Each column represents 1/3 second of motion.

(Bottom) Lagged Pearson correlation peaks at a positive lag of approximately 20 frames (333 ms), consistent with eye motion preceding head motion in these recordings. papers.title: Eye, Robot: Learning Expressive Gaze Dynamics via a VLM-Guided Transformer-VAE

papers.abstract: Recent work has explored visual reasoning through image generation, where models solve visual-reasoning problems by directly generating solution images. Intuitively, iterative samplers such as flow matching are well suited to this task, since each sampling step may resemble one reasoning step. However, in this work, from a circuit complexity perspective, we show that this intuition is misleading. We prove that as long as the model outputs satisfy certain mild regularity conditions, the trajectory of the vanilla flow-matching sampler can be simulated by a constant number of sequential rounds of parallel model evaluations. Consequently, additional sampling steps cannot increase the expressive power of a constant-depth backbone model under the standard complexity-theoretic model of transformers. We then reveal that self-conditioning, which conditions the model on the previous step's estimate of the final image, plays a previously unrecognized role in removing this bottleneck. Controlled experiments on diverse visual-reasoning tasks show that flow matching with self-conditioning achieves higher accuracy and greater reasoning depth than vanilla flow matching, and its performance improves with more sampling steps. Theoretically, we prove that with self-conditioning, a constant-depth backbone can achieve expressive power equivalent to that of space-bounded Turing machines. Our study suggests a design principle for future visual reasoning research: carry more information between sampling steps, so that additional steps translate into deeper reasoning.
authors: Zeyang Zhang, Linxiang Gao, Meiqi Gu, Xingyan Chen, Minrui Luo, Kaifeng Lyu, Tianxing He
bullets: Vanilla flow-matching trajectories can be simulated with only a constant number of parallel model-evaluation rounds under mild regularity conditions.
Therefore, adding sampling steps alone does not increase the expressive power of constant-depth transformer backbones.
Self-conditioning passes the previous estimate of the final image between steps, removing this computational bottleneck.
Experiments across diverse visual-reasoning tasks show higher accuracy, greater reasoning depth, and continued improvement with more sampling steps when self-conditioning is used.
The theory shows that self-conditioned constant-depth backbones can match the expressive power of space-bounded Turing machines.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes self-conditioning in flow matching for visual reasoning, providing a transferable technical insight for deep sequential reasoning in generative models.
papers.title: Self-Conditioning Enables Deep Sequential Reasoning in Flow Matching
papers.tldr: Self-conditioning allows flow-matching samplers to use additional steps for genuinely deeper visual reasoning, overcoming a limitation of vanilla flow matching.

papers.abstract: Differentiable reinforcement learning shows strong promise for robot policy learning, but its application to legged locomotion has remained limited to blind walking or simulated 2D tasks. Extending it to end-to-end visual obstacle avoidance is challenging because hard collision constraints and early termination upon contact corrupt first-order gradients, trapping optimizers in local minima. We present E2DRL, which addresses this with a soft differentiable obstacle-interaction formulation: penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints with velocity-conditioned stop-gradient shaping to provide the first-order training signals for 3D obstacle avoidance. To realize a deployable perception-control system, a privileged teacher trained via Soft Analytic Policy Optimization (SAPO) in a differentiable simulator is distilled into a recurrent depth-based student via DAgger, then blended with a base locomotion policy using a terrain-aware gating module for deployment. In simulation, E2DRL achieves higher sample efficiency than PPO and demonstrates superior velocity-tracking performance and 3D obstacle-avoidance capability compared with both PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC. We present the first sim-to-real validation of end-to-end differentiable RL for 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.
authors: Cheng Fan, Bingyang Zhou, Gang Yang, Zixuan Zhuang, Aoqian Zhang, Pengzhi Yang, Xin Liu, Chunzheng Wang, Yan Rui Tan, Fan Shi
bullets: Addresses gradient corruption from hard collisions and early termination in differentiable RL for legged obstacle avoidance.
Uses velocity-conditioned, stop-gradient shaping with penetration penalties across multiple body keypoints.
Distills a privileged SAPO teacher into a recurrent depth-based student using DAgger, then blends it with locomotion control through terrain-aware gating.
In simulation, shows higher sample efficiency than PPO and improved velocity tracking and obstacle avoidance versus PPO and Duality-based DCBF NMPC.
Demonstrates sim-to-real 3D obstacle avoidance on a Unitree Go2 in static and dynamic environments.

papers.selection_reason: Differentiable RL with soft obstacle interaction for 3D visual obstacle avoidance in quadruped robots, with sim-to-real deployment.
papers.title: E2DRL: End-to-End Differentiable Reinforcement Learning for 3D Obstacle Avoidance in Quadruped Robots
papers.tldr: E2DRL enables end-to-end differentiable visual 3D obstacle avoidance for quadruped robots by replacing hard collision handling with soft, gradient-preserving interaction penalties and deploying a distilled perception-control policy.

papers.abstract: We propose DAGFormer, a Transformer language model whose cross-layer connections are planned by a jointly trained topology predictor. Beyond the residual connections in a standard Transformer, DAGFormer adds direct connections from earlier layers to later ones, and the predictor controls the strength of every connection based on input tokens. Unlike existing cross-layer routing architectures, which set each layer's connections separately, DAGFormer plans the routing of the whole model at once. On matched OLMo-2 pairs from 75M to 1B parameters, DAGFormer lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 17% to 25% over the vanilla Transformer, and a 1B DAGFormer trained on 5B tokens outperforms the vanilla model trained on 10B. Against four routing baselines with the same data and budget, it reaches the lowest perplexity at 75M, 300M and 1B. The gain carries over to 13 commonsense, science, reading and math evaluation tasks (2.0 to 2.5 points higher mean accuracy at 300M and 1B) and to instruction finetuning (63% to 70% AlpacaEval win rate against the vanilla Transformer, leading every routing baseline), and under structured pruning DAGFormer degrades the least in five of six settings.
authors: Xiaocong Yang, Yuren Hao, ChengXiang Zhai
bullets: Adds direct connections from earlier to later layers beyond standard residual links.
A jointly trained topology predictor plans the full model’s routing at once, rather than layer by layer.
Reduces WikiText-2 perplexity by 17–25% over matched vanilla Transformers from 75M to 1B parameters.
Improves mean accuracy on 13 downstream tasks and achieves higher AlpacaEval win rates after instruction finetuning.
Shows greater robustness to structured pruning in five of six tested settings.

papers.abstract: Single-image 3D reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet standalone garments remain challenging due to thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered structures. Existing datasets and evaluation protocols provide limited support for systematic evaluation in this setting. We introduce MagicGarment, a benchmark for single-image standalone 3D garment reconstruction with 1,518 professionally constructed assets across 17 composite garment types, aligned multimodal annotations, and a unified evaluation protocol. We further establish a garment-aware reference baseline by adapting a pretrained image-to-3D backbone at two levels: Grounded Semantic Refinement (GSR) provides garment-focused visual conditioning, while Flow-Time-Route LoRA (FTR-LoRA) adapts the frozen 3D generative backbone using flow-timestep, token-routing, and expert-load information. Experiments demonstrate MagicGarment's benchmark utility and the effectiveness of garment-aware adaptation. Project page: https://1019538157.github.io/MagicGarment/.
authors: Jia Chen, Ruyang Zhao, Jun Bai, Chao Huang, Saishang Zhong, Xinrong Hu
bullets: Addresses challenges from thin-shell geometry, open boundaries, and layered garment structures.
Provides 1,518 professionally constructed assets spanning 17 composite garment types.
Includes aligned multimodal annotations and a unified evaluation protocol.
Adapts a pretrained image-to-3D model with garment-focused visual conditioning and flow-aware LoRA refinement.
Experiments show the benchmark is useful and the garment-aware adaptation is effective.

papers.abstract: Object-goal navigation requires an embodied agent to explore an unfamiliar environment, identify a target object, navigate toward candidate instances, and reliably determine whether the observed object satisfies the mission goal. This work investigates this problem through a two-stage development process. In Stage I, a fixed modular framework is used to examine combinations of exploration, object detection, and target validation methods. The results reveal clear trade-offs among navigation performance, validation reliability, execution time, and model-related cost, with no single fixed configuration remaining preferable across all evaluated conditions. These observations motivate F2A-ObjectNav (Fixed-to-Adaptive Object-Goal Navigation), an adaptive agentic architecture in which a rule-based Supervisor coordinates specialized components for navigation and exploration, object detection, target validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory. The architecture uses event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional semantic guidance while retaining lightweight execution during normal operation. F2A-ObjectNav is evaluated over 25 episodes in each of AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, achieving success rate (SR) / success-weighted path length (SPL) values of 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37, respectively. In addition to task-level metrics, architecture-specific behavioral metrics are used to characterize semantic-guidance usage, strategy switching, recovery activation, memory-supported behavior, and decision stability. The results show different patterns of adaptive intervention across the three environments, with higher intervention frequencies observed in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR than in AI2-THOR.
authors: Seyed Ali Mirghasemi, Alireza Taheri
bullets: Object-goal navigation requires exploration, object detection, target validation, and reliable mission completion in unfamiliar environments.

A rule-based Supervisor dynamically manages navigation, exploration, detection, validation, semantic guidance, and Mission Memory.
Event-driven recovery, strategy revision, candidate management, and conditional guidance support adaptive behavior while keeping normal execution lightweight.
Across AI2-THOR, RoboTHOR, and ProcTHOR, SR/SPL were 0.84/0.52, 0.40/0.22, and 0.44/0.37; adaptive interventions were more frequent in RoboTHOR and ProcTHOR.

papers.abstract: Instruction-Conditioned Motion Control (ICMC) separates parameter specification, instruction generation, and code synthesis for language-driven robot control, making execution outcomes traceable to instructions and programs. We compare one-shot generation with ICMC under o1 and o4-mini on cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks for a UR5e arm in MuJoCo. We then train an open-weight instruction policy by GRPO through a frozen code generator on cube placement onto two- and five-cube letter layouts, averaging the rewards of five programs per instruction. The logged positive-reward rate rose from 31.6% to 35.3% (253/800 to 282/800) between the first and last five training steps. A log audit identifies positive binary labels associated with geometric-failure messages: at least 19 in that run, 18 in the dense-reward run, and 5 in the run with one program per instruction. In one case, all five rewards were 1.0 while the log reports a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance; the verdict came from the program's own output stream. We distinguish logged reward rates from independently verified task success and report descriptive results for each configuration's single training trajectory. We introduce an independent evaluation protocol that checks task completion against fixed specifications, separating robot control from success assessment to support reproducible evaluation.
authors: Fan Huang, Dezhong Tong, Changyu Chen, Haewoon Kwak, Jisun An
bullets: Evaluates one-shot generation versus ICMC on UR5e cube pick-and-place and letter-reshaping tasks in MuJoCo using o1 and o4-mini.
Trains an open-weight instruction policy with GRPO through a frozen code generator, averaging rewards from five programs per instruction.
Logged positive-reward rates increased from 31.6% to 35.3% over the reported five-step trajectory, but these rates were not always consistent with independently verified task success.
Audits found positive labels for geometric failures, including a case where all five rewards were 1.0 despite a 0.9515 m miss against a 0.05 m tolerance.
Proposes independent evaluation against fixed task specifications to separate robot control from success assessment.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot's URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.

papers.abstract: Modern vision-language models can accept multi-image contexts, but aggregate accuracy rarely reveals where a multi-image reasoning pipeline fails. We study a controlled schema-application task in which a model must locate two target characters in a 16-image sequence, identify their visual attributes, consult an item-specific visual codebook, and compose two ordered nonce code names. We introduce a within-item 2-by-2 factorial Oracle design: Oracle-A supplies a verified textual schema, Oracle-B supplies a verified ordered target-appearance representation, and both interventions retain the original images and final question. Across 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed model responses, Oracle-B increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 46.3 to 63.0) and outperformed Oracle-A by 60.6 points (Holm-adjusted p-value no greater than .0002). An auxiliary retrieval diagnostic reached only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy even after removing code-name generation. Providing both Oracle sources yielded 100% accuracy across all models. These results localize the dominant recoverable deficit to upstream ordered instance recovery rather than primarily to downstream schema use and composition.
authors: Yiliu Xu, Xinjin Li, Yu Ma
bullets: The task requires locating two characters across 16 images, identifying their attributes, consulting a visual codebook, and composing ordered nonce names.

Providing ordered target appearances increased strict exact accuracy by 54.6 percentage points; it outperformed schema provision by 60.6 points.
An auxiliary diagnostic achieved only 49.1% ordered-appearance accuracy, while supplying both Oracle sources produced 100% accuracy across all models.
Findings are scoped to this controlled schema-application task and its 72 new items and 1,188 analyzed responses.

papers.abstract: Long-output inference in large language models suffers from severe KV cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks. While KV cache quantization alleviates this issue, low-bit quantization (e.g., 2-bit) severely degrades model accuracy. Recent mixed-precision key-cache quantization methods mitigate this degradation by allocating higher precision to important key channels, but estimate channel saliency using only key statistics. Through attention logit perturbation analysis at the RoPE channel-pair level, we show that quantization errors in channel pairs with large query--key pair-norm products contribute significantly to logit variation. Based on this insight, we propose PN-Mix, a mixed-precision key-cache quantization method for RoPE-based decoder-only LLMs, which allocates higher precision to salient channel pairs identified once during the prefill stage and reused throughout decoding. Across standard reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks, PN-Mix with 2.26-bit average precision achieves comparable or better average accuracy than prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32--2.39 bits. Furthermore, in our Pareto sweep, PN-Mix degrades gracefully down to 1.5 bits, whereas the compared baselines exhibit sharper performance drops below 2.25 bits.
authors: Gil Jae Song, Sungjoo Yoo
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory and bandwidth bottlenecks in long-output LLM inference.
Uses RoPE channel-pair attention-logit perturbation analysis to identify salient pairs via query–key pair-norm products.
Assigns higher precision to salient key pairs once during prefill and reuses the allocation during decoding.
At 2.26-bit average precision, matches or outperforms prior mixed-precision methods using 2.32–2.39 bits across reasoning, code-generation, and AIME benchmarks.
Degrades more gracefully to 1.5 bits than compared baselines, which show sharper drops below 2.25 bits.

papers.abstract: Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with physical observations that can guide action selection and execution. However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol. ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with 1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria. We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on a shared $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves success rates across all three task categories. Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on physical-property inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on assembly. Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline, but only Prompt Fusion improves every task. These findings support ForceBench's practical value for identifying the benefits and limitations of force integration across manipulation demands. The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/.
authors: Xuan Han, Zinuo Jin, Tianlin Li, Yunfan Lou, Xin Liu, Yuchen Xue, Yuanpeng He, Boxian Yao, Shuhan Zhan, Ruihai Wu, Zhibo Pang

Predictive and temporal benefits are strongest for physical-property inference, while temporal designs underperform on assembly.

papers.abstract: Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong performance on local robot manipulation, yet their success does not readily translate to long-horizon mobile manipulation. In our experiments, a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks but only 19% when these skills are composed into mobile manipulation. We argue that this gap stems from failures across the execution process rather than from local manipulation capability alone. To uncover these bottlenecks, we systematically diagnose failures in long-horizon mobile manipulation and identify three dominant regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. Based on this diagnosis, we develop failure-guided agentic intervention that augments a fixed subtask VLA with demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment. On RoboCasa365, these interventions progressively improve task success from 19% to 47%, with the finalized system reaching 49% on held-out episode seeds, compared with 18% for the baseline. The same design improves performance from 14% to 37% on BEHAVIOR-1K and from 5/20 to 13/20 on real-robot tasks. These results suggest that reliable mobile manipulation can be advanced by diagnosing and intervening on the current bottleneck, rather than uniformly scaling the underlying policy. Our code will be released at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/Cracking-Mobile-Manipulation.git.
authors: Zixuan Wang, Jia-Ning Li, Yinzhou Tang, Yanzhao Yu, Biao Wu, Meng Fang, Xin Li, Yiwu Zhong

Success improves from 19% to 47% on RoboCasa365, reaching 49% on held-out seeds versus 18% for the baseline.
The approach also improves results on BEHAVIOR-1K and real-robot tasks, supporting bottleneck-focused intervention over uniform policy scaling.

papers.tldr: Diagnosing bottlenecks across planning, navigation, and manipulation enables targeted agentic interventions that substantially improve long-horizon mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20\% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
authors: Keqiang Ren, Xuecheng Ye, Hanyu Liu, Zhihua Wang, Tao Jian, Yunsheng Ma, Jiayi Wen, Xinran Li, Zhigong Song
bullets: Addresses motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arms, and hands, plus error accumulation in long-horizon tasks.
Decouples the 29-DoF action space into hand, arm, and mobile-base branches within a Hierarchical Modular Framework.
Uses COMET cross-attention for inter-module coordination and vision-language-model task decomposition to limit temporal error propagation.
Adds full-palm 2D tactile sensing to represent distributed contact signals across modules.
On a physical 29-DoF robot, achieves over 20% higher task success than mainstream baselines across varied long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory -- rather than a chat conversation -- is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool -- machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.
authors: Carson Eisenach, Robert Joseph George, Vincent Quenneville-Belair, Kate Gwimm, Dean Foster
bullets: Targets multi-call agent work involving tools, external systems, other agents, humans, and self-written code.
Stores the full computation state in Git, enabling resume, rewind, fork, comparison, and merge instead of relying on chat history.
Provides primitives for waiting, communication, delegation, and undo; agents can turn procedures into sealed Lean tools whose types specify permissions.
Uses reversibility to assign tool review tiers, allowing autonomous execution where effects can be safely undone.
An untuned system achieves roughly two-thirds of its unsafe shell-equipped pass rate on Terminal-Bench using only safe tools.
