Figure 11: Two ways to collect the TODOs in a tree. Left: the agent is the loop, and every file costs model calls and context. Right: the agent writes the scan as a sealed program that runs under the tokens it already holds; each file is read and matched with no model call, and the model reasons once, over the summary.

Figure 7: From grant to system call, for a child with one project worktree and no network. The grant decides which tokens exist, the tokens decide which tools the model is offered, and each call carries its token to the provider, which checks its scope again.

Figure 12: L3M on one host. One daemon serves every hub on the host, and a hub is a folder: a bare repository, a forest of ACRs, its settings and a cache. Sessions are processes that the daemon starts and that call the model themselves. The human’s own settings name the hubs, the models and the credentials.

Figure 2: The body of an agent. Its write roots are worktrees on its own branches; the harness’s checkouts are denied to it; the rest of the agent is refs the harness writes and the agent reaches only through tools.

Figure 4: What the model sees is a pure function of the Log. Record 6 is retracted by the rewind at 7; the machine record at 3 lowers to nothing; the budget note at 5 becomes a delta that the dialect folds into the next user turn.

Figure 9: How a ceiling is known. An undo is a Reversible instance, which carries its proof; each class’s evidence is typed by the ceiling it supports; and the file class cites the round trip of one anchored write. The law that reversing twice is the identity is omitted.

Figure 20: One instance of improving agents inside L3M. Every arrow is an L3M primitive: a persona branch forks and syncs, a parent reads its children’s Logs, a program summarizes them and the model proposes edits, and a human publishes the result.

Figure 13: A tree of agents at spawn time. Each child’s grant lies within its parent’s, and its fuel is lent from the parent’s. A request that exceeds either is refused. The private child keeps the project’s refs but not the right to push them. The two children are the peers of Section 5.2.

Figure 15: Mail between hubs. The sender’s authority ends at its own outbox; carrying mail across machines is the postmaster’s duty, and only the human’s settings name the offices. Read marks travel back the same way, as receipts.

Figure 14: A letter, and its address. The host writes every field that says who sent a letter and when; the model writes the rest. An address names five parties, the persona being the agent’s name, and stars one. A letter for another hub adds the office and the recipient.

Figure 6: An effect class, its token, and a tool body written over them. The body’s type is its permission: it names NetEffects and nothing else, so it cannot reach IO, and the hosts it may fetch from are the ones its token carries.
Figure 8: A grant is a record of axes, a child’s grant is a meet with its parent’s, and the bound is a theorem.

Figure 10: A sealed program’s type is its permission request. The body is polymorphic in the host monad, so it can reach the world only through the eleven classes it is given, and Confined admits only the classes the program lists in footprint. ProgramCaps holds the tokens the agent’s grant minted, including the child-lifecycle door when the grant may spawn.

Figure 17: A staged build across two agents. Fetch sees only public lockfiles and warms a cache; build and run have no network. The builder cannot run what it built, though its build recipes execute inside the build sandbox; the runner receives the artifact by digest, cannot change it, and writes only a fresh output directory.

Figure 21: The bottleneck. A private parent P holds the secrets and has no network; its child C has the network and no secrets. Every message across the boundary is a metered edge, and the charged direction is private to public (orange). P seeds C with k bytes (1); C works publicly and returns a menu of N options (2); P answers with a selection (3), so at most log2 N bits leave the private side however much P read. In L3M this is a spawn pattern over the grants of Section 5.2.

Figure 5: The event loop. Signal sources and activities only post signals, and the sequencer alone appends to the Log. Each pass accepts what is consistent with the Log, journals the hooks’ decisions, folds the Log to decide what is owed, stores it, and only then starts the activities it names, so a kill at any point is repaired by the next pass.

Figure 18: Why the split bounds leakage. (a) An agent whose grant holds both the source and the network can leak through every byte it sends. (b) Split into peers with different grants that talk only by mail, the private side’s contribution to anything leaving is the seed, however much traffic the researcher does, under the channel model of the text. Arrow width stands for volume; orange marks bytes that may carry the source.

Figure 19: A quarantined reader. The program hands the page to a fresh subagent Q whose grant is empty, and parses its reply into one of three words fixed in advance. A page that hijacks Q gains a model that holds nothing, and can change only which word reaches A. Arrow width stands for volume; orange marks bytes that may carry an injected instruction.

Figure 16: Write, gate, execute: W⊕X for authority. No party both writes bytes and runs them, and the gate’s approval names the exact bytes. The staged build of Figure 17 is the same shape with two agents.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice. We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy's progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model $\pi_{0.5}$ and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control. Additional results and videos are available on the project website (https://policy-improvement-wm.pages.dev/).
authors: Colton Crosby, Hao Wang, Mac Schwager, Somil Bansal
bullets: Addresses deployment-time failures that nominal policies cannot predict or recover from without retraining or new data collection.
Learns a policy-conditioned liveness value from labeled on-policy rollouts to measure progress toward task completion.
Trains a compact latent world model from on-policy rollouts and play data, then plans short corrective interventions when progress is lost.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Goal and a Franka Panda using π₀.₅ and a diffusion policy, with reported task-success improvements and real-time control.
Scope: interventions rely on offline training data and black-box query access to the nominal policy.

papers.abstract: Real-world engineering drawings are often large-format and information-dense. Answering practical engineering questions therefore requires both fine-grained understanding of engineering information and complex reasoning over objects, relations, and evidence distributed across different regions or views. Existing benchmarks cover a range of engineering-drawing understanding tasks involving local regions, individual views, specific elements, or more constrained visual settings. However, systematic evaluation of understanding over realistic, large-format engineering drawings remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce LED-BENCH, a multidisciplinary benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained understanding and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings, spanning the mechanical, architectural, and transportation domains. Extensive evaluation of 11 representative multimodal large language models, including 8 proprietary models and 3 open-source models, reveals substantial remaining difficulty: GPT-5.6 Sol achieves 52.65% average accuracy, performance varies across engineering domains, and all evaluated models perform worse on questions requiring broader evidence integration. These results highlight fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning over large-format engineering drawings as persistent challenges for current multimodal models.

bullets: Covers mechanical, architectural, and transportation engineering domains.

Results identify fine-grained understanding, evidence integration, and complex reasoning as persistent challenges.

papers.abstract: A spatial answer depends on the reference frame specified in language and its supporting visual evidence. Item accuracy alone obscures whether correctness persists when either changes. We introduce Frame Evidence, a benchmark of 320 matched triplets and 960 Chinese multiple-choice questions from captured and rendered scenes. One family compares three grounded reference frames over fixed images. The other pairs image deletion annotated as insufficient with answer-preserving addition. Joint metrics require correct answers across all three frames and paired evidence variants. Across 20 configurations on 288 held-out questions, GPT three-shot reaches 50.00\% item accuracy, but the best three-frame group accuracy is 5/48 (10.42\%), reached by GPT two-shot. Few-shot prompting and task-specific adaptation improve item accuracy without consistently improving joint correctness. Input controls show where images support matched success, while repeated executions reveal answer instability beneath similar scores.

papers.abstract: An early mistake in the generated reasoning can constrain all subsequent reasoning. Repeated-generation methods, like MCMC-based approaches, attempt to improve output quality by sampling multiple generations, but their effectiveness can be limited by randomly selecting where to regenerate. On MATH500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B, we find that incorrect responses have substantially higher mean token entropy than correct responses, with an average within-question relative increase of approximately 112%, suggesting that entropy can signal reasoning errors. Motivated by this finding, we introduce REWIND, a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to propose targeted suffix regenerations. Across three model families and five benchmarks, REWIND outperforms all baselines, with gains of 0.51-10.00 percentage points over the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted, uncertainty-guided trajectory repair across models and tasks. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rewind-D310.
authors: Yi Ding, Mengyu Wang, Min Zhou, Menglin Yang
bullets: Early reasoning mistakes can constrain all later generated steps.
Incorrect responses show substantially higher mean token entropy than correct ones, motivating entropy-based error detection.
REWIND is a training-free controller that uses entropy dynamics to target suffix regeneration instead of choosing regeneration points randomly.

The approach is evaluated for targeted trajectory repair across multiple models and tasks.

papers.abstract: Lipreading remains challenging due to the inherent ambiguity of visual speech cues and their sensitivity to head pose and video resolution. In this work, we propose FLARE, a framework for robust visual speech representation learning via cross-modal distillation and joint face-lip modeling. FLARE leverages semantically rich Whisper representations as the acoustic teacher signal, converting them into discrete distillation targets through a random-projection quantizer and pretraining the model with a masked prediction objective. To capture complementary visual information, FLARE employs a dual-stream architecture that jointly processes lip region-of-interest (ROI) and full-face inputs, where the lip stream captures finegrained articulatory motion and the face stream encodes broader facial dynamics. During pretraining, auxiliary audio input is incorporated to facilitate cross-modal alignment, and modality dropout is applied to encourage robust visual-only representations. For downstream lipreading, FLARE serves as a visual encoder coupled with either a lightweight Transformer decoder or an LLM-based decoder. Evaluated on LRS2, LRS3, and the out-of-domain WildVSR benchmark, FLARE achieves strong lipreading performance, with word error rates of 11.7%, 13.2%, and 34.3%, respectively. A progressive design study confirms the contribution of each major component. Further analyses demonstrate that joint face-lip modeling improves robustness under degraded video resolution and large head pose variation, while yielding more phoneme-discriminative visual representations. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/jxzhanggg/FLARE.

papers.abstract: Foundation models for dynamical systems can forecast unseen partial differential equations (PDEs), ordinary differential equations (ODEs), and time series during inference. However, it remains an open question whether these foundation models truly learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies. We show that looped transformers are capable of emulating propagators for dynamical systems in-context by first establishing a link between linear attention and (extended) dynamic mode decomposition. We then generalize this insight into the $\textit{Test-Time Forecasting}$ (TTF) framework in which a one-step forecaster leverages iterations of gradient descent as recurrent depth. We demonstrate that lightweight TTF models trained on ODEs and PDEs generalize to out-of-distribution system dynamics during autoregressive rollout after being trained for one-step prediction. Our results reinforce TTF as a theoretically motivated framework for designing recurrent depth models capable of forecasting unseen dynamical systems at test-time.
authors: Jeffrey B. Lai, John Quinn, Anthony Bao, William Gilpin
bullets: Addresses whether foundation models learn generalizable in-context forecasting strategies for unseen ODEs, PDEs, and time series.
Links looped transformers and linear attention to dynamic mode decomposition, motivating their ability to emulate dynamical propagators.
Introduces TTF, where repeated gradient-descent iterations provide recurrent depth at test time.
Shows models trained only for one-step prediction on ODEs and PDEs can generalize to out-of-distribution dynamics during autoregressive rollout.
Scope: the abstract does not report specific datasets, numerical gains, or limitations beyond the demonstrated ODE/PDE setting.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation requires a global planner that connects visually specified endpoints while providing observations that a local policy can follow. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides map-registered RGB, opacity, and depth renderings, but does not explicitly encode navigable topology. We introduce \method, a Gaussian visual roadmap whose milestones, local connections, and visual references are constructed directly through 3DGS rendering without deriving an occupancy grid or signed distance field. We define render-based collision-free (RC-free) configurations and paths. Panoramic depth supplies conservative clearance for milestone validation and adaptive coverage, while edge-aligned orthographic rendering tests the robot's swept volume. We establish conditional soundness and sufficient conditions for deterministic query completeness and probabilistic construction completeness of GS-PRM. To validate the performance of GS-PRM, we conduct experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating long-horizon navigation using goal-conditioned policies guided by GS-PRM. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS-based navigation system, our GS-PRM-based navigation system achieves up to a twice higher average success rate and reduces travel time by up to 57.2% when both systems complete the navigation task.
authors: Ashraf Siddique, Kyung Min Han, Young J. Kim
bullets: Addresses the gap between 3DGS visual rendering and explicit navigable topology for global planning.
Constructs milestones, local connections, and visual references using 3DGS-rendered RGB, opacity, and depth.
Uses panoramic depth for conservative clearance and adaptive coverage, plus edge-aligned orthographic rendering to test swept-volume collisions.
Provides conditional soundness and completeness guarantees for deterministic queries and probabilistic roadmap construction.
Validated in simulated and real-world environments, achieving up to 2× higher average success and 57.2% shorter travel time than a state-of-the-art 3DGS navigation system when tasks are completed.

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis but requires significant storage and transmission resources. Mapping Gaussian attributes to 2D representations enables efficient compression using mature image codecs. However, Gaussian representations that achieve comparable rendering quality are generally treated similarly during optimization, despite substantial differences in coding rate, leading to limited rate-distortion (R-D) performance after compression. To address this limitation, we propose RDCompGS, a 3DGS compression method that enables overall R-D optimization of Gaussian representations with respect to subsequent coding. A differentiable estimate of the coding rate is incorporated into the R-D optimization with rendering distortion. The rate constraint adjustment model further regulates the R-D trade-off across different compression conditions. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that RDCompGS achieves average Bj{\o}ntegaard Delta Rate reductions of 37.84% and 49.31% with H.265/HEVC and JPEG XL, respectively. The estimated rate also shows a strong correlation with the actual bit-rate under different compression conditions.
authors: Huiping Ren, Shuai Wan, Luqian Bai, Zhang Chen, Fuzheng Yang
bullets: Targets the high storage and transmission cost of 3DGS while preserving novel-view rendering quality.
Maps Gaussian attributes to 2D representations and incorporates differentiable coding-rate estimates into rate-distortion optimization.
Uses a rate-constraint adjustment model to control the trade-off across compression conditions.
Across three benchmark datasets, reduces average BD-Rate by 37.84% with H.265/HEVC and 49.31% with JPEG XL.
Estimated rates strongly correlate with actual bitrates under varying compression conditions.

papers.abstract: As a lightweight and highly accurate method for nearest-neighbor search in 3D point clouds, approaches based on space-filling curves (SFC) have been proposed. However, due to the inherent properties of SFC, a gap arises between proximity relationships along the SFC and those in the original Euclidean space. In this study, we propose a loss function that reduces the influence of this gap. Specifically, we compute the distances between adjacent points along the SFC and train the model to optimize feature similarity between pairs of points that are distant from each other in the original 3D space. We incorporate the proposed method into a high-performing 3D point cloud segmentation model and evaluate its effectiveness on three datasets. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms conventional methods on both indoor and outdoor point cloud datasets.
authors: Konan Sasaki, Junya Komori, Kazuhiro Hotta
bullets: SFC-based neighbor search is efficient but can connect points that are far apart in 3D space.
The method computes distances between adjacent points along the SFC.
It trains feature similarity for point pairs that are distant in Euclidean space but close along the SFC.
The loss is integrated into a high-performing 3D point-cloud segmentation model.
Evaluation on three datasets shows improvement over conventional methods in both indoor and outdoor settings.

papers.abstract: Retrieving external knowledge can improve large language model (LLM) translation by providing supplementary information such as idiom interpretations and terminology. However, existing retrieval-augmented machine translation systems typically apply predefined retrieval strategies uniformly across all inputs. We argue that translation operates in a partial-evidence regime: LLM's parametric knowledge suffices for many inputs, while external evidence benefits a subset and usually supports rather than directly provides the desired translation. This creates two challenges: deciding when to retrieve and what evidence to acquire. We introduce Selective Retrieval-Augmented Translation (SRAT), an agentic reinforcement learning framework that learns when to translate directly or retrieve, what to retrieve, and how to integrate these decisions by optimizing final translation quality. To align evidence retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than simple semantic similarity, we further develop joint Plackett--Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training for retriever-training. Experiments on idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation with offline or online retrieval show that SRAT consistently outperforms never- and always-retrieve baselines, and quality-aligned retriever training provides further gains when similarity-based retrieval is insufficient. The results demonstrate the benefit of treating retrieval as a learnable translation action rather than fixed preprocessing.
authors: Shijun Li, Yang Liu, Najmeh Sadoughi, Dongmei Wang, Xinjie Li, Zhu Liu, Rohith Mysore Vijaya Kumar, Yuzong Liu
bullets: Existing retrieval-augmented translation retrieves uniformly, despite many inputs being solvable from the LLM’s parametric knowledge.
SRAT uses agentic reinforcement learning to decide whether to retrieve, what evidence to seek, and how to use it.
Joint Plackett–Luce optimization and translation-quality contrastive training align retrieval with downstream translation quality rather than similarity alone.
Experiments across idiom, knowledge-intensive, and document-level translation show consistent gains over never- and always-retrieve baselines.
The approach treats retrieval as a learnable translation action, with benefits shown under both offline and online retrieval.

papers.abstract: We devise a dual-arm cooperative planning framework for wiping table surface in the presence of scattered objects. Unlike conventional surface-cleaning strategies that only cover free areas and detour around obstacles, our framework explicitly assigns one arm to rearrange objects while the other performs coverage wiping, thereby enabling access to previously obstructed regions. Specifically, we first construct a set of wiping and object-rearrangement action primitives. Based on these primitives, we introduce Geo-MILP, a geometry-aware task planner formulated as Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP). By integrating Logic-Based Benders Decomposition (LBBD), Geo-MILP iteratively optimizes action sequencingand timing to resolve geometric conflicts, promoting efficient cooperation between wiping and object rearrangement. We then employ K-Order Markov Optimization (KOMO) to generate smooth, collision-free motions to ensure feasible execution. Simulation and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework not only increases reachable coverage by enabling access to obstructed areas, but also significantly improves time efficiency compared to Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) baselines, reducing planning time by up to 9 times and execution makespan by approximately 40%.
authors: Pengqi Zhang, Longchang Yu, Daohan Li, Liang Yan, Hangxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the limited coverage and detours of wiping methods that avoid scattered objects.
Assigns one arm to move objects while the other performs surface wiping using predefined action primitives.
Uses geometry-aware MILP planning with Logic-Based Benders Decomposition to optimize action order and timing under geometric conflicts.
Applies K-Order Markov Optimization to generate smooth, collision-free executable motions.
Simulation and physical experiments show up to 9× lower planning time and approximately 40% shorter execution makespan than TAMP baselines.

Unlike static single-arm CPP detouring, our reversible relocation strategy achieves complete workspace coverage without leaving uncleaned patches.

The Master Problem (MILP) optimizes the high-level task schedule based on logical dependencies, while the Geometric Sub-Problem iteratively verifies the feasibility of candidate schedules and injects logic-based cuts to resolve geometric conflicts. This closed-loop process ensures the generated plan is both time-efficient and physically executable.

papers.abstract: Temporal action detection in long untrimmed videos suffers from inaccurate localization and low-quality proposals, especially with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries. For open-ended video understanding and LLM-driven event analysis, reliable proposals connect temporal localization, event annotation, and semantic understanding. However, conventional temporal action detection (TAD) pipelines lack explicit modeling of proposal localization quality, cross-representation support, and inter-proposal relations. We propose Hybrid Rank-Calibration of Action Proposals (HyrCap), a proposal-centric query-based TAD framework for temporal event understanding. Hybrid combines complementary video features with different localization cues, while Rank-Calibration adjusts proposal ranking confidence to reflect localization reliability and candidate competition. HyrCap treats dense query-based predictions as an over-complete temporal event hypothesis space. Cross-Representation Consensus Calibration, Localization Quality Estimation, and Proposal Redundancy Suppression improve proposal ranking reliability, localization quality, and candidate discrimination. Inspired by LLMs' capabilities in fine-grained semantic recognition, event description, and reasoning, we introduce HyrCap for Semantic Action Understanding, using calibrated proposals for standard TAD and as inputs to LLM-based semantic understanding. We define a staged evaluation protocol to separately measure event localization, segment-level semantic understanding, and combined event understanding performance. Experiments on public benchmarks show that HyrCap achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and provides a finer-grained paradigm and evaluation protocol for query-based event segmentation and annotation.
authors: Rui Chen, Xingyu Chen, Pengxin Xu, Kai Chen, Junzhi Yu
bullets: Addresses inaccurate temporal localization and low-quality proposals in long, untrimmed videos, particularly with sparse annotations and ambiguous boundaries.
Uses complementary video representations and treats dense query predictions as an over-complete set of temporal event hypotheses.
Introduces consensus calibration, localization-quality estimation, and redundancy suppression to improve proposal ranking and candidate discrimination.
Supports both standard temporal action detection and LLM-based semantic event understanding through calibrated proposals.
Experiments on public benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics and propose a staged evaluation protocol for localization, semantic understanding, and their combination.

papers.abstract: Robotic exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment algorithms require reproducible environments with controllable geometry and visibility. This paper presents the Dungeon and Visibility World Generator, an open-source framework for constructing two- and three-dimensional environments and evaluating geometric line-of-sight. The framework supports orthogonal, polygonal or polyhedral, and curvilinear geometries, with six construction families covering scattered rooms, clusters, winding passages, caverns, branches, and loops. Room dimensions, passage structures, obstacles, and spatial placement can be controlled through configurable parameters and probability distributions. Each generated environment provides continuous free-space geometry and a corresponding discrete occupancy representation. A Rust-based visibility engine supports line-of-sight queries in both representations, enabling the evaluation of observable regions from arbitrary agent positions. The framework records configurations, generated geometries, occupancy grids, and visibility results to support reproducible experiments. We demonstrate the generator across all six geometry classes, examine how geometry and spatial resolution affect visibility, and evaluate generation time and reproducibility. The resulting framework provides a configurable foundation for evaluating robotic exploration, coverage, and multi-agent deployment algorithms in diverse environments.
authors: Edwin M\'eriaux, Antonio Lor\'ia, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Supports orthogonal, polygonal/polyhedral, and curvilinear environments.
Provides six construction families, including rooms, passages, caverns, branches, and loops.
Offers continuous free-space and discrete occupancy representations with configurable obstacles and spatial placement.
Includes a Rust-based visibility engine for line-of-sight queries from arbitrary agent positions.
Evaluates geometry, resolution, generation time, and reproducibility across the six environment classes.

papers.abstract: While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors. Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning. However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact. Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution. To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks. Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation. This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation. Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances. The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/.
authors: Linyi Huang, Guowei Huai, Weibin Liu, Shulong Jiang, Ping Tan, Weixuan Zhang, Hui Zhang, Jie Song
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of learning precise contact, coordinated arm–hand motion, and recovery from execution errors.
Decouples control into a functional hand skill for contact execution and an arm–hand policy for arm control and skill activation.
Uses real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and Dynamic Movement Primitive augmentation for data-efficient training.
Achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands.
Remains robust to dynamic disturbances, though its evaluation scope is limited to the reported tasks and hardware.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with \textit{in-context reinforcement learning} capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
authors: Diyuan Shi, Yiqi Tang, Hongyin Zhang, You Wu, Donglin Wang
bullets: Addresses the lack of continual adaptation in conventional pretrained VLA policies.
Adds a reinforcement-learning module that uses past observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals.
Refines action generation during deployment without updating the underlying model parameters.
Designed to support diverse history-construction strategies and VLA training pipelines.
Experiments in simulation and real-world deployment demonstrate adaptation to unseen scenarios.

papers.abstract: Block-diffusion language models denoise a whole block of token positions in parallel so each forward pass can emit many tokens. However, blocks are still denoised in strict sequence, a cost that within-block acceleration leaves untouched. Here, we investigate decoding blocks concurrently and propose One Block Ahead (OBA), a training-free decoding algorithm that denoises the next block alongside the current one. We demonstrate that for uniform-state diffusion LMs, where a block's denoising progress is not visible in its intermediate tokens, concurrent decoding is advantageous if the next block's tokens are promoted together with the corresponding sampler state, including the self-conditioning signal and the denoising time. We also derive a break-even criterion that relates the benefit of OBA to the relative cost of a paired-block forward pass. On DiffusionGemma, a state-of-the-art diffusion LM, OBA increases the tokens per forward pass by 42.3% (from 15.64 to 22.25) and the single-request denoising throughput by 16.3%, averaged over ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.
authors: Yangyi Shen, Pin-Jui Ku, Nicolai Oswald, Jean-Marie Lemercier, Yonggan Fu, Stefano Ermon, Jure Leskovec, Boris Ginsburg, Ante Juki\'c
bullets: Block-diffusion LMs generate tokens in parallel within blocks but traditionally denoise blocks sequentially.
OBA is a training-free decoder that advances the next block alongside the current block.
For uniform-state diffusion LMs, effective promotion requires carrying the next block’s sampler state, including self-conditioning and denoising time.
A break-even criterion relates OBA’s benefit to the cost of paired-block forward passes.
On DiffusionGemma, OBA raises tokens per forward pass by 42.3% and single-request denoising throughput by 16.3% across ten benchmarks, with a small accuracy regression.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | One Block Ahead (OBA). The current block 𝑥c and the warm-up block 𝑥w are denoised in one forward pass over the input sequence [𝑥c | 𝑥w]. A block-causal attention mask lets 𝑥w attend to 𝑥c but not the reverse, so 𝑥c is denoised as if it were alone. When 𝑥c is committed and encoded under causal attention, 𝑥w is promoted in its place, retaining the tokens and sampler state it has accumulated, and a new warm-up block follows.

Figure 2 |Warm-up progress of promoted and newly initialized blocks. For each benchmark, the grey bar corresponds to Native (𝐶=256) and the blue bar to OBA. The full height of a bar is the fraction of the 256 positions accepted on a block’s first pass as the current block, and its dark portion is the fraction whose token at that pass is retained until commitment, so the light segment on top is the fraction of first-pass acceptances later revised. Under OBA the first pass is the one after promotion, and every first block, which has no predecessor, is excluded. Fractions are averaged over three generation seeds. On average, a promoted block under OBA begins its first pass as the current block with 39.9% of its positions already holding their committed tokens, against 5.1% for a newly initialized block under Native (𝐶=256). papers.selection_reason: Concurrent decoding for diffusion LMs improves throughput; fits efficient inference.
papers.title: One Block Ahead: Promoting Sampler State in Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: One Block Ahead (OBA) accelerates block-diffusion language model decoding by denoising the next block concurrently with the current one, improving throughput with a small accuracy trade-off.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires scalable 3D environments that are both photorealistic and semantically grounded, yet existing indoor datasets are dominated by room-scale captures and costly LiDAR acquisition. Online real-estate platforms offer abundant panoramas of diverse multi-room homes, but sparse viewpoints and texture-poor regions make reconstruction severely under-constrained. We introduce Holi-Spatial 360, a generative reconstruction and data curation framework for converting these panoramas into annotated multi-room 3D environments. Because reconstruction quality bounds subsequent generation, our Correspondence-Guided Geometric Optimization converts feed-forward reconstruction priors into reliable cross-view constraints and builds a coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting representation as 3D spatial memory. Adapted single-image and video priors then restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content. The reconstructed scenes support arbitrary RGB-D rendering and an automated curation pipeline that combines end-to-end 3D grounding with VLM-based verification. Holi360 contains over 1K multi-room 3DGS scenes, more than 100K instance annotations, and 2M spatial question-answer pairs. We also introduce the Holi360 benchmark to evaluate the spatial understanding of VLMs in real-world, multi-room indoor environments. Experiments demonstrate superior reconstruction and curation quality under sparse panoramic inputs, while fine-tuning VLMs on Holi360 substantially improves spatial reasoning capabilities.
authors: Yuanyuan Gao, Zhirui Liu, Yuning Gong, Yifei Liu, Yifan Zhan, Kuixuan Jiao, Xiaolong Zhou, Yifan Yang, Hongjie Zhang, Xue Yang, Dan Xu, Zhihang Zhong
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of scalable, photorealistic, semantically grounded indoor 3D data and the under-constrained nature of sparse panoramas.
Uses correspondence-guided geometric optimization to turn reconstruction priors into cross-view constraints and build coherent 3D Gaussian Splatting spatial memory.
Applies image and video generation priors to restore appearance and complete continuous trajectories while preserving observed content.
Provides RGB-D rendering and automated 3D curation with grounding and VLM-based verification.
Introduces over 1K scenes, 100K+ instance annotations, 2M spatial QA pairs, and a benchmark; fine-tuning on the data improves VLM spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching its task, execution stage, and the continuation that should follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first vision-language-action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations. Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints, enabling historical continuations to serve as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, with 4,000 queries and a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, exceeding action-free Gemini Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Controlled retrieval studies show that removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision. We study two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning, increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8% on the LIBERO difficult subset, while improving task progress on real robots. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow task-local memory and refine context use around a frozen GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success, compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout, counting both successes and failures. These results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can support robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
authors: Yunze Liu, Jing Wang, Shenrui Wu, Wenkun He, Guanqi Zhan, Xianzheng Ma, Junyu Chen, Wenhang Ge, Haozhan Tang, Yuchao Gu, Zhuoyang Zhang, Zekai Wang, Dantong Niu, Zhen Dong, Yuke Zhu, Trevor Darrell, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Song Han, Han Cai

Achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, outperforming the action-free Gemini Embedding 2 baseline in the reported comparisons.
Retrieved experience improves policy success in DROID-Sim and LIBERO, and execution-feedback memory evolution improves performance across five ManiSkill tasks.
Ablations indicate that removing action information harms retrieval more than removing vision; evaluation focuses on the reported simulated and real-robot settings.

papers.abstract: Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate \textit{Active Generative Simulation}: optimizing a simulator's data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim, a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable. Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io
authors: Liqian Ma, Vaibhav Saxena, Utkarsh Aashu Mishra, Shuo Cheng, Yongxin Chen, Danfei Xu
bullets: Addresses fixed or manually tuned simulator data distributions that may poorly support real-world policy learning.
Uses meta-learning and meta-gradients to train an auxiliary rater that selects high-utility generation distributions within a user-defined parameter space.

Outperforms uniform-generation and retrieval baselines across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, with a reported 150% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation.
Matches expert manual parameter alignment and transfers proxy-policy-curated distributions to VLA fine-tuning.
Supports partial sim-real alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MetaGenSim. We propose a meta-learning framework for Active Generative Simulation with three stages: (a) Rater network learning: We meta-learn a rater network that weights simulation samples according to their contribution to policy performance on a held-out validation set of real demonstrations. (b) Parameter utility landscape: We map these scores back to their corresponding simulation parameters and use kernel density estimation (KDE) to construct a probability landscape that identifies high-utility regions. (c) Targeted synthesis and co-training: We sample from the constructed distribution to generate a targeted simulation corpus, then co-train the final policy on this synthetic data and few-shot real demonstrations to maximize realworld success.

Figure 1: Active Generative Simulation via MetaGenSim. Sim-and-real co-training (top) boosts robot performance but traditionally relies on manual alignment (middle), where experts must laboriously tune data generation parameters (such as tasks, object placements, camera poses). We propose MetaGenSim (bottom), which meta-learns a Rater to score synthetic data based on policy utility. This induces a utility landscape over parameters, enabling active generation of targeted simulation data that matches the real-world distribution without manually tuning the generation parameters.

The top-scored trajectories can be observed to match the visual and spatial arrangements of the real task, while the lowest-rated trajectories differ significantly in either aspect. (Bottom) Samples from the final MetaGenSim dataset, generated by sampling from the induced data generation parameter distribution.

papers.abstract: Post-training often improves the performance of large audio-language models on audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks. However, these improvements may reflect adaptation to specific question formats, such as multiple-choice questions, rather than genuine advances in audio understanding and reasoning capabilities. To investigate what LALMs actually learn from post-training, we conduct controlled experiments that disentangle improvements in audio understanding from adaptation to specific question formats. Across different models and post-training methods, we find that much of the reported improvement persists even without informative audio, but largely disappears when the question format changes. These findings suggest that post-training often teaches models to exploit task-specific textual cues and answer patterns rather than developing generalizable audio understanding and reasoning capabilities.

papers.abstract: Multimodal in-context learning (ICL) is an important capability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Its performance is closely tied to the demonstrations it uses, making demonstration retrieval a core problem for ICL. Common methods use fixed scoring methods to retrieve all the demonstrations at once, which may introduce redundancy and noise. Context-aware retrieval methods have emerged to address this problem by allowing incremental retrieval from a growing context. However, none of them lets the MLLM learn how to judge what new demonstrations it needs and then carry out progressive retrieval on its own. To this end, we introduce ActICL, which trains an MLLM agent to acquire and use an ICL context via tool-augmented reasoning. An ActICL agent analyzes its own information gaps during iterative reasoning and tool-use actions. Based on these gaps, it performs targeted retrieval to acquire a set of initial candidates. It can then use the existing context to further filter the candidates and refine the context, or it can iteratively perform a new retrieval. When the agent judges that the context is sufficient for the task, or when the resource limit is reached with the user request met, it sends the acquired context to an answering model, either the agent itself or another MLLM. We use a two-stage post-training procedure that jointly optimizes the agent's acquisition and answering. With an adaptive number of demonstrations, ActICL improves average performance by 11.6 percentage points over standard similarity-based retrieval across seven benchmarks and three MLLMs, and by 4.4 points compared to the strongest prior baseline. The contexts acquired by ActICL agents can also be used effectively by frontier models. When GPT-5.6-Sol performs 4-shot ICL, ActICL's contexts improve its performance by 3.5 points over standard retrieval, averaged over three benchmarks.
authors: Yanshu Li, Ruixiang Tang, Junyi Jessy Li, Elias Stengel-Eskin
bullets: Fixed, one-shot demonstration retrieval can introduce redundant or noisy context.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Given a multimodal query, we seek to construct a context with demonstrations that helps an MLLM answer the query correctly. Prior work has largely (a) used off-the-shelf similarity-based retrievers, which often return redundant demonstrations, or (b) trained context-aware retrievers, which can fail to generalize at test time. Our approach (c), ActICL, treats ICL context construction as an iterative agentic task, training an agent to formulate complex search queries, process and filter retrieved evidence, and decide when to submit a context to an answering model.

Figure 2: The overall illustration of ActICL. Given a query and acquisition instructions, the agent reasons at every step to choose among four actions: search submits a goal whose enabled channels retrieve previews from the demonstration bank, read reveals full demonstrations, and curate adds or removes read demonstrations in the retained context, until solve commits an admissible context. The agent learns on-policy which contexts make ICL effective and how to acquire them.

papers.abstract: Native multimodal pre-training trains a single model from scratch on text and multimodal data, enabling it to understand both language and visual inputs. However, how visual signals shape scaling behavior and support capabilities beyond visual understanding remains unclear. We investigate this question through controlled visual-content ablations across model sizes and training budgets. Specifically, we replace image embeddings with content-free padding token embeddings. Retaining visual content improves text prediction on image-text examples without materially changing the lowest text-only loss at a given compute budget, the optimal balance of model size and training data, or aggregate language scores. The relative multimodal loss benefit grows approximately as a power law of compute. To test benefits beyond understanding images, we evaluate spatial reasoning from text descriptions alone. Both conditions improve with model and data scaling. During training of the largest model, visual gains are most sustained in localization, navigation, and symbolic planning, which involve maintaining object configurations or composing spatial updates; gains in spatial relations, geometry, and physical commonsense are less consistent. These findings identify visual content as a scalable anchor for multimodal learning, with benefits that extend beyond visual inputs while preserving aggregate language performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA's success by -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores -28.0. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy's success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points, against -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy's reliance on the instruction unchanged.
authors: Hanlong Li, Sihan Tan, Takeshi Ashizawa, Benjamin Yen, Kazuhiro Nakadai
bullets: Rewording instructions reduces base OpenVLA success by 38.0 points on LIBERO, despite using semantically equivalent commands.
Test-time prompt ensembling, paraphrase medoids, and confidence-based selection fail to recover the lost performance; aggregation mainly reduces variance while preserving paraphrase bias.
A wrong-instruction probe links paraphrase sensitivity to how much policy success depends on the instruction, with stronger policies losing a smaller fraction.
LoRA training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to +2.0 points versus −32.0 for a matched control, replicating across seeds and OpenVLA-OFT.
The robustness improvement transfers to withheld phrasings without changing the policy’s overall reliance on instructions.

papers.abstract: This paper presents $S^3$-Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework for language-guided robot navigation under partial observability. Rather than assuming a complete environment representation in advance, $S^3$-Nav incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while exposing only a capacity-controlled, task-conditioned view to the high-level policy. This separation decouples what the robot must retain from what the policy needs to inspect, allowing decision complexity to be controlled without discarding grounded evidence required for subsequent reasoning and validation. High-level navigation outputs remain provisional and are independently grounded and validated against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric observations before physical execution or task termination. Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks demonstrate that separating persistent state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority improves closed-loop navigation reliability while reducing policy reasoning cost.
authors: Chaemin Lee, Hae Min Cho
bullets: Incrementally builds a persistent spatial-semantic representation instead of requiring a complete environment model.
Provides the high-level policy with a compact, task-conditioned view to control decision complexity.
Independently grounds and validates provisional navigation decisions using stored semantic evidence and current geometry.
Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks show improved closed-loop reliability with lower policy reasoning cost.

Fig. 4. The robot subsequently identifies goal-compatible relational evidence, approaches the selected target, and terminates after execution-layer validation. The final map shows the occupancy representation and trajectory accumulated during the episode.

papers.abstract: LLM system capabilities depend not only on model parameters but also on the executable harnesses that organize information acquisition, tool use, reasoning, and memory. Recursive harness evolution can automate their design, but how it can reliably discover generalizable systems from limited, noisy, and repeatedly reused feedback remains unclear. We study this question in agentic video understanding, where rich multimodal evidence and coupled mechanisms make harness optimization challenging. We first introduce VideoHarness-BRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework that evolves video harnesses around a frozen vision-language model. Analyzing over 4,000 evolved candidates, we find it competitive with hand-engineered systems but identify three interconnected failure modes: validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap. We trace all three to a common root: the same imperfect validation evidence drives both harness revisions and the proposer's search strategy. We therefore propose VideoHarness-SRSI, an evidence-governed framework in which every search decision rests on evidence that is transferable, sufficient, and gathered before the search commits. It restricts the proposer to content-free feedback, informs exploration with instrumented warm-up experiments, and develops mechanisms in isolated probe-race branches before factorial composition and joint refinement. Across four video understanding benchmarks, VideoHarness-SRSI improves the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to VideoHarness-BRSI and reduces the mean validation-test gap by 37.9%. Reliable harness evolution thus depends on how search is organized and informed, not only on how well it optimizes validation performance.
authors: Zihao Lin, Haoyu Dong, Haobo Xu, Chi-Chih Chang, Xuying Ning, Yinglong Xia, Shuang Yang, Zhuokai Zhao, Xinying Song, Dongfang Liu, Lifu Huang, Yang Song, Qifan Wang
bullets: Recursive harness evolution is studied for agentic video understanding with a frozen vision-language model.
Analysis of over 4,000 candidates identifies validation overfitting, search-budget dilution, and the early-experience trap.
SRSI uses transferable, sufficient, pre-commitment evidence; content-free proposer feedback; instrumented warm-up experiments; and isolated probe-race branches.
Across four benchmarks, it raises the equally weighted mean held-out score by 6.2% relative to BRSI and reduces the validation-test gap by 37.9%.
The findings suggest that reliable harness evolution depends on search organization and evidence quality, not validation optimization alone.

figures.caption: Figure 4 Overview of VideoHarness-SRSI. Top: under information isolation, the harness executes on the validation videos and questions, but the proposer receives only scores and content-free traces, never the videos, question text, options, or answers. Bottom: evolution proceeds in three stages under this policy. Stage I (instrumented warm-up) adds a removal and an intensity change to the free proposals of each round, summarizes the evidence in a per-mechanism report, and selects a seed pool and a backbone H0. Stage II (isolated branch evolution) evolves each mechanism axis in its own branch from H0; every axis is probed with three candidates, the top half race on to fifteen, and at most three axes are kept. Stage III (factorial composition) distills each kept axis into a fixed modification, evaluates all combinations against H0 to measure transfer and interactions, and then jointly refines them into the final harness H⋆.

papers.abstract: Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.
authors: Yue Zhang, Han Lin, Zun Wang, Yidong Huang, Zaid Khan, Mohit Bansal
bullets: Generic realism, diversity, and task coverage may not target the distinct failure modes of different pretrained navigation policies.
An LLM extracts and validates weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, then selects the strongest weakness by success-rate gap.
The framework maps validated weaknesses to controllable environmental factors and generates environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles.
Across three navigation agents, weakness-conditioned adaptation outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR; gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini transfer to HM3D.
Iterative re-diagnosis tracks weaknesses that persist or shift as policies improve, enabling updated environment generation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of WEDGE. Unlike existing environment generators, which are largely policyagnostic, WEDGE uses agent failures to guide generation. (a) We mine policy-specific weaknesses from successful and failed rollouts. (b) The mined weaknesses determine which environmental factors to control and which learnable regimes to target. Training on the resulting environments improves the agent and can yield cross-domain transfer beyond the generation simulator.

Figure 3: Weakness-conditioned environment construction and rollout verification. (a) Each policy is associated with its top mined weakness. (b) Candidate episodes are constructed by modifying the factors relevant to that weakness, such as target placement for target visibility or start state and layout for blind path ratio. Candidates are retained only when their feature values fall within the weakness range, with new layouts generated when existing ones are insufficient. (c) The policy is rolled out five times in each retained candidate, and episodes with two or three successful rollouts are selected for training.

Figure 2: LLM-guided discovery and validation of executable policy weaknesses. (a) We construct a diagnostic set by contrasting successful and failed episodes represented with a shared vocabulary of measurable primitives. (b) An LLM uses these structured examples to propose candidate weakness features and their executable definitions. (c) Each candidate is evaluated on the full diagnostic set, and (d) retained only if it satisfies the validation criteria for coverage, non-redundancy, predictiveness, and incremental value. Candidates that fail any criterion trigger a new round of episode sampling and feature proposal. This proposal–validation process repeats until the stopping criterion is met, with validated weaknesses retained for subsequent environment generation.

Figure 4: Analysis of weakness-conditioned adaptation. (a) We re-diagnose each agent after every adaptation round and track the SR gap associated with its dominant weakness. DD-PPO and Uni-NaVid retain the same dominant weakness, while Gemini develops a new weakness after the first round. (b) Adaptation gains are larger in weakness-associated regimes. For Uni-NaVid and Gemini, we compare gains across blind path ratio regimes. For DD-PPO, gains are reported by target category, with larger improvements on small, hard-to-see targets.

papers.abstract: MLLM-based detectors formulate vision-language grounding as autoregressive coordinate generation, yet in dense scenes, they often collapse into a box repetition loop, repeatedly emitting identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted. We trace this failure to historical-answer attention takeover: Under full-history autoregression, repeated coordinate tokens in the growing answer history attract disproportionate attention, crowding out the attention sinks needed to attend to new visual evidence. % To break this loop, in this paper, we propose \textbf{Compressed Window Auto-Regression} (WinAR). This new mechanism partitions a long answer sequence into consecutive generation windows and restricts full token-level autoregression to the current window only while compressing each previous window into a fixed set of latent tokens that condition subsequent decoding. This design reduces the repeated exposure to raw historical coordinates that triggers the attention takeover, yet preserves cross-window dependencies essential for coherent multi-object generation. On RSDense, which contains 200-2,000 objects per image, our model WinARDet improves RexOmni F1-score (IoU=0.5) from 32.16 to 39.36 over the baseline, while reducing the redundancy rate from 35.48% to 13.00%. WinARDet also generalizes across decoding strategies and output formats, including parallel box decoding and polygon generation, providing a practical paradigm for long-horizon vision-language grounding across scene densities.
authors: Chenxu Wang, Hangyi Kuang, Bo-Wen Yin, Yuxuan Li, Quan-Sheng Zeng, Yang Zhang, Xu Guo, Xiang Li, Qibin Hou
bullets: Dense-scene autoregressive detectors can repeatedly emit identical boxes until the decoding budget is exhausted.
The proposed Compressed Window Auto-Regression limits token-level attention to the current generation window.
Each previous window is compressed into fixed latent tokens, preserving cross-window dependencies while reducing historical-coordinate interference.
On RSDense, WinARDet raises F1 at IoU 0.5 from 32.16 to 39.36 and lowers redundancy from 35.48% to 13.00%.
The approach also extends to parallel box decoding and polygon generation across varying scene densities.

papers.abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet strengthening their reasoning through reinforcement learning (RL) remains an open challenge. Any-order generation can suffer from entropy degradation, which narrows the reasoning paths available for exploration. Recent work mitigates this issue by applying standard GRPO with left-to-right generation. However, independently generating every rollout from the input prompt can leave alternative continuations from intermediate states underexplored, while trajectory-level advantages assign uniform credit to all tokens without distinguishing the contributions of individual reasoning segments. We propose ForkGRPO, an RL framework that couples efficient exploration with fine-grained segment-level credit assignment. It samples multiple continuations from high-entropy intermediate states along a reference trajectory, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes. The continuations provide complementary learning signals: within-state group-relative advantages guide which continuations to reinforce, while Monte Carlo state-value differences indicate which reasoning segments improve expected outcomes. Among the evaluated architecture-preserving RL methods, ForkGRPO achieves the best performance on three of four benchmarks, while improving over the directly comparable JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points and using up to 27.8% fewer generated tokens. ForkGRPO-Fast further achieves a $2.49\times$ training wall-clock speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
authors: Zhaoyan Jia, Chengwei Zhou, Gourav Datta, Massoud Pedram
bullets: Addresses entropy degradation and insufficient exploration in any-order diffusion generation.
Samples continuations from high-entropy intermediate states, prioritizing textual boundaries and reusing shared prefixes.
Uses group-relative advantages for continuation selection and Monte Carlo value differences for segment-level credit assignment.
Achieves the best results among evaluated architecture-preserving methods on three of four benchmarks, improving over JustGRPO by up to 1.2 percentage points.
Reduces generated tokens by up to 27.8%; ForkGRPO-Fast provides a 2.49× training speedup with negligible accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models must reconcile conflicting text and images. Prior work has characterized the resulting behavior in terms of modality biases--e.g., a "blind faith in text"--but why preferences vary across models, domains, and input conditions remains unclear. We develop a predictive account from a Bayesian perspective, positing that VLMs combine conditionally independent evidence from each modality with prior beliefs, subject to modality-specific biases. The resulting two-parameter cue combination model accurately predicts VLM preferences under unseen combinations of input degradation and transfers to new forms of unreliability without refitting. Separating evidence strength from integration bias explains how VLMs can follow text even while weighting visual evidence more heavily, reconciling reports of text and vision dominance under a single combination rule.
authors: Josh Barua, Kyle Mahowald, William Rudman
bullets: Models combine conditionally independent visual and textual evidence with prior beliefs.
The framework separates evidence strength from integration bias, clarifying seemingly contradictory text- and vision-dominance findings.
It predicts model preferences for unseen combinations of input degradation.
The model transfers to new types of unreliability without refitting.
It offers a unified account of why modality preferences vary across models, domains, and conditions.

papers.abstract: Whole-body control plays a crucial role in enabling humanoid robots to execute expressive motions. Faithful execution requires preserving both the intended action and its expressive characteristics. Existing whole-body trackers typically balance joint and keypoint tracking with physical stability across diverse motions, but these objectives do not necessarily prioritize the expressive characteristics of each action. Our analysis shows that lower average positional tracking error does not guarantee better preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics. To address this gap, we propose a residual learning framework with compensation objectives targeting amplitude, energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. To concentrate compensation while limiting interference with the underlying tracking behavior, motion-aware gating allocates correction capacity according to body-part activity, preserving larger correction ranges in more active parts and restricting them elsewhere. For each frozen tracker, we train motion-specific residual policies and distill them into a unified policy shared across motion categories. Simulation and physical experiments on the Unitree G1 across eight motion categories demonstrate superior preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics compared with the corresponding baselines.

papers.abstract: User feedback enables LLMs to refine reusable personalized skills, but often mixes persistent preferences with request-specific corrections. Indiscriminately retaining both risks negative transfer, motivating selective retention at the level of individual requirements. We frame this challenge as selective transfer over atomic rules and propose SkillGrain, a framework for learning reusable personalized skills from user feedback. SkillGrain decomposes feedback into independently actionable rules, predicts their transferability, and retains only those suitable for future requests. To learn these decisions, we combine rubric-guided skill rewards with fine-grained credit assignment that separately evaluates rule content and retention decisions. We further jointly optimize skill induction and skill-conditioned generation through reinforcement learning, ensuring that learned skills support downstream personalization. We construct a benchmark spanning five personalized writing tasks to evaluate cross-request generalization. Experiments across three base models in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings show that SkillGrain achieves the best overall average performance among competing methods.

papers.abstract: Does a language model answer better because its compressed memory contains useful document information? Replacing memory vectors with zeros can lower a trained model's score without showing that it outperforms a model trained without memory. We combine zeroing with separately trained models that cannot access stored text or receive the same constant input for every document. Across nine systems, some models rely on memory yet perform worse than the trained alternative. For example, in experiments that predict states in generated stories, zeroing memory worsens a model's prediction loss, yet a model trained without memory achieves lower loss than the original model with intact memory. On TriviaQA, giving xRAG memory from another question's passage raises F1, which measures word overlap with accepted answers, from 19.38 without a document to 24.78. Its effect on how often outputs contain an accepted answer is statistically uncertain. The question's retrieved passage scores higher still (29.88 F1). Thus a gain over no document alone does not establish that the gain requires the question's passage. Evaluations must therefore specify the comparison model, absolute performance, and generation and scoring conditions.
authors: Minsu Oh, Seunghui Jwa, Chanjun Park, Yeo-Chan Yoon
bullets: Zeroing memory can hurt performance without proving memory improves over a model trained without memory.
Across nine systems, some depend on memory yet perform worse than memory-free trained alternatives.
In story-state prediction, intact memory underperformed a separately trained no-memory model despite zeroing worsening loss.
On TriviaQA, unrelated passage memory increased xRAG F1 from 19.38 to 24.78, while the question’s passage reached 29.88; accepted-answer rates were statistically uncertain.
Evaluations should report comparison models, absolute performance, and generation/scoring conditions.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for multi-turn agentic tasks that require interactions with users and environments over extended sequences of actions. A common approach to improving LLM agents is to use more capable expert models to provide training supervision, either by behavior cloning the expert's trajectories or by using the expert to correct the actions in trajectories generated by the weaker student model. However, expert LLMs can provide richer supervision than actions alone: they can directly generate textual critique that explain why specific actions are incorrect. We study whether training on such feedback benefits LLM agents and propose Critique-Augmented Agentic Fine-Tuning (CAFT), a framework that elicits textual expert feedback on student-generated trajectories. For each incorrect action, the expert yields both a corrected action and a textual critique explaining the student's mistake--which we then use as the training target for fine-tuning. Across four student models from the Nemotron 3 and Gemma 4 families on the agentic domains $\tau^2$-Bench Airline+Retail and WebShop, adding critiques to action-level supervision improves performance by 8% on average over action-only distillation. Additionally, CAFT checkpoints can also provide a better warm start for reinforcement learning than expert-trajectory distillation. Our results demonstrate that textual critiques can strengthen supervision for multi-turn LLM agents.
