papers.abstract: Multimodal models and agents have emerged to enable AI systems to learn from and interact with the real world more like humans by integrating information across multiple modalities. However, enabling multimodal agents to continually acquire useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data remains a significant challenge as they move toward long-horizon tasks and lifelong settings. Addressing this challenge requires effective memory mechanisms that can maintain continuity across sessions, adapt to changing users and environments, and refine memory-management policies through accumulated experience. We introduce a two-axis analytical framework for multimodal agent memory structured around two key questions: how multimodal information is formed and represented (Axis I, Formation and Representation), and how its management adapts with accumulated experience (Axis II, Memory Management). Axis I, Formation and Representation, characterizes what information is retained and how it is encoded (e.g., modality-specific embeddings, textual and structured records, latent and parametric representations) to support subsequent reasoning and action. Axis II, Memory Management, distinguishes three tiers: T1 Static Memory reuses fixed memory; T2 Dynamic Memory updates memory through a stable policy; and T3 Self-Evolving Memory updates memory through an evolving policy. Based on this framework, we synthesize recurring design patterns and derive principles for balancing source fidelity with abstraction, maintaining temporal validity and provenance, grounding memory use in recoverable evidence, and evolving memory policies over time. Furthermore, we discuss the challenges and potential future directions for the memory mechanism of multimodal agents.
authors: Minghao Guo, Qingyue Jiao, Xiujin Liu, Jianhong Pang, Ruimeng Yang, Naihao Xu, Liwei Che, Haochen Xue, Ziqi Wang, Xinying Cai, Jiaxuan Luo, Jiaxin Deng, Xuesong Ye, Jintao Qu, Wenyao Gao, Jingwen Gu, Chenyang Zhao, Shichun Liu, Guibin Zhang, Zefang Liu, Siyin Wang, Wujiang Xu, Danrui Li, Zeru Shi, Woongyeong Yeo, Shuang Liu, Wei-Chieh Huang, Weizhi Zhang, Tianyu Yang, Kangsan Kim, Yebowen Hu, Bowen Wen, Bowen Jiang, Haohao Su, Ming Yin, Sheldon Yu, Mian Zhang, Yuyan Chen, Hanrong Zhang, Kai Mei, Zihao Zhang, Mingyu Jin, Xi Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Tianxin Wei, Linyong Nan, Zhenwen Liang, Zhendong Chu, Ziqi Huang, Yongye Su, Sixun Dong, Shujian Liu, Kaiqu Liang, Jiaojiao Han, Zhaoye Fei, Kun Wang, Shihan Dou, Zhichun Guo, Xingjian Diao, Zeqi Gu, Heng Wang, Tao Feng, Cheng Qian, Hamid Palangi, Silei Xu, Xi Yun, Yi Zhu, Shilong Liu, Qingsong Wen, Sung Ju Hwang, Zuxuan Wu, Yu-Gang Jiang, Yiyu Shi, Dimitris N. Metaxas, Jiaxuan You, Julian McAuley, Mengdi Wang, Jiawei Han, Philip S. Yu, Ziyi Ye
bullets: Motivated by the difficulty of continually retaining useful information from complex, heterogeneous multimodal data.
Axis I classifies memory by how information is formed and represented, including embeddings, textual or structured records, and latent or parametric forms.
Axis II categorizes memory management into static, dynamically updated, and self-evolving policies.
The framework synthesizes design patterns and principles for abstraction, temporal validity, provenance, evidence grounding, and policy evolution.
It outlines open challenges and future directions for multimodal agent memory.

The shaded interval highlights the recent growth period after 2025.

Figure 6: Representations in multimodal agent memory. Multimodal experience may be retained close to the source modality, transformed into explicit textual or structured records, or internalized as latent states or parametric memory. We classify each memory path by the representation ultimately supplied to downstream computation, rather than by formats used only for storage or indexing. These families expose recurring trade-offs among recoverability, interpretability, compactness, and tight integration with the agent policy. Hybrid architectures combine multiple representations, often linking compact abstractions to recoverable source evidence.

Figure 9: T2 Dynamic Memory predominates across image, video, GUI, and embodied memory systems in our taxonomy. Architecture-level incidence is shown for image, video, GUI, and embodied memory systems in the taxonomy-current corpus. Within each modality panel, rows correspond to memory-management tiers and columns correspond to representation families: source-preserving modality-native memory, cross-represented explicit memory, latent or parametric memory, and hybrid multi-path memory. Each dot denotes one architecture, positioned horizontally by publication year from approximately 2023 to 2026; architectures published before 2023 are grouped near the ∼’23 position. Irregular envelopes summarize the density of architectures in each cell, and cell labels report counts. Representation-family counts are non-exclusive, so an architecture may be counted in multiple columns when it combines multiple memory representations.

Figure 2: Publication landscape of multimodal agent memory. Representative methods across image, video, GUI, and embodied settings from 2023 to 2026, organized by memory-management tier: T1 Static Memory, T2 Dynamic Memory, and T3 Self-Evolving Memory.

Figure 11: Systems realization and lifecycle of multimodal agent memory. A conceptual organization of the mechanisms that connect logical memory with runtime execution and physical storage, rather than an architecture implemented in full by any single analyzed system. The control plane (§6.4) covers logical-memory and execution-state lookup, reuse validation, and resource-aware admission and scheduling. The cross-layer runtime (§6.5) connects memory to computation through materialization and connects execution history to retained memory through write-back. The physical memory hierarchy (§6.2, §6.3) covers residency, replication, transfer, compression, and reconstruction across accelerator HBM, host DRAM, local SSDs, and remote resources. Consistency and coordination (§6.6) concern identity, visibility, provenance, invalidation, and isolation across these paths; the guarantees of individual mechanisms remain scoped to the artifacts they manage.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
authors: Kyusong Lee, Heting Ying, Tiancheng Zhao
bullets: Targets the challenge of following the intended person in shared spaces with visual distractors.

On-policy refinement raises distractor-tracking success from 55.80% to 58.22% and reduces collision rate by 1.99 percentage points.
The study is preliminary and motivates further work on on-policy refinement for person following.

papers.abstract: Multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) organize information across different modalities to support multimodal Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to improve the performance of multimodal large language models (MLLMs). The effectiveness of these multimodal Graph RAG methods largely depends on the quality of the constructed MMKGs. However, most existing methods construct MMKGs without explicit guidance on graph quality, while reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods that rely on final-answer correctness may provide only indirect feedback on MMKG quality. To address these limitations, we propose MMKG-R1, a novel MMKG-quality-driven RL framework for training an MLLM as a multimodal knowledge constructor. To be specific, MMKG-R1 introduces multiple quality-aware rewards to directly evaluate both the quality of information extracted from individual knowledge sources and the quality of the assembled MMKG. These rewards are then used to guide the RL training. Experiments across multiple datasets show that MMKG-R1 constructs MMKGs that improve downstream question-answering accuracy.

papers.abstract: This paper presents LLM-jp-4, a family of Japanese sovereign large language models (LLMs) developed with an emphasis on transparency, reproducibility, and practical usability. LLM-jp-4 comprises an 8B dense model and a 32B-A3B mixture-of-experts model, both trained from scratch on approximately 12 trillion tokens. To support independent verification and reproduction, we establish explicit criteria for selecting training data, external models, and software, and make the development process publicly available. Evaluation results demonstrate substantial improvements over previous LLM-jp models and competitive performance against open-weight models of similar scale. By documenting the development principles, training procedures, and empirical findings of LLM-jp-4, we aim to provide a reference for future sovereign AI development.

papers.abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.

papers.abstract: Robotic ultrasound can standardize image acquisition and reduce operator workload and variability, but policy learning remains limited by the lack of realistic, controllable simulation environments. While controllable world models have advanced rapidly in natural-image domains, ultrasound world modeling remains challenging because each frame captures only a cross-section of unobserved 3D anatomy, causing small probe motions to induce large appearance changes. Existing approaches rely on robot-tracked poses and latent-space prediction, but do not directly generate the observations required for interactive control. We propose SonoWorld, a causal ultrasound world model that learns video dynamics from unlabeled clinical videos and grounds them to 6-DoF control using a small set of freehand clinical scans tracked with an EM sensor. SonoWorld is trained in three stages: pretraining a latent-action-conditioned video diffusion model on around 6.9 million unlabeled multi-organ ultrasound frames; grounding the learned video dynamics to metric probe poses with a small EM-tracked thyroid dataset; and applying distribution matching distillation to enable causal, long-horizon autoregressive generation with selectively caching eviction tokens at inference time. We evaluate controllability through pose-following fidelity, round-trip consistency, and axis-specific control under synthetic actions on held-out tracked scans, and further validate it with a user study. In model-based action discrimination, SonoWorld correctly ranks the target-directed probe motion over an equal-magnitude opposite motion in up to 74.8% of trials. To our knowledge, SonoWorld is the first causal, pose-controllable ultrasound world model learned primarily from freehand clinical videos, providing a data-driven interactive environment for robotic ultrasound data acquisition and policy evaluation.

Evaluated pose-following, round-trip consistency, axis-specific control, and user-study performance on held-out tracked scans.

papers.abstract: Jailbreak attacks against large language models (LLMs) are evaluated using attack success rate (ASR), which depends on correctly identifying responses that fulfill prohibited requests. Existing evaluators can mistake refusals or topically related responses for successful attacks. We show that changing only the judge LLM can alter reported ASR by up to $82$ percentage points. We introduce the semantic reconstruction game, a training-free evaluator that decomposes compliance judgments into constrained semantic comparisons. Given only a response, an LLM reconstructs the request answered by its substantive content, excluding information merely repeated or refused. The game compares this reconstruction against similar decoy requests to determine whether it matches the original request, allowing abstention when neither candidate matches. Across three off-the-shelf LLM judges, the game achieves the lowest mean error against human labels among evaluated methods and reduces variation in reported ASR. It prioritizes avoiding false positives, even at the cost of missing some successful jailbreaks.

It compares the reconstruction with the original and decoy requests, while allowing abstention when neither matches.
Across three off-the-shelf judges, it had the lowest mean error against human labels and reduced ASR variation, but may miss some successful jailbreaks.

papers.abstract: One-step diffusion distillation achieves strong performance on small datasets but remains insufficient for high-resolution or complex text-to-image settings. Extending to multistep distillation often requires training data, suffers from early-step degradation, inconsistent outputs across sampling budgets, and incurs high computational cost. We identify that these limitations stem from simultaneous training, where a single adapted network approximates multiple score functions of different student distributions at once, causing biased distribution matching and unstable optimization. Therefore, we propose Progressive Multistep Data-free Distillation (PMDD), which assigns a dedicated adapted network per student distribution while avoiding the memory overhead of maintaining multiple adapted networks. Combined with a stage-wise unforget loss to preserve earlier-step generations, PMDD reduces optimization bias in the student, provides faster convergence, and a single unified model that supports multiple inference budgets. Extensive experiments show that PMDD matches or outperforms data-free few-step baselines at every multistep budget, reaches FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64x64 in two steps, below its 512-NFE teacher (2.32), and achieves FID 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512x512, while requiring 4-5x less training compute than data-free DMDv2 to support three inference budgets.
authors: Ngoc Duy Tran, Kien Do, Duc Thanh Nguyen, Truyen Tran
bullets: Multistep distillation is challenging for high-resolution and complex text-to-image generation because it can require data, degrade early steps, produce inconsistent budgets, and be computationally expensive.
PMDD assigns a dedicated adapted network to each student distribution without retaining all networks simultaneously, reducing optimization bias.
A stage-wise unforget loss preserves earlier-step generations during progressive training.
The unified model matches or exceeds data-free few-step baselines across budgets, reaching FID 1.99 on ImageNet 64×64 in two steps and 7.76 on zero-shot COCO 512×512.
It uses 4–5× less training compute than data-free DMDv2 when supporting three inference budgets.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision on student rollouts, but this supervision can become unreliable when the student and teacher diverge, either because of a large initial policy gap or compounding errors in long-horizon reasoning and tool use. We introduce Divergence-Triggered Dynamic Distillation (DTDD), an adaptive OPD framework that uses segment-level student-teacher divergence to trigger teacher takeover during training. When divergence triggers an intervention during reasoning, the student prefix continues to receive standard OPD supervision. The teacher then generates a recovery suffix, which the student learns through behavior cloning, using cross-entropy on the teacher-generated tokens. We evaluate DTDD in three regimes: long-horizon reasoning, distillation from a base initialization without offline supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-turn agents. We also compare alternative trigger designs and teacher-intervention rates. DTDD reduces the post-warmup peak gradient norm by $8.6\times$ and, from a base initialization, reaches $21.3\%$ held-out math accuracy in $2.6\times$ fewer optimizer updates than OPD; both methods finish near $22\%$. It improves best-observed performance by $4.8$ and $4.1$ percentage points on ALFWorld with LoRA and agentic code, respectively. Ablations show that segment-averaged triggers outperform token-spike triggers. Behavior cloning is also more effective than the tested OPD surrogate for training teacher-generated recoveries. Across 23 experimental arms, takeover tends to help when the teacher substantially outperforms the OPD-trained student, provided that the teacher can recover from student-visited states, the student can learn those recoveries, and teacher intervention is neither excessive nor insufficient.
authors: Qijia He, Zequn Li, Spencer Luo, Tianle Chen, Pradyumna Narayana, Zixian Ma, Ranjay Krishna, Lan Nie, Sugato Basu
bullets: Problem: OPD supervision can become unreliable after large policy gaps or compounding reasoning and tool-use errors.
Method: Segment-level divergence triggers teacher intervention; the student prefix receives OPD supervision, while a teacher-generated recovery suffix is learned via behavior cloning.
Results: DTDD reduced post-warmup peak gradient norm by 8.6× and reached 21.3% held-out math accuracy in 2.6× fewer updates from a base initialization, with similar final accuracy to OPD.
It improved best-observed ALFWorld and agentic-code performance by 4.8 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively.
Scope: Takeover helps when the teacher is substantially better and can recover from student states, while intervention rates must avoid being too high or too low.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for code usually rewards passing tests, which a model can do while remaining wrong on the inputs the tests do not cover. A program verifier instead decides whether a program satisfies a formal specification for all inputs. Language models are almost always paired with verifiers at inference time only, and turning a verifier into a reward raises two difficulties. It reports only acceptance or rejection, which gives no gradient when every attempt fails, and a policy can cheat it, most simply by telling it to assume what the proof was supposed to establish. We build an agentic environment and reward that address both. The reward reads the verifier's diagnostics rather than its verdict, scoring a candidate by the weighted fraction of proof obligations it discharges, extended with hidden probes from a reference proof's annotations. An integrity audit outranks the verifier, rejecting any candidate that alters the specification or assumes what it was meant to prove. The model works as an agent against a live verifier over many turns, with a separately trained proof specialist as a frozen collaborator. Across Qwen3 models from 1.7B to 14B and a 35B Qwen3.6 mixture-of-experts model, held-out verification on code generation rises from 66.1% to 93.5% on DafnyBench and from 56.3% to 100% on SWE-Proof. This reward leads every other training signal we compare, including a binary pass-or-fail reward trained under otherwise identical settings, with the widest margin on code generation. When the agent must also deliver the repository patch, graded by each project's withheld tests, the fraction of held-out issues it resolves rises from 59.6% to 72.5%. Evaluated unchanged on three verification suites withheld from training, the checkpoints improve on all of them, including one whose language and verifier are absent from training.
authors: George Ma, Yuhao Zhang, Bing He, Zeren Shui, Ferhat Erata, Murali Krishna Ramanathan, Somayeh Sojoudi, Hao Zhou
bullets: Addresses sparse verifier rewards and policies that exploit or weaken specifications.
Scores partial progress from discharged proof obligations, augmented with hidden reference-proof probes.
Uses an integrity audit to reject specification changes or circular assumptions.
Agents interact with a live verifier over multiple turns alongside a frozen proof specialist.
Verification improves across model sizes and unseen suites, while held-out issue resolution rises from 59.6% to 72.5%.

papers.abstract: We present Keypoint Constraint Learning (KCL), a framework for learning task-relevant motion constraints from visual demonstrations and for planning safely with the extracted constraints. To make constraint learning tractable from RGB-D observations, we represent demonstrations using sparse 3D object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted through segmentation, visual feature clustering, and point tracking. In this reduced geometric space, we learn keypoint dynamics and infer distance- and orientation-based constraints that make the expert trajectories feasible and approximately locally optimal by enforcing KKT optimality conditions in the reduced state space. We then plan with the learned constraints under uncertainty, using robustness margins derived from accumulated prediction error, and provide a theoretical analysis of how keypoint perception error and learned dynamics error affect the recovered constraints. We evaluate KCL on visual demonstrations from navigation to rigid/deformable manipulation, showing that it recovers multi-stage geometric constraints and outperforms baselines in downstream safe planning.
authors: Zheng Qiu, Zhouyu Zhang, Ninghan Zhong, Glen Chou
bullets: Represents RGB-D demonstrations with object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted from segmentation, feature clustering, and tracking.
Learns keypoint dynamics and infers distance- and orientation-based constraints using KKT optimality conditions.
Plans safely under uncertainty by adding robustness margins based on accumulated prediction error.
Analyzes how perception and learned-dynamics errors affect the recovered constraints.
Evaluations across navigation and rigid/deformable manipulation show recovery of multi-stage constraints and improved downstream safe planning over baselines.

papers.abstract: This work concerns our submission for the Multilingual track of the 2026 BabyLM Challenge. We improve on our baseline using data that has been summarized and translated by an LLM, showing that higher-quality data can come from synthetic sources. We further improve with 2 simple changes: using a larger model, and using a character-level vocabulary. Both of these changes require LoRA-style fine-tuning for realizing their full potential. We dub our final Qwen3-based model Qwenfant, which, at the time of submission, ranks 1st in the Multilingual track.

papers.abstract: In so-called "Industry 4.0," integrated sensors, analytics tools, and other digital technologies supplement industrial workflows, potentiating enhanced visibility and automation. Prognostics and health management (PHM) and natural language processing (NLP) practitioners alike have explored the application of large language models (LLMs) to industrial asset management, but many prior works' focus on exam-like benchmarks has limited their assessment of LLMs' ability to automate practical operations. Herein, we introduce CoffeeBench, a fault diagnostics task for LLM agents, using a simulated appliance. The LLMs we evaluate struggle to consistently identify faults from the sensor information alone, but the best-performing ones can iteratively refine the fault-option space to eventually obtain a successful diagnosis. Our subsequent analyses, therefore, focus on: differentiating models by diagnostic efficiency (RQ1); examining the lagging performance of the three worst models (RQ2); and identifying viable heuristics for selective prediction (RQ3), including that initial diagnostic uncertainty and LLM-judged soundness of reasoning are high-signal predictors of diagnostic success. In addition to our benchmark results (Section 3.1), we provide practical insights for improving the performance of the open-weight models on CoffeeBench, such as by explicitly tracking episode state on their behalf to reduce timeouts (Section 3.2) or applying a deliberation loop to refine diagnostic hypotheses (Section 3.3).
authors: Lucas H. McCabe, Sarah Lukens, H. Howie Huang
bullets: Introduces CoffeeBench, a fault-diagnosis benchmark for LLM agents operating on a simulated appliance.
Evaluates diagnostic efficiency, poor-performing models, and heuristics for selectively trusting predictions.
The strongest models can narrow the fault-option space iteratively to eventually reach successful diagnoses.
Initial diagnostic uncertainty and the model’s judged reasoning soundness predict diagnostic success.
Practical improvements include explicitly tracking episode state to reduce timeouts and using deliberation loops to refine hypotheses.

papers.abstract: We present Kandinsky S2V 1.0, an open family of speech-to-video models for controllable audio-driven human animation, comprising Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite (2B parameters) and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro (21B parameters). From a single reference image, a speech waveform, and a text prompt, the models generate long-form 25 FPS video in which lip motion, expression, pose, and gesture follow the speech. The architecture draws text and audio conditioning from one Qwen2.5-Omni model and adds a reference-aware three-scale visual memory. Training starts from the Kandinsky 5.0 Video foundation models [1] and combines mixed reference-memory layouts with an area-adaptive face loss. The training corpus contains 1.17M single-speaker clips selected by active-speaker detection, with captions generated directly in English and Russian. A side-by-side human evaluation against the strongest open-source baseline and two proprietary commercial models shows that Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro performs comparably to or better than these models on average and is also preferred for lip synchronization. On common speech to video benchmarks, Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro rank among the top performing models according to mean rank over five reported metrics. Beyond the base models, we provide {\pi}-Flow distilled variants of both Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Lite and Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro. The distilled Kandinsky S2V 1.0 Pro model generates video in 16 sampling steps without classifier-free guidance, achieving a 5.4 times end-to-end speedup over the base model, while matching or exceeding it on nearly all reported benchmark metrics. To accelerate open research and deployment in speech-to-video generation, we release the code, model checkpoints, and diffusers integration under the MIT license.
authors: Nikolay Semenov, Artem Riabinin, Sergey Bassenko, Anna Averchenkova, Julia Agafonova, Anastasia Aliaskina, Kirill Kozlov, Lev Novitskiy, Nikita Samsonov, Nikolai Gerasimenko, Denis Dimitrov
bullets: Generates long-form 25 FPS avatar video from one image, speech waveform, and text prompt.
Uses unified text/audio conditioning, three-scale reference-aware visual memory, and area-adaptive face loss.
Includes Lite (2B) and Pro (21B) models trained on 1.17M active-speaker clips.
Pro performs comparably to or better than evaluated open and proprietary models, with preferred lip synchronization; both rank highly on common benchmarks.
π-Flow distillation enables the Pro model to generate in 16 steps without classifier-free guidance, delivering a reported 5.4× end-to-end speedup while largely preserving quality.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the Kandinsky S2V 1.0 architecture. Text features from the frozen Qwen2.5-Omni Thinker and audio features from its frozen audio tower [17] feed trainable text and audio encoder stacks in the DiT, with Nt text blocks and Na audio blocks. The reference image is encoded by a frozen Hunyuan 3D VAE [2], and its latent is concatenated (denoted by C) with the noisy target latent zt and a multi-scale FramePack [14] memory of past frames to form the visual sequence consumed by the DiT. Each DiT block applies self-attention (V2V), cross-attention to the text tokens (V2T), an optional cross-attention to the audio tokens (V2A) injected periodically across the stack, and a feed-forward layer. The denoised visual latent is decoded back to pixel space by the frozen VAE decoder.

Figure 4: Frame-aligned audio cross-attention (V2A). Audio features from the frozen Qwen2.5Omni audio tower pass through the trainable audio encoder. In each V2A layer the target video tokens of latent frame i attend only to the audio tokens of the same time span, which gives a block-diagonal attention pattern. Memory and reference tokens skip this layer. The strips at the bottom left mark the visual decoder blocks that contain a V2A layer in the 2B and 21B models.

The memory tokens are concatenated (C) with the reference and target tokens into one visual sequence for the DiT. papers.abstract: Understanding neural scaling laws is increasingly important for theory and practice, yet first-principles explanations remain limited even in simple settings. In this work, we study capacity-limited scaling in a bottlenecked bigram model with power-law (Zipf) token statistics, viewed as an analytically tractable toy model of a large language model. Fixed random embeddings serve as a proxy for representational capacity and induce an explicit bottleneck of width, allowing us to derive scaling laws for prediction regret as a function of model width, vocabulary size, and the Zipf exponent. Our results complement recent theoretical accounts based on optimization dynamics by isolating scaling due purely to representational constraints. In the appropriate regime, the theory recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws and suggests that heavy-tailed language statistics may underlie both optimization- and capacity-driven scaling. Experiments natural language datasets (WikiText2, OpenWebText) closely match the predicted curves.
authors: Julian Enoch, Elvis Dohmatob
bullets: Studies prediction regret under Zipf-distributed token statistics.
Uses fixed random embeddings to impose an explicit representational bottleneck of variable width.
Derives scaling with model width, vocabulary size, and Zipf exponent.
Recovers the functional form of classical neural scaling laws in an appropriate regime.
Predicted curves closely match results on WikiText2 and OpenWebText.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision on the student's own samples, but its targets still come from the teacher. Verifier reinforcement learning (RL) instead uses an outcome signal, but it provides no direct constraint on capabilities outside the verifier. Combining the two is difficult for diffusion language models (dLLMs), because bidirectional denoising makes the policy likelihoods required by ratio-based RL unreliable. We develop a likelihood-free pipeline for a mixture-of-experts dLLM. Each rollout group is routed by verifier outcome. Mixed groups use ratio-free, group-centred REINFORCE. If every student rollout fails but a teacher succeeds, the model receives dense KL supervision on the student's denoising canvases. All other groups are skipped. A KL term anchored to the distilled checkpoint limits changes outside the verifier reward. The tool-calling teacher succeeds on only 18.6% of the training prompts. At 24 denoising steps, distillation exceeds the teacher by 6.77 percentage points, and routing improves the distilled checkpoint by a further 18.31 points. Routing lowers reasoning-trace accuracy by 0.71 points but raises direct-answer accuracy on the same items by 13.21 points. The anchored arm restores trace accuracy. Its tool-calling score differs by -0.16 points, with a confidence interval that includes zero, although this comparison also removes a small fallback distillation route. A domain-conditional recipe retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; a second seed gives 18.23 points and reproduces both preservation results, but the math result is seed-dependent. We pre-registered every arm and evaluated each comparison on paired items in a single sweep on one machine.
authors: Wentao Lu, Tianyu Zhu, Jesse Clark
bullets: Addresses unreliable policy likelihoods in bidirectional denoising, which hinder ratio-based RL for diffusion language models.
Routes rollout groups by verifier outcomes: mixed outcomes use group-centred, ratio-free REINFORCE; all-failure groups with teacher success receive dense KL distillation; other groups are skipped.
Anchors training to the distilled checkpoint with KL regularization to limit changes outside the verifier objective.
At 24 denoising steps, distillation beats the teacher by 6.77 points, while routing adds 18.31 points; direct-answer accuracy rises 13.21 points despite a 0.71-point drop in reasoning-trace accuracy.
The anchored variant restores trace accuracy, and domain-conditional training retains a 16.37-point tool-calling gain; math improvements are seed-dependent.

papers.abstract: Existing illumination estimation methods primarily recover lighting distributions for rendering, but typically leave the contributions of individual physical light sources at specific scene locations implicit. We address this gap by leveraging the scene understanding capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to connect local illumination with its physical sources. We introduce LAMP, a framework for point-conditioned, source-aware illumination reasoning from a single RGB image with marked query points. LAMP constructs a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks contributing sources for each query, and predicts their 3D query-to-source directions. We supervise these relationships using procedurally controlled indoor scenes, reusing independently rendered source responses to derive contribution targets across lighting configurations and obtaining exact directions from source and query positions. On the Infinigen test set, fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B increases dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m from 0% to 70.6%, with 94.5% of directions within 12.5 degrees of ground truth among correctly localized sources. Combined with a lightweight network predicting dense RGB irradiance, LAMP achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior lighting-estimation methods while additionally localizing individual physical sources in 3D and explicitly attributing local illumination to them.
authors: Yanqiao Wang, Jin Sun
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit source attribution in conventional illumination-estimation methods.
Builds a shared inventory of active light sources, ranks their contributions per query point, and predicts 3D query-to-source directions.
Trains on procedurally controlled indoor scenes with source-response contribution targets and exact geometric directions.
On Infinigen, fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B reaches 70.6% dominant-source 3D PCK@0.5m; 94.5% of correctly localized directions are within 12.5° of ground truth.
Combined with dense RGB irradiance prediction, achieves probe-rendering quality comparable to prior methods while adding explicit 3D source localization and attribution.

A dense network predicts RGB irradiance from the unmarked image. At inference, the ranked sources and the irradiance map are composed to render a probe at any query.

papers.abstract: Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target-room decisions without re-evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 evaluations against 15 to 18. Additional materials are available at https://mind-icra27.github.io/.
authors: Mohamed Abouagour, Junhyun Nam, Wonse Jo, Byung-Cheol Min
bullets: Compiles persistent language instructions into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection.
Intersects these dependencies with event footprints to refresh only affected room judgments, while updating reachability and selection separately.
On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences, reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 decisions.
Preserves all benchmark decisions with frozen Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B evaluators, and matches full recomputation in all 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes.
Scope: guarantees depend on fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, plus conservative dependency and footprint coverage; it does not improve evaluator accuracy.

papers.abstract: Memory for long-horizon video generation must satisfy two competing requirements: it must remain bounded so generation can continue indefinitely, while still recovering what was observed at a place when the camera returns, regardless of how long ago it was seen. Reconstruction-based memories provide spatial recall by caching and reprojecting explicit geometry, but require growing storage and depend on estimated 3D structure. Recurrent memories keep a constant-size state, but retention is governed by temporal recurrence, causing old observations to fade with time. We introduce SMART, a slot memory addressed by region tokens, which combines bounded storage with spatially addressed recall. SMART stores content in a constant-size slot recurrence whose writes are addressed by the observing camera and whose reads are queried by the rendering camera, without constructing an explicit 3D representation or maintaining a growing cache. Consequently, recall is conditioned on inter-view geometry rather than on recency. Each read additionally provides a confidence estimate that conditions a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, allowing it to selectively trust retrieved content while relying on its generative prior elsewhere. On long trajectories in Memory Maze and Minecraft, SMART maintains high-fidelity recall far beyond its training horizon while using constant memory and per-step cost.
authors: Eren Cetin, Julius Erbach, Vukasin Bozic, Hyojun Go, Zixiang Zhao, Nikolai Kalischek, Federico Tombari, Konrad Schindler, Dominik Narnhofer
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between bounded memory and recalling observations when the camera revisits a location.
Uses a constant-size slot recurrence with writes keyed by the observing camera and reads queried by the rendering camera.
Avoids explicit 3D reconstruction and growing caches by conditioning recall on inter-view geometry.
Provides confidence estimates to a chunk-causal diffusion transformer, which balances retrieved content with its generative prior.
On Memory Maze and Minecraft trajectories, maintains high-fidelity recall beyond the training horizon with constant memory and per-step cost.

papers.abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy's own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace's source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.
authors: Chang Liu, Sibo Tian, Litian Gong, Zhiwen Fan, Jiachen Li, Xiao Liang, Minghui Zheng
bullets: Targets product variation, prerequisite sequences, and precise contact-rich approaches in EoL disassembly.

papers.abstract: Transformers are intuitively considered to be efficient at copying from their inputs. We actually show that the ability of LLMs to copy in context can be improved through explicit modeling. We propose Copy-Paste Language Models (CPLMs), which add a lightweight Copy-Paste head to the conventional language modeling (LM) head. CPLMs improve training efficiency, downstream performance, and offer new operating points in long-context and retrieval setups. We validate our approach by pretraining models from 135M to 1.7B parameters, showing improvements across all scales and backbones with negligible training and inference overheads. We explain the success of CPLMs by showing that they partially mitigate the LM head gradient bottleneck through an alternative gradient path.
authors: Nathan Godey, Yoav Artzi
bullets: Transformers may copy from inputs inefficiently despite appearing naturally suited to copying.
CPLMs augment the standard language-modeling head with a lightweight Copy-Paste head.
The method improves training efficiency, downstream performance, and provides useful operating points for long-context and retrieval tasks.
Improvements hold across model scales from 135M to 1.7B parameters and across backbones, with negligible training and inference overhead.
The authors attribute the gains to an alternative gradient path that partially alleviates the LM-head gradient bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.
authors: Zachary Broveak, Christian Kubicka, Thierry Tambe
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of fixed per-layer expert utilization in dense-to-MoE conversion.
Introduces static per-layer allocation shared across tokens and dynamic per-token allocation schedules.
Both approaches improve analytic- and learning-based conversion methods over uniform utilization.
At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation lowers WikiText-2 perplexity by 1.04–6.26 points across the evaluated models and bases.
Dynamic allocation also improves six-task mean accuracy by 1.5–4.2 percentage points on the learned bases across tested utilization levels.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Spectral-MoE learned-base dynamic allocator architecture. During the forward pass, the allocator uses hidden states to initialize and revise per-token schedules, layers commit budgetconstrained expert counts, and the final layer consumes the remainder. During the backward pass, loss gradients pass through selections and budget commitments via STEs to train only the allocator, routers, and partition affinities.

papers.abstract: Transformer language models develop attention heads that specialize in syntactic relations, for example, attending from verbs to their subjects. Do these heads play a causal role in the model's syntactic predictions? Evidence for such a role is mixed to negative: even when we force these heads to attend to a distractor noun other than the subject, the model's syntactic predictions are still more consistent with the subject than with the distractor. Interventions on specialized syntax heads had a significantly stronger effect on syntactic predictions than interventions on random heads, but only in one of the two measures we propose.
authors: William Timkey, Tal Linzen
bullets: The study tests whether heads attending along syntactic relations, such as verbs attending to subjects, causally influence syntax.
Forcing syntax heads to attend to distractor nouns does not shift predictions away from the true subject.
Intervening on syntax heads affects syntactic predictions more than intervening on random heads under one proposed measure.
The findings provide limited evidence for a causal role and differ across evaluation measures.

papers.abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.
authors: Sitan Huang, Grace Gao
bullets: Addresses robustness challenges from extreme lunar illumination and deployment-time perceptual disturbances.
Uses an end-to-end vision-language-action policy mapping observations directly to rover control actions.
Trains with safety-aware expert demonstrations generated in a high-fidelity lunar simulation.
Performs competitively with a modular navigation baseline in closed-loop evaluation under unseen disturbances.
Adaptive execution horizons reduce inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates versus fixed horizons in evaluated scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the VLA policy and training. a) Prior to policy training, an RVQ-VAE is trained on expert trajectories from the policy’s training dataset, which then assigns each trajectory in the same dataset a primary and secondary code pair. b) The policy is trained to predict these primary and secondary codes from camera and BEV-map images. The quantized latent vector corresponding to predicted codes is decoded back to an RVQ-discretized trajectory, whose heading angles are refined by continuous offsets. An execution-horizon head predicts a categorical distribution over execution horizons for each curvature bound. At deployment, the maximum curvature demanded for closed-loop trajectory tracking selects the corresponding execution horizon.

papers.abstract: World models of visual information predict future image frames conditioned on given action sequences. This predicted scene evolution is driven by deterministic changes such as controlled motion on a robot platform, as well as stochastic changes such as rendering of manipulated objects or previously occluded regions. Our key insight is that the spatial location of these stochastic changes is itself learnable. We leverage this insight by jointly regressing both the deterministic next-state prediction and the spatial uncertainty map, then using the uncertainty map to guide a conditional diffusion process. We propose Decoupled Drift-Diffusion World Model (D3WM), which uses a transformer trained with a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood objective to produce both the deterministic next-state prediction and a spatial map of heteroscedastic aleatoric uncertainty. The learned uncertainty map then provides a structured spatial gate for a conditional diffusion model: deterministic regions are anchored to the predicted state, while uncertain regions, such as disocclusions or dynamic textures, are sampled by the diffusion process. We frame this decomposition under a variance-gated stochastic differential equation that separates deterministic drift from stochastic diffusion. D3WM shows improved results over competitive baselines in two distinct types of action spaces: robotic tabletop manipulation and camera motion.
authors: Anton Arapin, Aditya Singh, Yixin Wang, Jun Gao, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Targets world-model predictions containing both deterministic motion and stochastic changes such as disocclusions or dynamic textures.
A transformer jointly predicts the deterministic next state and a spatial heteroscedastic uncertainty map using Gaussian negative log-likelihood.
The uncertainty map gates a conditional diffusion process, anchoring predictable regions while sampling uncertain ones.
The method is formulated as a variance-gated stochastic differential equation separating drift from diffusion.
Improves over competitive baselines across robotic tabletop manipulation and camera-motion action spaces.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture of D3WM. The input action sequence is denoted a[0,t), and t corresponds to the time shift into the future that the model aims to predict. The deterministic prediction network fµ θ is labeled ‘Drift Network’ in the figure for compactness, while in the text, “drift” refers only to the SDE coefficient fθ (Section 3.1).

papers.abstract: Transformers are efficient to pre-train at scale because attention permits parallel computation across sequence positions, but long-context inference requires increasingly large KV caches. Efficient recurrent alternatives reduce the asymptotic complexity of inference, but their sequential dependence limits token-wise parallelism during training, making them harder to scale. Further, the current paradigm of extending long context tasks creates competing notions of retaining information precisely and keeping long-context inference efficient. To address this gap, we introduce Titan-Llama, a post-training method for retrofitting attention-based language models with a hierarchical memory architecture that updates parameters at test-time. Titan-Llama applies a blockwise attention mask and preserves full-fidelity attention over recent tokens while compressing historical context into recurrent, fixed-size neural memory modules (NMMs). Our formulation allows pre-trained attention layers to be replaced without training a new language model from scratch. On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Titan-Llama raises accuracy over segmented attention windows from 23.87\% to 40.51\% on QuALITY and from 14.50\% to 40.75\% on LongHealth. Inference benchmarks show more than 20\% faster prefill, 37\% faster decode at medium context lengths, and 24\% lower steady-state decode memory usage in the evaluated configurations. Together, these results demonstrate that incorporating memory architecture mechanisms that utilize test-time training effectively modulates long-context behavior of pre-trained models, offering a practical route to adapting pre-trained transformers for efficient long-context inference. Our code is released on Github \href{https://github.com/sarahpannn/titans-pytorch/tree/main}{GitHub}
authors: Sarah Pan, Ali Behrouz
bullets: Addresses the tension between precise information retention and efficient long-context inference.
Uses hierarchical neural memory modules, blockwise attention, and full attention over recent tokens while compressing older context into fixed-size memory.
Replaces attention layers post-training, avoiding training a new language model from scratch.
On Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, improves QuALITY and LongHealth accuracy over segmented attention windows and reports faster prefill/decode with lower steady-state decode memory.
Evaluated configurations show benefits at medium context lengths; broader scope beyond the reported model and tasks is not established by the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Titan-Llama architecture at a glance. Left: The inner loss generates gradients at test-time w.r.t. MLP weights, teaching it to memorize historical attention key-value bindings. Right: The query associated with a local hidden state is used to retrieve a value from the NMM. This value, approximating the historical attention output, is then used as a residual and injected into the lambdagated output stream.

Figure 2: Long-context language modeling and decode latency. Left. Change in per-token negative log-likelihood relative to full attention, measured on Pile. Titan-Llama with 1024-token segments beats full attention from 16K through 128K. Right. Median single-token decode latency on an A100 at batch size one, after prefill and warmup (lower is better). Titan-Llama’s CUDA-graph-enabled decode is faster than the measured full-attention, Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, and In-Place TTT implementations across the reported lengths (Dao & Gu, 2024; Yang et al., 2025).

Figure 3: The effects of scaling chunk size on downstream performance and efficiency. Left. Scaling chunk size improves performance on long-context reasoning tasks like QuALITY and LongHealth. Middle. RULER trends are mixed. Longer chunks help at intermediate lengths but do not consistently improve associative recall. Detailed RULER results can be found in Table 5 in the Appendix. Right. Larger chunks increase prefill latency as memory bandwidth saturates.

Figure 4: Increasing the proportion of Llama 3.2 1B layers retrofitted with NMMs increases token decode throughput, decreases prefill latency, and also decreases memory footprint during token decoding. Peak memory footprint during prefill for partial Titan-Llama hybrids exceeds full-attention Llama while retrofitting all layers leads to lower peak memory footprint. Benchmarking was performed on a single 80GB NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Figure 5: Inference cost when later attention layers are restricted to local windows. The plot shows a 512-token window. Restricting more layers limits the growth of the KV cache and makes decode throughput less sensitive to prefill length.

papers.abstract: While work on LLM-based regression has largely focused on scalar prediction, multi-output text regression remains less explored. We present DualView, a parameter-efficient approach to leverage LLMs for multi-output text regression. \method{} first extracts broad and output-specific representations from a frozen LLM, then uses a dual-branch architecture to produce the full score vector. Across five heterogeneous regression tasks and eight LLMs (up to 122B), DualView outperforms seven supervised regression baselines while requiring 82--1842 times fewer fitted parameters than the three strongest baselines. These improvements extend across individual output dimensions and persist even with limited training data. Notably, DualView using a smaller open-weight LLM can outperform unsupervised prediction with Gemini 3.1 Pro. Controlled ablations show that broad and output-specific evidence provide complementary predictive benefits, while lightweight shared predictors achieve strong performance with fewer trainable parameters.
authors: Yiheng Su, Junyi Jessy Li, Matthew Lease
bullets: Addresses the underexplored problem of predicting multiple regression outputs from text with LLMs.
Extracts broad and output-specific representations, then combines them through a dual-branch architecture.
Evaluated across five heterogeneous tasks and eight LLMs, including models up to 122B parameters.
Outperforms seven supervised baselines while fitting substantially fewer parameters; gains persist with limited training data.
Ablations show complementary value from both evidence types and effective lightweight shared predictors.

papers.abstract: We present LidarVerse, a real-time unified LiDAR world model for sensor simulation across tasks and sensors. Existing LiDAR simulators largely follow one of two complementary paradigms: reconstruction-based methods preserve the geometry of a captured scene but require lengthy per-scene optimization, whereas generative methods amortize learning across data but lack the consistency needed for long-horizon rollouts. LidarVerse brings both paradigms into a single, unified conditional generative framework. A universal tokenizer maps LiDAR range sequences into a shared latent space, where a bidirectional teacher learns a common interface for conditioning on a LiDAR prefix, an HD-Map, a persistent spatial cache, and optionally, text. Varying the available scene evidence turns the same model into a generator of new worlds, a point-cloud forecaster, or a generalizable resimulator of observed scenes without per-scene optimization. We distill the teacher into a four-step autoregressive causal student and maintain both a rolling temporal K/V cache and a world-aligned spatial cache, enabling persistent long-horizon rollouts with real-time inference at 11 FPS on a single H100 GPU. LidarVerse achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across all three evaluation protocols, while its tokenizer supports 32-, 64-, and 128-beam LiDAR and generalizes to an unseen scanning pattern. These results demonstrate that generative and reconstruction-grounded LiDAR simulation can be realized within one model, providing the core capabilities for future closed-loop sensor simulation.
authors: Henry Che, Xuanchi Ren, Sanja Fidler, Shenlong Wang, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Shengyu Huang
bullets: Combines reconstruction-based scene consistency with the scalability of generative modeling in one conditional framework.
Uses a universal tokenizer and a shared latent interface conditioned on LiDAR prefixes, HD maps, spatial memory, and optionally text.
A single model supports new-world generation, point-cloud forecasting, and resimulation without per-scene optimization.
A distilled four-step causal student with temporal and spatial caches enables persistent long-horizon rollouts at 11 FPS on one H100 GPU.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on most metrics across three evaluation protocols and generalizes across LiDAR beam counts and an unseen scanning pattern.

papers.abstract: With the growing number of LLMs available, selecting which one to use for a prompt has become a key question. A large part of the routing literature relies on semantically embedding prompts into a vector space and then applying a lightweight classifier to the embedded representations. These methods perform robustly in-distribution but they struggle to generalize to unseen tasks. By studying the geometry of semantic embeddings, we trace a clear failure mode: features that determine the neighbors of unseen prompts are an unreliable proxy for LLM selection. We therefore replace the semantic embedding with the following map: we run a partial forward pass of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on the prompt and use the hidden state of its last token at a deep layer as the representation. When applying kNN and other simple classifiers to this new representation, we obtain a clear result in generalization: on average across cost penalties, their performance improves. Moreover, kNN and another simple classifier that we propose outperform every evaluated semantic-embedding baseline. Our two simple methods also beat a recent SoTA hidden-states based router on RouterBench.
authors: Leonardo Torti, Emanuele Rimoldi, Tomer Galanti, Tomaso Poggio, Pierfrancesco Beneventano

Simple kNN and a proposed classifier improve average generalization across cost penalties and outperform evaluated semantic-embedding baselines.
Both methods also outperform a recent hidden-state router on RouterBench.

papers.abstract: Scientific imaging data involving medical (e.g., 3D radiographic, microscopic images) and astronomical sensors pose different challenges from natural images. One key challenge is that these datasets are often orders of magnitude larger than natural images. Efficient training and inference on such data is challenging due to the increased hardware requirements, often needing bespoke solutions. Moreover, the relevant objects such as tumors and astronomical phenomena are sparsely distributed with respect to the background information. Standard efficiency techniques like quantization and pruning apply uniform scaling of all regions, potentially compromising the precision/fidelity of predictions. Thus, efficient methods that reduce computational requirements without losing resolution for relevant parts of the data and with uncertainty estimates on predictions are essential. We present \textit{Conformal Adaptation} with risk guarantees for uncertainty-aware sparse computations. Our formalism is general, spanning dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks where hierarchical models predict at low resolution, certify the signal using conformal risk control, and refine the certified predictions. We benchmark our method on multiple tasks such as 3D medical image segmentation, 2D galaxy flux prediction, and 1D calcium spike rate prediction, achieving $2.5$--$72\times$ wall-clock speedup across the various tasks, including on commodity CPUs.
authors: Shehtab Zaman, Aneesh Rangnekar, Nancy Lee, Harini Veeraraghavan
bullets: Targets oversized medical, astronomical, and other scientific data with sparsely distributed signals.
Uses hierarchical low-resolution prediction, conformal risk control, and selective refinement of certified regions.
Supports dense pixel-level classification and regression tasks across 3D, 2D, and 1D data.
Benchmarks report 2.5–72× wall-clock speedups, including on commodity CPUs.
Scope: focuses on reducing computation without sacrificing resolution for relevant signals or uncertainty estimates.

papers.abstract: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful tool for high-resolution subsurface model reconstruction, but it remains highly nonlinear and ill-posed, especially when the initial model is inaccurate or the acquired data are noisy and incomplete. Annealed Stein variational gradient descent (ASVGD) provides a particle-based Bayesian framework for FWI by approximating the posterior distribution with an ensemble of velocity models, thereby enabling uncertainty quantification beyond a single deterministic solution. However, conventional ASVGD-FWI commonly relies on simple handcrafted priors, such as Gaussian or smoothing assumptions, which are often insufficient to represent complex geological structures. To address this limitation, we introduce a learned diffusion model (DM) as an implicit regularization mechanism within the ASVGD-FWI framework. Instead of explicitly evaluating the diffusion prior density, the trained diffusion model acts as a learned geological projection operator that guides updated particles toward the distribution of plausible velocity models. In this way, the proposed method combines data consistency from FWI, posterior diversity from ASVGD, and structural realism from the diffusion prior. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the diffusion-regularized ASVGD-FWI produces more geologically consistent mean models, suppresses nonphysical artifacts, and yields uncertainty estimates that are more concentrated around structurally complex and poorly constrained regions. These results suggest that learned diffusion priors can effectively enhance Bayesian FWI by improving both inversion stability and the interpretability of posterior uncertainty.
authors: Chao Li, Mrinal K. Sen, Sergey Fomel, Yangkang Chen
bullets: Addresses the nonlinearity and ill-posedness of FWI under inaccurate initial models and noisy or incomplete data.
Integrates a learned diffusion model into annealed Stein variational gradient descent as an implicit geological prior.
Combines FWI data consistency, ASVGD posterior diversity, and diffusion-based structural realism.
Produces more geologically consistent mean models, fewer nonphysical artifacts, and more focused uncertainty in complex, poorly constrained regions.
The evidence is based on numerical experiments; the approach depends on a trained diffusion prior to represent plausible velocity models.

papers.abstract: Evaluation of large language models (LLMs) remains largely pre-scientific: it involves many design decisions, with little guidance on how to make them. These choices can substantially affect measured performance and, consequently, decisions about subsequent pretraining. To identify effective evaluation setups, we investigate 8 aspects, such as task formulation or the number of in-context examples. We compare the setups using three widely-used signal criteria, repurposed as normative meta-measures: monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency of the evaluation scores across intermediate checkpoints. In an early pretraining scenario, we evaluate these setups on 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models trained on different types of data, using 80 tasks in four languages. We also examine the setups on three larger LLMs ($\geq$7B) in the same four languages and explore how the preferred setups change with model scale. Our results yield concrete recommendations: some choices, such as the use of multiple prompts, are consistently useful, whereas others, such as task formulation, depend on model scale. More generally, our framework serves as a recipe for the choice of evaluation setups in new scenarios.
authors: Shenbin Qian, David Samuel, Jind\v{r}ich Helcl, Andrey Kutuzov, Stephan Oepen
bullets: Studies eight evaluation aspects, including task formulation and the number of in-context examples.
Uses monotonicity, non-randomness, and ranking consistency as normative meta-measures.
Evaluates setups across 26 monolingual 2B-parameter models, 80 tasks, and four languages, plus three larger models.
Finds that multiple prompts are consistently helpful, while task formulation preferences vary with model scale.
Provides practical recommendations and a general recipe for choosing evaluation setups in new scenarios.

papers.abstract: Can AI agents carry out research on open scientific problems? We introduce Into the Unknown, a benchmark that provides an agent with a science paper along with a research direction to pursue and tasks it to write a follow-up paper. We work with scientists at US Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories, who each contribute an unpublished follow-up direction from their own work together with the necessary conditions a submission must meet. While assessing the quality of a follow-up paper is challenging in general, using these conditions to form a rubric makes evaluation more tractable for research problems that have no reference answer. We have nine frontier agents write 15 follow-ups each, spanning quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science, and scientific machine learning domains. None of the 135 submissions satisfies all the conditions, and 114 fail our integrity check, most often because the paper claims work that was never done or reports numbers that contradict the recorded evidence. Overall, agents readily produce papers that look like follow-ups, but none meets the standard of the domain scientist, leaving substantial headroom. Our code and data are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.
authors: Zhi Cao, Yining Hong, Jiaolong Yang, Yejin Choi, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Huang Huang
bullets: Problem: Most human manipulation datasets lack force measurements, limiting force-aware human-to-robot transfer.
Method: FACT cascades a track-guided coarse planner with a force-action joint refiner that predicts future video, visual tracks, actions, and interaction forces.
Data: The model is pretrained on the EgoForce human tactile dataset together with robot demonstrations.
Results: Across ten fine-grained manipulation tasks, FACT improves success rates by up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex using as few as 10 robot and 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning.
Scope: Force supervision, visual-track prediction, and future-force prediction each support improved dexterous execution; the study focuses on tasks requiring fine coordination and force feedback.

papers.abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.
authors: Maria Attarian, Yifan Ruan, Claas Voelcker, Chenyang Cao, Amy Zhang, Peter Stone, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski

papers.abstract: Learning a collective policy for state-based Cartesian manipulation across diverse robotic embodiments presents a fundamental challenge due to embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. Collective learning aggregates multi-robot experience to discover shared task structure, yet naive aggregation can average incompatible action modes when different embodiments realize the same Cartesian command through different transition behavior. This leads to strategy ambiguity and performance collapse on dynamically outlying embodiments. To address this, we propose PACE, a two-stage collective learning framework that separates shared task-space intent from embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. The first stage employs a representation layer pre-trained on offline trajectories to extract task-level context from collective data. The second stage introduces a decision layer equipped with a predictive dynamics adapter. By forcing the latent state to predict future transitions, this adapter acts as a latent regularizer that grounds the policy in the transition behavior of the executing robot while preserving real-time inference without online planning. Evaluations across simulated embodiments demonstrate that our method prevents performance collapse on distinct robots. It achieves over 93\% overall success and 89\% on dynamically out-of-distribution zero-shot simulated robots, outperforming the Transformer behavior cloning (82\%) and diffusion policy baselines (66\%). Physical KUKA deployment further validates the feasibility of the full state-based pipeline under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Shaocheng Liu, Yuan Meng, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses performance collapse caused by aggregating incompatible action-transition behaviors across embodiments.

The adapter predicts future transitions to ground actions in the executing robot’s dynamics without online planning.
Achieves over 93% overall success and 89% success on dynamically out-of-distribution simulated robots.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real feasibility on a physical KUKA platform.
