papers.abstract: Tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in almost all large language models (LLMs). One of the most popular frameworks is BPE tokenization, which consists of special token segmentation, pretokenization, and byte-pair encoding (BPE). However, existing algorithms are sequential, with each stage only processing complete output from the previous stage. In order to reduce latency and memory footprints, recent works (Jiang and Gong, ICML 2026) (Li, Yang and Mamouras, ASPLOS 2026) (Mamouras, Li and Yang, PLDI 2026) have initiated the study of online algorithms for subroutines such as pretokenization and BPE with a goal of streaming input to output as the input arrives online. However, the search for efficient online tokenization remains open. In this work, we formalize and resolve online tokenization. We introduce the notion of delay for online tokenization which characterizes the extent to which the algorithm output lags behind the (possibly computationally intractable) optimum. We give a near-linear time algorithm with optimal delay (up to constant factors). We complement this algorithm with a conditional lower bound: unless $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$, there is no polynomial time algorithm that beats the delay of our algorithm by more than a constant factor. We implement a practical variant for tokenizers from OpenAI's tiktoken and HuggingFace's tokenizers. We obtain a $7.9\times$-$34.8\times$ latency advantage (measured as time to first token) over tiktoken (as well as the recent gigatoken tokenizer) and our implementation maintains approximately constant memory usage independent of input size. Our implementation also achieves a $2.4\times$-$7.0\times$ improvement in throughput over tiktoken and $15.8\times$-$38.1\times$ over tokenizers.
authors: Mina Dalirrooyfard, Christopher Ye
bullets: Defines delay for online tokenization relative to an offline optimum, even when computing that optimum may be intractable.
Provides a near-linear-time online algorithm whose delay is optimal up to constant factors.
Shows conditionally that, unless P = NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can improve its delay by more than a constant factor.
A practical implementation for tiktoken and HuggingFace tokenizers achieves lower time-to-first-token, higher throughput, and approximately constant memory usage with respect to input size.

papers.abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.
authors: Daniel Lawson, Dhruv Sreenivas, Adriana Hugessen, Khimya Khetarpal, Glen Berseth
bullets: Addresses poor generalization from static offline datasets, especially on unseen tasks requiring composition of known skills.
Proposes TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model to generate achievable future outcomes.
Uses imagined outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned behavioral cloning policies.
Demonstrates significant generalization gains on stitching-based OGBench tasks.
Scope: focuses on zero-shot goal generalization and avoids the difficulty of long-horizon world-model generation.

papers.abstract: Generating novel molecules with desired properties is a central challenge in drug discovery. Although foundational work focused on de novo generation, practical use cases require a more complex setting: conditioning on an initial seed molecule, optimizing multiple properties, and operating in data-sparse regimes. We introduce PairIT, a flexible training framework for autoregressive transformers over SMILES sequences that enables seeded generation by learning from pairs of structurally similar molecules. By leveraging matched pairs, the model learns to generate local, chemically meaningful edits that improve a property of the seed molecule. Prompt tokens extend this framework by specifying the target property, desired direction, and approximate magnitude of change. Multiple prompt tokens can be concatenated to enable multi-property optimization at inference time. For properties where pair supervision alone is insufficient, reinforcement learning post-training can further improve optimization, providing a tunable trade-off between proximity to the seed and the optimization objective. PairIT naturally supports pretraining on a large dataset and fine-tuning on a smaller dataset, which is critical for performance in data-sparse regimes. Surprisingly, we observe diminishing returns to the scale of the pretraining dataset. We demonstrate empirically on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons datasets that, with appropriate paired-data curation, a standard transformer model of modest size (68M parameters) can achieve robust seeded molecular optimization in low-data regimes.
authors: Hannah Lawrence, Bodhi P. Vani, Ji Won Park, Natasa Tagasovska, Samuel Don Stanton, Andrew Martin Watkins, Michael Maser, Ewa M. Nowara
bullets: Addresses molecule optimization with a starting seed, multiple property goals, and sparse training data.
Learns local chemical edits from structurally similar molecule pairs represented as SMILES sequences.
Uses prompt tokens to specify target properties, optimization direction, and approximate change; prompts can be combined for multi-property optimization.
Optional reinforcement-learning post-training improves optimization while controlling similarity to the seed.
Experiments on MoleculeNet and Therapeutics Data Commons show robust optimization with a modest 68M-parameter transformer; larger pretraining data offers diminishing returns.

papers.abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
authors: Elena Sorina Lupu, Hannah Grauer, Phaedrus Leeds, Nikhil Ranganathan, Connor Lee, Sulekha Kishore, Cailyn Smith, Shon Cortes, Brian Hardy, Benjamen Bycroft, Darren W. Rowen, Soon-Jo Chung
bullets: Addresses spacecraft autonomy under communication delays and limited bandwidth by moving learning pipelines onboard.
Deploys a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU for real-time image-based control.
Integrates ROS 2 Foxy for data transport and an open-source, integrity-focused self-healing file system.
Conducted 12 spacecraft experiments over approximately one year in Low Earth Orbit.
Demonstrates that learning-based software, commercial hardware, and open-source tools can operate under LEO constraints.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces LLM inference costs by removing model components to produce smaller dense models. However, existing methods can cause reasoning performance to collapse on long-form reasoning tasks such as AIME. We propose \textit{LayerTrim}, a training-free structured pruning method that identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features while preserving attention and decoder depth. LayerTrim is the first training-free structured pruning method designed to preserve long-form reasoning without gradients or recovery training. Across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, LayerTrim outperforms existing structured pruning methods in most evaluated settings, improving average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP. On \texttt{Qwen3-14B}, LayerTrim achieves 1.24$\times$ faster prefill and 19.7\% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model, while better preserving reasoning ability. It also achieves the shortest average generation length among evaluated pruned models, while retaining the highest average accuracy. These results demonstrate that LayerTrim improves reasoning efficiency through both structural compression and reduced token generation.
authors: Woosang Lim, Haneul Yoo, Vincent-Daniel Yun, Sungjoo Yoo
bullets: Targets reasoning degradation caused by conventional structured pruning on long-form tasks such as AIME.
Identifies redundant decoder layers and selectively trims their MLP features without gradients or recovery training.
Evaluated across three reasoning language models and five benchmarks, outperforming existing pruning methods in most settings.
Improves average accuracy by up to 21.4 percentage points over RESP.
On Qwen3-14B, delivers 1.24× faster prefill and 19.7% lower peak GPU memory than the dense model while preserving reasoning ability.

papers.abstract: Emerging decision models such as JEV provide typed interfaces that map task instructions and observations directly to choices, judgments, and scores. As these models are increasingly used for automated decision-making, understanding their reliability under adversarial manipulation becomes critical. We introduce DecisionRobust, a benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of decision models across textual and visual inputs. Our benchmark covers practical decision-making scenarios and a diverse suite of attacks, including semantics-preserving text perturbations, image perturbations, and prompt injection in both modalities. We curate evaluation sets through external validity checks and cross-model candidate selection. We evaluate 30 model configurations on text tasks and 17 on vision tasks, including 24 and 12 held-out models, respectively, that are excluded from candidate selection. Our experiments reveal several key findings. First, attacks expose vulnerabilities beyond the models used for construction and selection, although optimized image perturbations transfer weakly to many targets even with multiple surrogates. Second, relative model robustness varies across tasks and attack types, and resistance to input perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Third, label-consistency checks substantially reduce measured attack success across text and image settings, highlighting the importance of validating apparent failures. The benchmark is available at https://yifan-lan.github.io/DecisionRobust/.
authors: Yifan Lan, Zhongye Liu, Yurui Chang, Hanyu Wang, Yongkang Du, Lu Lin, Jinghui Chen
bullets: Evaluates robustness across textual and visual inputs using semantics-preserving perturbations, image attacks, and multimodal prompt injection.
Tests 30 text-model configurations and 17 vision-model configurations, including held-out models for external evaluation.
Finds vulnerabilities transfer beyond benchmark-construction models, while optimized image attacks often transfer weakly.
Shows that robustness depends on the task and attack type; perturbation resistance does not guarantee prompt-injection resistance.
Label-consistency checks substantially lower measured attack success, underscoring the need to validate apparent failures.

papers.abstract: Activation steering controls large language models at inference time, but its effectiveness depends on the choice of reference data. We introduce genesis steering, which derives a genesis vector from contrastive examples in the model's own fine-tuning data. When these data are unavailable, we draw on the membership inference literature to identify likely training examples and construct a proxy dataset. We establish two theoretical results on optimal displacement to the decision boundary and reduced proxy-estimation bias. We evaluate genesis steering and membership-based proxy construction on T\"ulu-3-8B, whose fine-tuning data are publicly available, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as a control. We find that safety data from T\"ulu-3-8B's training mixture yield stronger steering than external datasets on both models. On T\"ulu-3-8B, membership scores largely agree in identifying training examples, and vectors built from top-ranked examples achieve competitive performance against random subsets of the same size. In contrast, the results on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct hint that a MIA method will only have a positive effect if the mean direction shift with MIA-filtered in-distribution data is much less severe than the direction shift with OoD data.
authors: Tora Bodin, Eric Aubinais, Ilaria Torre, Chih-Hong Cheng
bullets: Activation steering is sensitive to the choice of reference data.
The method builds a genesis vector from contrastive examples in training data; membership inference identifies likely examples when the data are unavailable.
Theoretical analysis characterizes optimal displacement toward decision boundaries and reduced proxy-estimation bias.
On Tülu-3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, in-distribution safety data produced stronger steering than external datasets.
Membership-ranked examples were competitive on Tülu-3-8B, while benefits on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct depended on limiting the induced mean-direction shift.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows language models to adapt their behavior from instructions and demonstrations in a prompt, but accuracy alone does not reveal how contextual information controls their predictions. We study the acquisition and trainability of ICL with a controlled diagnostic that separates copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt. Across 17 models, about a third prefer the copied answer, a few are undecided, and the rest prefer the rule-consistent answer, which goes with higher accuracy and with control by the requested value rather than the closest conflicting example. Checkpoint analyses show that models begin prioritizing task-relevant prompt tokens over conflicting examples long before their accuracy improves beyond chance level. In matched training experiments, synthetic documents that define endings and then query them shift models toward compositional responses on the controlled diagnostic, whereas fine-tuning on definition exercises built from rewritten real documents improves accuracy when prompts reassign label meanings. The results suggest that ICL is not acquired as a single, uniform capability. Instead, prompt control, answer preference, construction without candidates, and transfer can develop along distinct trajectories.
authors: Minglai Yang, Xinyu Guo, Renxiong Wang, Sunjie Hou, Daniel Yue Zhang, Yunzhong He
bullets: A controlled diagnostic distinguishes copying a nearby demonstration from integrating information across the prompt.
Across 17 models, many favor copied answers, while rule-consistent preferences align with higher accuracy and better prompt control.
Checkpoint analyses show sensitivity to task-relevant tokens emerges before accuracy rises above chance.
Synthetic training promotes compositional responses, while rewritten-document exercises improve accuracy when label meanings are reassigned.
ICL components—including prompt control, answer preference, candidate-free construction, and transfer—follow distinct developmental paths.

papers.title: From Copying to Composition: How Language Models Develop In-Context Learning
papers.tldr: Language models develop in-context learning through separable abilities, gradually shifting from copying nearby examples to composing answers from task-relevant prompt information.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have been widely applied in embodied agents and robotics for vision tasks. However, MLLMs suffer from limitations in spatial reasoning and perception. Post-training techniques have shown promise for improving these capabilities; yet, there are limited data-driven surveys of such approaches. In this survey, we consider approaches to fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs for spatial reasoning tasks, ranging from supervised to reinforcement learning, with an emphasis on the datasets used. We investigate themes of dataset construction, data modality and annotation, and evaluation of the resulting models. Based on these themes, we categorize research into three groups: dataset design, dataset construction and evaluation. We find four main methods for constructing fixed spatial annotations: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop. We also observe substantial variation in evaluation approaches, including different scoring methods, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types. Finally, we identify opportunities for future research in unified dynamic annotation, efficient spatial reasoning, standardization of evaluation, expanded spatial range, and human-centered spatial interactions.
authors: Mahdieh Mallahnezhad, Masoud Jafaripour, Mohamadali Tofigh, Sheila Schoepp, Osmar R. Zaiane
bullets: Reviews supervised- and reinforcement-learning approaches for fine-tuning pretrained MLLMs on spatial reasoning tasks.
Categorizes research into dataset design, dataset construction, and evaluation.
Identifies four fixed-annotation strategies: rules and templates, LLM prompting, procedural generation, and human-in-the-loop methods.
Highlights substantial variation in scoring, tolerance metrics, and benchmark types.
Proposes future directions including dynamic annotation, efficient reasoning, standardized evaluation, broader spatial ranges, and human-centered interaction.

papers.abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning enables large language model agents to learn from sparse outcome rewards in long-horizon tasks. Recent methods derive step-level credit by comparing observation-matched experiences across trajectories. However, identical observations can occur in different contexts, and matched peers are not equally informative for a given decision. Moreover, favorable terminal outcomes can obscure redundant actions or detours within successful trajectories. To address these two challenges, we propose Contextual Credit Policy Optimization (CCPO). For the first, CCPO weights observation-matched peers from other trajectories by contextual similarity, computed from frozen LLM representations and accumulated trajectory statistics, allowing peers from similar contexts to contribute more to a step's baseline. For the second, CCPO pairs historical credit, which compares the realized return against the weighted peer baseline, with future credit, which measures the change in contextual outcome value over a short realized continuation. A step is thus credited for the progress it makes, not only for its trajectory's eventual outcome. Both credits are computed in hindsight from rollouts already collected for training, enabling CCPO to address these challenges without an auxiliary value critic. Across two Qwen2.5-Instruct backbones (1.5B and 7B), CCPO achieves up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop and outperforms GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points. Ablations show that contextual weighting outperforms uniform weighting, and that historical and future credit serve as complementary learning signals.
authors: Huiwen Han, Ziyao Zeng, Zihao Zhu, Sisong Bei, Hao Wang, Hongyu Xu, Yan Han, Degui Zhi, Zhiwen Fan
bullets: Addresses misleading peer comparisons across contexts and redundant actions hidden by successful final outcomes.
Weights observation-matched peers using frozen LLM representations and trajectory statistics.
Combines historical credit from peer baselines with future credit from short-term contextual value changes.
Computes both signals retrospectively from existing rollouts, avoiding an auxiliary critic.
Reaches up to 97.4% success on ALFWorld and 79.4% on WebShop, outperforming GRPO by up to 21.6 and 18.5 points.

papers.abstract: Aerial and remote sensing video is increasingly evaluated like web video, by posing multiple-choice questions to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) over sampled frames and reporting accuracy. This paper argues that this recipe measures the wrong aspect, and supports the claim with a convergent meta-analysis of a broad set of published results, organized in four evidence tiers, in which a claim becomes a position only when collected evidence agrees. Parameter scale exhibits a median of +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase on aerial benchmarks, far below a human gap of at least 19 points, whereas acquisition conditions control perception, as 315 of 318 evaluations in 19 within-paper contrasts lose accuracy when conditions such as altitude, view, object size or time horizon become harder. No aerial benchmark in the corpus combines video input with per-task human and random baselines, competence collapses from answering to acting in closed-loop navigation, and the same MLLMs score higher on the aerial benchmark than on ground spatial ones, but lower on studies that test cross-view geometry. From these findings the current study derives five falsifiable principles and proposes the AVU-Card, a reporting card for aerial video benchmarks
authors: Georgios Angelidis, Aggelos Psiris, Maria Vakalopoulou, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos, Giorgos Sfikas, Iraklis Varlamis
bullets: A convergent meta-analysis synthesizes published aerial and remote-sensing video results across four evidence tiers.
Model parameter scaling yields limited gains: a median +3.4 accuracy points per tenfold increase, versus a human gap of at least 19 points.
Perception degrades in 315 of 318 within-paper contrasts when altitude, viewpoint, object size, or time horizon becomes harder.
Current benchmarks lack video-input evaluations with both task-specific human and random baselines, and competence drops sharply from answering to closed-loop navigation.
The paper proposes five falsifiable principles and the AVU-Card for reporting aerial video benchmark properties.

papers.abstract: Constructing robust GUI agents relies on multimodal visual grounding: the ability to precisely map natural language intents to actionable on-screen components. Despite abundant desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks, high-fidelity resources tailored for diverse environments are surprisingly scarce. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Screen Referring Grounding Dataset (ScreenRef), a comprehensive GUI grounding dataset consisting of GUI screenshots paired with natural language referring expressions and box or point annotations. Spanning desktop, web, and mobile domains, ScreenRef comprises 586K screenshots and over 633K referring expression instances, covering tasks such as text recognition, visual matching, spatial understanding, and refusal scenarios. To boost the model's grounding performance, we propose the Distillation-to-Reinforcement Learning (D2RL) method to address the limited generalization of supervised fine-tuning and the sparse reward problem in reinforcement learning. Utilizing ScreenRef, we train Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct via sequential SFT and D2RL training, yielding GroundGUI-8B. GroundGUI-8B achieves 95.2% on ScreenSpot-V2, 63.9% on ScreenSpot-Pro, 65.4% on OSWorld-G, 86.8% on MMBench-GUI L2, and 38.3% on UI-Vision. Among 8B-scale models, it produces substantial gains over models trained on open-source datasets, with performance comparable or even superior to models trained on closed-source data. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/PrentisAI/GroundGUI.

papers.abstract: As the Arctic transitions toward a seasonally ice-free state, capturing the complex morphology of submerged sea ice is crucial for advancing models of ocean-ice-atmosphere heat exchange and monitoring under-ice habitats. Currently, sub-surface ice mapping is predominantly achieved through acoustic sensors such as multibeam sonar. While sonar provides robust large-scale geometry, it lacks spectral and high-resolution textural information required to record fine morphological features - a critical limitation in under-ice environments, where sparse visual features and degraded sensing conditions challenge the capture of detailed structural and optical surface properties. We present a benchmark for vision-based under-ice 3D reconstruction using real-world data from the MOSAiC expedition and synthetic data generated in an Unreal Engine-based underwater robotics simulator. The benchmark evaluates Structure-From-Motion (SfM) and monocular depth estimation, with quantitative comparison enabled through cross-modal registration to upward-looking multibeam sonar.

Enables quantitative assessment through cross-modal registration with upward-looking multibeam sonar.

papers.abstract: Chatbot Arena ranks language models with the Bradley-Terry model, which gives each model one score and so assumes Luce's choice axiom. Choice theory predicts where this fails: near-copies are told apart more decisively than their scores imply. On 1.8 million Arena votes, votes between versions of one model are 1.37 times as decisive as Bradley-Terry predicts, between sizes of one generation 1.26 times and between models of one lab 1.12 times; a release a year later gives consistent multipliers, and the effect survives alternative tie treatments, prompt subsets and topics, and timing checks. How alike two models' answers are worded and formatted tracks the effect. A correction with four to six parameters predicts held-out votes better than Bradley-Terry and than models with hundreds of parameters, mostly by modelling ties; frozen and carried to new releases in a test fixed in advance, its gains are concentrated in ties, and better head-to-head odds are not established. The leaderboard order barely moves. With language-model judges and three-answer menus, a near-copy takes votes mostly from its twin when choices are pooled over prompts (log-odds shift +0.10, 95% interval 0.05 to 0.16); within a prompt the shift is smaller and clear for two of four judges.
authors: Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose, Aishwarya Bose, Sandip Nandi
bullets: Near-duplicate models are distinguished more decisively than Bradley–Terry predicts: 1.37× for model versions, 1.26× for same-generation sizes, and 1.12× for models from the same lab.
The effect persists across release timing, tie treatments, prompt subsets, topics, and other checks, and is associated with similarity in answer wording and formatting.
A compact 4–6-parameter correction predicts held-out votes better than Bradley–Terry and much larger alternatives, mainly by modelling ties.
The correction’s gains carry to new releases, but improved head-to-head odds are not established and leaderboard rankings change little.
Language-model judges also favor a near-copy’s twin when votes are pooled across prompts, with weaker and less consistent within-prompt effects.

papers.abstract: Achieving human-like dexterous manipulation remains a central challenge in robotics. Learning from human hand-object interaction (HOI) datasets offers a promising pathway to diverse dexterous skills, yet existing physics-based approaches train specialist policies for individual trajectories, thereby limiting skill reuse at scale. We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand-object tracking policy jointly trained across diverse HOI trajectories. Efficient joint training requires allocating each rollout to both an undertrained phase and a starting state that supports continued tracking. DexMimic realizes this insight through Value-Guided Reset Allocation, which adapts the initialization distribution online to prioritize difficult phases and select reset states with higher expected tracking returns. We further introduce a benchmark spanning training, fine-tuning, and generalization. Experiments show improved tracking success and training efficiency, faster fine-tuning, and the potential for zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects; larger training sets further improve efficiency and generalization. Finally, we validate DexMimic on a real-world dexterous manipulation platform.
authors: Zhexi Luo, Zhixuan Xu, Rui Yang, Zeyu Xiao, Yiwen Hou, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the limited skill reuse of specialist physics-based policies trained on individual human hand-object trajectories.
Jointly trains across diverse hand-object interaction trajectories as a generalist policy.
Uses Value-Guided Reset Allocation to prioritize undertrained phases and reset states with higher expected tracking returns.
Introduces a benchmark covering training, fine-tuning, and generalization, with experiments showing improved tracking success and training efficiency.
Demonstrates faster fine-tuning, potential zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects, and real-world platform validation.

papers.abstract: Automatic prompt optimization (APO) uses feedback from model responses to improve prompts automatically. However, its effectiveness is usually measured through overall scores, which do not reveal which questions become correct, which previously correct answers become wrong, or whether improvements extend to unseen questions. We introduce Reflective Feedback-Driven Prompt Optimization (RFDPO), a tool that tracks recoveries (incorrect to correct), regressions (correct to incorrect), and churn (all changed outcomes). RFDPO uses this feedback to guide subsequent revisions and records prompt changes throughout optimization. We evaluate RFDPO across five benchmarks covering law, knowledge, instruction following, mathematics, and privacy, using GPT-5 as the optimizer and GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4.1 Mini as solvers. Our results show that overall accuracy can hide substantial changes: in five of nine configurations, churn was at least five times the absolute net change, and a single-item net change concealed up to 17 changed outcomes. Average validation gains were 7.9 percentage points, compared with 5.2 points on held-out tests. In a controlled ablation on LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% ($p=0.024$) while maintaining similar net gains. These findings motivate reporting recovery, regression, churn, and performance on unseen data alongside overall accuracy.
authors: Chinmoy Mitra, Tarek Mahmud
bullets: Overall accuracy may obscure substantial question-level changes: churn was at least five times the net change in five of nine configurations.
RFDPO uses item-level feedback to guide prompt revisions and records how prompts evolve.
Across five benchmarks, average gains were 7.9 percentage points on validation data and 5.2 points on held-out tests.
On LegalBench-Hearsay, item-level feedback reduced churn by 40% while preserving similar net gains.
The study recommends reporting recoveries, regressions, churn, and unseen-data performance alongside accuracy.

papers.abstract: Robotic systems that must acquire information about a specific target often face severe occlusion from sur- rounding structures or from the target itself, such that a single camera viewpoint provides only partial information. Active perception must therefore select viewpoints that progressively reveal unobserved regions. However, conventional local next- best-view (NBV) methods typically select viewpoints according to their immediate utility, which can overlook views that provide limited information initially but enable more informative obser- vations from subsequent viewpoints. We formulated local target perception as a short-horizon sequential view-planning problem and proposed a Receding-Horizon Next-Best-View (RH-NBV) planner that evaluates candidate sequences of future viewpoints rather than isolated views. RH-NBV is evaluated on a UR5e manipulator with an eye-in-hand RGB-D camera in simulation as well as on physical robot against a gradient-based NBV planner, and random search, using a coffee mug and Stanford bunny under controlled occlusion and a tomato plant with natural self-occlusion. Under heavy occlusion, RH-NBV achieves substantially higher target information recovery, reaching 63.8% ROI coverage versus 34.2% and 85.5% occluded-surface recall versus 7.4% for the single-step NBV baselines on the most occluded mug configuration. A controlled horizon ablation shows that this improvement arises from multi-step reasoning rather than additional computation. RH-NBV provides the greatest benefit for strongly occluded targets, while myopic NBV remains competitive and substantially cheaper when visibility is less constrained.
authors: Ayse Gul Yildiz, Rekha Raja
bullets: Severe occlusion makes single-view target perception incomplete and can cause local NBV methods to miss strategically useful viewpoints.
The planner evaluates candidate multi-step viewpoint sequences in a receding-horizon framework, then executes the next view.
On a UR5e with an eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, it was tested in simulation and on a physical robot across synthetic and natural occlusion scenarios.
Under the most occluded mug configuration, RH-NBV achieved 63.8% ROI coverage and 85.5% occluded-surface recall, versus 34.2% and 7.4% for single-step NBV baselines.
Its advantage is greatest under strong occlusion; myopic NBV remains cheaper and competitive when visibility is less constrained.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved the reasoning of autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language models. Language models that generate continuous token embeddings are emerging as a strong alternative, but RL post-training for them remains understudied. We propose \method{}, a post-training framework for continuous flow language models. Such a model denoises token embeddings over multiple steps and decodes them into discrete tokens only at the last step. To obtain pathwise gradients, which backpropagate through continuous actions and have much lower variance than REINFORCE, we introduce a critic that estimates the value of intermediate token embeddings, bypassing the non-differentiable decoding step. The critic must also keep track of the value function as the policy changes; to this end, we design a critic that predicts a value from every token representation and improves policy optimization. Across four reasoning tasks, \method{} reliably improves a continuous flow language model through RL post-training and outperforms baseline methods of the same type.
authors: Xu Han, Jiajing Hu, Li-Ping Liu
bullets: Addresses the understudied problem of RL post-training for language models that generate continuous token embeddings.
Uses a critic to estimate values for intermediate embeddings, avoiding the non-differentiable final token-decoding step.
Employs pathwise gradients, which offer lower variance than REINFORCE for continuous actions.
Introduces a critic that predicts values from every token representation while tracking policy changes.
Reliably improves the model across four reasoning tasks and outperforms same-type baseline methods.

papers.abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification remains an important challenge in AI. Hierarchical Bayesian methods provide a principled framework for this by representing unknown quantities through posterior distributions. Joint inference of neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters is challenging for conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods due to strong dependencies. In this work, we introduce the multilevel particle marginal Metropolis-Hastings (MLPMMH) method, which combines pseudo-marginal inference for the hyperparameters with coupled sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) across hierarchy of network-width truncations for conditional parameter inference. The hierarchy is induced by a trace-class neural network (TNN) prior with width-dependent decay, motivated empirically by the compressible structure observed in trained neural-network parameters. Under standard multilevel coupling assumptions, we establish that MLPMMH achieves mean-square error (MSE) $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$ at expected computational cost $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$, and verify the predicted rate on a Bayesian regression problem. To address larger-scale applications, we further introduce S-MLPMMH, a practical approximation that replaces the exact sampling components with a PCA-based hierarchy and scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo. Experiments on MNIST demonstrate competitive predictive performance and uncertainty quantification while exploiting the parallel structure of the approximation. Software has been made publicly available at https://github.com/submission-code-anon/mlpmmh-anon.
authors: Neil K. Chada, Simon Cotter, Kody J. H. Law, Xinzhu Liang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of jointly inferring neural-network parameters and prior hyperparameters with conventional MCMC.
Proposes MLPMMH, combining pseudo-marginal hyperparameter inference with coupled SMC over network-width truncations under a trace-class neural-network prior.
Provides a theoretical MSE–cost guarantee of O(ε²) error at O(ε⁻²) expected computational cost under standard coupling assumptions.
Introduces S-MLPMMH, a practical PCA-based approximation with scalable Bayesian Monte Carlo for larger applications.
Regression experiments verify the predicted rate, while MNIST experiments show competitive prediction and uncertainty quantification with parallelizable computation.

papers.abstract: Monocular 3D object detection methods increasingly rely on depth-guided transformers, but they operate entirely in the perspective image plane where spatial relationships are distorted by foreshortening. We propose MonoMIP, a dual-decoder framework that adds complementary 3D geometric reasoning through Bird's-Eye View (BEV) features constructed via Multi-Height Inverse Perspective Mapping. We perform IPM at K elevation planes spanning ground to rooftop, producing an ordered stack of height-conditioned metric BEV features that reduces above-ground misprojection and exposes depth-dependent appearance variation across planes. A BEV decoder with multi-scale deformable attention aggregates this multi-height evidence per query, while a depth-guided 3D decoder provides complementary perspective-space predictions. Without extra training data, MonoMIP attains 25.84% Moderate AP3D|R40 on KITTI val and 21.66% on the official test set for Car, outperforming recent published monocular methods on both the KITTI and Waymo benchmarks.
authors: Emir Ulurak, Furkan K{\i}ra\c{c}
bullets: Addresses perspective distortion and above-ground misprojection in monocular 3D detection.
Constructs ordered metric BEV features using inverse perspective mapping across K elevation planes from ground to rooftop.
Uses a deformable-attention BEV decoder alongside a complementary depth-guided 3D decoder.

papers.abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) across geographically distributed and poorly interconnected compute pools or data centers has become a topic of significant interest. This has led to increased study of local optimization methods such as DiLoco for LLMs, especially those that use local (or inner) adaptive or preconditioned optimizers, which are critical for high-performance LLM training. However, a central challenge remains: it is well known that increasing the number of model replicas (replica scaling) while fixing the total training budget leads to monotonically decreasing performance. Existing work has empirically demonstrated that the choice of inner optimizer (Muon v.s. AdamW) can significantly improve this trend, but offers only limited explanation of the performance difference. In this work, we consider a range of inner-optimizers and identify two important factors that impact replica scaling: (1) the covariance structure of the pseudo-gradients and (2) the impact of batch size on the pseudogradient's noise scale. Based on these insights, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that whitening-based pre-conditioning is a powerful inner-optimizer desideratum. Our empirical evaluation extends the results to reveal that whitening-based inner-optimizers achieve strong replica scaling (for 8-96 replicas), with performance relative to DP improving as parameters and data are scaled.
authors: Eugene Belilovsky, Stefan Horoi, Edouard Oyallon, Benjamin Th\'erien
bullets: Replica scaling under a fixed training budget typically degrades performance as the number of replicas grows.
The study examines how different local or inner optimizers affect this scaling in methods such as DiLoCo.
Two key factors are identified: pseudo-gradient covariance structure and batch-size effects on pseudo-gradient noise.
Theory and experiments indicate that whitening-based preconditioning is a desirable inner-optimizer property.
Across 8–96 replicas, whitening-based optimizers show strong scaling, with relative performance improving as model and data scales increase.

papers.abstract: As video models enable longer and more realistic interactive experiences, maintaining a world consistent with its history becomes essential. This requires both preserving previously observed content and ensuring coherent world evolution over time. World memory is a critical capability to evaluate alongside visual fidelity and video duration. We introduce WorldMemBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating world memory in video world models. Across 260 test cases, it assesses static memory through the retention of human identity and appearance, object appearance and geometry, and environmental content and geometry, and dynamic memory through event progression and state persistence. Using controlled camera departures and multi-revisit trajectories, the benchmark evaluates static content against fixed initial references and dynamic events against expected state transitions. It combines appearance and geometry metrics with event-specific assessments, and reports video quality and camera-following accuracy as complementary diagnostics. Evaluation of nine representative models shows that strong static retention does not imply reliable dynamic state evolution, while repeated revisits reveal memory degradation beyond the first return. Human studies support the alignment between our automatic evaluations and human judgments. WorldMemBench provides a systematic testbed for diagnosing memory failures and guiding the development of persistent, temporally coherent video worlds.

papers.abstract: Video-based remote physiological measurement (RPM) has broad applications, while Vision-Language Models (VLMs) provide a promising opportunity to enable end-to-end physiological monitoring for future human-aware intelligent systems. However, existing RPM methods rely on task-specific models and cannot be seamlessly integrated with the multimodal understanding and interaction capabilities of VLMs. We revisit RPM with VLMs and provide empirical evidence for two major bottlenecks: generic visual semantic representations fail to preserve fine-grained physiological cues; while discrete token prediction in autoregressive generation is inherently misaligned with continuous numerical measurement. To address these challenges, we propose VITAL (Visual-physiological Token Alignment for Language Models), a visual-physiological token alignment framework for RPM and preserving general vision tasks. VITAL retains the original visual pathway for semantic understanding and introduces an independent physiological pathway to jointly model semantic and physiological information. Moreover, we propose a structured numerical alignment approach to improve the reliability of generative heart rate estimation by enhancing numerical relationship modeling. Extensive experiments show that VITAL improves cross-domain estimation performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving the general visual understanding capability of VLMs, demonstrating its effectiveness as a unified visual-physiological model. Code will be released.
authors: Xiao Yang, Zekun Zhang, Yuxuan Fan, Duoxun Tang, Ziyang Liu, Dengbo He, Kaishun Wu, Jiyao Wang
bullets: VLM-based RPM is limited by generic visual features that miss fine-grained physiological cues.

VITAL adds an independent physiological pathway alongside the original semantic visual pathway.

Experiments report improved cross-domain performance on multiple rPPG datasets while preserving general visual understanding.

papers.abstract: Dense cardiac dynamics are essential for assessing cardiac function, yet in practice clinicians often observe only extremely sparse measurements. However, recovering full dynamics from such sparsity is a highly ill-posed problem due to the lack of temporal cues. While auxiliary time-series signals like ECG provide physiological guidance, effectively exploiting them is challenging due to the cross-modal representation gap and phase misalignment. In this work, we present CardioFAD, a Focus--Align--Diffuse paradigm that reformulates sparse cardiac dynamic synthesis as a recoverability--alignability anchor discovery problem. Our core insight is that resolving extreme temporal ambiguity requires a compact set of anchor states that are both sufficient to recover the visual trajectory and reliable for ECG--visual alignment. We therefore learn motion-salient keyframes under two complementary principles: trajectory sufficiency, which preserves trajectory-critical intra-modal motion content, and anchor alignment, which promotes consistent inter-modal correspondence at these anchors. We implement the Focus and Align modules optimized by the two aspects. Diffuse then performs two-stage generation by first synthesizing keyframes and subsequently interpolating the remaining frames. Extensive experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography videos demonstrate superior visual quality, temporal coherence, and improved functional consistency under the extreme one-shot regime.
authors: Junkai Liu, Haofan Wu, Nay Aung, Joao A. C. Lima, Steffen E. Petersen, Le Zhang
bullets: Addresses the severe temporal ambiguity of cardiac dynamic synthesis from extremely sparse observations.
Learns motion-salient keyframes that are both trajectory-sufficient and aligned with ECG signals.

Experiments on cardiac MRI and echocardiography show improved visual quality, temporal coherence, and functional consistency in the one-shot setting.

papers.abstract: Information-theoretic exploration is of primary interest in methodological studies of reinforcement learning (RL) and computational cognitive neuroscience, while the established RL theory builds regret guarantees on confidence sets. This situation leaves open the conditions under which the information-driven exploration found in nature is more advantageous than the exploration of the established RL theory. We put the state-of-the-art methods of these two paradigms, Active Inference (AIF) and Bayes-UCBVI, on an equal footing: both act through the same state abstraction of a tabular MDP with $S$ states, and their greedy forms differ only in the exploration term. We find that AIF's information gain decays too fast to serve as a confidence width, locking greedy agents that explore by it out of the optimal action. Calibrating the information gain by a square root yields calibrated AIF, which attains regret of order $\sqrt T$ for an exact abstraction, but no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI for a fixed reward. When an adversary chooses rewards from the agent's data, Bayes-UCBVI's value-specific widths lock out, whereas calibrated AIF pays a factor $\sqrt S$, which no goal-memoryless agent avoids on some MDP whose start states the adversary also chooses. Calibrated information gain thus acts as a reward-agnostic $\ell_1$ confidence set, preferable to value-specific widths when rewards are chosen from the agent's data, not when they are fixed.
authors: Melih Kandemir, Mustafa Mert \c{C}elikok
bullets: AIF and Bayes-UCBVI are compared under the same tabular-MDP state abstraction, differing only in exploration bonuses.
Uncalibrated AIF information gain decays too quickly, causing greedy agents to miss optimal actions.
Square-root calibration gives AIF order-$\sqrt{T}$ regret under an exact abstraction.
For fixed rewards, calibrated AIF offers no better guarantee than Bayes-UCBVI.
For rewards chosen from the agent’s data, calibrated AIF remains effective with a $\sqrt{S}$ factor, while Bayes-UCBVI can be locked out.

papers.abstract: Understanding the mechanism behind why diffusion models memorize their training data remains an open question in generative modeling. In this paper, we examine this question from two perspectives: (a) the model-level perspective concerning the onset of memorization in a model during training, and (b) the sample-level perspective concerning the proclivity of an individual sample to be memorized by a given model. We show that the so-called input loss curvature, or the Frobenius norm of the Hessian of the diffusion model's training loss, is an effective metric for quantifying both perspectives on memorization. In particular, we empirically demonstrate that input curvatures averaged across training and validation samples can identify when a model is likely to start regurgitating its training data when tracked over training time. However, this metric is not sufficient for measuring an individual sample's likelihood of being memorized. To address this perspective, we introduce a counterfactual definition of memorization in diffusion models, extending the analogous notion from supervised learning proposed by [Feldman, 2019]. We prove that this counterfactual memorization is controlled by the input curvature of the leave-one-out model, thus establishing a direct theoretical link between a sample's local loss landscape and its generation likelihood. We validate our derived bounds through several empirical experiments and show that input-dependent curvature provides a proxy for memorization.
authors: Shashank Sule, Xinyue Yu, Boonam Shin, Yuxuan Liu, Abolfazl Hashemi, Hayden Schaeffer
bullets: Memorization is studied both as a training-time model behavior and as an individual sample property.
Average input curvature over training and validation samples can signal when a model begins regurgitating training data.
Curvature alone does not adequately measure whether a specific sample will be memorized.
The paper defines counterfactual memorization for diffusion models and proves it is controlled by input curvature of a leave-one-out model.
Experiments validate the theoretical bounds and support input-dependent curvature as a memorization proxy.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates memorization in diffusion models using loss curvature, providing a theoretical and empirical framework for understanding generative model behavior.
papers.title: Loss Curvature as a Sampling-Free Proxy for Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.tldr: Input loss curvature, measured via the diffusion-loss Hessian, is a sampling-free proxy for detecting model-level memorization and estimating sample-level memorization under a counterfactual definition.

papers.abstract: Understanding the dynamics of language acquisition in Large Language Models (LLMs) is crucial for uncovering how statistical representations evolve into structured linguistic capabilities. However, most existing studies focus primarily on fully trained models, leaving the developmental trajectory across intermediate training stages largely underexplored. In this work, we leverage intermediate checkpoints from open-source models (e.g., Pythia and OLMo) under teacher-forcing evaluation to systematically investigate language acquisition across training steps and model scales. We focus on four core characteristics: morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects. Our findings reveal that models acquire morphological structures well before semantic embeddings stabilize. Furthermore, we show that training dataset size has a positive impact on divergence recognition, while co-occurrence during pre-training and repetition during inference have a negative impact on divergence recognition and associative link generation.
authors: Forough Shirin Abkenar, Haoshuo Fu, Liang Feng, Ning Yan, Masood S. Mortazavi
bullets: Studies language acquisition across training stages and model scales rather than only at convergence.
Analyzes morphological structure acquisition, embedding drift, repetition dominance, and co-occurrence effects.
Finds morphological structures emerge earlier than stable semantic embeddings.
Larger training datasets improve divergence recognition.
Pre-training co-occurrence and inference-time repetition negatively affect divergence recognition and associative link generation.

papers.abstract: Pluralistic alignment needs to accommodate diverse preferences under limited human feedback. Using AI simulators to label preference comparisons reduces annotation costs, but variation in simulation accuracy across individuals can leave some people's preferences poorly represented in training. We study how to allocate human feedback across people to construct training data for pluralistic alignment, and how this allocation affects the trained policy. To make this allocation explicit and controllable, we define a social welfare objective over individual supervision utilities that measure label quality. Each query's marginal welfare gain depends on its expected supervision improvement, the recipient's current utility, and application-designated priority. Welfare-Aware Preference Acquisition (WAPA) uses auxiliary reference models to estimate query gains and individual utilities, then selects queries by estimated marginal welfare gain while updating recipient utilities. We prove exact optimality of the acquisition algorithm for the estimated welfare objective under a fixed query budget and model predictions. Experiments on six Roleplay collections and four OpinionQA regions demonstrate improved supervision and controllable allocation tradeoffs. Policy training on four Roleplay collections improves preference prediction for both seen and unseen individuals. When prioritizing a designated group and poorly represented individuals, acquiring human labels for 20% of comparisons recovers 75-86% of the average predictive utility gap between policies trained entirely on AI-generated labels and entirely on ground-truth labels.

Across Roleplay and OpinionQA experiments, 20% human labels recovered 75–86% of the average predictive-utility gap between fully AI-labeled and fully ground-truth-trained policies when prioritizing designated or poorly represented groups.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) applies every rank-one component of its update to every token, and mixture-of-experts variants replace this with a learned router that activates a fixed number of components. We argue that the number of components a token needs is a detection question with a classical answer. A token's responses to the rank-one components of a trained LoRA consist of a few large values on a Gaussian noise floor whose width matches that of an untrained adapter, and the floor carries cross-talk rather than adaptation. We introduce SQUELCH, a router-free mixture of rank-one experts that (i) soft-thresholds each token's responses at a multiple of its own robust noise level, so the active rank varies per token; (ii) chooses that multiple for each module by Stein's unbiased risk estimate, so no rank budget is specified; and (iii) replaces the resulting marginal keep-or-drop decisions by one explaining-away step on the value Gram matrix, which suppresses redundant co-active components and recruits complementary ones. SQUELCH adds no trainable parameters to LoRA. We prove that the squelch is within a logarithmic factor of the oracle input-dependent allocation, that the selected threshold is risk-consistent, and that explaining away is a descent step toward the joint sparse code whose error is controlled by the coherence of co-active components. On commonsense reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE with LLaMA-3.1-8B, Qwen3, and DeBERTaV3, SQUELCH improves over LoRA by 2.2--3.2 points and over the strongest mixture baseline by 0.8--1.2 points while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.
authors: Mei Okonkwo, Owen Castellanos, Ingrid Solberg, Yusuf Demirel
bullets: Motivation: LoRA applies every rank-one component to every token, although many responses appear to be cross-talk on a Gaussian noise floor.
Method: A router-free mechanism estimates each token’s robust noise level and soft-thresholds component responses, allowing the active rank to vary without a preset rank budget.
Thresholds are chosen per module using Stein’s unbiased risk estimate; an explaining-away step suppresses redundant components and favors complementary ones.
Theory: The method is near-optimal up to a logarithmic factor, has risk-consistent threshold selection, and provides coherence-based error control for joint sparse coding.
Experiments across reasoning, knowledge, math, code, and GLUE tasks report gains over LoRA and a mixture baseline while activating 8.6 of 32 components per token on average.

papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces the KV-cache traffic that dominates long-context LLM decoding, but practical methods largely operate at coarse granularity. Token-level selection offers finer control, yet presents two challenges: low-dimensional scoring may lose query--key structure needed for accurate ranking, while gathering scattered selected tokens can offset the resulting latency benefit. We introduce Joint Subspace Sparse Attention (JSSA) to address both challenges. For selection quality, JSSA learns a shared low-dimensional query--key subspace by minimizing token-score preservation error. We upper-bound the resulting non-convex objective with a tractable marginal objective that admits a closed-form spectral solution; direct refinement of the exact objective provides no measurable improvement in the tested settings. For execution efficiency, we develop a gather-free token-level indexed-attention kernel that supports distinct per-KV-head selections under the standard grouped-query attention (GQA) KV-cache layout. Across standard GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) models, JSSA consistently remains close to full-KV accuracy while avoiding the substantial generation-length inflation and architecture-dependent failures observed with competing methods. On an NVIDIA B200 GPU, JSSA achieves up to $6.43\times$ the decoding throughput of full-KV attention at 128K context. JSSA achieves reasoning accuracy comparable to model-native DSA without model training and reaches 96--99\% of its decoding throughput even at 700B scale large models.
authors: Jiwon Song, Yoongon Kim, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Addresses low-dimensional token-ranking errors and the latency cost of gathering scattered KV-cache tokens.
Learns a shared query–key subspace via a tractable spectral objective for token selection.
Introduces a gather-free indexed-attention kernel supporting distinct selections per KV head under GQA.
Remains close to full-KV accuracy across GQA, hybrid sliding-window/global attention, and MLA models.
Matches model-native DSA reasoning accuracy without training and reaches 96–99% of its decoding throughput at 700B scale.

papers.abstract: Modern image generation largely relies on specialized generative models that leave the process of image construction implicit in learned parameters. We explore an alternative: general-purpose coding agents that construct images through executable programs. Our study of zero-shot drawing on AgentDrawBench, a 200-prompt benchmark, reveals a distinctive capability profile. Agents excel at preserving structure and satisfying precise visual constraints, achieving competitive results in domains where compositional accuracy matters more than photorealistic appearance, while remaining limited in perceptual richness. Their visual expressiveness varies with the drawing interface, and a qualitative study on reconstruction shows how procedural skills extracted from human demonstrations support different artistic media. We then examine code as an external visual language of thought: a structured, executable representation that agents can construct and inspect. We test it in visual question answering task and find reconstructed visual code retains substantial information for question answering and, in some domains, supports higher accuracy than the original image. These abilities raise a further question: do agents draw on a shared internal representation of scene content beyond a particular drawing program? We explore an internal visual language-of-thought hypothesis, in which a shared, compositionally structured representation supports visual operations across drawing languages. Cross-harness drawings and images assembled from independent single-pixel queries exhibit related layouts and tones. Agents also maintain self-generated room arrangements across viewpoints after visible drawings are removed. These results demonstrate that the coding agent would maintain a consistent and coherent world inside its imagine even before the harness gets involved and the generation starts.
authors: Hengguang Zhou, Yuanhao Ban, Jiaqi Feng, Xiaohuan Pei, Justin Cui, Cho-Jui Hsieh
bullets: On the 200-prompt AgentDrawBench, agents perform well when compositional accuracy and precise constraints matter more than photorealism.
Their expressiveness depends on the drawing interface, while procedural skills from human demonstrations transfer across artistic media.
Executable visual code retains substantial information for visual question answering and can outperform the original image in some domains.
Cross-harness and single-pixel experiments suggest agents maintain a shared, compositionally structured internal representation of scenes.
The findings indicate coherent scene understanding before image generation begins, though perceptual richness remains a limitation.

papers.abstract: Real measurements are too limited to train an accurate indoor pathloss predictor that works across a wide range of buildings. Large-scale synthetic pretraining offers a way forward, but real building layouts are also scarce, and accurate ray-tracing simulators are slow, expensive, and often proprietary. We address both problems by introducing a generator that automatically creates diverse indoor layouts and a fast, open-source approximate ray tracer that computes radio maps for them. Using this pipeline, we generate 128M synthetic samples, pretrain ResNet-101 and Swin-T encoder-decoders, and fine-tune them on high-quality benchmark data. Despite simulator mismatch, our ResNet-101 model reduces error by 15% on average relative to the best known methods across five indoor radio-map prediction tasks and improves transfer on a small real-measurement dataset. Both architectures show predictable data-scaling trends: power laws fitted on 2M-16M samples predict the mean normalized downstream RMSE at 32M-128M with 3.33% mean absolute percentage error for ResNet-101 and 7.10% for Swin-T. These results show that pretraining on large amounts of cheap simulated data can improve indoor radio-map prediction, even when real measurements and high-quality simulations are limited.
authors: Khoren Petrosyan, Artashes Mkrtchyan, Rafayel Mkrtchyan, Hrant Khachatrian, Theofanis P. Raptis

papers.abstract: Current scaling law formulations suggest that increasing the number of unique samples in a dataset improves model performance, while repeated exposure to the same samples provides diminishing value. In this work, we examine this assumption for image self-distillation models. Through systematic experiments across diverse datasets, namely Maxar, SATLAS, Waymo, nuPlan, Ego4D, ImageNet, and YFCC15M, we demonstrate that the effects of sample repetition on downstream performance are non-trivial and dataset-dependent. We identify settings where repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on a larger set of unique samples. This finding highlights a limitation of existing scaling laws. To address this gap, we propose a modified version of a Chinchilla-style scaling law that explicitly accounts for two factors: the number of unique samples and repetition per sample. This formulation provides a framework for understanding data-compute trade-offs and improves prediction in some regimes where repetition plays a central role, although its benefits are not consistent across datasets. Finally, we examine how subset selection and augmentation affect downstream performance.
authors: Alvard Barseghyan, Ani Vanyan, Hakob Tamazyan, Hrant Khachatrian
bullets: Finds that sample repetition has non-trivial, dataset-dependent effects across seven diverse image and video datasets.
Shows that repeatedly training on a smaller random subset can outperform training on more unique samples in some settings.
Proposes a Chinchilla-style scaling law incorporating both unique-sample count and repetition per sample.
The modified law improves prediction in some repetition-dominated regimes, but gains are inconsistent across datasets.
Also studies the effects of subset selection and data augmentation on downstream performance.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a modified scaling law for image self-distillation models that accounts for sample repetition, addressing a gap in current understanding of data efficiency for foundation models.
papers.title: Data Density Scaling Laws for Image Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Image self-distillation does not follow a simple “more unique data is always better” rule: repetition can sometimes outperform larger unique datasets, motivating repetition-aware scaling laws.

papers.abstract: World models are a powerful means of reasoning and planning, but many of these action-conditioned predictive models are high dimensional and computationally expensive. These challenges limit the number of action candidates that can be evaluated by a planner. We show that this cost is avoidable for planners over short horizons, which only require local information with respect to the current state. For a fixed state, the frames reachable by varying a low-dimensional action (a camera movement or an end-effector command) lie on a low-dimensional manifold. We estimate the local shape of that manifold directly via a network trained to estimate how each image region moves per unit of each action axis supervised by data collected from samples by the generator. A correction head fit to trajectory data estimates the shape of this manifold region up to a third-order Taylor polynomial. We call this network estimating the Taylor polynomial describing the manifold shape an Action Jet and compute its radius of validity in closed form. By traversing this approximation of the local manifold shape, we only have to perform inference once per state for any number of candidate actions. Scoring sixteen candidates from a single extraction is over 300x faster than with either source generator, and this gap widens with the number of candidates a planner evaluates. We measure against state-of-the-art action-conditioned generators, IRASim and WorldGym on BridgeData V2, a real 7-DoF manipulation benchmark, and FrameCrafter on DL3DV scenes, where we chart from the novel-view generators DepthSplat and LagerNVS. Because only the tangent comes from the generator and every other term from the data, the Action Jet also predicts held-out frames more accurately than IRASim, the generator that supplied its tangent, at short horizons and at over 100x less compute.
authors: Anton Arapin, Chahyon Ku, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Problem: High-dimensional world models make evaluating many action candidates computationally expensive.
Method: Learn image-region motion per action dimension and fit a correction head that approximates the local manifold with a third-order Taylor polynomial.
The approximation’s closed-form validity radius defines where the local prediction can be trusted.
Result: Sixteen candidate actions are scored from one extraction at over 300× lower cost than the source generators, with larger gains for more candidates.
Scope: Evaluated on BridgeData V2 manipulation data and DL3DV novel-view scenes against several action-conditioned or view-synthesis generators.

Figure 1: A chart of the action-conditioned data manifold. (a) For a fixed state x, varying the action traces a curved surface in latent space, the manifold Mx, on which transitions recorded from x lie. (b) Probing the frozen generator T at ±δ (blue) gives the tangent plane at the current latent zt. While T ’s own response bends away from the manifold, the Action Jet (orange) fits the Taylor polynomial to the recorded transitions in the data and so follows Mx up to the radius r∗1 (green) it computes from its own coefficients. (c) One token of the chart is marked on the tangent plane in (b). The geometry encoder writes the fields of all A action axes in one orthonormal frame Q with coefficients G.

Figure 4: Parallel Octo policy candidate prediction and evaluation. Candidate trajectories sampled from Octo are predicted by the Action Jet, and the winning candidate is the one with the lowest latent MSE to the true t+4 observation. Octo takes the goal image as its target and proposes candidate trajectories four steps into the future at each planning step, and the planning loop repeats until the goal state is reached.

Figure 5: Architecture. (A1) probing; (A2) the geometry encoder, emitting Q and G; (A3) the correction head, whose coefficient fields depend on the state and a noise draw but never on the action. Everything in the red region is arithmetic on tensors already in memory.

Figure 6: Extracting and tracing a local chart. A held-out state is encoded once and the correction head’s coefficient fields are extracted once. The six branches then read that one extraction along each action axis. Each branch shows a surface of the local action manifold Mx and a corresponding decoded frame, predicted from the step along the labeled axis. Reading a surface render: x and y are commanded action in the plane spanned by the labeled axis and one companion axis, the latter present only so that the patch is a surface rather than a curve. The dashed circle is the query radius for that axis for that episode, and red dashed circle is the validity radius. The dashed line on the tangent plane is the departure from the tangent basis plane. The flat gray sheet is the first-order chart zt +QGa, which is the zero-height plane in this embedding and so is flat by construction. The blue sheet adds the correction head, zt + QGa + r̃(a, ε). The two touch at the origin but the blue sheet leaves it with a nonzero slope. Every vertex of both sheets is arithmetic on the single extraction, no network is re-run anywhere in the figure, and only the displayed frames are decoded.

papers.title: Action Jets: Learning the Local Shape of the Action-conditioned Data Manifold
papers.tldr: Action Jets approximate the local action-conditioned image manifold so planners can evaluate many short-horizon action candidates with one model inference, achieving over 300× faster scoring and improved short-horizon prediction accuracy.

papers.abstract: Humanoid policies trained in simulation can transfer qualitatively to hardware while failing to transfer the force interactions learned during training, compromising torque efficiency, load regulation, and robustness to impacts. This failure can arise from actuator sim-to-real gaps because forces depend on actuator torques. We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world model that preserves a simulator's physics priors while correcting actuator dynamics to align simulated rollouts with recorded hardware rollouts. For humanoid motion with contact, this requires contact-consistent replay: if hardware playback in simulation begins with misaligned contact wrenches, the residual model learns to correct reset artifacts rather than actuator discrepancies. Using only onboard proprioception, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose needed to initialize replay with consistent contact forces. We show that a UAN trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data generalizes to tasks that benefit from accurate force and impulse regulation and produces policies that transfer seamlessly to the real world, yielding 20% lower running torque, 43% lower force-tracking error, extreme compliance, accurate impedance control, and dynamic, robust jumps.
authors: Nolan Fey, Khai Nguyen, Yash Prabhu, Gabriel B. Margolis, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Addresses actuator sim-to-real gaps that degrade torque efficiency, load regulation, and impact robustness.
Uses a residual world model that preserves simulator physics while aligning simulated rollouts with hardware behavior.
Infers simulator-side stance-foot pose from proprioception to initialize contact-consistent replay and avoid reset artifacts.
Trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data, it supports force and impulse regulation, impedance control, compliance, and dynamic jumps.
Reports 20% lower running torque and 43% lower force-tracking error during real-world transfer.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly. Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution. We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion. Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination. We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations. Building on this pipeline, we develop $\lambda_0$, a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training. Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. $\lambda_0$ achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks. We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world. Homepage: https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/
authors: humanoid Team
bullets: Human robot demonstrations are costly, while existing egocentric data often lacks locomotion, posture, and accurate embodiment transfer.

The system reaches 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Finite safety assessments cannot exclude an adversary that preserves unattacked behavior until certification and activates afterward. We characterize this limitation for embodied and tool-use AI. An adversary that matches the complete observation law until observable, irrevocable certification and retains intervention access afterward attains $v\mathbb{E}[(n-S_0)_+]$ expected post-certification events over $n$ trials, where $v$ is the active event probability and $S_0$ the unattacked certification time. The result covers adaptive and privately randomized evaluators. Switching at certification is exactly optimal for a fixed likelihood-ratio test under memoryless, event-increasing interventions without a binding intervention budget. A positive clean-certification requirement forces linear worst-case expected excess when intervention raises event rates over an authorized deployment horizon, even if certification is deferred to the deadline. In simulated RoCo collaboration, switching yields commanded-separation violations in 34 of 36 post-certification episodes. Preregistered randomized AgentDojo trials estimate 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation (95% interval [1.67, 2.29]). An adversarial language-model controller infers hidden certification from noisy evaluation receipts and times intervention accordingly. With permanent revocation, a mixture likelihood-ratio monitor bounds cumulative excess above a prespecified reference rate at square-root order, up to logarithmic factors, on every sample path. A single fixed alternative can permit linear expected excess under stationary attacks. Against a controller observing the monitor's rule and statistic, live mixture monitoring reduces violations from 12.00 to 3.81 per 24 assigned task opportunities. Revocation also reduces tasks executed.
authors: Inderjeet Singh
bullets: An adversary can mimic safe behavior until observable, irreversible certification, then activate interventions; expected harm scales with remaining deployment opportunities.
Switching precisely at certification is optimal under fixed likelihood-ratio testing, memoryless event-increasing interventions, and no binding intervention budget.
Simulations and randomized tool-use trials show substantial post-certification violations, including 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation in AgentDojo.
Permanent revocation with mixture monitoring bounds cumulative excess at roughly square-root order up to logarithmic factors, but reduces tasks executed.
A controller aware of the monitoring rule still caused fewer violations under live monitoring: 3.81 versus 12.00 per 24 task opportunities.

Figure 5: The stopping rule that issues a rate certificate also determines the adversary’s remaining uninspected operation. Observed post-certification events on world 006 progress from the ratetracking controller through the language-model attackers to deterministic switching. Each row is a separate registered execution. All attempted 40 episodes, with defined counts shown. Grey denotes the rate tracker, blue language-model controllers, and orange deterministic switching. These counts have no estimated repeated-campaign intervals. The comparison describes executed policies rather than a causal effect of model choice or decision spacing. Under the stated memoryless intervention model, the exact per-trial optimum is vE[(n− S0)+]. The executed deterministic policies act at the indicated block boundaries.
