The dashed continuation reconstructs the statistic from retained outcomes for display. It is not evidence inspected before the retained certificate. The nominal-episode strip preserves the undefined execution failure without advancing the defined-trial clock.

The dotted lines mark the executed alternative q = 0.88. Solid curves are i.i.d. calculations. papers.abstract: This paper studies Wong--Zakai convergence and Fourier neural operator learning for stochastic Volterra integral equations (SVIEs) describing random systems with memory. A Wong--Zakai theorem establishes convergence of pathwise solutions driven by piecewise linear approximations of Brownian motion to the corresponding SVIE solution. This convergence provides a foundation for using mirror-padded Fourier neural operators to learn the solution operator mapping initial conditions and driving noise to entire solution trajectories. Numerical experiments demonstrate competitive prediction accuracy and generalization to temporal grids finer than those used for training, while assessing the influence of padding and computational cost. As a follow-up to \citet{LKP:26}, this study extends their operator-learning framework to SVIEs through separate convergence and approximation analyses tailored to convolutional memory.

bullets: Addresses stochastic Volterra integral equations, which model random systems with memory.
Proves convergence from piecewise linear Brownian-motion approximations to pathwise SVIE solutions.
Trains Fourier neural operators to map inputs and noise to entire solution trajectories.
Numerical experiments show competitive accuracy and generalization to finer temporal grids than those used in training.
Evaluates padding choices and computational cost; the framework is tailored to convolutional memory.

papers.abstract: Token-selection methods for on-policy distillation (OPD) prioritize student-visited positions using diverse signals, including uncertainty, teacher-student disagreement, and mismatch direction. We instead derive token importance from the distillation objective itself: how much can each position's loss decrease under an equal local KL budget on the student's predictive distribution? The answer is the utility $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$, where $g_t$ is the logit gradient and $F_t$ is the categorical Fisher matrix. For reverse-KL it equals the student-weighted variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio, and for forward-KL it equals the Pearson $\chi^2$ divergence, so the appropriate utility follows from the choice of objective. On shared training checkpoints, several independently motivated criteria, including student entropy, KL disagreement, and TIP, concentrate their importance on nearly the same positions as the derived utility at a 50\% selection fraction, while diverging at stricter fractions and for direction-specific criteria. We instantiate the utility as Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW), a continuous, mean-normalized token weighting. Across seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 student-teacher pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD under both reverse-KL (1.35-4.0 macro points) and forward-KL (1.08-2.71 macro points), and is competitive with existing selective methods using a single closed-form score derived from the training objective.
authors: Narayanan Sadagopan, Yilan Chen, Vijay Lingam
bullets: Defines token utility as the loss reduction achievable under an equal local KL budget: $s_t=g_t^\top F_t^\dagger g_t$.

Implements the score as continuous, mean-normalized Fisher Utility Weighting (FUW).
On seven math-reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 teacher–student pairs, FUW improves over matched uniform OPD for both KL directions.
Several existing criteria align with the derived utility at moderate selection rates but diverge under stricter selection or direction-specific scoring.

papers.abstract: Protein function annotation operates over an expanding label space, making class-incremental learning (CIL) a natural framework for incorporating newly discovered functions without full retraining. Yet existing CIL methods have been developed largely in vision and have not been systematically evaluated over frozen protein representations. We conduct a controlled benchmark of nine representative CIL methods across five sequence-, structure-, and sequence--structure-based protein encoders and two enzyme function datasets at different scales, while keeping the encoders frozen and evaluation settings consistent across representations. We find that no method transfers reliably across encoders, and that these failures persist across alternative phase constructions. Diagnostic analyses reveal that this instability arises from weak gradient-based stability signals, substantial heterogeneity in embedding geometry, and covariance assumptions whose appropriate capacity changes with both dataset scale and encoder. These findings suggest that the representation itself should be treated as a central component of continual-learning design rather than a passive feature extractor. More generally, reliable protein CIL will require encoder-aware methods that adapt their statistical assumptions and capacity to the geometry of the representation on which they operate. Code is available at https://github.com/zygao930/ProteinCIL.

papers.abstract: Post-training reasoning LLMs often requires making a tradeoff between costly supervision and compute inefficiency: supervised finetuning typically requires reasoning traces, which is data inefficient since in many applications one only has prompt-answer tuples and lacks the groundtruth chain-of-thought (CoT) sequence. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (with verifiable rewards, for example) can operate without CoT data but it is much more compute-inefficient since it requires multiple autoregressive completions per optimization step, none of which are guaranteed to give a non-zero policy gradient. In this work we explore a middleground, a self-distillation technique that uses answer-only data, treating CoT as latent variables. This relies on training a partner ``inverse reasoning LLM" that generates the original's reasoning traces conditioned on the answer. The inverse model is trained once and reused across incoming batches of answer-only data, with all generation happening offline and up front, making the approach particularly suited to continual post-training. Using Qwen3-0.6B on the Countdown and GSM8K tasks, we show that after GRPO training has saturated, a single offline distillation round from the inverse model roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts and, on Countdown, outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation on every hard-tail metric at every mix ratio (with smaller gains on GSM8K); rejection sampling by construction has no signal on problems the model never solves on its own. Continued GRPO on the fresh data retains an edge at hard pass@1 but trails distillation at pass@8 and pass@32 while regenerating rollouts at every step. As an added bonus we see that the inverse model has a second application as an accurate verifier of correctness. When used for best-of-$n$ selection at test time, it raises selection accuracy on Countdown from 0.753 (majority voting) to 0.969.
authors: Eric O. Korman
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between trace-dependent supervised fine-tuning and compute-heavy reinforcement learning when only prompt–answer pairs are available.

On Qwen3-0.6B evaluations, one distillation round after GRPO saturation roughly doubles pass@1 on hard prompts; gains are smaller on GSM8K.
On Countdown, inverse-model distillation outperforms rejection-sampling self-distillation across reported hard-tail metrics and mix ratios.
As a verifier for best-of-n selection, the inverse model improves Countdown selection accuracy from 0.753 with majority voting to 0.969.

This is a training prompt, so (b) is the actual SFT training datum, letting us see the supervision and what was learned from it side by side. Notably, even though the model trained on this very prompt, (c) is not a replay of (b): the student reaches 61 by a different route (75 − 7 − 7 rather than 75 − (7 + 7)), slips and self-corrects (“- 4” before “* 4”), and brackets the final expression differently—what transfers is the strategy, not the memorized sequence. papers.abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs. Although such supervision encourages linguistic representations, it does not explicitly require them to preserve information about how the underlying time-series signal evolves. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in LOTUS, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, LOTUS achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that LOTUS uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25 to 50 times their size on TSRBench.
authors: Van Dai Do, Huu Hiep Nguyen, Minh Hoang Nguyen, Manh Nguyen, Hung Le
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit temporal-information preservation in label- or language-supervised time-series models.
Uses non-overlapping channel patches mapped into LLM embedding space and predicts the next patch from hidden states.

Evaluated across three LLM backbones and six downstream datasets, LOTUS achieves 59.91% accuracy and improves over the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%.
Representation analyses indicate that LOTUS uses numerical inputs and retains temporal structure; it also outperforms models 25–50× larger on TSRBench.

papers.abstract: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/
authors: Chih-Hai Su
Tsung-Wei Ke
Yu-Lun Liu
bullets: Addresses the failure of geometry-specific residual priors and cross-family scaling differences.
Learns a dimensionless motion prior, then estimates scale from observations with a lightweight training-source correction.
Works without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence.
Outperforms harmonic extension across evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies.
Transfers without retraining to point-tracked animal video and robot–soft-body grasping.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Demo: densifying video point tracks. Across frames 4–39, the model observes the same 12 tracked vertices in every frame. (a) Twelve observed points and 120 completed points. (b) 120 camera-opposed far-side points (0 of 2,164 ever observed). Without ground truth, this shows the checkpoint connects to a tracker and completions exist on the far side, not that either is accurate. Overlays degrade away from fitted frame 18 (Appendix D).

Figure 2: CEPHEID constructs dense motion by decoupling residual structure from physical scale. Given a mesh M with coordinates X and sparse observed displacements O on vertex subset Ω (A), harmonic extension first yields a closed-form base field H (B). Amplitude recovery then estimates physical scale ŝ using frozen fitted coefficients (C; Algorithm 1). Conditioned on H and O, the flow-matching network learns the normalized target R/ŝ with R = F −H during training, while mapping k Gaussian noise draws to samples averaged into R̄θ at inference (D); it is the sole component trained by gradient descent (flame icon). Finally, the completed field is assembled as F̂ = H + ŝ · R̄θ (E).

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on cloth, a family no model trained on. Completion from 32 observed vertices of the 1,577 free vertices, shown as geometry above and per-vertex error below on a shared ramp; the observed points are marked on the ground truth. NSDP tears the sheet and DOMA loses its shape and self-intersects, while our completion keeps the flag intact and its error field dark. The first panel is the true residual; the three that follow show the same frozen network output, differing only in the scale applied to it. papers.abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
authors: Mingxuan Yan, Litian Gong, Dihong Huang, Zhixu Li, Tianyu Zhang, Wenqian Zhang, Hefeifei Jiang, Peihao Li, Jian Zhang, Mengfei Zhao, Yikai Tang, Hai Zhai, Zehao Wang, Ruijian Liang, Yanjia Huang, Lin Shao, Changliu Liu, Kaiyu Hang, Zhiwen Fan, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Jianfei Yang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Benchmarks weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks.
Across three VLAs, approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning, while the best label granularity depends on the approach and model.
Constant-tag fine-tuning further improves mean success after conditioned pretraining, regardless of tagged or untagged inference.
AXIS-Bench provides replayable simulation trajectories with object and contact states for controlled, user-defined quality-label comparisons.
In a real-world experiment, simulation pretraining increased success from 9.6% to 31.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. AXIS-Bench workflow for quality-aware VLA pretraining. The simulation benchmark evaluates performance after fine-tuning on 24 target tasks, with matched pretraining data, training budgets, and target-task demonstrations within each VLA comparison. The real-world workflow supports user-defined workspaces and tasks by aligning the simulation workspace, re-rendering demonstrations under the target workspace and camera configuration, fine-tuning on real-world target-task demonstrations, and evaluating task success. papers.abstract: Personal-agent memory has largely focused on learning what users know, prefer, and want. However, knowing the user does not necessarily mean knowing what the user and the agent have established together. An assistant's proposal should not become an authorized instruction merely because it is remembered. We introduce Grounding Awareness, the ability to distinguish accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scoped arrangements when selecting actions. We develop a controlled benchmark to test whether agents can tell the difference between proposals users have accepted and those they have not, and whether they apply accepted arrangements only where appropriate. Across multiple agents and memory systems, we find that strong memory performance does not ensure Grounding Awareness. More surprisingly, providing more complete user information can increase execution of unacknowledged proposals, while persistent memory can cause agents to treat these proposals as if they were user instructions. We trace these failures through memory writing, retrieval, and action selection. Finally, we introduce Grounding Layer, a lightweight, training-free extension that explicitly tracks grounding status and checks consequential actions, substantially improving agent behavior without modifying models or memory systems.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Xinyue Chen, Yicheng Jiang, Hua Shen
bullets: Introduces Grounding Awareness: distinguishing accepted, unacknowledged, revised, and scope-limited arrangements.
Presents a controlled benchmark for testing whether agents apply only accepted arrangements in appropriate contexts.
Finds that strong memory can still lead agents to execute unacknowledged proposals, especially when more user information is available.
Traces failures to memory writing, retrieval, and action selection.
Grounding Layer, a lightweight training-free extension, improves behavior by tracking grounding status and checking consequential actions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally invalid actions in preferred trajectories and ignores the downstream cascading influence of early pivotal deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9\% and 94.3\% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7\% and 70.8\% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to $2.44\times$ while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

papers.abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.
authors: Haldun Balim, Yilun Du, Na Li
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between short-horizon value bootstrapping and costly trajectory optimization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP). Planning proceeds via iterative beam search. Starting from an initial beam, GTP repeatedly (1) branches candidate trajectory prefixes by duplicating, (2) refines action suffixes through partial forward diffusion and denoising under the diffusion prior, and (3) prunes candidates using rollouts through learned dynamics, reward, and value models. The top-scoring trajectories are retained and expanded at the next depth, progressively constructing long-horizon plans toward high-return regions.

papers.abstract: Large language models rely on prompt context to perform in-context learning, follow formats, and adapt to local evidence. This ability, however, also raises a robustness concern: models may reuse irrelevant tokens from earlier context when answering a later query. Prior work identifies this behavior as contextual entrainment and finds attention heads whose ablation reduces it, arguing that these heads are largely task- or relation-specific. But are the mechanisms behind contextual entrainment truly isolated by relation, or do relation-conditioned searches recover reusable components shared across relations? Using factual-distractor relation-completion prompts across 19 lexical-semantic subtypes, we identify attention heads whose ablation reduces entrainment and test how the resulting head sets transfer recovery ability across exact relations, semantic families, and mixed relation distributions. Same-family transfer exceeds different-family transfer, family residuals weaken once globally shared heads are removed, and subtype-specific searches repeatedly rediscover many global heads. Clean-completion and context-use probes further suggest that this shared intervention can reduce harmful copying while preserving ordinary relation completion and simple in-context abilities. Our findings provide a more precise perspective on contextual entrainment and its mitigation: harmful context following is not best addressed by searching for isolated relation-specific circuits, but by using heterogeneous attack prompts to reveal reusable intervention targets whose effects are shaped by semantic relation structure.
authors: Jinghan Zheng, Jiajun Shi
bullets: The study examines whether heads linked to harmful copying are relation-specific or reusable across relations.

papers.abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.

Targets both more flexible KV-cache memory compression and lower full-attention computation cost.

papers.abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.
authors: Augusta van Haren, Hanna Hoogen, Luca Pattavina, Quincy Rommen
bullets: Targets the complexity of PredRNN-V2’s dual-memory ST-LSTM recurrent unit.
Introduces an ST-GRU with update and reset gates, merging temporal memory into the hidden state.
Evaluated on Moving MNIST using the original experimental protocol over ten predicted frames.
Reports MSE 55.1, SSIM 0.883, LPIPS 0.065, and PSNR 19.53 dB.
Does not outperform PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM, or PSNR, but achieves lower LPIPS and matches earlier PredRNN performance with a simpler cell.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Side-by-side comparison of the ST-LSTM-based and ST-GRU-based PredRNN(-V2) architectures, with the flows of information shown in different colours. The ST-LSTM-based PredRNN(-V2) has two memory states: the temporal memory Cl t flows horizontally from the previous time step to the current one (t), whereas the spatiotemporal memory Ml t zigzags through the layers (l) of PredRNN(-V2), capturing short-term dynamics. Both memory states are used to update the hidden state Hl t. The ST-GRU-based PredRNN(-V2), in contrast, integrates the horizontal memory flow into the hidden state Hl t, while the spatiotemporal memory is still carried by Ml t.

Figure 2: Frame-wise MSE, SSIM, LPIPS and PSNR on the Moving MNIST test set. All models were trained and evaluated following the protocol described in Section 2.5. Results for the LSTM-based models are taken from Wang et al. (2021), and those for the GRU-based models from Dong et al. (2025). PSNR for the ST-LSTMbased PredRNN-V2 was computed with the official trained model (Wu, 2022). All results for the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 are from our own evaluation.
Figure 4: Side-by-side mathematical comparison of the ST-LSTM and ST-GRU building blocks.

Figure 6: Side-by-side comparison of the ST-LSTM and ST-GRU building blocks, with the flows of information shown in different colours. The ST-LSTM has two memory states: the temporal memory Cl t across time steps (t), and the spatiotemporal memory Ml t, which captures short-term dynamics across layers (l). Each memory state is modulated by three gates, it, ft and gt (respectively i′t, f ′ t and g′t), and both contribute to the hidden state Hl t via the output gate ot. The ST-GRU, in contrast, integrates the horizontal memory flow into the hidden state Hl t, while the spatiotemporal memory is still carried by Ml t. Each of these states is modulated by two gates, zt and rt (respectively z′t and r′t), and they are combined via the output gate ot. The reduction in both gates and memory states is what makes the ST-GRU simpler than the ST-LSTM.

papers.abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) has become a widely adopted approach for aligning vision-language models (VLMs), yet the security of multimodal preference data remains largely unexplored. Existing preference poisoning attacks either corrupt explicit supervision signals or require visible triggers, making them detectable under human inspection. We introduce DPOison-VL, the first clean preference poisoning attack against VLM-DPO, which manipulates model alignment solely through imperceptible perturbations on a small fraction of training images, while leaving all prompts, responses, and preference annotations semantically intact. We formulate poison construction as a bilevel optimization and derive a gradient alignment surrogate that efficiently steers image perturbations toward the attacker-specified preference. We further introduce a preference displacement score for principled poison selection with provable first-order optimality under a fixed poison budget, and derive a sufficient condition for preference inversion. Extensive experiments across diverse attack tasks, different VLM architectures and scales, and baseline comparisons demonstrate that DPOison-VL achieves up to 98\% ASR with only 2\% poisoned data and exhibits cross-model transferability, while largely preserving clean accuracy and general utility. Our findings reveal a critical vulnerability in VLM-DPO, where imperceptible image perturbations in preference training data can silently redirect alignment.
authors: Chengtao Jian, Kai Yang

papers.abstract: 3D part assembly aims to reconstruct a complete shape from a set of unassembled parts by predicting a rigid SE(3) transformation for each part. Because the placement of a part is rarely determined by its own geometry, the task demands reasoning over the entire part set, and existing methods, which rely on pairwise relations or iterative generation and verification, scale poorly to objects with many parts. We present LLM2R, which casts part assembly as sequence modeling with a pretrained decoder-only large language model (LLM): a Point-BERT encoder and a Q-Former compress each part into a block of geometric tokens, the blocks of all parts are concatenated, and a causal LLM adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) processes the sequence in one forward pass. Causal attention, however, lets the hidden states of a part observe only the parts that precede it. LLM2R therefore appends a block of learnable summary tokens after the last part: these tokens follow every part, so their states aggregate the whole assembly at a constant token cost, and a part-aware pose head fuses each part's states with them before predicting its rotation and translation. One architecture thus handles semantic and geometric assembly and predicts all poses in a single non-autoregressive pass. LLM2R achieves the highest part accuracy and success rate on all three PartNet categories, the best rotation error, translation error, and part accuracy on PartNeXt, and the lowest translation error and fastest inference on Breaking Bad, where only a fracture-specialized method is more accurate. Its advantage grows with the number of parts: at 100 parts it exceeds GARF by 33.5 points in part accuracy on Breaking Bad and Assembler by 29.1 points on PartNet, and it transfers zero-shot to unseen categories with more than 16 points higher part accuracy than the strongest of three baselines.
authors: Zhouhan Zhong, Qiuhong Shen, Xingyi Yang, Jinyi Xu, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Problem: Pairwise and iterative assembly methods struggle as the number of parts grows because placement depends on the full set.
Method: Point-BERT and a Q-Former encode each part into geometric-token blocks, which a LoRA-adapted causal LLM processes in one pass.
Key design: Learnable summary tokens aggregate information from all parts and are fused with each part’s states to predict rotation and translation.
Results: LLM2R achieves leading or competitive accuracy, pose errors, success rate, and inference speed across PartNet, PartNeXt, and Breaking Bad.
Scope: It transfers zero-shot to unseen categories and its advantage increases for assemblies with many parts.

papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.
authors: Fabian Gr\"oger, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Shuo Wen, Maria Brbi\'c
bullets: Using only 10–20% of projector-training data recovers most downstream gains.
Projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated with little performance loss.
PORTAL maps Gaussian approximations of vision and language features via optimal transport on a shared principal subspace.
It uses only per-modality summary statistics and requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient optimization.
Across six backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks, PORTAL matches the standard 558k-pair pipeline; it outperforms it in 3 of 7 settings and averages 98% of its score in the other 4.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Projector alignment as a coarse alignment with a broad solution space. (Left) Standard pipeline: during projector alignment, the vision encoder and language model are frozen, and only the projector is trained to map visual tokens into a representation space compatible with the LLM using image-caption pairs. (Middle) We show that projectors trained on different image-caption datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving downstream performance, indicating that there is a large solution space for the weights of the projector. (Right) This observation motivates a closedform solution of projector alignment. We propose a training-free projector PORTAL constructed by optimal transport between the two modalities’ marginal statistics.

papers.selection_reason: Core multimodal LLM alignment research; analyzes projector training and proposes a training-free initialization.
papers.title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
papers.tldr: Projector training in multimodal LLMs mainly provides coarse alignment, enabling PORTAL to replace it with a training-free, statistics-based initialization that nearly matches the standard pipeline without paired data.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents often struggle to recover from failures whose causes lie several steps earlier, beyond what local reflection or backtracking can resolve. We introduce BELIEFWEAVER, a framework that combines persistent evidence across attempts with prospective reasoning over repair directions. It maintains a relational belief state over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints. Execution evidence updates related frontier priorities across attempts and rollback, while diagnostic evidence gates execution. An implicit world model (IWM) evaluates repair hypotheses, predicts progress, and identifies relations among frontiers to guide exploration. We further distill these recurring IWM reasoning components into a 9B student through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy distillation (OPD). Across three terminal-based benchmarks, BELIEFWEAVER improves aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive trends in exploration efficiency. The distilled 9B student improves final score by 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline while reducing estimated teacher API cost by 54.8% relative to the matched teacher. These results show that persistent evidence and prospective reasoning can improve recovery in long-horizon agent tasks while substantially reducing reliance on teacher-model inference.
authors: Xiyang Wu
Zhichao Liu
Shengxin zhang
Zongxia Li
Ming Li
Tianyi Zhou
Dinesh Manocha
bullets: Addresses failures whose causes occur several steps before the observed error, beyond local reflection or backtracking.
Maintains relational beliefs over frontiers, attempts, observations, and checkpoints; execution and diagnostic evidence guide priorities and actions.
Uses an implicit world model to evaluate repair hypotheses, predict progress, and identify relationships among exploration frontiers.
Across three terminal-based benchmarks, it raises aggregate final score by 5.1 percentage points over native Terminus-2 continuation, with positive exploration-efficiency trends.
A distilled 9B student gains 9.8 percentage points over the reported native baseline and reduces matched teacher API cost by 54.8%.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of BELIEFWEAVER. BELIEFWEAVER combines evidence from past attempts with prospective reasoning over candidate repairs. Given the task and current context (Blue Box), the implicit world model (Yellow Box) proposes repair hypotheses, gathers diagnostic evidence, and estimates their outcomes. The persistent exploration graph (Gray Dashed Box) retains hypotheses, attempts, observations, and relations across rollback. Belief-guided selection (Purple Box) uses this evidence to update frontier priorities, while diagnostic evidence determines execution eligibility. The agent harness and verifier (Pink Box) execute the selected frontier and feed the outcome back into the graph.

Figure 3: Failure to improve despite belief updates. Four stages trace how updated evidence redirects exploration without improving the retained checkpoint. The log contrast below shows a mismatch between local startup success and the subsequent controller probe. Monospaced excerpts and checkpoint fields are taken from the archived teacher trace; descriptions are condensed. q denotes the logged controller belief, and scores are retained-checkpoint test-pass fractions.

Figure 2: Successful continuation with residual failures. Four stages trace how evidence against one candidate shifts belief-based selection toward a successful partial repair. Monospaced excerpts and checkpoint fields are taken from the archived teacher trace; descriptions are condensed. q denotes the logged controller belief, and scores are retained-checkpoint test-pass fractions.

papers.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.
authors: Adri\'an Szlatincs\'an, Filippo Ziliotto, Bruno Lepri, Luciano Serafini, Massimiliano Luca, Tommaso Campari
bullets: The study tests partner-state observation, object knowledge exchange, and next-action prediction under strict partial observability without intentions or task-level messages.
Other Agent’s State (OAS) improves task quality and reduces unnecessary effort across all planners.
Knowledge Exchange (KE) mainly improves efficiency, reducing simulation steps by up to 25%, with limited effect on success.
Next-action prediction decreases success in most model–context settings, despite increasing explicit partner mentions.
Coordination primarily comes from reacting to shared context—especially OAS—rather than explicit anticipation, with planner-dependent partner modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Decoupled architecture with Other Agent’s State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE), and Other Agent’s Next Action (OANA) prediction. Both agents build a world graph using their own environmental object observations and their actions. The graph’s nodes represent the house, rooms, furniture, receptacles, objects, and agents. The edges represent the type of relation between them. If allowed, the agents also observe the OAS and exchange their knowledge about the objects when they are in the same room. Their high-level LLM planners call a High-Level Action (at replanning) and the corresponding low-level skills (action execution in the simulator), and predict the OANA. The predicted OANA is then compared with the other agent’s current and next actions (union target, Section 3.3), retrieved from its list of all called high-level actions.

Figure 3: Success Rate against episode length (Simulation Steps) for every configuration in Table 1. For Gemini and DeepSeek, KE and OAS both shorten episodes, and OAS also raises Success Rate; all arrows but one point down, since prediction lowers Success Rate in fifteen of sixteen model×context pairs (the exception is the Llama 8B with KE only). The y-axis ranges differ per panel.

Figure 1: Observation settings and OANA prediction. With object KE, co-located agents synchronize their accumulated object knowledge. With OAS observation, agents also observe the partner’s state, but only when co-located. With OANA prediction, each replanning step predicts the partner’s next action before the agent selects its own. papers.selection_reason: Studies partner information and coordination in embodied multi-agent collaboration, fitting the embodied AI scope.
papers.title: Observe, Share, or Predict? Disentangling Partner Information in Embodied Multi-Agent Collaboration
papers.tldr: In embodied multi-agent collaboration, sharing a partner’s state improves coordination more reliably than exchanging object knowledge or predicting actions.

papers.abstract: Target-aware multimodal instruction selection requires useful examples and an appropriate balance of supervision. Sample-level rankings can overrepresent similar content without optimizing this balance; group-level methods face coarse units, predefined set-level validation signals, and costly or inaccurate mixture search. We propose CLIVO, a target-aware framework connecting fine-grained semantic allocation, automatically learned validation objectives, and differentiable mixture search. Specifically, semantic clusters provide independently adjustable shares at the hundred-cluster scale. Correlations between per-example merged-proxy losses and real probe performance identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. A single backward pass through the merged proxy supplies gradients for all shares, avoiding an additional mixture-response regression model. Selecting 100K instructions from an 8M pool, CLIVO attains 97.2% of the full-data four-target average score with only 1.25% of the data. It improves on the strongest evaluated selection baseline by 1.16 points using random within-cluster sampling; combining learned quotas with sample ranking increases this advantage to 1.55 points. Analyses show that finer units benefit most targets, short-trained experts preserve mixture responses, sample weighting retains useful validation information, and direct search consistently reduces the learned objective. CLIVO also supports interpretable allocation, modular selection, and reuse across targets and granularities.
authors: Yuhan Wang, Rui Hu, Batian Di, Tan Jiang, Dongsheng Ma, Leichao Dong, Yuanzi Li, Yalin Feng
bullets: Addresses redundancy in sample-level ranking and inefficiency or coarseness in group-level instruction selection.
Uses fine-grained semantic clusters with independently adjustable shares, learned nonnegative validation-example weights, and gradient-based mixture search.
Selects 100K instructions from an 8M pool while reaching 97.2% of the full-data average score across four targets using 1.25% of the data.
Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline by 1.16 points with random within-cluster sampling and by 1.55 points when combined with sample ranking.
Supports interpretable, modular allocation and reuse across targets and granularities; scope includes the evaluated multimodal instruction-selection setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CLIVO overview: learning what to train on and how to evaluate the mixture. (1) Unit: a fixed multimodal encoder and K-means organize the instruction pool into semantic clusters with adjustable training shares. (2) Signal: probe models are trained on sampled mixtures and evaluated on downstream benchmarks. Cluster experts are merged using the same shares to construct proxies. Correlations between per-example proxy losses and real scores identify target-relevant validation examples; learned nonnegative weights combine their losses into an objective. (3) Learning: with experts and validation weights frozen, gradients update the training shares through the merged proxy under budget and capacity constraints. papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

papers.abstract: Geospatial reasoning links VLMs to real-world action and decision making. Reliable reasoning requires accurate spatial information and effective spatial representations. However, current VLMs obtain this information mainly from language and vision. At larger geographic scales, limited visual observations make it difficult to establish accurate spatial references and recover precise spatial relations. This leads to a bottleneck for VLM spatial perception and reasoning. This paper proposes that geospatial vector geometry can become a native spatial modality within a VLM and introduces GeoVec-VLM. First, we develop a structured geometry representation that preserves the spatial structure and arrangement of vector objects, building an explicit spatial basis. Second, we introduce a geometry interaction strategy that brings this basis into multimodal computation, where it interacts with visual content and language references according to the queried spatial relations. Together, these designs allow perception and reasoning to operate on shared geometric references. Across five spatial reasoning tasks, GeoVec-VLM improves mean accuracy by about 11\% relative to the strongest baseline, maintains its gains under geographic transfer, and shows greater geometric consistency. Our results show that geospatial vector geometry offers a promising internal spatial basis for VLM spatial reasoning. https://github.com/TXFR/GeoVector-VLM

bullets: Current VLMs struggle with precise spatial references at large geographic scales because visual observations are limited.

A geometry interaction strategy combines this basis with visual content and language references based on queried spatial relations.
Across five spatial reasoning tasks, it improves mean accuracy by about 11% over the strongest baseline and retains gains under geographic transfer.
The model also demonstrates greater geometric consistency, supporting vector geometry as an internal basis for VLM reasoning.

papers.abstract: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary

Improves mean successful coverage by approximately 10% over the strongest baseline on four Multi-Goal docking variants.
Achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks and remains broadly competitive on five MuJoCo tasks, with added nonlinear and linear solve costs.

papers.abstract: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.
authors: Tianhao Guo
bullets: For arbitrary-depth linear networks, fixed compensation strengths in [0,1] do not increase mean-square error when calibration Gram matrices are invertible and rounding errors satisfy suitable zero-conditional-mean and shared second-moment conditions.
The gain comes from both directly removing inherited error and reducing the excitation of later quantization noise.
Guarantees can fail with ReLU activations, bounded codebooks, or fixed rounding errors—even for two scalar linear layers; stable activations admit bounds based on projection–activation commutators.

Experiments on two 8B models at 4 bits found fixed half-strength compensation consistently better than uncompensated rounding across tested models and inputs, but no strength-selection rule was consistently best or reliably transferable to new text.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a common generative recipe for robot foundation models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) generate action chunks, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally generate future visual states. Both start generation from a fixed Gaussian prior, despite temporal continuity between past and future states and actions. This requires costly training and iterative sampling, especially for WAMs with an additional visual branch. We introduce $Δ$-flow, which constructs the source from recent history with mild noise rather than from a fixed Gaussian prior. This moves the source closer to the target, reducing transport to a small residual $Δ$ that can be learned efficiently and enables single-step inference. We integrate $Δ$-flow into the VLA policy $π_{0.5}$ and the WAM policies ImageWAM and Fast-WAM. On LIBERO, ImageWAM reaches 90% success in one epoch rather than six, and Fast-WAM reaches 95% in two epochs rather than eight. With LoRA fine-tuning, $π_{0.5}$ exceeds its baseline's five-epoch performance after one epoch. Single-step inference gives $1.54\times$, $2.49\times$, and $4.45\times$ speedups on $π_{0.5}$, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, respectively. It preserves action smoothness, achieving a $4.5\times$ reduction in action jerk compared with one-step Gaussian sampling. $Δ$-flow reaches state-of-the-art generalization performance on LIBERO-Plus. Action-history sources can be applied to pretrained WAM policies without retraining. Replacing the Gaussian action source at inference largely preserves task success with a single sampling step and can slightly improve it. We further study how action representation and visual information in action learning affect history-to-future prediction in $Δ$-flow. These results show that $Δ$-flow is simple yet effective, improving the efficiency and generalization of robot foundation models.

Tuo An
Xinying Guo

bullets: Targets costly iterative sampling and training in vision-language-action and world-action robot models.
Builds the flow source from recent action and visual history, learning only the residual transition to future actions and states.
Integrated into π₀.₅, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, it achieves faster training and 1.54×–4.45× inference speedups on LIBERO.
Maintains smooth actions, reducing action jerk 4.5× versus one-step Gaussian sampling, and reaches state-of-the-art generalization on LIBERO-Plus.
History-based action sources can be applied to pretrained world-action models without retraining, though visual and action representations affect prediction quality.

figures.caption: Figure 6 Action continuity at chunk boundaries on ImageWAM. The panels show mean action change (left) and action jerk (right) around transitions between consecutive action chunks. The four curves compare Gaussian sampling with ten or one step, one-step action-only ∆-flow, and one-step complete ∆-flow. All four methods are evaluated on the same LIBERO-Long tasks with identical initial states. Each policy predicts a 16-action chunk and executes the first 12 actions before replanning. Step 0 is the first action of the new chunk. Background shading indicates the new chunk, and bands around the curves show paired-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. Arrows annotate relative differences in boundary peaks.

Figure 1 ∆-flow matching learns past-to-future changes for efficient robot foundation models. Unlike Gaussian-source flow matching, which reconstructs future visual states and actions from noise through iterative sampling, ∆-flow constructs each source from its corresponding recent history with mild Gaussian perturbation and learns only the residual change ∆. This shorter transport substantially improves training efficiency, enables fast single-step inference, strengthens generalization under distribution shift, and preserves smooth action generation across chunk boundaries.

Figure 3 Training progress on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. Success rates are shown over training epochs for ImageWAM, Fast-WAM, and π0.5. The top panels show LIBERO and the bottom panels show LIBERO-Plus, evaluated without additional fine-tuning. papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
authors: Angen Ye, junjie xie, Yujia Song, Junkai Huang, Dapeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the precision, opacity, and data-scarcity challenges of end-to-end low-level action prediction in surgical robotics.
Uses an MLLM for visual understanding, structured explanations, and skill selection, while verified control programs execute actions.
Trains on a state-to-skill dataset augmented with visual and state perturbations, then optimizes correctness, prerequisites, and output validity.
For brain–machine-interface implantation, reaches 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1 on a fixed test set.
Achieves 88.0% task success across 50 closed-loop real-robot trials.

Starting from raw image, robot-state, instruction, and skill-label samples, the pipeline expands the data through image/text augmentation and constructs structured rationales using three MLLMs. Candidate outputs are filtered by rule-based checks, leaveone-generator-out cross-validation, and human spot inspection before being retained in the final structured dataset.

Fig. 3. Closed-loop decision example for flexible-electrode implantation. At each step, SurgiCLAW receives the current microscopic image, robot state, and operation query, then outputs a structured rationale, an operator-facing answer, and a single atomic-skill call. The example illustrates a typical decision sequence from spatial registration and image-quality correction to needle alignment and final insertion. surgical data: a multi-MLLM data-generation pipeline expands 5,000 state–skill samples into 30,000 structured ones, and a three-reward group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization objective improves skill selection, prerequisite safety, and output parseability. On the fixed test set SurgiCLAW reaches 94.6% accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1, and it completes 88.0% of 50 closed-loop implantation trials. We interpret these results as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of clinical efficacy: the evaluation covers a single high-precision task using phantom and ex-vivo material, and the closed-loop comparisons are constrained by the modest number of paired trials. Whether the safety and interpretability benefits generalize to other tasks, to more stringent clinical conditions, or to long-horizon unattended operation remains to be established.

papers.abstract: Parametric Computer-Aided-Design (CAD) modeling from human intent remains challenging, particularly during the conceptual design stage, where design goals are expressed through incomplete and unstructured modalities (e.g., hand-drawn sketches and textual descriptions). In this work, we rethink the human intent-to-CAD pipeline and propose a unified method that directly maps multi-level human intents to executable codes, without assuming the prior existence of target CAD models. To support our study, we construct HiCAD, the first large-scale dataset aligning hand-drawn sketches, textual descriptions, and parametric CAD codes. Based on this, we introduce HiCAD, a two-stage framework comprising Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge the representational gap between heterogeneous inputs, and Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to enforce geometric and topological consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing baselines across multiple tasks, validating its effectiveness and robustness in transforming heterogeneous human intents into high-fidelity parametric CAD models. Our project page: https://zqwlearning.github.io/HiCAD.
authors: Qingwang Zhang, Jiahao Li, Xiangdong Zhou
bullets: Addresses conceptual CAD design from incomplete, heterogeneous human intents without requiring pre-existing target CAD models.

Uses Cooperative Multi-Task Alignment to bridge representations across input modalities.
Applies Spatial-Aware Reinforcement Learning to promote geometric and topological consistency.
Reports improved performance and robustness over existing baselines across multiple tasks.

papers.abstract: Training-free story visualization without reference images must preserve recurring entities across frames while scaling to long narratives. Existing methods typically maintain consistency by conditioning each frame on other frames of the same story, coupling generation time, VRAM, or both to story length. We introduce ELECT, which instead settles cross-frame identity before final rendering through a language-guided scene-entity mapping and stationary anchors elected from the model's own drafts. This makes the per-frame cost of the final rendering pass independent of story length. Joint attention exceeds 96 GB of VRAM at 32 scenes, whereas ELECT remains at 8.3 s per frame and under 20 GB VRAM from 10 to 1000 scenes. On the Story50 long-story benchmark, ELECT reaches 0.833 average Character Consistency Similarity (aCCS), compared with 0.826 for ten-round refinement, at one seventh of its generation cost, with lower text alignment (0.327 vs. 0.340). At 1000 scenes, to our knowledge, the first evaluation of training-free story visualization at this length, ELECT exceeds ten-round refinement by 0.017 aCCS and the nearest flat-cost baseline by 0.091, while also surpassing refinement in text alignment at one twenty-fourth of its generation time. These results show that long-horizon consistency need not require increasingly expensive inter-frame conditioning as stories grow.
authors: Mehrajul Abadin Miraj, Md. Mahmudul Hasan, Meherun Farzana, Aniket Joarder, Mahmudul Hasan, Abir Chakraborty Partha, Md. Ahasanul Alam, Redwan Ahmed Rizvee, Md. Fahim Arefin, Md Mahmudur Rahman, Md. Tanvir Alam, Md Mosaddek Khan
bullets: Addresses the memory and generation-time growth caused by conditioning each frame on other story frames.
Uses language-guided scene-entity mapping and stationary anchors selected from the model’s own drafts before final rendering.
Maintains 8.3 seconds per frame and under 20 GB VRAM across 10–1000 scenes, while joint attention exceeds 96 GB at 32 scenes.
On Story50, achieves 0.833 aCCS versus 0.826 for ten-round refinement at one-seventh the generation cost.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) by permanently removing neurons and weight rows, yielding dense, hardware-agnostic speedup. Existing post-training methods couple neuron selection and weight reconstruction through a shared calibration dataset, introducing domain bias and out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. We propose SARATHI, a framework that decouples these two stages. A data-free \emph{NMF Residual Subspace Probe} scores neurons using intrinsic weight geometry, without accessing any calibration data, and carries a formal connection to Robust PCA. \emph{Adaptive OBS} then reconstructs the pruned weights with a localized calibration batch, operating in $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ peak memory per layer and eliminating the global memory bottleneck of coupled methods. A \emph{Bias Shift Compensation} step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise cause perplexity collapse at high sparsity. Experiments across six models from two architecture families (gated and non-gated FFN) at 15--40\% sparsity show that SARATHI achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.
authors: Sankar Behera, Dhruv Singh, Satyadev Ahlawat, Yamuna Prasad
bullets: Addresses domain bias and out-of-memory failures caused by coupling pruning decisions with reconstruction on one calibration dataset.
Uses an NMF Residual Subspace Probe to score neurons from intrinsic weight geometry without calibration data.
Applies Adaptive OBS with localized calibration batches and O(d²) peak memory per layer for weight reconstruction.
Adds Bias Shift Compensation to mitigate activation drift and perplexity collapse in post-LayerNorm models.
Across six models at 15–40% sparsity, achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds structured-pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The coupling flaw in existing structured pruning vs. SARATHI’s decoupled design. (b) SARATHI separates these two stages: neuron selection is entirely data-free (NMF Residual Probe, green), while weight reconstruction uses only a small localized batch with O(d2) memory per layer (Adaptive OBS, blue). The result is an architecturally native pruned model with Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) Cosine Similarity of 1.0000 and no OOM failures, even at 40% sparsity on OPT-6.7B.

papers.abstract: KV caches make long-context serving efficient by reusing past computation, but model switching breaks this reuse and forces the receiver to prefill the context again. We study \emph{zero-prefill cross-model context handoff}: translating a sender cache into a receiver-compatible state so that the receiver can continue directly without prefilling same context. Existing affine transport methods show that receiver KV states can be substantially reconstructed from sender caches. However, through extensive analyses, we find that reconstruction fidelity is a poor proxy for receiver utility. Similar K/V reconstruction errors can lead to substantially different attention patterns, predictive distributions, and downstream accuracy, because conventional reconstruction objectives overlook the query-dependent functional importance of K and V in receiver attention. We thus introduce CACHELINK, which learns a coupled K/V correction through the receiver behavior directly. Across four independently trained sender--receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, CACHELINK improves the equal-weight mean over all methods for every pair. In matched diagnostics, CACHELINK changes K/V squared error by less than 0.4% while substantially changing receiver attention and next-token behavior. At 32K context, it reduces handoff latency by up to $7.27\times$ relative to receiver re-prefill. Our findings verify that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient and that preserving the receiver computation induced by the transported cache is important for effective cross-model KV transport.
authors: Haomiao Qiu, Yining Tang, Zijia Song, Ruizi Han, Ziyue Qiao, Miao Zhang
bullets: Cross-model switching normally forces the receiver to re-prefill the shared context, reducing KV-cache reuse.
The work finds that similar K/V reconstruction errors can produce very different attention patterns, predictions, and downstream accuracy.
CacheLink learns a coupled K/V correction guided directly by receiver computation and behavior.
Across four sender–receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, it achieved the best equal-weight mean for every pair.
At 32K context, it reduced handoff latency by up to 7.27× versus receiver re-prefill.

papers.abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high-quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low-bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training-free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T-BGR introduces a tail-aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution-tail coefficients and preserving fine-grained information without introducing additional parameters or high-precision branches. CAPS performs coarse-to-fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low-bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full-precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm-lc/HGA-Quant.
authors: Xinmeng Liu, Xianglong Yan, Kaicheng Yang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high computational and memory costs that hinder ARVG deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
T-BGR uses a tail-aware reconstruction objective to better preserve important weight-distribution information during quantizer calibration.
CAPS allocates mixed activation precision across generation stages based on stage importance and computational cost under a bit budget.
Experiments across multiple ARVG backbones show improved robustness to aggressive low-bit quantization.
On Infinity, it achieves near full-precision quality at effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while W4A6 existing methods show degradation or inconsistency.

papers.abstract: We present Co-DSL, a framework in which users and LLMs co-design reusable spatial concepts for layout generation. In the first stage, our system allows users to create a library of personalized operations. To add a concept, a user provides a description, which the LLM converts into an initial implementation. The user can then observe the concept's execution behavior over example scenarios and provide lightweight feedback to the LLM, which revises the concept's implementation logic. In the second stage, given a library, an LLM can author a layout program that meets a new layout request from a user. Executing a layout program instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts. In this way, we require the LLM only to specify which concepts should hold, while we use a solver to search for a layout that satisfies them. Across five spatial layout domains, we find that Co-DSL libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that are challenging for prior fixed-operation systems, and demonstrate that our concept-graph representation is needed for LLMs to reliably compose concepts together. We further find that Co-DSL lets LLMs author generative layout programs that expose high-level parametric controls users can manipulate to explore a distribution of related layouts without re-prompting.
authors: R. Kenny Jones, Jiajun Wu, Maneesh Agrawala
bullets: Users describe personalized spatial operations; the LLM implements and revises them based on lightweight feedback and observed examples.
For new requests, the LLM authors a layout program represented as a concept graph, specifying which concepts should hold.
A solver searches for layouts satisfying the composed concepts, reducing the need for the LLM to generate exact layouts directly.
Across five spatial layout domains, the framework captures patterns beyond fixed-operation systems and reliably composes concepts.
Generated programs expose parametric controls for exploring related layouts without repeated prompting.

papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) by routing domain-specific data to specialized teachers, integrating their capabilities through dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories. However, domain routing only distinguishes the supervision sources for different domains; updates from all domains still act on shared parameters. When teachers differ substantially in response style and domain expertise, supervision that is effective in isolation may still lead to persistent gradient conflicts and capability degradation during joint optimization. To address this challenge, we propose Cross-Teacher Guarding for MOPD (Road MOPD), which introduces non-routed teachers as auxiliary cross-domain critics on the same student trajectories and coordinates multi-teacher supervision through token-level credit assignment and gradient updates. Specifically, cross-teacher-guided credit assignment uses teacher agreement to strengthen token-level corrections jointly supported by the teachers and attenuate conflicting signals; preventive multi-teacher gradient projection uses auxiliary gradients from the same trajectories to constrain potentially conflicting updates and adaptively controls projection strength to retain target-domain learning signals. In experiments, Road MOPD mitigates degradation in the disadvantaged domain, gains over 5 percentage points under high conflict, and improves overall performance in low-conflict and three-domain settings.
